### [1] [IDSPACE: A Novel Document Generator for Reliable Evaluation of Digital Identity Verification Systems [Extended Technical Report]](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03052)
*Lulu Xie,Yancheng Wang,Kanchan Chowdhury,Rolando Garcia,Yingzhen Yang,Jia Zou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: IDSpace is a synthetic identity document generation system that addresses the scarcity of real identity documents for fraud detection evaluation. It introduces model-guided Bayesian optimization to tune generation parameters, decouples user metadata from control parameters, and supports scanned/mobile-captured documents beyond template images.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As services move online, trust institutions need to verify remote user identities. However, evaluating fraud detection tools is difficult because identity documents are sensitive and scarce. Synthetic data generation offers a solution, as evidenced by prior work being downloaded over 11,000 times.

Method: IDSpace extends prior research in three directions: (1) Model-guided Bayesian optimization that tunes generation parameters to maximize visual similarity and prediction consistency with target-domain models using only a few target domain samples; (2) Decoupling user-specified metadata (demographics, fraud patterns, capture device) from automatically tuned control parameters (font styles, noise levels, image quality); (3) Expanding beyond template images to support scanned and mobile-captured documents.

Result: IDSpace improves evaluation consistency by 15-45% over baselines (CycleGAN, diffusion inpainting, non-guided optimization) using only a few real samples, while improving training accuracy by up to 9% and SSIM similarity with the target domain by 10%. A new dataset of 359,240 high-quality synthetic documents across ten European ID types was also released.

Conclusion: IDSpace provides an effective solution for generating synthetic identity documents for fraud detection evaluation, requiring only minimal real samples from target domains while achieving significant improvements in consistency, accuracy, and visual similarity.

Abstract: As services move online, trust institutions such as banks, lenders, and governments must verify the identity of remote users. Fraud detection tools are widely available, but evaluating and fine-tuning them remains difficult because identity documents are sensitive and therefore scarce. Synthetic data generation offers a path forward, and demand is clear: our prior work in this area has been downloaded over $11{,}000$ times (aggregated from eight parts). We introduce IDSpace, extending this line of research in three directions. First, we propose model-guided Bayesian optimization, which tunes generation parameters to maximize both visual similarity and prediction consistency with target-domain models given only a few samples from a target domain. Second, we decouple user-specified metadata (demographics, fraud patterns, capture device) from automatically tuned control parameters (font styles, noise levels, image quality), allowing users to configure evaluations without low-level expertise. Third, we expand beyond template images to support scanned and mobile-captured documents. Experiments show IDSpace improves evaluation consistency by $15-45\%$ over baselines including CycleGAN, diffusion inpainting, and non-guided optimization, using only a few real samples, while improving training accuracy by up to $9\%$ and SSIM similarity with the target domain by $10\%$. We also released a new dataset consisting of $359{,}240$ high-quality synthetic documents across ten European ID types.

</details>


### [2] [Mudragen: Geometrically Supervised Generation of Interacting Two-Hand Mudras for Preserving Indian Classical Dance Heritage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03415)
*Jagadish Kashinath Kamble,Jayanta Mukhopadhyay,Debaditya Roy,Partha Pratim Das*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MudraGen is a conditional diffusion framework that synthesizes realistic RGB images of Samyukta Hasta Mudras (two-hand gestures from Bharatanatyam Indian classical dance). It addresses low-resource dataset challenges and lack of precise textual descriptions by introducing geometry-aware supervision with three objectives: Keypoint Loss, Joint Offset Loss, and Shape Consistency to ensure anatomical validity and inter-hand coordination.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Indian classical dance gesture datasets are inherently low-resource, and canonical Sanskrit definitions of many mudras lack precise textual descriptions, limiting the effectiveness of conventional text-conditioned image generation models. There was a need for a method that can accurately generate complex two-hand interaction gestures while preserving anatomical validity and cultural nuance.

Method: MudraGen uses a conditional diffusion framework with three geometry-aware objectives: (1) Keypoint Loss for 3D joint alignment, (2) Joint Offset Loss for inter-hand spatial coherence, and (3) Shape Consistency as an anatomical regularizer that encourages consistent hand morphology while allowing independent hand poses. These objectives guide the diffusion model toward anatomically plausible and well-coordinated hand configurations.

Result: MudraGen surpasses existing state-of-the-art generative approaches in visual realism, anatomical correctness, and preservation of fine hand-pose structure, enabling faithful reproduction of complex Samyukta Hasta mudras.

Conclusion: The ability to generate culturally grounded and structurally consistent gestures highlights practical applications in cultural preservation and dance education, addressing the unique challenges of synthesizing interactive two-hand gestures in Indian classical dance.

Abstract: Automatic generation of hand gestures is essential for the transmission of Indian classical dance and critical for its preservation. Indian classical dance gesture datasets are inherently low-resource, and the canonical Sanskrit definitions of many mudras lack precise textual descriptions, limiting the effectiveness of conventional text-conditioned image generation models. We present \textbf{MudraGen}, a conditional diffusion framework that synthesizes realistic RGB images of \textit{Samyukta Hasta Mudras} -- interactive two-hand gestures from Bharatanatyam (an Indian classical dance form). Unlike prior work on simple hand signs or single-hand gestures, MudraGen introduces geometry-aware supervision to capture the precise coordination, anatomical validity, and cultural nuance of interacting hands. We formulate three geometry-aware objectives: Keypoint Loss for 3D joint alignment, Joint Offset Loss for inter-hand spatial coherence, and Shape Consistency, which serves as an anatomical regularizer by encouraging consistent hand morphology while allowing independent hand poses. Together, these objectives guide the diffusion model toward anatomically plausible and well-coordinated hand configurations, enabling the synthesis of photorealistic and pose-accurate gesture images. Experimental results show that MudraGen surpasses existing state-of-the-art generative approaches in visual realism, anatomical correctness, and preservation of fine hand-pose structure, enabling faithful reproduction of complex Samyukta Hasta mudras. Beyond quantitative gains, its ability to generate culturally grounded and structurally consistent gestures highlights practical applications in cultural preservation and dance education.

</details>


### [3] [Position: Unlabeled IS NOT Equal to No Human Supervision in Visual Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03077)
*Dong Lao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This position paper argues that the term "unsupervised learning" in computer vision is too broad and ambiguous, as different methods using unlabeled data embed substantially different human priors. The authors urge the community to explicitly disclose assumptions about data selection and learning objectives to improve comparison and methodological clarity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observe that while unsupervised learning research has grown, the term "unsupervised" has become misleading - many methods that claim to be unsupervised actually rely on human supervision through data curation and training objectives. This ambiguity hinders research comparison and methodology assessment.

Method: This is a position paper presenting an argumentative analysis. The authors examine the decline in papers using "unsupervised" in titles at flagship CV conferences since 2021, and analyze how different data curation schemes and training objectives embed different human priors.

Result: The paper identifies that different unsupervised methods rely on substantially different human priors through data selection and learning objectives. The term "unsupervised" no longer accurately captures these distinctions, making fair comparison difficult.

Conclusion: The authors advocate for standardized disclosure practices where authors explicitly state priors in data selection and learning objectives, and specify which pipeline components depend on which assumptions. This will improve academic communication, enable fairer comparisons, and preserve methodological diversity.

Abstract: This position paper argues that the absence of labels does not imply the absence of human supervision in visual learning, and urges the research community to identify sources of supervision more explicitly. Many recent methods in computer vision build upon representations learned from large-scale unlabeled data, and are therefore grouped under the same umbrella term ``unsupervised.'' However, different data curation schemes and training objectives embed substantially different human priors on which models rely, and we argue that one ``unsupervised'' umbrella term is no longer capturing these distinctions. This ambiguity makes it harder to compare unsupervised learning research conducted under different assumptions, coinciding with a sharp decline in papers titled with ``unsupervised'' in flagship computer vision conferences since 2021, despite continued growth of the field. While we fully embrace pre-training as a strong foundation for modern computer vision, we advocate for a community-level effort toward greater conceptual clarity: authors are encouraged to disclose priors in data selection and learning objectives, and to specify which components of a learning pipeline depend on which assumptions. Standardized disclosure practices can improve academic communication, ensure fairer comparisons, and preserve methodological diversity in unsupervised learning.

</details>


### [4] [Exemplar: Classical Priors Complement Frozen Features for Few-Shot Microscopy Segmentation at Native Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03080)
*Michal Průšek,Adam Novozámský,Filip Šroubek*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Exemplar is a few-shot biomedical image segmenter that combines frozen DINOv3 features with classical filter responses in a lightweight head, achieving state-of-the-art performance across 11 biomedical imaging datasets with minimal annotation (1-8 masks).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Biomedical dataset segmentation typically requires either domain-specific models with substantial annotations or foundation models at inference time. This paper addresses the need for a lightweight, few-shot segmenter that can generalize across diverse biomedical imaging datasets without extensive training or fine-tuning.

Method: Exemplar fuses a frozen DINOv3 backbone with a fixed bank of classical native-resolution filter responses in one lightweight head, fitted from support masks alone. The approach leverages complementary information: classical priors (filter bank alone: 0.693 IoU) and frozen self-supervised features (DINOv3 alone: 0.672 IoU). The fused head achieves 0.782 across 11 datasets.

Result: Exemplar outperforms five forward-pass few-shot methods in 54/55 comparisons (52 significant after Holm correction). From a single mask, it achieves 0.703 vs 0.682 for from-scratch nnU-Net. nnU-Net only overtakes at 8 masks but requires 16-77x longer training time.

Conclusion: The fusion of classical filter responses with self-supervised features provides complementary information that enables superior few-shot segmentation across diverse biomedical datasets with minimal annotation requirements and fast inference.

Abstract: Segmenting a new biomedical dataset usually means a domain-specific model trained on substantial annotation, or a foundation model steered at inference time. We present Exemplar, a few-shot segmenter that fuses a frozen DINOv3 backbone with a fixed bank of classical native-resolution filter responses in one lightweight head, fitted from the support masks alone. In the few-mask, native-resolution regime, classical priors and frozen self-supervised features are complementary: fused in one head, a single fixed configuration spans eleven biomedical imaging datasets. Under the same head, the classical bank alone reaches 0.693 on the eleven-dataset panel, scored by foreground intersection-over-union or centreline Dice, and the frozen features alone 0.672; the bank leads on seven of the eleven and the features on the rest, and fused they reach 0.782. Against five forward-pass few-shot methods, Exemplar leads in 54 of 55 method-dataset comparisons, 52 of them significant after Holm correction. From a single annotated mask it reaches 0.703 on the same panel, against 0.682 for a from-scratch nnU-Net trained on that same mask. At eight masks nnU-Net overtakes it on the panel mean, chiefly on centreline agreement, but takes 16-77x longer to fit.

</details>


### [5] [PointGT: Simultaneous Geometry and Texture Editing for Point-Based Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03341)
*Yanshu Zhang,George Shramko,Pratul P. Srinivasan,Ke Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: PointGT is a point-based 3D representation that enables simultaneous editing of object geometry and appearance, combining a point-based representation suitable for geometry deformations with a learned UV mapping technique for high-resolution texture editing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing volumetric 3D representations (e.g., 3D Gaussian Splatting) produce high-quality, photorealistic results but are difficult to edit. Specifically, texture editing methods for such representations are incompatible with geometry edits and deformations.

Method: PointGT combines a point-based representation (well-suited for geometry deformations) with a learned UV mapping technique to enable high-resolution texture editing while maintaining compatibility with geometry modifications.

Result: PointGT enables fine-grained editing of both geometry and texture in point-based neural representations with high rendering quality.

Conclusion: The proposed PointGT successfully bridges the gap between high-quality 3D reconstruction and editable representations, enabling simultaneous geometry and texture editing in point-based neural representations.

Abstract: We present PointGT, a point-based 3D representation that enables simultaneous editing of object geometry and appearance. Existing reconstruction and view synthesis techniques produce volumetric 3D representations that are high-quality and photorealistic, but are difficult to edit. In particular, recent efforts to enable texture editing for 3D Gaussian Splatting representations are not compatible with geometry edits and deformations. Our method combines a point-based representation that is well-suited for geometry deformations with a learned UV mapping technique that enables high-resolution texture editing. We show that PointGT enables fine-grained editing of both geometry and texture in point-based neural representations with high rendering quality.

</details>


### [6] [Solving the Needle-in-a-Haystack Problem in Mammography Vision-Language Model with Differentiable Subset Sampling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03085)
*Young Seok Jeon,Beatrice Brown-Mulry,Rohan Satya Isaac,Anjana Dissanayaka,Theo Dapamede,Mohammadreza Chavoshi,Judy Gichoya,Hari Trivedi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TopKSigLIP is a vision-language model for mammography that addresses two key limitations of standard CLIP: high-resolution image requirements and report homogeneity. It uses a TopK-Patch module to sample informative patches from high-res images and a Sup-sigmoid loss with soft labels to improve learning from predominantly negative reports. The model outperforms existing VLMs on zero-shot benchmarks for density assessment, BI-RADS classification, finding subtyping, and cancer prediction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard CLIP-style vision-language models exhibit limited zero-shot performance in mammography tasks due to two overlooked characteristics: (1) the high-resolution nature of mammography images, and (2) the homogeneity of radiology reports driven by a predominance of negative/benign findings. The standard CLIP architecture forces a tradeoff between resolution and batch size due to GPU memory constraints, and the contrastive loss falsely repels semantically similar pairs in this context.

Method: TopKSigLIP introduces two novel components: (1) TopK-Patch module that learns to sample a sparse set of high-res patches likely to contain lesions, sidestepping the resolution-batch size tradeoff while providing built-in localization; (2) Sup-sigmoid loss that extends SigLIP's sigmoid loss with soft labels derived from structured data to address report homogeneity.

Result: TopKSigLIP outperforms existing open-source mammography and general medical VLMs on both internal and external benchmarks across density assessment, BI-RADS classification, finding subtyping, and cancer prediction under zero-shot evaluation. It remains competitive under linear probing despite using a significantly smaller vision encoder and smaller training batches than baselines. The TopK-Patch module also achieves superior lesion localization compared to post-hoc Grad-CAM.

Conclusion: TopKSigLIP successfully addresses the limitations of standard CLIP for mammography by introducing a TopK-Patch module for efficient high-res image processing and a Sup-sigmoid loss for handling report homogeneity. The model demonstrates superior performance on multiple clinically important tasks while maintaining computational efficiency.

Abstract: There is growing interest in adopting CLIP-style vision--language model (VLM) pretraining for mammography. However, models that directly employ the standard CLIP architecture and training objective exhibit limited zero-shot performance in clinically important tasks such as cancer, finding-type, and BI-RADS predictions. We argue that this underwhelming performance is due to neglecting two characteristics of mammography data: (1) its high-res nature, and (2) homogeneity of radiology reports, largely driven by a predominance of negative/benign findings on examinations. We propose TopKSigLIP, a VLM designed to address these two limitations through a novel architecture and learning objectives. Instead of downscaling high-res mammography images to satisfy GPU memory constraints, TopKSigLIP introduces TopK-Patch module that learns to sample a sparse set of high-res patches likely to contain lesions, sidestepping the resolution--batch size tradeoff of VLM training. The sampled patch locations additionally serve as a built-in localization tool. To address report homogeneity, we replace the contrastive loss, which falsely repels semantically similar pairs, with a Sup-sigmoid loss. Sup-sigmoid loss extends the sigmoid loss from SigLIP with soft labels derived from structured data. TopKSigLIP outperforms existing open-source mammography and general medical VLMs on both internal and external benchmarks on density assessment, BI-RADS classification, finding subtyping, and cancer prediction under zero-shot evaluation. TopKSigLIP remains competitive under linear probing despite using a significantly smaller vision encoder and smaller training batches than baselines. The TopK-Patch module additionally achieves superior lesion localization over post-hoc Grad-CAM. Code and weights are made public:https://github.com/Youngseok0001/TopKSigLIP.

</details>


### [7] [P-CORE: Self-Supervised Surface Consistency for Point-Based Neural Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03349)
*Yanshu Zhang,Shichong Peng,Mehran Aghabozorgi,Alireza Moazeni,Ke Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the challenge of enabling point-based neural representations to handle large deformations in free-form non-rigid shape editing. The proposed self-supervised method generates random deformations and ensures consistency between surface predictions before and after deformation, incorporated into attention-based point representations with learned interpolation kernels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Point-based neural representations are desirable for multi-view reconstruction due to their lack of fixed connectivity, which allows flexible surface topology. However, they struggle with holes and surface discontinuities under large deformations, limiting their applicability for non-rigid shape editing.

Method: The key innovation is a self-supervised consistency approach: (1) Generate random deformations applied to the point cloud, (2) Ensure the surface prediction from the deformed point cloud equals the deformation applied to the original surface prediction. This is incorporated into attention-based point representations using a learned interpolation kernel (instead of Gaussian splatting) that can adapt to large deformations without adding/removing points.

Result: The framework significantly enhances robustness to large deformations. Experiments on synthetic benchmarks (Neural Editor, Objaverse) show superior zero-shot editing performance and reduced artifacts compared to existing point-based methods. Qualitative results on real-world datasets (DTU, Mip-NeRF 360) demonstrate effectiveness on practical scenes.

Conclusion: The proposed self-supervised deformation consistency approach, combined with attention-based learned interpolation kernels, successfully enables point-based neural representations to handle large non-rigid deformations without requiring ground truth multi-view images of deformed geometry.

Abstract: Advances in neural rendering have enabled high-fidelity multi-view reconstruction of 3D scenes. However, free-form non-rigid shape editing remains a significant challenge. Point-based neural representations are highly desirable for multi-view reconstruction because they lack fixed connectivity, which does not constrain the learned surface topology to that of the initialization. Yet this same property causes point-based representations to struggle with holes and surface discontinuities under large deformations. To address this, we propose a novel self-supervised method to enable point-based representations to adapt to large deformations without requiring ground truth multi-view images of deformed geometry. The key idea is to generate random deformations and to ensure consistency in the predicted surface before and after deformation. In particular, the surface prediction from the deformed point cloud should be the same as the deformation applied to the surface prediction from the original point cloud. We incorporate our approach into attention-based point representations, which differ from splatting-based point representations in their use of a learned interpolation kernel between points as opposed to a Gaussian kernel around each point. This learned interpolation kernel can learn to adapt to large deformations, without requiring addition or removal of points. We show that our framework significantly enhances its robustness to large deformations. Experiments on synthetic geometry editing benchmarks (Neural Editor, Objaverse) demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing point-based methods in zero-shot editing and significantly reduces artifacts. Furthermore, qualitative results on the DTU and Mip-NeRF 360 datasets demonstrate our method's effectiveness on real-world scenes.

</details>


### [8] [WireSeg-32K: A Physics-Grounded Synthetic Dataset for Wire Instance Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03102)
*Zilin Dai,Lehong Wang,Yi Yang,Xiang Fei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WireSeg-32k is a synthetic dataset of 32,000 RGB images with instance masks and depth maps for wire instance segmentation, generated using DeformX - a co-simulation pipeline coupling Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering. LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on this dataset improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deformable linear objects (wires and cables) are difficult to segment due to being thin, highly deformable, and frequently self-occluded. Large-scale instance-level annotations are expensive to obtain in real scenes. Existing resources either focus on cable tracing or semantic segmentation under constrained settings, or generate visually plausible images without physically grounded wire deformation.

Method: The authors developed DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline that couples Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering. This enables physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes, CAD-based wire assets, and diverse visually grounded scenes. They also created a complementary real-world test set with annotations.

Result: LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k alone improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, demonstrating that physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception.

Conclusion: Physically grounded synthetic data (WireSeg-32k generated via DeformX) can effectively transfer to real wire perception tasks, achieving significant improvement in wire instance segmentation performance.

Abstract: Deformable linear objects such as wires and cables are difficult to segment because they are thin, highly deformable, and frequently self-occluded, while large-scale instance-level annotations are expensive to obtain in real scenes. Existing resources either focus on cable tracing or semantic segmentation under constrained settings, or generate visually plausible images without physically grounded wire deformation. We present WireSeg-32k, a synthetic dataset for wire instance segmentation with 32,000 RGB images, instance masks, depth maps, and a complementary real-world test set with annotations. To generate this dataset, we develop DeformX, a co-simulation pipeline that couples Cosserat-rod dynamics with photorealistic Isaac Sim rendering, enabling physically plausible, contact-consistent wire shapes, CAD-based wire assets, and diverse visually grounded scenes. As a simple baseline, LoRA fine-tuning SAM3 on WireSeg-32k alone improves real-world mAP@75 by 10.2% over the off-the-shelf model, showing that physically grounded synthetic data can transfer to real wire perception.

</details>


### [9] [TruncGradGS: Improved 3D Gaussian Splatting via Truncated Gradient Updates](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03534)
*Theo Morales,Nhat-Quynh Le-Pham,Robin Atkins,Binh-Son Hua*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the gradient vanishing problem in 3D Gaussian Splatting optimization by proposing a piecewise truncated gradient formulation that improves stability and robustness to initializations. The method works with both static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting, and includes a new benchmark dataset for dynamic scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard gradient-based optimization in 3D Gaussian Splatting suffers from gradient vanishing, where pixels far from Gaussian primitives have diminishing gradient magnitudes, leading to suboptimal scene reconstruction.

Method: The authors propose a piecewise truncated gradient formulation that modifies how gradients influence primitive attributes during optimization, improving stability and robustness to initializations.

Result: The method consistently improves 3D Gaussian Splatting with random and COLMAP initializations across static and dynamic settings, demonstrated on public benchmarks and a newly proposed synthetic 3D dataset.

Conclusion: The piecewise truncated gradient formulation effectively addresses gradient vanishing in 3D Gaussian Splatting, providing improved optimization stability and robustness while being generalizable across different scene types and initialization methods.

Abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting has become a de facto scene representation for novel view synthesis, yet robustly learning 3D Gaussian primitives from visual input remains challenging. Standard optimization relies on gradient-based updates, but a common issue is the gradient vanishing phenomenon: a pixel far from a Gaussian primitive often has diminishing gradient magnitudes to influence primitive attributes, resulting in suboptimal scene reconstruction. In this paper, we propose a method to address gradient vanishing with a piecewise truncated gradient formulation that improves the optimization stability and robustness to initializations. We show that our method consistently improves 3D Gaussian Splatting with random and COLMAP initializations while being generalizable across static and dynamic Gaussian Splatting. As a by-product, we also examine the limitations of current benchmarks for dynamic scenes, and introduce a novel dataset for benchmarking dynamic Gaussian Splatting using synthetic 3D scenes. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in both static and dynamic settings for the public benchmarks and our proposed dataset.

</details>


### [10] [SLIDEFORGE: An LLM Agent for Controllable Editing of Slides as Structured Artifacts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03109)
*Haozhen Zheng,Fulin Wang,Tianhu Xiong,Yingjie Yu,Shengyi Qian,Hanchao Yu,Alex Schwing,Klara Nahrstedt,Mingyuan Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SLIDEFORGE is an agentic framework for AI-assisted slide editing that solves critical limitations of existing approaches (which operate on screenshots and lose editability). It builds a "Deck State Graph" that links visual decomposition, native PPTX object structure, and perceptual organization to enable theme-preserving reconstruction while maintaining native editability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI agents for slide editing operate on screenshots or weak document representations, which fragment visual units, rasterize editable content, and break layout. AI-assisted slide editing requires not just understanding but also retaining layout, style, component structure, and native editability - which existing approaches fail to achieve.

Method: SLIDEFORGE introduces a Deck State Graph - an executable slide state that links: (1) visual decomposition, (2) native PPTX object structure, and (3) perceptual organization. The framework recovers human-referable components while retaining fine-grained editable structure, supports theme-preserving reconstruction through slide-native operations, and uses rendered-state verification for quality control.

Result: SLIDEFORGE outperforms direct prompting, screenshot-based agents, and generic code-agent baselines across multiple dimensions including component recovery, preservation, restyling consistency, visual quality, and native editability.

Conclusion: SLIDEFORGE represents a significant advance in controllable slide editing by bridging the gap between AI capabilities and practical presentation editing needs. The introduced evaluation paradigm provides comprehensive metrics for assessing AI-assisted slide transformation, and the open-source implementation enables further research and development.

Abstract: Current AI agents compellingly describe slides. However, AI-assisted slide editing requires more than understanding: the output must retain layout, style, component structure, and native editability. Towards, AI-assisted slide editing, existing agents operate on screenshots or weak document representations and often fragment coherent visual units, rasterize editable content, or break layout. In contrast, for controllable slide editing, we introduce an agentic framework, SLIDEFORGE, which builds a Deck State Graph, an executable slide state that links visual decomposition, native pptx object structure, and perceptual organization. By recovering human-referable components while retaining fine-grained editable structure, SLIDEFORGE supports theme-preserving reconstruction through slide-native operations and rendered-state verification. We further introduce an evaluation paradigm for controllable slide transformation that jointly measures component recovery, preservation, restyling consistency, visual quality, and native editability. Experiments show that SLIDEFORGE outperforms direct prompting, screenshot-based agents, and generic code-agent baselines across these dimensions. Code is available at https://github.com/UIUC-MONET/SLIDEFORGE.

</details>


### [11] [Building Pretraining Data for World Models: An Unreal Engine-Based Pipeline for Action-Conditioned Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03557)
*Haoyu Wang,Songchun Zhang,Haoran Li,Haoyang Huang,Zeyue Xue,Nan Duan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A large-scale synthetic data production pipeline built on Unreal Engine for generating action-conditioned, multi-view video. The pipeline uses a two-stage approach: Stage I runs real-time physics simulation to record trajectory data, Stage II replays trajectories for high-quality offline rendering. The system includes distributed production features and produced 2,691 hours of 1080p video and 6,076 hours of 720p video from 429 levels and 40 humanoid characters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Action-conditioned video models require large-scale visual data paired with control signals that are temporally aligned with scene transitions. Obtaining such supervision from real-world video is difficult because the actions that caused each visual change are typically unknown.

Method: Two-stage pipeline: (1) Stage I executes real-time physics in PIE (Play In Editor), recording per-frame character states, control inputs, and camera states into an intermediate trajectory representation; (2) Stage II replays trajectories in a separate engine process and renders them offline with Movie Render Queue (MRQ) for high-quality output. The production system includes cache-aware task partitioning, node-local slot scheduling, automated scene screening, aesthetic and luminance filtering, partial-output recovery, asynchronous upload, and continuous cluster health monitoring.

Result: Production cluster: 25 servers with 8 NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs each. From 2,384 asset packs, 429 levels were retained for production along with 40 humanoid characters. Output: 2,691 hours of 1080p video and 6,076 hours of 720p video. This pipeline constitutes the Unreal Engine synthetic-data production component used in EchoWM.

Conclusion: The paper describes the system architecture, implementation decisions that emerged from production failures, and limitations of using perceptual quality proxies for world-model data curation. The pipeline successfully produces large-scale synthetic action-conditioned video data for training world models.

Abstract: Action-conditioned video models require large-scale visual data paired with control signals that are temporally aligned with the resulting scene transitions. Such supervision is difficult to obtain from ordinary real-world video because the actions that caused each visual change are typically unknown. We present a large-scale synthetic data production pipeline built on Unreal Engine for generating action-conditioned, multi-view video. To accommodate the different execution requirements of real-time physics and high-quality offline rendering, the pipeline executes trajectory generation and final rendering in two stages: Stage I runs real physics in PIE and records per-frame character states, control inputs, and camera states into an intermediate trajectory representation; Stage II replays those trajectories in a new engine process and renders them offline with Movie Render Queue (MRQ). Around this core, we develop a distributed production system with cache-aware task partitioning, node-local slot scheduling, automated scene screening, aesthetic and luminance filtering, partial-output recovery, asynchronous upload, and continuous cluster health monitoring. The production cluster contains 25 servers with eight NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPUs per server. From 2,384 asset packs, 429 levels were retained for production together with a pool of 40 humanoid characters. The pipeline has produced 2,691 hours of 1080p video and 6,076 hours of 720p video. We describe the system architecture, the implementation decisions that emerged from production failures, and the limitations of using perceptual quality proxies for world-model data curation. The pipeline described in this report constitutes the Unreal Engine synthetic-data production component used in EchoWM.

</details>


### [12] [Beyond Small Patches: Black-Box Detection and Purification of Diverse Backdoor Triggers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03139)
*Ahmed Abdelnaby,Mohamed Elmahallawy*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TRIM is a black-box defense against backdoor attacks that detects and removes malicious triggers at inference time without requiring model internals, training data, or clean samples. It uses region-based segmentation, adaptive trigger discovery via inpainting/diffusion, and selective purification, achieving ASR as low as 1.16% while preserving clean accuracy up to 87.87%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing backdoor defenses often require access to model internals, training data, or clean validation samples, making them impractical for deployed black-box vision systems where only API access to the model is available. There is a need for a deployment-oriented defense that can work with zero auxiliary information.

Method: TRIM employs three key components: (1) Region-based segmentation using deep feature representations to identify potential trigger locations, (2) Adaptive trigger discovery through inpainting and diffusion-based reconstruction to isolate regions causing misclassification without assumptions about trigger type/shape/location, and (3) Selective region purification that cleans poisoned regions while preserving benign content. Additionally, it caches feature embeddings of previously identified triggers for efficient recognition.

Result: TRIM consistently outperforms existing black-box defenses across diverse datasets and backdoor types (blended, sparse, varying-size, and multiple triggers). It reduces attack success rates (ASR) to as low as 1.16% while preserving clean accuracy of up to 87.87%.

Conclusion: Effective backdoor mitigation is possible at inference time even when the defender has no access to any auxiliary data (model internals, training data, or clean samples). TRIM demonstrates that black-box defenses can achieve strong performance without requiring internal model access or clean data.

Abstract: Deep neural networks (DNNs) are increasingly deployed in real-world vision systems, yet their predictions can be covertly manipulated by backdoor attacks, in which malicious triggers cause targeted misclassification while preserving high clean accuracy. Existing defenses often rely on model internals, training data, or clean validation samples, making them difficult to deploy when only black-box access to a trained model is available. We propose TRIM (Trigger Removal by Identifying Manipulated Regions), a deployment-oriented black-box defense that detects and selectively removes backdoor triggers at inference time without requiring model internals, training data, or clean samples. The key insight behind TRIM is to identify image regions that are responsible for anomalous model behavior and purify only those regions while preserving benign content. TRIM innovates via three key components: (i) region-based segmentation with deep feature representations, (ii) adaptive trigger discovery through inpainting and diffusion-based reconstruction to isolate regions responsible for misclassification---without assumptions about trigger type, shape, or location, and (iii) selective region purification that cleans poisoned regions while retaining benign content. To support practical deployment, TRIM further caches feature embeddings of previously identified triggers, enabling efficient recognition and avoiding redundant detection and purification. Extensive experiments across diverse datasets and backdoor types, including blended, sparse, varying-size, and multiple triggers, show that TRIM consistently outperforms existing black-box defenses, reducing attack success rates (ASR) to as low as 1.16% while preserving clean accuracy of up to 87.87%. These results demonstrate that effective backdoor mitigation is possible at inference time even when the defender has no access to any auxiliary data.

</details>


### [13] [VeriPhy: Agentic Physical Reasoning for World Model Evaluation and Refinement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03153)
*Wenzhuo Xu,Yuchen Zhu,Chongjian Ge,Xuan Shen,Jing Shi,Jason Kuen,Yongxin Chen,Molei Tao,Christopher McComb,Noelia Grande Gutiérrez,Jiuxiang Gu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VeriPhy is an auditable physical-verification system for generated videos that identifies physical violations and their timing, rather than just providing a quality score. It uses a text-only planner to compile prompts into typed physical obligations, with execution gated by observations and returning provenance-carrying evidence records.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Visual fluency in generated video does not imply physical reliability. Existing scalar quality scores cannot indicate what physical obligation a clip violates or when it fails. There is a need for an auditable system that can trace verdicts to the evidence that produced them.

Method: VeriPhy uses a text-only planner that compiles prompts into typed physical obligations and a statically validated execution plan before any frame is observed. During execution, observations gate and scope only declared calls to frozen low-level experts (segmentation, tracking, counting, 11 typed physical measurements, depth, OCR, audio-event detection). Each action returns a provenance-carrying evidence record. Typed resolvers and fixed composition map usable records to a three-valued state (supported, contradicted, or unknown, surfaced as plausible, implausible, or abstain).

Result: On a 149-clip core carrying 304 flaw records, VeriPhy accounts for 228, against 164 for a published question-decomposition evaluator. Prompting the backbone monolithically reaches 222. What separates VeriPhy is that each decision retains its evidence record and provenance, making traces auditable one verdict at a time.

Conclusion: VeriPhy provides auditable physical verification for generated videos with full provenance. While recall (228) is comparable to monolithic prompting (222), its key advantage is auditability—every verdict is traceable to the evidence that produced it, enabling critic verdicts to be written back into generation.

Abstract: Visual fluency in generated video does not imply physical reliability, and a scalar quality score alone is incapable of indicating the obligation a clip violates or the moment it fails. We present VeriPhy, an auditable physical-verification system in which a text-only planner compiles the prompt into typed physical obligations and a statically validated execution plan before any frame is observed. During execution, observations gate and scope only declared calls to frozen low-level experts (e.g., segmentation and tracking, counting, eleven typed physical measurements over the resulting tracks, depth, OCR, and audio-event detection). Each action returns a provenance-carrying evidence record whose payload, when usable, is either a typed measurement or an explicitly tagged learned state. Typed resolvers and fixed composition map usable records to a three-valued state (supported, contradicted, or unknown, surfaced as plausible, implausible, or abstain) with full provenance, so that every verdict is traceable to the evidence that produced it. We anchor evaluation in a 1,500-clip corpus of human-annotated flaw records that localize real generation failures in prompt reference, space, and time. On a 149-clip core carrying 304 such records, VeriPhy accounts for 228, against 164 for a published question-decomposition evaluator given the same clips and the same claims. Recall alone does not separate it from prompting the same backbone monolithically, which reaches 222; what separates them is that each decision retains its evidence record and provenance, making the traces auditable one verdict at a time and usable as the interface through which a critic verdict could be written back into generation.

</details>


### [14] [Who Speaks for the Pruned? Visual Token Pruning as Coverage Optimization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03158)
*Qingchan Zhu,Weihang You,Hanqi Jiang,Changdi Yang,Tianming Liu,Geng Yuan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CoverPruner is a training-free visual token pruning method for vision-language models (VLMs) that asks a complementary question to existing methods: which surviving token best represents a removed token? It formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM) using projector-space coverage and a lightweight attention probe, achieving superior accuracy across various VLM architectures and compression rates, especially under aggressive compression.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing visual token pruning methods only ask which tokens to keep (retained-token view). This approach has a critical flaw: it can keep redundant high-scoring tokens while leaving discarded evidence without a close representative. The motivation is to address this gap by asking the complementary demand-side question: after a token is removed, which surviving original token represents it for the target VLM?

Method: CoverPruner formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM), which covers the full projected visual-token set with query-weighted demand. It instantiates RCM with two key components: (1) projector-space coverage - using the project's output space to measure representational coverage, and (2) a lightweight first-layer attention probe - a lightweight mechanism to identify which surviving tokens can best represent discarded ones.

Result: CoverPruner achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods across multiple VLM architectures and compression rates. The largest gains typically appear under aggressive compression scenarios.

Conclusion: The proposed demand-side perspective (asking which surviving token represents a removed token) is complementary to the traditional supply-side approach (asking which tokens to keep). This Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM) framework with projector-space coverage and attention probe proves effective for training-free visual token pruning in VLMs, particularly under high compression rates.

Abstract: Visual token pruning reduces the inference cost of vision-language models (VLMs), but most methods only ask which tokens to keep. This retained-token view can keep redundant high-scoring tokens while leaving discarded evidence without a close representative. We propose CoverPruner, a training-free pruner that asks the complementary demand-side question: after a token is removed, which surviving original token represents it for the target VLM? CoverPruner formulates pruning as Representational Coverage Maximization (RCM), covering the full projected visual-token set with query-weighted demand. It instantiates RCM with projector-space coverage and a lightweight first-layer attention probe. Across multiple VLM architectures and compression rates, CoverPruner achieves the best average accuracy among all compared methods, with the largest gains usually appearing under aggressive compression.

</details>


### [15] [RoboTok: An Internet-Scale Data Engine for Human Demonstration Retrieval and Dexterous Manipulation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03199)
*Howard Qian,Yiting Chen,Yunfei Xie,Kejia Ren,Podshara Chanrungmaneekul,Gaotian Wang,Bowen Wen,Chen Wei,Kaiyu Hang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RoboTok is an internet-scale data engine that retrieves manipulation-relevant human demonstrations from web videos for training dexterous robot policies, using a learned latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories in actor-centered reference frames.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Robot learning requires broad and diverse demonstrations, but collecting robot data is expensive and cannot cover the long tail of real-world tasks. Web videos represent a scalable and continuously growing source of supervision, but efficient retrieval of relevant human demonstrations remains challenging.

Method: The method learns a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories expressed in estimated actor-centered reference frames. This representation enables manipulation behaviors to be compared across variations in camera viewpoint, scene appearance, and actor occlusions while remaining compact enough for efficient search and continual indexing over internet-scale video collections.

Result: RoboTok retrieves more relevant manipulation demonstrations compared to existing robot-data retrieval approaches and improves downstream task success on retrieval benchmarks and downstream robot policy performance.

Conclusion: Hand-pose trajectory-aware retrieval makes web video a scalable and continuously growing source of supervision for robot learning, establishing this approach as a way to address the data bottleneck in robot learning.

Abstract: Robot learning increasingly depends on broad and diverse demonstrations, yet collecting robot data remains expensive and poorly suited to covering the long tail of real-world tasks. To address this bottleneck, we introduce RoboTok, an internet-scale data engine that, given a query human manipulation video, retrieves manipulation-relevant human demonstrations from web videos for training dexterous robot policies. Specifically, we learn a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories expressed in estimated actor-centered reference frames. This representation enables manipulation behaviors to be compared across variations in camera viewpoint, scene appearance, and actor occlusions, while remaining compact enough for efficient search and continual indexing over internet-scale video collections. We evaluate RoboTok against existing robot-data retrieval approaches on retrieval benchmarks and downstream robot policy performance. Our results show that RoboTok retrieves more relevant manipulation demonstrations and improves downstream task success, establishing hand-pose trajectory-aware retrieval as a way to make web video a scalable and continuously growing source of supervision for robot learning.

</details>


### [16] [Learning to Zoom Efficiently with a Contrastive Curriculum](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03206)
*Falko Helm,Iryna Gurevych*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A paper proposing an intrinsic reward-based method for teaching Multimodal Large Language Models to use zoom-in tools without supervised fine-tuning, using InfoNCE-style contrastive learning with hard negative examples, and introducing the synthetic M&C dataset for evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous zoom-in learning methods require extensive warm-start SFT phases with additional labels, which is inefficient. This work aims to eliminate this requirement by enabling intrinsic learning of zoom-in tool use.

Method: InfoNCE-style intrinsic reward using curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls as contrastive training signal; introduced M&C dataset with region-of-interest labels for direct zoom-in ability measurement.

Result: Competitive with SFT methods while being more efficient; outperforms all baselines when used as drop-in replacement for SFT; recall metric most strongly correlates zoom-in region with task performance.

Conclusion: Intrinsic rewards with contrastive learning can effectively teach MLLMs zoom-in tool use without warm-start SFT, providing a more efficient and label-free alternative. The M&C dataset enables scalable evaluation of zoom-in abilities.

Abstract: Using a zoom-in tool is an important foundational part of modern visual agents, because it allows to efficiently handle tasks involving high-resolution images. Most previous methods need an extensive warm-start supervised fine-tuning phase for teaching models zoom-in. We show that this is not necessary by proposing a new intrinsic reward for learning tool use in MLLMs without the need for additional labels or warm-start SFT. Our InfoNCE-style reward uses a curriculum of increasingly hard negative tool calls as a contrastive training signal. Empirical experiments on $V^*$, HRBench and MME-RealWorld show that our approach is competitive while being more efficient. When used as a drop-in replacement for SFT, we even outperform all baselines. To directly measure the zoom-in ability of models, we further introduce the scalable synthetic Muffin&Chihuahua (M&C) dataset. Each image consists of a grid with every cell either showing a muffin or chihuahua. Leveraging the M&C dataset's unique region of interest labels, we find that recall is the metric that most strongly correlates the zoom-in region with final task performance. Our model and code for reproduction is publicly available under https://github.com/UKPLab/emnlp2026-zoom-in

</details>


### [17] [ProgResViT: Progressive Resolution and Width for Adaptive Vision Transformers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03216)
*Ali Hojjat,Janek Haberer,Olaf Landsiedel*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ProgResViT is an input-adaptive Vision Transformer that dynamically adjusts computation based on image complexity by progressively processing images across multiple rounds - starting with low-resolution/narrow subnetwork and refining with higher-resolution/wider subnetwork when needed. Uses Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG) to condition token fusion and layer outputs on current round, block, and input resolution.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision Transformers typically process every image using fixed input resolution and model width, even though many images can be classified with substantially less computation. This leads to inefficient resource usage for simpler images.

Method: Progressive inference across multiple rounds: (1) First round processes low-resolution image with narrow subnetwork; (2) If prediction confidence is insufficient, reuse representations and proceed with higher-resolution input and wider subnetwork; (3) All rounds share a single backbone with Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG) that conditions token fusion and layer outputs on current round, block, and input resolution.

Result: ProgResViT applied to DeiT yields better accuracy-compute trade-offs than adaptive-width, adaptive-depth, and dynamic-token baselines. With knowledge distillation, achieves 84.9% top-1 accuracy, slightly exceeding DeiT-III-S. Also provides favorable trade-offs for self-supervised DINO representations and downstream semantic segmentation.

Conclusion: ProgResViT demonstrates that progressive, input-adaptive inference can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy while dynamically allocating computation based on image complexity, applicable to both supervised and self-supervised settings across classification and segmentation tasks.

Abstract: Vision Transformers (ViTs) typically process every image using a fixed input resolution and model width, even though many images can be classified with substantially less computation. We introduce ProgResViT, an input-adaptive ViT that performs inference progressively across multiple rounds. The first round processes a low-resolution image with a narrow subnetwork. Inference terminates when the prediction is sufficiently confident; otherwise, the model reuses the representations produced in the current round and proceeds with a higher-resolution input and a wider subnetwork to refine its prediction. As all rounds share a single backbone, we propose Progress-Conditioned Soft Gating (PSG), which conditions token fusion and layer outputs on the current round, block, and input resolution. On image classification, applying ProgResViT to DeiT yields better accuracy-compute trade-offs than adaptive-width, adaptive-depth, and dynamic-token baselines. With knowledge distillation, a DeiT-based ProgResViT achieves 84.9% top-1 accuracy, slightly exceeding the reported DeiT-III-S accuracy under a comparable evaluation setting. We show that the same design also provides favorable accuracy-compute trade-offs for self-supervised DINO representations and downstream semantic segmentation. Code is available at https://github.com/ds-kiel/ProgResViT.

</details>


### [18] [Counting Animals in Camera-Traps Image Sequences without Count Labels: Winning Solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03233)
*Fagner Cunha,Juan G. Colonna,Eulanda M. dos Santos*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents MaxBoxCount, the winning solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge for counting unique animals in camera trap image sequences without requiring count annotations for training.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Camera traps are essential for wildlife monitoring, but counting unique individuals across short image sequences remains challenging due to large temporal discontinuities (1 frame/second) and the high cost of manual annotation for individual counts.

Method: The approach combines a strong species classification pipeline with a counting heuristic based on MegaDetector detections to estimate the number of unique individuals without requiring count annotations during training.

Result: Won the iWildCam 2021 Challenge, establishing a benchmark for animal counting at the sequence level under realistic annotation constraints where count annotations are unavailable for training.

Conclusion: MaxBoxCount demonstrates that effective individual counting can be achieved without expensive manual count annotations by leveraging species classification and detection-based heuristics, advancing automated wildlife monitoring capabilities.

Abstract: Camera traps have become an essential tool for wildlife monitoring, motivating the development of computer vision methods for the automated extraction of information from these data. While most prior work has focused on species identification, many ecological applications also require estimating the number of unique individuals appearing across short image sequences. This task is particularly challenging because camera traps typically acquire bursts of images at approximately one frame per second, creating large temporal discontinuities that may make conventional multi-object tracking methods unreliable, and because manually collecting individual count annotations is prohibitively expensive. In this work, we describe the winning solution to the iWildCam 2021 Challenge, which introduced a benchmark for counting animals at the sequence level under realistic annotation constraints where count annotations are unavailable for training. Our approach, MaxBoxCount, combines a strong species classification pipeline with a simple yet effective counting heuristic based on MegaDetector detections to estimate the number of unique individuals without requiring count annotations. Code is available at https://github.com/alcunha/iwildcam2021ufam.

</details>


### [19] [An Ensemble-Based Self-Taught Learning Approach for Parking Space Classification Under Limited Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03258)
*Lucas de Oliveira Cunha,Joelton Deonei Gotz,Paulo Lisboa de Almeida,Andre Gustavo Hochuli*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a self-taught learning framework for parking spot classification using convolutional autoencoders for unsupervised representation learning. The approach learns transferable visual representations from unlabeled data and uses an ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders with independent classifier heads to improve robustness and reduce annotation requirements, achieving 93-96% accuracy on PKLot and CNRPark benchmarks under cross-dataset evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Address limitations of deep learning approaches for parking spot classification that rely on large amounts of annotated data and exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous environments.

Method: Self-taught learning framework using unsupervised representation learning with convolutional autoencoders. The learned encoders serve as fixed feature extractors for supervised classification with limited annotated samples. An ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders is employed with independent classifier heads and prediction fusion at inference time.

Result: Achieves accuracies between 93% and 96% in data-constrained scenarios. Substantially reduces annotation requirements while improving robustness under significant domain shifts on PKLot and CNRPark benchmarks under cross-dataset evaluation protocols.

Conclusion: The ensemble-based self-taught learning strategy effectively addresses the data annotation bottleneck and domain generalization challenges in parking spot classification, enabling effective classification with limited annotated data while maintaining robustness across heterogeneous environments.

Abstract: Parking spot classification is a fundamental task in intelligent transportation systems, yet most deep learning approaches rely on large amounts of annotated data and exhibit limited generalization across heterogeneous environments. To address these limitations, we investigate a self-taught learning framework based on unsupervised representation learning with convolutional autoencoders. The proposed approach learns transferable visual representations from unlabeled data and reuses the learned encoders as fixed feature extractors for supervised classification with limited annotated samples in the target domain. To further enhance robustness and mitigate architectural bias, an ensemble of heterogeneous autoencoders is employed, with independent classifier heads and prediction fusion at inference time. Experiments conducted on the PKLot and CNRPark benchmarks under cross-dataset evaluation protocols show that the proposed ensemble-based strategy substantially reduces annotation requirements while improving robustness under significant domain shifts, achieving accuracies between 93\% and 96\% in data-constrained scenarios.

</details>


### [20] [MedQA-MM: Shortcuts Behind Medical Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03261)
*Benlu Wang,Yifan Zhang,Jiaqing Yu,Chin Siang Ong,Juncheng Huang,Zhuohao Li,Zhenyu Zhang,Arman Cohan,Hong Yu,Zonghai Yao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper identifies "reasoning inflation" in medical multimodal MCQ benchmarks, where models can achieve correct answers through spurious cues (answer wording, non-visual text, image artifacts) rather than intended image findings. The authors propose analyzing observable "routes" rather than hidden cognition, and demonstrate via experiments that current benchmarks significantly overattribute visual reasoning ability to models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current medical multimodal benchmarks credit final answers without examining whether the intended image finding was actually used. A correct answer could be supported by benchmark-preserved cues in answer wording, non-visual clinical text, visible image text, artificial annotations, or device/context artifacts. This leads to "reasoning inflation" - overestimating models' true medical image reasoning capabilities.

Method: The authors conducted: (1) Prompt- and image-side audits, (2) Modality ablations (text-only, options-only settings), (3) Matched repairs preserving medical target and answer key. They tested across 6 medical multimodal MCQ datasets using a 13-configuration open-model panel. They also constructed MedQA-MM, a 1,000-item shortcut-mitigated subset.

Result: Full-input accuracy: 62.63%. Text-only: 53.96%. Options-only: 29.71%. Removing length-gap cues: -6.58pp. Removing absolute/conspicuous cues: -3.50pp. Removing spatial/prepositional cues: -4.77pp. In MedQA-MM: text-only dropped to 5.21%, options-only to 12.33%.

Conclusion: Medical image-reasoning claims require route-level evidence. The significant performance with non-visual inputs and the drops when removing spurious cues demonstrate that benchmarks overestimate true multimodal reasoning. Models may not actually use images as intended; route-level analysis is necessary to validate genuine visual reasoning in medical MCQs.

Abstract: A benchmark score credits final answers, but not the route by which an item can be answered. In medical multimodal multiple-choice questions (MCQs), this distinction matters because a correct answer can be supported by the intended image finding or by benchmark-preserved cues in the wording of answers, non-visual clinical text, visible image text, artificial annotations, or device/context artifacts. We call the resulting score-level overinterpretation reasoning inflation. Here, a route is an observable input path that can support answer selection, not a claim about the model's hidden cognition. Across six medical multimodal MCQ datasets, we separate candidate cues from behavioral evidence through prompt- and image-side audits, modality ablations, and matched repairs that preserve the medical target and answer key. In a 13-configuration open-model panel, full-input accuracy is 62.63%, while text-only and options-only settings achieve 53.96% and 29.71%, respectively. Removing length-gap, absolute/conspicuous, and spatial/prepositional cues lowers accuracy by 6.58, 3.50, and 4.77 percentage points. We also construct MedQA-MM, a 1,000-item shortcut-mitigated subset, where text-only and options-only accuracy fall to 5.21% and 12.33%. This does not imply that models never use images; it shows that medical image-reasoning claims require route-level evidence.

</details>


### [21] [Tensor-based Brain Surface Modeling and Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03302)
*Moo K. Chung,Keith J. Worsley,Steve Robbins,Alan C. Evans*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A unified computational framework for tensor-based morphometry (TBM) that detects brain surface shape differences between clinical groups from MRI data, combining surface modeling, Laplace-Beltrami diffusion smoothing, and statistical analysis to localize cortical regions with structural changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Brain cortical surface shape differences between clinical groups are not uniform across the cortex. Existing methods lack a unified framework that combines surface modeling, smoothing, and statistical analysis to detect and localize these regional variations in surface area and curvature.

Method: The approach combines surface modeling, surface data smoothing using diffusion based on explicit Laplace-Beltrami operator estimation, and statistical analysis in a unified mathematical framework. Surface metrics (local area and curvature) are computed from cortical surfaces extracted from MR images, then smoothed to increase signal-to-noise ratio before statistical comparison between groups.

Result: The method successfully localizes cortical regions with the most rapid structural differences, demonstrated by identifying gray matter tissue growth and loss regions in longitudinal brain images of children.

Conclusion: This unified tensor-based surface morphometry approach provides an effective tool for detecting and localizing regional brain surface shape differences in clinical studies, with applications in developmental neuroimaging.

Abstract: We present a unified computational approach to tensor-based morphometry in detecting the brain surface shape differences between two clinical groups based on magnetic resonance images. Our approach is novel in a sense that we combined surface modeling, surface data smoothing and statistical analysis in a coherent unified mathematical framework. The cerebral cortex has the topology of a 2D highly convoluted sheet. Between two different clinical groups, the local surface area and curvature of the cortex may differ. It is highly likely that such surface shape differences are not uniform over the whole cortex. By computing how such surface metrics differ, the regions of the most rapid structural differences can be localized. To increase the signal to noise ratio, diffusion smoothing based on the explicit estimation of Laplace-Beltrami operator has been developed and applied to the surface metrics. As an illustration, we demonstrate how this new tensor-based surface morphometry can be applied in localizing the cortical regions of the gray matter tissue growth and loss in the brain images longitudinally collected in the group of children.

</details>


### [22] [Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies for Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03334)
*Yixiong Yang,Sisheng Zhang,Qingsong Yan,Shaohuai Shi,Qiang Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies addresses the computational bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting training caused by continual growth of Gaussian primitives. The method combines Laplacian image decomposition with coarse-to-fine frequency-staged training, archiving lower-frequency Gaussian fields after fitting so subsequent fields can optimize higher-frequency residuals independently. This reduces active Gaussians during training, lowering optimization overhead and accelerating convergence. The approach is plug-and-play and orthogonal to existing accelerations like Taming-3DGS and FastGS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) suffers from continual growth of Gaussian primitives during training, which creates a key bottleneck by increasing optimization cost and slowing convergence, particularly at high resolutions. This primitive growth problem becomes increasingly severe at higher resolutions, limiting the practical applicability of 3DGS for high-quality rendering tasks.

Method: The proposed Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies scheme combines Laplacian image decomposition with coarse-to-fine, frequency-staged training. After fitting lower-frequency structure, the corresponding Gaussian field is archived so that subsequent fields can optimize higher-frequency residuals without carrying the full primitive burden. At inference time, the rendered components are composed in the image domain via a Laplacian-style reconstruction. This method is designed to be plug-and-play and orthogonal to existing 3DGS acceleration methods.

Result: The method achieves average speedups of 1.73x and 1.21x at 1K resolution setting, and 1.74x and 1.33x at 4K resolution setting on Taming-3DGS and FastGS backbones respectively. The speedups are larger on more challenging scenes, and benefits become increasingly pronounced at higher resolutions, with competitive reconstruction quality maintained.

Conclusion: Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies provides an effective solution to the Gaussian primitive growth problem in 3DGS training. By decomposing the problem into frequency-staged components and archiving lower-frequency fields, the method significantly reduces active Gaussians during training. Its orthogonal nature allows combination with existing accelerations (Taming-3DGS, FastGS) for synergistic improvements. The approach demonstrates particularly strong benefits at higher resolutions, making it promising for practical high-quality 3D rendering applications.

Abstract: A key bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting training is the continual growth of Gaussian primitives, which increases optimization cost and slows convergence, especially at high resolutions. We propose Laplacian Frequency Hierarchies, a simple yet efficient 3DGS scheme that combines Laplacian image decomposition with coarse-to-fine, frequency-staged training. After fitting lower-frequency structure, we archive the corresponding Gaussian field so that subsequent fields can optimize higher-frequency residuals without carrying the full primitive burden, and we compose the rendered components in the image domain via a Laplacian-style reconstruction at inference time. This design reduces the number of active Gaussians during training, thereby lowering optimization overhead and accelerating training. The proposed scheme is plug-and-play and orthogonal to prior 3DGS accelerations: it can be directly combined with strong backbones such as Taming-3DGS and FastGS to improve training speed with competitive reconstruction quality. It achieves average speedups of 1.73x and 1.21x at 1K setting, and 1.74x and 1.33x at 4K setting on Taming-3DGS and FastGS, with larger gains on more challenging scenes and increasingly pronounced benefits at higher resolutions.

</details>


### [23] [When Depth Hurts: Reliability-Aware Geometry Distillation for Depth-Free RGB-D Salient Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03378)
*Xuehao Wang,Jiaxin Hua,Runmei Li,Zhenyu Wu,Chenglizhao Chen,Ke Gu,Aimin Hao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: A reliability-aware geometry distillation framework for RGB-D salient object detection that uses a frozen Depth Anything V2 model as a training-time teacher to transfer geometry knowledge to an RGB-only inference network, eliminating dependence on defective sensor depth.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sensor depth in RGB-D SOD is unreliable (missing regions, blurred boundaries, artifacts), which can make RGB-D detectors less accurate than RGB-only. Existing quality-aware approaches still depend on the same defective modality.

Method: Use a frozen Depth Anything V2 model as teacher to transfer dense relative geometry, hierarchical spatial attention, and boundary structure to a compact edge-aware geometry branch. Pooled bidirectional interaction aligns geometry with appearance. A pixel-wise reliability estimator selectively injects compatible geometry. Teacher is removed after training, leaving an RGB-only network.

Result: Trained on 2,985 RGB-mask pairs, achieves best or tied-best in 26/36 metric-dataset comparisons against 10 RGB-D SOD methods. 13.4% relative MAE reduction on ReDWeb-S. When retrained on DUTS-TR, improves F-measure by 4.2% on PASCAL-S, demonstrating cross-domain transferability.

Conclusion: Geometry distillation from pre-trained depth models can effectively replace defective sensor depth, creating an RGB-only inference network that outperforms RGB-D methods that rely on actual sensor depth. The approach generalizes beyond the training dataset domain.

Abstract: Depth can resolve appearance ambiguity in RGB-D salient object detection (SOD), yet sensor depth is not uniformly reliable. Missing regions, blurred boundaries, and structural artifacts can propagate through multimodal fusion and make an RGB-D detector less accurate than its RGB-only counterpart. Existing quality-aware approaches regulate observed depth but remain dependent on the same potentially defective modality. We propose \method, a reliability-aware geometry distillation framework developed for RGB-D SOD benchmarks without using dataset-provided depth during training or inference. A frozen Depth Anything V2 model serves only as a training-time teacher, transferring dense relative geometry, hierarchical spatial attention, and boundary structure to a compact edge-aware geometry branch. Pooled bidirectional interaction aligns geometry with appearance, and a pixel-wise reliability estimator selectively injects geometry that is compatible with the current RGB representation. The teacher is removed after training, leaving an RGB-only inference network. Trained on 2,985 RGB-mask pairs, \method{} achieves the best or tied-best result in 26 of 36 metric-dataset comparisons against ten recent RGB-D SOD methods, including a 13.4\% relative MAE reduction on ReDWeb-S. When retrained on DUTS-TR, it also improves the strongest prior $F$-measure by 4.2\% on PASCAL-S, showing that the distilled geometry transfers beyond a particular sensor or dataset domain. Code will be released upon publication.

</details>


### [24] [FoRIS: Progressive Foreground Refinement for Training-Free In-Context Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03384)
*Ming Hu,Jianfu Yin,Mingyu Dou,Miaomiao Zhang,Yao Wang,Cong Hu,Bingliang Hu,Quan Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FoRIS is a training-free in-context segmentation framework that treats ICS as a coarse-to-fine progressive refinement process, consisting of three stages: Foreground Purification, Foreground Localization, and Foreground Consolidation. It achieves SOTA performance with 4.5 and 4.8 mIoU improvements in 1-shot and 5-shot settings respectively.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In-Context Segmentation (ICS) aims to segment arbitrary semantic concepts given few annotated visual exemplars. Existing approaches directly predict final masks through reference-query matching, which may be suboptimal. The authors revisit ICS from a classical segmentation perspective, viewing it as a coarse-to-fine progressive refinement process.

Method: The proposed FoRIS framework consists of three key stages: (1) Foreground Purification - suppresses background distractions, (2) Foreground Localization - localizes discriminative target regions, (3) Foreground Consolidation - recovers complete foreground structures through semantic aggregation. The method is training-free.

Result: FoRIS achieves SOTA performance across semantic and part segmentation tasks, with average improvements of 4.5 mIoU points in 1-shot setting and 4.8 mIoU points in 5-shot setting over existing approaches.

Conclusion: The coarse-to-fine progressive refinement perspective provides a promising direction for in-context segmentation, and FoRIS demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach through significant performance improvements over existing methods.

Abstract: In-Context Segmentation (ICS) aims to precisely segment arbitrary semantic concepts, such as objects or parts, given one or a few annotated visual exemplars. In this paper, we revisit ICS from a more classical segmentation perspective, viewing it as a coarse-to-fine progressive refinement process. Rather than directly predicting the final mask through reference-query matching, we progressively refine the segmentation from coarse and ambiguous foreground responses to precise and complete foreground structures. Building upon this perspective, we propose a training-free in-context segmentation framework, termed FoRIS. Specifically, FoRIS consists of three key stages: Foreground Purification, Foreground Localization, and Foreground Consolidation, which progressively suppress background distractions, localize discriminative target regions, and recover complete foreground structures through semantic aggregation. Experimental results demonstrate that FoRIS achieves SOTA performance across semantic and part segmentation tasks, with average improvements of 4.5 and 4.8 mIoU points over existing approaches in the 1-shot and 5-shot settings, respectively.
