Code: https://github.com/Xi-Mu-Yu/FoRIS.

</details>


### [25] [Exploring the Potential of Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training for Multi-Source Remote Sensing Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03391)
*Xiangyang Miao,Kelu Yao,Yekai Huang,Xiaogang Xu,Junxiao Xue,Minjun Shen,Chenghui Lv,Shanji Liu,Yaying Chen,Chao Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OmniRSCLIP is a contrastive learning framework that extends CLIP to support heterogeneous remote sensing modalities (SAR, MSI, HSI) beyond RGB, using Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition (SSBD) to adapt arbitrary-channel inputs while preserving pretrained visual knowledge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing remote sensing contrastive learning methods are built on RGB-oriented CLIP architectures, making it difficult to exploit heterogeneous sensors such as SAR, multi-spectral imaging (MSI), and hyperspectral imaging (HSI).

Method: The paper proposes: 1) Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition (SSBD) which formulates arbitrary-channel adaptation as a basis recomposition problem using pretrained CLIP patch embeddings as transferable spatial bases and wavelength-conditioned coefficients for sensor-specific embedding kernels; 2) A spectral-context-aware mask-based contrastive learning scheme to suppress modality-specific redundant features; 3) Construction of OmniRS5M, the first large-scale remote sensing image-text corpus covering RGB, SAR, MSI, and HSI.

Result: Experiments on retrieval, zero-shot classification, and semantic localization show that OmniRSCLIP preserves strong RGB-domain performance while effectively extending CLIP to heterogeneous remote sensing modalities.

Conclusion: OmniRSCLIP successfully extends CLIP beyond its fixed RGB input interface to support multi-source sensor inputs for remote sensing vision-language modeling, without breaking the pretrained visual knowledge. The approach aligns heterogeneous sensors in a unified image-text semantic space while maintaining RGB performance.

Abstract: Contrastive language-image learning (CLIP) has become a key paradigm for remote sensing vision-language understanding. However, existing remote sensing contrastive learning methods are mostly built on RGB-oriented CLIP architectures, making it difficult to exploit heterogeneous sensors such as SAR, multi-spectral imaging (MSI), and hyperspectral imaging (HSI). To address this limitation, we propose OmniRSCLIP, an end-to-end contrastive learning framework that supports multi-source sensor inputs for remote sensing vision-language modeling. The key idea is to extend CLIP beyond its fixed RGB input interface without breaking the pretrained visual knowledge. To this end, OmniRSCLIP introduces Spectral-Spatial Basis Decomposition (SSBD), which formulates arbitrary-channel adaptation as a basis recomposition problem: pretrained CLIP patch embeddings provide transferable spatial bases, while wavelength-conditioned coefficients span sensor-specific embedding kernels within a constrained visual prior space. This design avoids forcing heterogeneous sensors into a fixed-channel input space, while aligning them in a unified image-text semantic space. We further introduce a spectral-context-aware mask-based contrastive learning scheme to suppress modality-specific redundant features and enhance fine-grained image-text alignment. Finally, to support multi-modal training, we construct OmniRS5M, the first large-scale remote sensing image-text corpus covering RGB, SAR, MSI, and HSI. Experiments on retrieval, zero-shot classification, and semantic localization show that OmniRSCLIP preserves strong RGB-domain performance while effectively extending CLIP to heterogeneous remote sensing modalities.

</details>


### [26] [Neural-Collapse-guided Task-Free Continual Anomaly Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03406)
*Xiaotong Kong,Chaoyang Song,Ziai Zhou,Jinxia Zhang,Kanjian Zhang,Haikun Wei*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: NC-TFAD is a task-free continual learning framework for industrial anomaly detection that uses neural collapse theory and ETF (Equiangular Tight Frame) geometry to stabilize representation learning from non-stationary data streams without task boundaries. It generates synthetic anomalies as anchors, uses FNCC loss for contrastive learning, and combines normal-patch prototypes with self-attention for anomaly localization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world manufacturing environments have unpredictable data distribution shifts, making task-dependent continual learning assumptions impractical. Existing methods require clear task boundaries, which don't exist in practical industrial settings.

Method: 1) Freeze pretrained backbone and align streaming features to simplex ETF prototype space; 2) Generate synthetic anomaly samples as auxiliary anchors to satisfy NC-inspired geometric construction; 3) Apply inter- and intra-class regularization with Focal Neural Collapse Contrastive (FNCC) loss to suppress representation drift; 4) Use normal-patch-prototype-guided localization branch with weak self-attention prior to produce anomaly heatmaps without pixel-level annotations.

Result: NC-TFAD consistently outperforms representative task-free continual learning methods and unified anomaly detection baselines on MVTec AD and VisA datasets in both image-level detection and pixel-level localization under the task-free continual learning protocol.

Conclusion: Geometry-driven modeling via neural collapse and ETF prototypes offers an effective and robust solution for task-free continual anomaly detection in real-world industrial applications, outperforming both task-free continual learning methods and unified anomaly detection baselines.

Abstract: Recent years have witnessed growing interest in continual anomaly detection for industrial visual inspection. However, real-world manufacturing environments exhibit unpredictable shifts in data distributions, rendering task-dependent continual learning assumptions impractical. To address this limitation, we formulate industrial anomaly detection as a task-free continual learning problem and propose NC-TFAD, a neural-collapse-inspired, geometry-driven framework for learning from non-stationary data streams without task boundaries. NC-TFAD freezes a pretrained backbone and aligns streaming features to a simplex Equiangular Tight Frame (ETF) prototype space to stabilize representation geometry under non-stationary streams. To satisfy the NC-inspired geometric construction in the absence of real anomalies, we generate synthetic anomaly samples as auxiliary anchors during training. Building on this geometry, we further introduce inter- and intra-class regularization together with a Focal Neural Collapse Contrastive (FNCC) loss to suppress representation drift and improve normal-anomaly separability. Finally, a normal-patch-prototype-guided localization branch constructs calibrated patch-wise deviation maps from normal training samples and fuses them with a weak self-attention prior, producing anomaly heatmaps without pixel-level annotations. Extensive experiments on MVTec AD and VisA show that NC-TFAD consistently outperforms representative task-free continual learning methods adapted from general vision, as well as unified anomaly detection baselines, in both image-level detection and pixel-level localization under the task-free continual learning protocol. These results highlight that geometry-driven modeling offers an effective and robust solution for task-free continual anomaly detection in real-world industrial applications.

</details>


### [27] [When Do Frozen VLMs Respond to Image-Free Object-Token Edits? An Answer-Key-Free Protocol and What It Reveals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03429)
*Wonbin Son,Gyumun Choi,Junil Seo,Seungmin Rho,Mi Young Lee,Hyungjoon Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper proposes a novel approach to answering "what-if" queries about scenes by editing Vision-Language Model (VLM) representations at the token level, rather than modifying text or regenerating images. Instead of passing the original image to the VLM, they abstract images into object-level tokens, enabling representation-level edits. They introduce an answer-key-free protocol to evaluate when frozen VLMs respond to such token edits.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current approaches to what-if queries in VLMs require either injecting assumptions as text or repainting scenes with generative models. This paper aims to move the edit to the representation level before model input, which is a fundamentally different approach that could provide more direct manipulation of the VLM's understanding.

Method: The authors introduce an answer-key-free protocol that scores edits whose answers are logically determined without requiring post-edit answer annotations. The protocol audits itself by reversing each scoreable choice. They test this across two remote-sensing datasets (iSAID, VRSBench) and three frozen LM backbones.

Result: Three key structures were discovered: (1) The response is not free - explicit edit teaching (not ordinary VQA training) produces responses in dense scenes and multiplies them in sparse scenes; (2) Once activated, the response is governed by token cleanliness and density, with detector+segmenter tokens competitive with oracle and outperforming it on VRSBench; (3) The image-free token route preserves 92-96% of a matched patch-token baseline's free-text VQA, and answers measurably depend on the tokens.

Conclusion: The response, cleanliness, and reading structures are sign-preserved across remote-sensing datasets and different frozen LM backbones. This approach enables representation-level editing for what-if queries while maintaining most of the VQA capabilities, opening new possibilities for understanding and manipulating VLM representations.

Abstract: Answering what-if queries about a scene with a VLM usually means injecting the assumption as text or repainting the scene with a generative model. We instead move the edit to the representation level, before the model input. The image is abstracted into a set of object-level tokens, and the original image never enters the VLM. This design rests on an open question: when do frozen VLMs actually respond to such token edits? We introduce an answer-key-free protocol: no post-edit answer is annotated. It scores edits whose answers are logically determined, and audits itself by reversing each scoreable choice. The protocol reveals three structures. The response is not free: explicit edit teaching, not ordinary VQA training, produces it in dense scenes and multiplies it in sparse ones, on all three operations. Once on, it is governed by token cleanliness and density, with deployable detector+segmenter tokens competitive with the oracle and outperforming it on VRSBench. And reading is a separable axis: the image-free token route preserves 92-96% of a matched patch-token baseline's free-text VQA, and the answers measurably depend on the tokens. The response, cleanliness, and reading structures are sign-preserved across two remote-sensing datasets (iSAID, VRSBench) and three frozen LM backbones. We release the probe generator, records, judge logs, and code.

</details>


### [28] [OCR-EDR: Rendering-Aware Diagnosis and Repair for Closed-Loop OCR Improvement](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03445)
*Linnan Zhao,Kang Liu,Hao Yu,Jiabo Zhan,Chong Sun,Chen Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OCR-EDR is a rendering-aware framework for fine-grained OCR error diagnosis and iterative repair. It assesses consistency between OCR predictions, their renderings, and source images, while preserving valid predictions including rendering-equivalent ones. The framework includes OCRErrBench dataset and DocEDR model, achieving 94.78% diagnostic accuracy and significant improvements in formula recognition.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current OCR systems struggle with complex formulas, structured text, and long-tail formats, producing errors like omissions and hallucinations. Existing evaluation methods only provide aggregate metrics without supporting case-level error analysis or performance improvement. There is a need for a framework that can diagnose errors at fine-grained level and iteratively repair them while preserving rendering-equivalent valid predictions.

Method: OCR-EDR framework consists of two main stages: (1) Joint assessment - verifies whether OCR prediction and its rendered version are consistent with the source image, preserving valid predictions including rendering-equivalent ones while diagnosing and localizing genuine errors; (2) Iterative repair - applies executable edits and may request updated rendering for iterative reassessment. The approach uses OCRErrBench dataset (diverse real OCR predictions covering text/formulas, exact/rendering-equivalent positives, and genuine errors) and DocEDR model to execute the diagnosis-repair loop.

Result: DocEDR achieves 94.78% diagnostic accuracy on OCRErrBench. It repairs 86.23% of erroneous inputs to visual consistency. On DOCRcaseBench, it raises formula Case-F1 by 30.99 percentage points over DOCR-Inspector-7B. On UniMER-Test's identified Bad subsets of four OCR systems, it improves formula CDM by up to 4.62 percentage points.

Conclusion: OCR-EDR successfully transforms fine-grained OCR analysis into verified corrections and measurable performance gains. The rendering-aware approach effectively handles both exact matches and rendering-equivalent predictions while providing iterative error repair capabilities.

Abstract: Although document OCR systems perform increasingly well on routine documents, complex formulas, structured text, and long-tail formats remain error-prone. OCR predictions may omit fine-grained content or hallucinate unsupported outputs, while equivalent encodings of the same visible content must be accommodated. Existing OCR evaluation methods mostly report aggregate metrics, offering limited support for analyzing case-level errors and improving OCR performance. We propose OCR-EDR (OCR Error Diagnosis and Repair), a rendering-aware framework that advances from fine-grained diagnosis to iterative repair. Given a source image, an editable OCR prediction, and its rendered image, OCR-EDR first jointly assesses whether the prediction and its rendering are consistent with the source, preserving valid predictions, including rendering-equivalent ones, while diagnosing and localizing genuine errors. It then applies executable edits and may request an updated rendering for iterative reassessment. We construct OCRErrBench from diverse real OCR predictions, covering text and formulas, exact and rendering-equivalent positives, and genuine errors, and develop the DocEDR model to execute the diagnosis--repair loop. On OCRErrBench, DocEDR achieves 94.78% diagnostic accuracy. It repairs 86.23% of erroneous inputs to visual consistency, raises formula Case-F1 by 30.99 percentage points over DOCR-Inspector-7B on DOCRcaseBench, and improves formula CDM by up to 4.62 percentage points on the identified Bad subsets of four OCR systems on UniMER-Test. These results show that OCR-EDR turns fine-grained OCR analysis into verified corrections and performance gains.

</details>


### [29] [Preserving Knowledge across Space and Time for Continual Video Deepfake Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03446)
*Taehoon Kim,Jongwook Choi,Heejae Jo,Byungmin Park,Jongwon Choi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MSFD is a continual learning framework for deepfake video detection that decomposes video features into spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal modalities in the frequency domain, preserving each modality independently during sequential model updates to adapt to new forgery patterns while maintaining performance on previous tasks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing deepfake detection approaches are designed for images and fail to capture video-specific cues. Deepfake videos contain distinct evidence along both spatial and temporal axes, requiring separate preservation of each modality during sequential model updates to handle new forgery patterns while preventing catastrophic forgetting.

Method: The framework decomposes video features into spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal modalities in the frequency domain. It uses cross-modality decorrelation loss to encourage spatiotemporal representations to remain orthogonal to single-modality cues, enabling independent preservation of each modality as different deepfake types exhibit varying reliance on spatial and temporal cues across tasks.

Result: MSFD achieves stronger adaptation and preserves performance more effectively than state-of-the-art methods across diverse continual deepfake video scenarios.

Conclusion: The modality-specific approach in the frequency domain effectively addresses the challenge of continual deepfake video detection, successfully balancing adaptation to new forgery patterns with preservation of performance on previous tasks.

Abstract: The continuous emergence of high-quality video deepfakes requires detectors that continually adapt to new forgery patterns, yet existing approaches, which are designed for deepfake images, fail to capture video-specific cues. Unlike deepfake images that contain only spatial artifacts, deepfake videos leave distinct evidence along both spatial and temporal axes, necessitating the separate preservation of each modality during sequential model updates. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a continual deepfake video detection framework, Modality-Specific Frequency Distillation (MSFD), that explicitly decomposes video features into spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal modalities in the frequency domain. This decomposition enables independent preservation of each modality, as different deepfake video types exhibit varying reliance on spatial and temporal cues across tasks. Furthermore, MSFD adopts a cross-modality decorrelation loss that encourages spatiotemporal representations to remain orthogonal to single-modality cues. Extensive experiments show that our framework achieves stronger adaptation and preserves performance more effectively than state-of-the-art methods across diverse continual deepfake video scenarios.

</details>


### [30] [STARS-GS: Structure-Aware Regularized Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale Aerial Surface Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03447)
*Bocheng Li,Wenjuan Zhang,Jie Pan. Dongxu Han,Xuesong Ma,Yiling Yao,Yaning Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: STARS-GS is a structure-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting framework designed for large-scale 3D surface reconstruction from aerial imagery. It addresses three key challenges in existing methods: (1) scene partitioning that splits continuous elements, (2) geometric constraints overlooking local organization, and (3) uniform regularization unsuitable for heterogeneous structures. The method introduces structure-aware scene partitioning with boundary refinement, neighborhood-aware Gaussian organization extending constraints to local geometry, and adaptive surface regularization that adjusts strength based on local characteristics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large-scale 3D surface reconstruction from aerial imagery is fundamental for geospatial mapping and urban modeling. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has shown promise, existing methods struggle with three major issues: scene partitioning breaks continuous elements across sub-regions, geometric constraints focus only on individual Gaussians ignoring local organization, and uniform regularization fails to handle heterogeneous geometric structures. These limitations lead to cross-region inconsistencies, stitching artifacts, and poor geometric accuracy in complex scenes.

Method: STARS-GS proposes three key innovations: (1) Structure-aware scene partitioning that preserves continuous scene structures during partitioning and reduces cross-region geometric inconsistencies through boundary refinement; (2) Neighborhood-aware Gaussian organization that extends geometric constraints from individual primitives to their neighborhood organization, encouraging Gaussians to conform to local surface geometry; (3) Adaptive surface regularization that adjusts regularization strength according to local geometric characteristics, promoting consistency in structured regions while preserving variations in unstructured regions.

Result: Extensive experiments on large-scale aerial photogrammetry benchmarks show STARS-GS consistently outperforms other Gaussian-based methods. The average F1-score increased from 0.640 (second-best method) to 0.698, representing a relative improvement of approximately 9.1%. This demonstrates effective improvements in both geometric accuracy and surface completeness.

Conclusion: STARS-GS successfully addresses the three major challenges in large-scale 3DGS surface reconstruction through its structure-aware approach. The combination of structure-aware partitioning, neighborhood-aware organization, and adaptive regularization leads to significant improvements in reconstruction quality, reducing artifacts and better handling heterogeneous geometric structures. The 9.1% relative improvement in F1-score demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed framework for aerial photogrammetry applications.

Abstract: Large-scale 3D surface reconstruction from aerial imagery is fundamental to geospatial mapping and urban modeling. Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have demonstrated considerable potential for this task. However, existing methods still face three major challenges in large and complex scenes: scene partitioning may split continuous scene elements across independently optimized sub-regions; geometric constraints mainly focus on the attributes of individual Gaussians while overlooking their local organization; and uniform regularization struggles to accommodate heterogeneous geometric structures. To address these issues, we propose STARS-GS, a structure-aware 3DGS framework for large-scale surface reconstruction. First, we introduce a structure-aware scene partitioning strategy that better preserves continuous scene structures during partitioning and reduces cross-region geometric inconsistencies and stitching artifacts through boundary refinement. Second, we develop neighborhood-aware Gaussian organization that extends geometric constraints from individual primitives to their neighborhood organization, encouraging Gaussians to better conform to local surface geometry. Third, we introduce adaptive surface regularization that adjusts the regularization strength according to local geometric characteristics, promoting geometric consistency in structured regions while preserving plausible variations in unstructured regions. Extensive experiments on large-scale aerial photogrammetry benchmarks demonstrate that STARS-GS consistently outperforms the evaluated Gaussian-based methods in surface reconstruction. It increases the average F1-score from 0.640 for the second-best method to 0.698, corresponding to a relative improvement of approximately 9.1\%, demonstrating effective improvements in geometric accuracy and surface completeness.

</details>


### [31] [Preprocessing Failure and Adversarial Detection in Depthwise-Separable Edge Vision Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03453)
*Jannatul Masruk Mukta,Rifa Sanjida,Adrita Rahman Tory,Md. Saifur Rahman,Khondokar Fida Hasan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper evaluates six preprocessing-based defenses against adversarial attacks on edge vision systems, comparing traditional residual/inception architectures with depthwise-separable CNNs (common in edge devices). The study finds that depthwise-separable architectures show consistently poor recovery compared to residual architectures, while also revealing a detection opportunity based on the asymmetry between clean and adversarial predictions under preprocessing. Standard image quality metrics are found to be unreliable proxies for defense effectiveness.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Preprocessing-based defenses are widely recommended as model-agnostic mitigations for adversarial attacks on edge vision systems, requiring no retraining or architectural changes. However, these defenses were only evaluated on residual or Inception-class architectures, not on the depthwise-separable CNNs that dominate edge deployments. This represents a significant gap in the security evaluation literature.

Method: The authors evaluated six preprocessing defenses against adversarial perturbations across both architecture families (residual and depthwise-separable). They conducted ablation studies to determine whether the failure mechanism is architectural rather than parametric. They also assessed the reliability of standard image quality metrics as proxies for defense effectiveness.

Result: Across all perturbation levels and defenses tested, depthwise-separable architectures showed consistently poor recovery while residual architectures showed partial recovery. The ablation results support an architectural rather than parametric explanation. Notably, preprocessing disrupts clean predictions while leaving adversarial predictions largely unchanged, creating a detection opportunity. Standard image quality metrics were found to be unreliable proxies for defense effectiveness.

Conclusion: The failure of preprocessing defenses on depthwise-separable CNNs is not merely a negative result—it reveals a detection opportunity for adversarial attacks. The paper provides a practitioner decision framework for adversarially resilient edge vision deployment. Limitations include evaluation on only three architectures and one attack family.

Abstract: Preprocessing-based defenses are the standard first-line response to adversarial attacks on edge vision systems, requiring no retraining, no architectural changes, and widely recommended as model-agnostic mitigations. Yet the foundational evaluations of these defenses were conducted on residual or Inception-class architectures, not on the depthwise-separable CNNs that dominate edge deployments. This untested assumption leaves a gap in the security evaluation literature. This paper closes that gap by evaluating six preprocessing defenses against adversarial perturbations across both architecture families. Across all perturbation levels and defenses tested, the two depthwise-separable architectures show consistently poor recovery while the residual architecture shows partial recovery; ablation results are consistent with an architectural rather than parametric explanation, though only three architectures and one attack family are evaluated. Crucially, this failure is not merely a negative result. The same output divergence that disqualifies preprocessing as a recovery mechanism reveals a detection opportunity: preprocessing consistently disrupts clean predictions while leaving adversarial predictions largely unchanged, an asymmetry that is directly measurable without retraining or architectural modification. We further show that standard image quality metrics are unreliable proxies for defense effectiveness, a methodological gap in current evaluation practice. A practitioner decision framework is provided for adversarially resilient edge vision deployment.

</details>


### [32] [BMCTrack-d: Pig re-identification and tracking via back marks in challenging camera settings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03463)
*David Brunner,Maciej Oczak,Marie Bordes,Jean-Loup Rault,Stephan M. Winkler,Viktoria Dorfer*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BMCTrack-d is a novel tracking-by-detection approach for individual-level pig monitoring using unique back marks for re-identification in challenging side-view camera settings, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Individual-level pig monitoring is essential for assessing health, behaviour, and welfare, but remains challenging due to pigs having uniform appearances within breeds. Existing solutions primarily use top-down view cameras which are not always practical. This work addresses the need for robust individual tracking in side-view settings with challenges like rapid movement, severe occlusions, and low resolution.

Method: The method uses a tracking-by-detection framework with: (1) a neural network-based back mark classifier for identity prediction, (2) a temporal prediction consistency check that validates identity assignments against recent prediction history, and (3) a deduplication stage to resolve conflicting identity assignments. The approach prioritizes accurate appearance-based re-identification over continuous tracking.

Result: On a demanding test set, BMCTrack-d outperforms BoT-SORT-ReID by 9.11% and TrackTrack-ReID by 1.03% in higher-order tracking accuracy.

Conclusion: Back mark-based re-identification combined with dedicated post-processing stages (temporal consistency check and deduplication) enables robust individual-level pig monitoring in challenging side-view camera settings with occlusions and low resolution.

Abstract: Automated pig monitoring is essential for assessing their health, behaviour, and welfare. To date, most pig monitoring solutions operate on the group-level, because individual-level monitoring requires reliable long-term identification and tracking of each animal. For domesticated pigs this remains challenging because pigs of the same breed often have highly uniform appearances. Moreover, research on pig monitoring is almost exclusively reported in top-down view camera settings, which considerably ease tracking, but are not always an option in practice. In this work, BMCTrack-d is presented, a novel tracking-by-detection approach that leverages unique back marks to enable robust pig re-identification and tracking in a challenging side-view camera setting, afflicted by rapidly moving pigs, severe occlusions and low resolution. The method first predicts the detected pigs' identities using a neural network-based back mark classifier. To improve re-identification reliability over time, two dedicated post-processing stages are introduced: a temporal prediction consistency check, which validates the identity assignments against the recent prediction history, and deduplication, which resolves conflicting identity assignments in each time step. By explicitly prioritising accurate, appearance-based re-identification over continuous tracking, the proposed approach addresses a key limitation of existing trackers for individual-level monitoring scenarios. On a demanding test set BMCTrack-d outperforms two strong baselines, BoT-SORT-ReID and TrackTrack-ReID, by 9.11% and 1.03%, respectively, in higher-order tracking accuracy. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of back mark-based re-identification and tracking for robust individual-level pig monitoring in challenging settings.

</details>


### [33] [SafeRestore: Detector-Relative Risk Certificates for Selective Industrial Image Restoration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03475)
*Shaoliang Yang,Jun Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical problem in industrial inspection pipelines: image restoration can inadvertently suppress defects or create false activations. The authors propose SafeRestore, a selective action framework that decides when to automatically return a transformed image versus requiring human review. The method uses action-specific fitted scores and exact binomial bounds for certification, evaluated on the Carinthia-S dataset.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In industrial inspection, images are typically restored before defect detection. However, restoration can either suppress actual defect structures (evidence loss) or create false activations in clean regions (excess activation). The authors recognize that restoration is not always beneficial and that a framework is needed to decide when to use restored vs. original images or human review.

Method: SafeRestore formulates restoration as a selective action problem over: (1) the measured display, (2) five restored candidates, and (3) review. The framework ranks candidates using action-specific fitted scores, selects a gate using threshold-tuning data, and evaluates on a disjoint certification sample using two one-sided exact binomial bounds—one for positive-conditional evidence-loss incident rate and one for all-accepted excess-activation incident rate. This provides marginal guarantees for one policy fixed before certification outcomes, under an image-level i.i.d. working model.

Result: On 4,591 Carinthia-S images, the primary all-action policy passed in only 1 of 5 training repetitions (12.0% ± 26.9% pass-gated test coverage). Fixed bicubic and reduced-complexity variants passed more often. On reserved morphologies, evidence-loss incidence rose to 81.1-90.3%. The KolektorSDD dataset lacked both detector competence and sufficient positive certification images.

Conclusion: The contribution is an auditable, detector-relative framework for deciding when to automatically return transformed images versus requiring human review. Importantly, the authors explicitly state this is NOT a claim that adaptive routing outperforms simpler policies—the evidence does not support such a claim. The framework provides verifiable risk-coverage guarantees rather than improved performance.

Abstract: Industrial inspection pipelines often restore a measured image before a detector acts on it, yet restoration can suppress detector-supported defect structure or create clean-region activations. We formulate restoration as a selective action problem over the measured display, five restored candidates, and review. SafeRestore ranks candidates with action-specific fitted scores, chooses a gate on threshold-tuning data, and evaluates the fixed gate on a disjoint certification sample with two one-sided exact binomial bounds: one for the positive-conditional evidence-loss incident rate and one for the all-accepted excess-activation incident rate. The guarantee is marginal for one policy fixed before its certification outcomes are observed, under an image-level i.i.d. working model. In a retrospective split-sample study of 4,591 public Carinthia-S images, the protocol yields auditable risk-coverage behavior. The primary all-action policy passes in one of five training repetitions (12.0% +/- 26.9% pass-gated test coverage when failures count as zero), whereas fixed bicubic and reduced-complexity variants pass more often. On reserved morphologies, evidence-loss incidence rises to 81.1-90.3%, and KolektorSDD lacks both detector competence and enough positive certification images for the stated target. The contribution is therefore an auditable, detector-relative framework for deciding when a transformed image may be returned automatically and when review remains necessary -- not a claim that adaptive routing outperforms simpler policies on the present evidence.

</details>


### [34] [Tree species mapping in Denmark: A comparison of spectral-temporal features with geospatial foundation model embeddings](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03480)
*Alkiviadis Koukos,Spyros Kondylatos,Thomas Nord-Larsen,Lotte Nyborg,Christian Tøttrup,Kenneth Grogan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This study maps tree species across Denmark at 10m resolution using National Forest Inventory plots and Earth Observation (EO) data, comparing manually engineered spectral-temporal features (STF) with embeddings from foundation models (TESSERA and AlphaEarth). The STF-based MLP achieved the best performance (macro F1: 0.843 for pure stands, 0.653 for mixed stands), while TESSERA embeddings showed advantages when training data is limited. The resulting map, with 79.9% accuracy, is the first high-resolution national tree species map of Denmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The need for large-scale forest characterization and tree species mapping, which is crucial for forest monitoring, ecological research, and land management, particularly at a national scale where traditional field-based methods are insufficient.

Method: The study used multi-temporal Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 observations combined with canopy height information. Two input representations were compared: (1) manually engineered spectral-temporal features (STF), and (2) embeddings from foundation models TESSERA and AlphaEarth. Three classifiers (Random Forest, XGBoost, MLP) were evaluated on pure and mixed forest stands. Ablation experiments were conducted to assess the contribution of different data sources.

Result: The STF-based MLP achieved the highest classification performance with macro F1 scores of 0.843 for pure stands and 0.653 for mixed stands. TESSERA embeddings delivered competitive performance for pure stands (within 1.1 percentage points of the best model) and demonstrated substantial advantages when fewer than 25% of training plots were available. Multi-year observations improved accuracy over single-year inputs. The best model was applied nationally to produce a 10m tree species map with 79.9% area-adjusted validation accuracy.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates the effectiveness of combining multi-temporal EO data with machine learning for large-scale tree species classification. Foundation models like TESSERA show promise, especially under limited training data conditions. The resulting 10m tree species map of Denmark is the first high-resolution national product of its kind, providing a valuable open-access resource for forest monitoring and management.

Abstract: We map tree species across Denmark using National Forest Inventory plots and EO data, while evaluating the potential of foundation models for large-scale forest characterization. We compare two alternative input representations for tree species classification: (i) manually engineered spectral-temporal features (STF) derived from multi-temporal Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 observations, and (ii) embeddings generated by the EO FMs TESSERA and AlphaEarth. Both representations are complemented with canopy height information. Random forest, XGBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) classifiers are evaluated for all input representations, with separate assessments for pure and mixed forest stands. The STF-based MLP achieves the highest classification performance, yielding macro F1 scores of 0.843 and 0.653 for pure and mixed stands, respectively. The MLP trained on TESSERA embeddings delivers competitive performance for pure stands, achieving results within 1.1 percentage points of the best-performing model. TESSERA consistently outperforms STF-based models when fewer than approximately 25% of training plots are available, demonstrating a substantial advantage under limited training data. Multi-year observations systematically improve classification accuracy relative to single-year inputs, while ablation experiments reveal the complementary contributions of Sentinel-1 backscatter, spectral indices, and canopy height data. The best-performing model is subsequently applied at the national scale to generate a 10 m tree species map of Denmark. Area-adjusted validation indicates an overall map accuracy of 79.9%. The resulting map, released as an open-access product, is the first high-resolution national tree species map of Denmark and provides a valuable resource for forest monitoring, ecological research, and land management applications.

</details>


### [35] [Residual Optimal Transport-Based Experts Collaboration Towards Modality-Aware Infrared-Visible Object Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03516)
*Yue Zhao,Hua Yu,Yukun Zhao,Yuzhi Zhang,Maoguo Gong,Xin Mei,Zhuping Hu,Yanchi Li,A. K. Qin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FlexibleFusion is a unified method for infrared-visible object detection that adapts to both complete and missing-modality scenarios. It uses a Modality-Aware Experts Collaboration (MAEC) mechanism for adaptive pathway allocation and a Residual Self-Paced Entropic Optimal Transport (RSPEOT) for aligning heterogeneous feature distributions across modalities.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current IVOD methods assume both visible and infrared modalities are always present, but in practice sensors may fail or drop frames. Additionally, reliably estimating semantic correlation across heterogeneous modalities with spectral distribution discrepancy remains challenging. Fixed fusion approaches collapse when one modality is missing.

Method: 1) MAEC mechanism: Selectively activates and aggregates cross-modal or intra-modal expert pathways, enabling cross-modal fusion when full modalities are available and fallback to self-fusion under missing conditions. 2) RSPEOT: Introduces residual-driven self-paced update for entropic optimal transport, prioritizing reliable matches and progressively refining harder ones, rather than using fixed sparsity coefficient.

Result: Comprehensive experiments under complete and missing-modality protocols show consistent performance across arbitrary modality configurations.

Conclusion: FlexibleFusion provides a unified and adaptive solution that seamlessly operates across complete and missing-modality regimes, addressing the limitations of existing fixed fusion approaches for IVOD.

Abstract: Infrared-visible object detection (IVOD) integrates complementary evidence from visible and infrared sensors for reliable perception in challenging scenes. In practice, sensors may fail or drop frames, leaving one modality unavailable or intermittent. Existing methods for IVOD assume both modalities are always present, and fixed fusion collapses when one stream is missing. Furthermore, it remains a critical challenge to reliably estimate semantic correlation across heterogeneous modalities, especially under spectral distribution discrepancy. We present FlexibleFusion, a unified and adaptive method that flexibly allocates integration pathways and fusion strength, operating seamlessly across complete and missing-modality regimes. At its core, the Modality-Aware Experts Collaboration (MAEC) mechanism selectively activates and aggregates cross-modal or intra-modal expert pathways. It allows cross-modal fusion when full modalities are available and falls back to self-fusion under missing conditions. Additionally, we design Residual Self-Paced Entropic Optimal Transport (RSPEOT) to align heterogeneous feature distributions from a transport perspective. Instead of relying on the fixed sparsity coefficient in standard entropic optimal transport (EOT), RSPEOT introduces a residual-driven self-paced update that prioritizes reliable matches and progressively refines harder ones. This design alleviates the additional optimization burden of standard EOT while preserving reliable semantic alignment. Comprehensive experiments under complete and missing-modality protocols show consistent performance across arbitrary modality configurations. Code will be released upon publication.

</details>


### [36] [Neural Video Compression Based on Deformable Temporal Alignment and Difference-aware Fusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03520)
*Chuyue Shan,Songlin Sun,Wang Chenwei,Shen Zihan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a neural video compression method that improves temporal context quality by combining deformable temporal alignment and difference-aware spatial selective fusion, addressing limitations in complex motion, occlusion, and high-frequency texture regions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing conditional coding-based neural video compression methods rely on propagated reference features for temporal context, but these are vulnerable to motion estimation and local alignment errors in regions with complex motion, occlusion, and high-frequency textures, leading to inaccurate temporal information.

Method: The proposed method consists of two key components: (1) A Context-aware Temporal Alignment Module that generates complementary temporal context, and (2) A Difference-aware Spatial Selective Fusion module that adaptively selects reliable temporal information and suppresses misalignment.

Result: The proposed method achieves certain rate-distortion performance improvement over DCVC-DC.

Conclusion: The combination of deformable temporal alignment and difference-aware spatial selective fusion effectively addresses the limitations of existing methods in handling complex motion regions, providing improved compression performance.

Abstract: In conditional coding-based neural video compression, the quality of temporal context directly affects compression per- formance. Existing methods mostly construct context from prop- agated reference features, but they are vulnerable to motion esti- mation and local alignment errors in regions with complex mo- tion, occlusion, and high-frequency textures, resulting in inaccu- rate temporal information. To address this issue, this paper pro- poses a method combining deformable temporal alignment and difference-aware spatial selective fusion. A Context-aware Tem- poral Alignment Module is used to generate complementary tem- poral context, while a Difference-aware Spatial Selective Fusion module adaptively selects reliable temporal information and sup- presses misalignment. Experiments show that the proposed method achieves certain rate-distortion performance improve- ment over DCVC-DC.

</details>


### [37] [SafeRI: Recognition and Intervention for Token-Level Safety Intervention in Large Vision Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03544)
*Caoyuan Ma,Tian Gu,Wenpu Liu,Weichu Xie,Shuai Dong,Yuqi Xu,Ji Zhao,Ziyue Wang,Wenzheng Chang,Taiqiang Wu,Yongfu Zhu,Wenqi Shao,Zheng Wang,Yinqiang Zheng*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a streaming recognition and gated LoRA framework for vision-language model (VLM) safety that enables on-demand intervention rather than permanent modification to model behavior. A lightweight recognizer monitors generation state and activates LoRA only when needed to redirect unsafe outputs to safe responses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current safety alignment methods apply interventions globally (always-on), which unnecessarily perturbs the model's original reasoning path and degrades general multimodal capabilities. The authors argue safety alignment should be an on-demand intervention, not a permanent modification to every decoding trajectory.

Method: The framework consists of: (1) A lightweight recognizer that estimates safety of current pre-token generation state during autoregressive generation; (2) A LoRA gate whose output updates based on recognizer output for the following decoding step; (3) When safe, generation follows the frozen-backbone policy; (4) The LoRA module is trained from unsafe prefixes, transition statements, and safe continuations to learn redirecting unsafe generations to safe responses.

Result: Experiments across multiple safety and general-purpose benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of the method in post-alignment settings.

Conclusion: The proposed streaming recognition and gated LoRA framework provides an effective on-demand safety intervention mechanism for VLMs, preserving general capabilities while selectively activating safety modifications only when needed.

Abstract: Existing safety alignment methods for vision-language models usually modify the model behavior globally: once the safety parameters are trained or loaded, they participate in both unsafe and already-safe generations. This always-on intervention can unnecessarily perturb the model's original reasoning path and degrade general multimodal capabilities. We argue that safety alignment should be an on-demand intervention rather than a permanent modification to every decoding trajectory. To this end, we propose a streaming recognition and gated LoRA framework for intrinsic VLM safety. During autoregressive generation, a lightweight recognizer estimates whether the current pre-token generation state is safe or unsafe. Its output updates the LoRA gate for the following decoding step; otherwise, generation follows the frozen-backbone policy. The LoRA module is trained from unsafe prefixes, transition statements, and safe continuations, so that it learns to redirect unsafe generations back to safe responses after activation. Experiments across multiple safety and general-purpose benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in post-alignment settings.

</details>


### [38] [WIDE: Wildcard Inference with Dynamic Expansion for Cross-Modal Generative Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03554)
*Teng Guo,Xin Wang,Jiayou Xu,Keying Zhou,Jifeng Shen,Haoxin Ruan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WIDE addresses forced hallucination in cross-modal generative retrieval by dynamically emitting wildcards when the model detects semantic blind spots due to information asymmetry between modalities (e.g., text queries vs visual candidates).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Cross-modal generative retrieval suffers from information asymmetry - text queries are concise while visual candidates are dense. This causes the autoregressive decoder to hallucinate fine-grained details absent from queries during identifier generation, allowing irrelevant candidates to rank highly.

Method: WIDE comprises three components: (1) Adaptive Entropy Thresholding (AET) calibrates layer-specific uncertainty boundaries offline; (2) Asymmetry-aware Wildcard Decoding (AWD) detects semantic blind spots during decoding and emits wildcards instead of forced deterministic identifiers, dynamically expanding search space without log-probability penalties; (3) Blind-Spot Re-ranking (BSR) evaluates expanded candidates using hybrid scoring combining discrete generation confidence with continuous semantic similarity.

Result: WIDE outperforms state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods on the M-BEIR benchmark, effectively suppressing forced hallucination while maintaining compact index structures.

Conclusion: The proposed WIDE framework successfully addresses the information asymmetry problem in cross-modal generative retrieval through dynamic wildcard expansion and hybrid re-ranking, offering a practical solution that balances generation accuracy with semantic understanding.

Abstract: Generative retrieval has demonstrated significant success by unifying representation learning and search into a single sequence-to-sequence generation task. However, extending this paradigm to cross-modal retrieval reveals a critical challenge arising from the inherent information asymmetry across different modalities, such as the gap between concise text queries and dense visual candidates. This structural mismatch causes the autoregressive decoder to suffer from forced hallucination when generating identifiers via standard trie-constrained beam search, where the model is severely penalized for failing to guess fine-grained details absent from the query, allowing irrelevant candidates to hijack top rankings. To address this issue, we propose Wildcard Inference with Dynamic Expansion (WIDE). WIDE employs Adaptive Entropy Thresholding (AET) to calibrate layer-specific uncertainty boundaries offline. During the decoding generation phase, Asymmetry-aware Wildcard Decoding (AWD) detects semantic blind spots and emits wildcards instead of forced deterministic identifiers, dynamically expanding the search space without incurring log-probability penalties. Finally, Blind-Spot Re-ranking (BSR) evaluates the expanded candidate pool using a hybrid scoring mechanism that combines discrete generation confidence with continuous semantic similarity. Extensive experiments on the M-BEIR benchmark demonstrate that WIDE outperforms state-of-the-art generative retrieval methods, effectively suppressing forced hallucination while maintaining compact index structures.

</details>


### [39] [FlashRender: Few-Step Generative Rendering via Camera-Controlled Video MeanFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03563)
*Byeongjun Park,Byung-Hoon Kim,Hyungjin Chung*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FlashRender is a few-step generative rendering framework that retakes a source video along a target camera trajectory in seconds. It addresses discretization error in multi-step generative rendering models through three complementary techniques: RETA for sampling-step-consistent camera control, MeanFlow for lower-curvature denoising trajectory, and on-policy flow map distillation for error correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper identifies sampling-step-dependent camera control as a prominent manifestation of discretization error in existing multi-step generative rendering models. Resolving this inconsistency substantially lowers denoising trajectory curvature, facilitating subsequent step distillation.

Method: The approach introduces three key techniques: (1) Representation Transformation and Alignment (RETA) - aligns hidden source-video representations with target-video features from a frozen visual geometry model to encode geometric transformation within the source-video stream; (2) MeanFlow objective - fine-tunes the model on the lower-curvature denoising trajectory induced by RETA to address discretization error; (3) On-policy flow map distillation - corrects self-rollout errors under fixed few-step sampling.

Result: The approach matches multi-step baselines in video quality and geometric consistency at 25x lower sampling cost while achieving superior camera controllability, even under out-of-distribution target camera trajectories.

Conclusion: RETA, MeanFlow, and on-policy flow map distillation play complementary roles in few-step generative rendering. Together, they enable efficient high-quality video generation with strong geometric consistency and camera control capabilities.

Abstract: We present FlashRender, a few-step generative rendering framework that retakes a source video along a target camera trajectory in seconds. We identify sampling-step-dependent camera control as a prominent manifestation of discretization error in existing multi-step generative rendering models and show that resolving this inconsistency substantially lowers denoising trajectory curvature, facilitating subsequent step distillation. To this end, we introduce Representation Transformation and Alignment (RETA), which aligns hidden source-video representations with target-video features from a frozen visual geometry model. This directly encodes the geometric transformation within the source-video stream, enabling sampling-step-consistent camera control. We then fine-tune the model with the MeanFlow objective on the lower-curvature denoising trajectory induced by RETA, allowing the model to more effectively address discretization error. Finally, we apply on-policy flow map distillation to correct self-rollout errors under fixed few-step sampling. Extensive experiments show that RETA, MeanFlow, and on-policy flow map distillation play complementary roles in few-step generative rendering. Together, they enable our approach to match multi-step baselines in video quality and geometric consistency at 25x lower sampling cost while achieving superior camera controllability, even under out-of-distribution target camera trajectories.

</details>


### [40] [Occlusion-Robust Multimodal Emotion Recognition in VR via Fusion of Facial Images and EMG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03569)
*Birgit Nierula,Karam Tomotaki-Dawoud,Mert Akguel,Mustafa Tevfik Lafci,David Przewozny,Anna Hilsmann,Peter Eisert,Sebastian Bosse*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses emotion recognition in VR by combining lower-face video with upper-face EMG to overcome HMD occlusion limitations. The late-fusion approach achieves 51% macro-F1, outperforming single-modality baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Head-mounted displays in VR occlude the upper face, making conventional image-based facial expression analysis incomplete for real-time affective assessment applications.

Method: Created a synchronized multimodal dataset from 20 participants pairing lower-face video with seven-channel upper-face EMG. Used a late-fusion architecture merging CNN visual embeddings with RBF-kernel EMG representations under subject-independent test conditions.

Result: The proposed late-fusion method achieves 51% macro-F1, outperforming both image-only (41%) and EMG-only (43%) baselines when classifying seven emotional categories.

Conclusion: Upper-face EMG provides robust complementary information under HMD-induced visual occlusion, establishing a foundation for multimodal emotion recognition in naturalistic VR environments for applications like communication training and therapeutic interventions.

Abstract: Head-mounted displays (HMDs) fundamentally limit emotion recognition in virtual reality (VR): by occluding the upper face, they render conventional image-based facial expression analysis incomplete, particularly for applications requiring real-time affective assessment. We address this challenge by fusing lower-face video with facial electromyography (EMG) from the occluded upper face to classify seven emotional categories (six basic emotions plus neutral). We introduce a synchronized multimodal dataset from 20 participants, pairing lower-face video with seven-channel upper-face EMG elicited by validated emotion stimuli. Under subject-independent test, our proposed late-fusion architecture merging convolutional visual embeddings with RBF-kernel EMG representations achieves 51% macro-F1, outperforming both image-only (41%) and EMG-only (43%) baselines. These results demonstrate that upper-face EMG provides robust complementary information under HMD-induced visual occlusion and establish a foundation for multimodal emotion recognition in naturalistic VR environments. This approach facilitates affect-adaptive applications, including communication training and therapeutic interventions. The dataset will be shared upon request under an ethical-use agreement.

</details>


### [41] [Drive-HWM: Hierarchical World Models for Dynamic-Latent Guided Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03572)
*Zhaoxin Fan,Tianbao Zhang,Wenjun Wu,Xiaofeng Wang,Yeying Jin,Jian Zhao,Zheng Zhu,Shuicheng Yan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Drive-HWM is a hierarchical slow-fast world modeling framework for autonomous driving that organizes future representation prediction and action generation at complementary temporal scales. The slow model predicts multi-step future representations for long-horizon anticipation, while the fast model jointly predicts next frames and immediate actions for responsive decision-making. It introduces Dynamic-Aware Latents learned through optical-flow prediction to model motion dynamics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing world model approaches for autonomous driving either separate future prediction from action generation or jointly predict them at the same temporal scale, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve long-horizon anticipation and responsive, observation-grounded decision making.

Method: The proposed Drive-HWM uses a hierarchical slow-fast architecture: (1) Slow world model predicts multi-step future representations to capture extended scene evolution; (2) Dynamic-Aware Latents are learned through optical-flow prediction to model motion dynamics; (3) Fast model uses a lightweight multimodal backbone and autoregressive expert to jointly predict next frame and immediate action from latest observation, with next-frame prediction encouraging capture of imminent scene evolution and one-step action generation allowing continuous updates as new observations arrive.

Result: Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 demonstrate strong driving performance of Drive-HWM. Comprehensive ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the hierarchical slow-fast design, dynamics-aware future representations, and joint next-frame and action prediction.

Conclusion: The hierarchical slow-fast world modeling approach successfully enables both long-horizon anticipation and responsive, observation-grounded decision making for autonomous driving. The integration of Dynamic-Aware Latents and joint next-frame/action prediction are key contributors to performance.

Abstract: World models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by predicting how traffic scenes may evolve and using such predictions to support action generation. However, existing approaches either separate future prediction from action generation or jointly predict them at the same temporal scale, making it difficult to simultaneously achieve long-horizon anticipation and responsive, observation-grounded decision making. We present Drive-HWM, a hierarchical slow--fast world modeling framework that organizes future representation prediction and action generation at complementary temporal scales. The slow world model predicts multi-step future representations to capture extended scene evolution. To explicitly model the abundant motion dynamics in driving environments, we introduce Dynamic-Aware Latents learned through optical-flow prediction. Guided by these future representations, the fast model uses a lightweight multimodal backbone and an autoregressive expert to jointly predict the next frame and the immediate action from the latest observation. Next-frame prediction encourages the fast model to capture imminent scene evolution, while one-step action generation allows decisions to be continuously updated as new observations arrive. Extensive experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 demonstrate the strong driving performance of Drive-HWM. Comprehensive ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the hierarchical slow--fast design, dynamics-aware future representations, and joint next-frame and action prediction.

</details>


### [42] [Text2Thermal: Physics-Aware Thermal Image Synthesis from Textual Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03585)
*Tayeba Qazi,Brejesh Lall,Prerana Mukherjee*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Text2Thermal proposes using text prompts to explicitly specify unobservable radiometric factors (material, weather, time-of-day, heat-emission state) for thermal image synthesis, adapting Stable Diffusion to the thermal domain without requiring registered RGB images at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Thermal infrared imaging offers reliable perception in darkness and adverse weather, but thermal datasets remain scarce. Existing RGB-to-thermal translation is fundamentally ill-posed because thermal appearance depends on surface emissivity and object temperature—factors not observable in the visible spectrum—causing a single RGB image to be consistent with many valid thermal outputs.

Method: The paper proposes Text2Thermal, a physics-aware thermal image synthesis framework that uses textual priors to resolve ambiguity. Instead of inferring unobservable radiometric factors from RGB, the method explicitly supplies them through thermally grounded captions encoding material, weather, time-of-day, and heat-emission state. A pretrained Stable Diffusion backbone is adapted to the thermal domain. An optional control signal provides spatial guidance while preserving prompt-specified radiometry.

Result: Text2Thermal achieves state-of-the-art FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) among thermal image synthesis methods on M3FD, FLIR, and FMB datasets, while offering text-level control that translation-based approaches cannot provide.

Conclusion: Language provides a natural means of resolving the ill-posed nature of RGB-to-thermal translation by explicitly specifying radiometric factors. The approach demonstrates that thermal imagery can be synthesized from text prompts alone, with optional spatial control, achieving superior quality and controllable synthesis compared to existing methods.

Abstract: Thermal infrared imaging offers reliable perception in darkness and adverse weather, but thermal datasets remain scarce, motivating extensive work on translating abundant RGB images into thermal. Such translation is fundamentally ill-posed as thermal appearance is governed by surface emissivity and object temperature, neither of which is observable in the visible spectrum, so a single RGB image is consistent with many valid thermal outputs. We argue that language offers a natural means of resolving this ambiguity, and propose Text2Thermal, a framework for physics-aware thermal image synthesis from textual priors. Rather than inferring the unobservable radiometric factors from RGB, we supply them explicitly through thermally grounded captions encoding material, weather, time-of-day, and heat-emission state, and adapt a pretrained Stable Diffusion backbone to the thermal domain. Because the radiometric content is determined entirely by the prompt, Text2Thermal synthesizes thermal imagery without requiring a registered RGB image at inference; where spatial guidance is desired, an optional control signal imparts scene geometry without disturbing the prompt-specified radiometry. Experiments on M3FD, FLIR, and FMB show that Text2Thermal achieves state-of-the-art FID among thermal image synthesis methods while offering text-level control that translation-based approaches cannot provide.

</details>


### [43] [SV-WAM: An Efficient Surround-View World-Action Model for End-to-End Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03602)
*Jinyang Wang,Shiwei Li,Junjian Wang,Zhiqiang Deng,Jianbin Gao,Yihang Zhao,Liu Liu,Yongjia Zhao,Jinlong Chen,Huirui Xu,Yifeng Pan,Kangwei Liu,Fan Ren,Ji Tao,Minghao Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SV-WAM is a surround-view world-action model for autonomous driving that uses all six cameras for full spatial coverage while maintaining efficient inference by discarding the video branch at deployment. It uses future-video prediction as training supervision (not at inference) and includes a drivable-area compliance regularizer for safety.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous driving world models used single front camera for efficiency, but this limits spatial coverage in safety-critical maneuvers like lane changes, merges, and turns. The goal was to preserve full six-camera observations while maintaining efficient inference.

Method: 1) Future-video prediction as dense training supervision for action learning within a shared generative model, rather than as inference-time output. 2) Action-centered causal mask prevents action tokens from attending to future-video tokens during joint action-video denoising. 3) Differentiable drivable-area compliance regularizer that penalizes vehicle-footprint corners approaching or crossing drivable boundaries.

Result: SV-WAM achieves state-of-the-art planning performance on NAVSIMv2 benchmark and competitive zero-shot transfer capability on nuScenes benchmark, with low inference latency.

Conclusion: The approach successfully balances full surround-view spatial coverage with efficient deployment by using video prediction only during training and discarding the video branch at inference time. The drivable-area regularizer improves planning safety and boundary awareness.

Abstract: World models (WMs) have demonstrated strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by learning predictive representations of future scene dynamics. However, generating future videos during inference introduces substantial computational overhead, leading many recent driving WMs to adopt a single front camera as input for efficient deployment. This design restricts spatial coverage in safety-critical maneuvers such as lane changes, merges, and turns. To address this limitation, we propose SV-WAM, a surround-view world-action model (WAM) that preserves full six-camera observations while maintaining efficient inference. SV-WAM leverages future-video prediction as dense training supervision for action learning within a shared generative model, rather than as an inference-time output. At the core of this design is an action-centered causal mask that prevents action tokens from attending to future-video tokens during joint action-video denoising. Consequently, the video branch can be discarded at deployment, enabling efficient action-only planning. Furthermore, we introduce a differentiable drivable-area compliance regularizer that penalizes vehicle-footprint corners approaching or crossing drivable boundaries, improving planning safety and boundary awareness. Extensive experiments on the closed-loop NAVSIMv2 benchmark and the open-loop nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that SV-WAM achieves state-of-the-art planning performance with low inference latency and competitive zero-shot transfer capability.

</details>


### [44] [Auditing Patient Privacy in Medical Generative Models: Scalable Memorization Detection with DeepSSIM++](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03615)
*Antonio Scardace,Francesco Guarnera,Sebastiano Battiato,Daniele Ravì*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DeepSSIM++ is a self-supervised similarity metric designed to detect memorization in medical generative models, addressing patient confidentiality concerns. It uses multi-scale feature aggregation and anatomy-preserving augmentations to learn an embedding space where cosine similarity approximates SSIM, enabling scalable memorization auditing without exact pixel-level registration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep generative models used for medical image synthesis can memorize and reproduce training samples, raising serious patient confidentiality concerns. Existing detection methods have limitations: pixel-based metrics are sensitive to generation artifacts, while generic embedding-based metrics lack anatomical sensitivity required for medical data.

Method: DeepSSIM++ leverages multi-scale feature aggregation and anatomy-preserving augmentations to learn an embedding space where cosine similarity approximates the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM). This approach eliminates the need for exact pixel-level registration while maintaining anatomical sensitivity.

Result: DeepSSIM++ achieves an average Macro F1 improvement of 33 percentage points under ideal alignment and 46 percentage points under realistic spatial and intensity perturbations compared to state-of-the-art baselines. It also accelerates large-scale similarity computation by several orders of magnitude compared with analytical SSIM.

Conclusion: DeepSSIM++ provides an open-source tool that combines anatomical sensitivity and computational efficiency for scalable memorization auditing in medical generative AI. Code and data are publicly available.

Abstract: While deep generative models offer new opportunities for medical image synthesis and data sharing, their ability to memorize and reproduce training samples raises serious concerns about patient confidentiality. Detecting such memorization at scale remains challenging: traditional pixel-based metrics are sensitive to generation artifacts, whereas generic embedding-based metrics often lack the anatomical sensitivity required for medical data. To address this challenge, we introduce DeepSSIM++, a self-supervised similarity metric for scalable memorization auditing in medical generative models. By leveraging multi-scale feature aggregation and anatomy-preserving augmentations, DeepSSIM++ learns an embedding space where cosine similarity approximates the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM), eliminating the need for exact pixel-level registration. Compared with state-of-the-art baselines, DeepSSIM++ achieves an average Macro F1 improvement of 33 percentage points under ideal alignment and 46 percentage points under realistic spatial and intensity perturbations. Furthermore, it accelerates large-scale similarity computation by several orders of magnitude compared with analytical SSIM. By combining anatomical sensitivity and computational efficiency, DeepSSIM++ provides an open-source tool for scalable memorization auditing in medical generative AI. Code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/brAIn-science/DeepSSIM.

</details>


### [45] [EraseSAE: Surgical Concept Erasure in Text-to-Video Diffusion Models via Sparse Autoencoders](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03629)
*Xinghao Wang,Dong Li,Wei Yu,Yingwei Pan,Tao Gong,Qi Chu,Nenghai Yu,Ting Yao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EraseSAE is a novel framework for surgical concept erasure in DiT-based text-to-video diffusion models. It uses sparse autoencoders to decompose activations into interpretable monosemantic features, then employs contrastive attribution to identify and erase target concepts with spatiotemporal precision while preserving generation quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current text-to-video diffusion models are trained on loosely curated data, raising safety and copyright concerns. Existing concept erasure methods operate at coarse granularity, misaligned with the fine-grained, distributed nature of concept representations, leading to incomplete removal or quality degradation. Surgical erasure requires intervention at the monosemantic feature level.

Method: The propose EraseSAE framework with a decompose-attribute-erase pipeline: (1) Partitioned Convolutional Sparse Autoencoder decomposes dense spatiotemporal activations into disentangled, interpretable sparse features while preserving spatiotemporal coherence; (2) Contrastive attribution mechanism contrasts activations from paired prompts to isolate concept-specific feature kernels; (3) Timestep-resolved spatiotemporal masks confine erasure to regions where target concept is active.

Result: Extensive experiments across diverse diffusion models and concept erasure tasks demonstrate that EraseSAE achieves precise and robust concept removal with minimal quality degradation, substantially outperforming state-of-the-art methods.

Conclusion: EraseSAE provides an effective solution for surgical concept erasure in T2V diffusion models by targeting monosemantic features, achieving precise removal while preserving generation quality. The code is available at https://github.com/HiDream-ai/EraseSAE.

Abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video (T2V) diffusion models have demonstrated remarkable generative capabilities, yet their reliance on loosely curated training data raises pressing safety and copyright concerns. Concept erasure offers a principled remedy by removing unwanted semantics from pretrained models while preserving remaining concepts. However, existing approaches typically operate at a coarse granularity misaligned with the fine-grained, distributed nature of concept representations, leading to incomplete removal or degraded generation quality. We argue that surgical erasure fundamentally requires intervention at the level of monosemantic features, where each unit encodes a single interpretable concept. To this end, we propose EraseSAE, a novel framework that leverages sparse autoencoders to achieve surgical concept erasure in DiT-based T2V diffusion models via a principled decompose-attribute-erase pipeline. We first introduce the Partitioned Convolutional Sparse Autoencoder, which decomposes dense spatiotemporal activations into disentangled, interpretable sparse features while preserving spatiotemporal coherence. A contrastive attribution mechanism then contrasts activations from paired prompts to isolate concept-specific feature kernels. At inference, timestep-resolved spatiotemporal masks derived from the identified kernels confine erasure to regions where the target concept is active, leaving unrelated content intact. Extensive experiments across diverse diffusion models and concept erasure tasks demonstrate that EraseSAE achieves precise and robust concept removal with minimal quality degradation, substantially outperforming state-of-the-art methods. The code is available at https://github.com/HiDream-ai/EraseSAE.

</details>


### [46] [Stabilizing Camera-Controlled Novel View Synthesis at Inference Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03639)
*Prajwal Singh,Arjun Badola,Seema Kumari,Hajime Nagahara,Shanmuganathan Raman*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses instability in training-free, camera-controlled novel view synthesis from single images using pre-trained video diffusion models. The key insight is that decomposing camera motion into small autoregressive steps is the main source of stability, limiting geometric distortion and error accumulation. Performance degrades when per-step motion exceeds 18-20°.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for camera-controlled novel view synthesis combine multiple inference-time components, making it unclear which design choices are most important. The method becomes unstable under large camera motion and long generation horizons, limiting practical applicability.

Method: The authors propose CamTrol++, which uses small autoregressive camera steps to limit per-step geometric distortion. They evaluate geometry-constrained spatial attention, low-frequency appearance anchoring, and an efficient registration-free warping pipeline as supporting refinements.

Result: CamTrol++ improves temporal and geometric consistency, downstream 3D reconstruction quality, and generation efficiency over training-free baselines. The method remains effective for 56-frame generation and under substantial controlled depth corruption. Performance is stable for small motions but degrades when per-step motion approaches 18-20°.

Conclusion: Careful control of camera motion at inference time can substantially improve the stability of camera-controlled novel view synthesis without retraining or modifying the diffusion backbone. The main stability factor is simple: small autoregressive steps rather than complex architectural additions.

Abstract: Training-free, camera-controlled novel view synthesis from a single image using pre-trained video diffusion models often becomes unstable under large camera motion and long generation horizons. Existing approaches commonly combine several inference-time components, making it unclear which design choices are most important for stability. We show that the main source of stability is simple. Decomposing camera motion into small autoregressive steps limits per-step geometric distortion and reduces error accumulation. A controlled camera-step study shows that performance remains stable for small motions and degrades more strongly as the per-step motion approaches $18$-$20^\circ$. We further evaluate geometry-constrained spatial attention and low-frequency appearance anchoring as supporting refinements, together with an efficient registration-free warping pipeline. Across RealEstate10K and MegaScene, CamTrol++ improves temporal and geometric consistency, downstream 3D reconstruction quality, and generation efficiency over training-free baselines. The method remains effective for 56-frame generation and under substantial controlled depth corruption. These results show that careful control of camera motion at inference time can substantially improve the stability of camera-controlled novel view synthesis without retraining or modifying the diffusion backbone.

</details>


### [47] [Tree-Structured Vector Quantization For Efficient And Progressive Image Compression](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03641)
*Xinkun Wang,Tianyi Xu,Qingyu Luo,Mingming Ma,Changzhe Jiao,Fu Li,Yi Niu*

Main category: cs.CV
