TL;DR: Tree-VQ is a progressive tree-structured vector quantization framework for learned image compression that organizes discrete codewords as a hierarchical binary tree, where each latent token is represented by a routed root-to-leaf path. Every prefix of this path corresponds to a valid quantized representation, enabling progressive decoding and refinement.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing vector-quantization based image compression methods produce separate compressed representations for each target bitrate, lacking progressive bitstreams where prefixes are decodable and can be refined by appending additional bits.

Method: Tree-VQ organizes discrete codewords as a hierarchical binary tree and represents each latent token by a routed root-to-leaf path. The method includes: (1) prefix-compatible tree entropy model that codes progressive continuation decisions using causally available decoded contexts, (2) rate-aware refinement scheduling to allocate tree bits to spatial blocks under a prefix budget, and (3) hierarchical prefix supervision to ensure internal nodes are directly decodable at low rates.

Result: Tree-VQ achieves superior performance-efficiency trade-off, delivering the best perceptual compression results with much fewer parameters and lower latency than competing methods.

Conclusion: Tree-VQ provides an effective solution for progressive image compression through its hierarchical tree structure, enabling efficient progressive decoding with fewer parameters and lower latency compared to existing methods.

Abstract: Vector-quantization based image compression has achieved strong rate--distortion performance, yet most of them still produce a separate compressed representation for each target bitrate. Such variable-rate behavior allows one model to operate at multiple rates, but it does not necessarily provide a progressive bitstream whose prefixes are themselves decodable and can be refined by appending additional bits. We propose \textbf{Tree-VQ}, a progressive tree-structured vector quantization framework for learned image compression. Tree-VQ organizes discrete codewords as a hierarchical binary tree and represents each latent token by a routed root-to-leaf path. Crucially, every prefix of this path corresponds to a valid quantized representation, so shallow internal nodes serve as coarse reconstruction codes and deeper nodes provide successive refinements. This allows a compressed image to be decoded from an early prefix and progressively improved as more branch symbols are received, rather than being re-encoded for different target rates. To make this structure practical for compression, we introduce a prefix-compatible tree entropy model that codes progressive continuation decisions and routed branch refinements using only causally available decoded contexts. We further use rate-aware refinement scheduling to decide which spatial blocks should receive additional tree bits under a given prefix budget, and hierarchical prefix supervision to ensure that internal nodes are directly decodable at low rates. Experiments show that Tree-VQ achieves a superior performance--efficiency trade-off, delivering the best perceptual compression results with much fewer parameters and lower latency than competing methods.

</details>

*Xiaoyu Yang,Qixing Wu,Huixian Zhao,Changlong Jin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Vision Foundation Models (VFMs) provide transferable patch representations for few-shot industrial anomaly detection, but their attention computation is typically inherited from pretraining objectives centered on semantic aggregation. This creates a potential mismatch: token relations that support semantic recognition may not adequately expose the localized texture and structural deviations required for anomaly localization. We therefore investigate the hypothesis that the attention computation of a frozen VFM can be reconfigured as a task-relevant component of anomaly detection. We instantiate this idea with Power-Law Self-Correlation Enhanced Attention (PL-SCEA), which retains the semantic context of pretrained query-key attention while constructing token-adaptive self-correlations over contextualized value features. Positive-correlation filtering and power-law reweighting then emphasize relations that are salient relative to each token's relational background, without introducing additional trainable attention projections. The resulting features are modeled by a lightweight variational autoencoder that provides a fixed-size reconstruction-based representation of category-specific normality. The two stages serve complementary roles: attention reconfiguration shapes how local relational deviations are represented, while reconstruction-based modeling converts deviations from learned normality into anomaly scores. Across MVTec AD and VisA, the complete framework achieves competitive image-level detection and consistently strong pixel-level localization across the evaluated few-shot settings. Ablations further show that PL-SCEA improves localization with either the VAE or a memory bank under the tested setting. These results support the view that task-aligned attention reconfiguration can improve the anomaly-localization capability of frozen pretrained representations.

</details>


### [49] [Rethinking 3D Noise: Learning 3D-Aware Video Priors via Optimization-Free Morphological Perturbations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03657)
*Onat Şahin,Mohammad Altillawi,George Eskandar,Carlos Carbone,Ziyuan Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes 3D Morphological Perturbations (3DMP) as an optimization-free regularizer for improving 3D scene representations (NeRF, 3D Gaussian Splatting) in sparse-view settings. The method treats each Gaussian as a fundamental building block and applies perturbations across scale, rotation, and pruning to preserve spatial consistency without requiring per-scene optimization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D scene representations like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting suffer severe artifacts in sparse-view settings. Existing generative 3D artifact fixers rely on paired corrupted and clean renders, requiring costly per-scene reconstructions across varying view configurations. While 2D image augmentations act as instant regularizers, no explicit equivalents exist for 3D representations to preserve spatial consistency across views, which is essential for 3D-aware training.

Method: The proposed method, 3D Morphological Perturbations (3DMP), treats each Gaussian in 3DGS as a fundamental building block (analogous to a 2D pixel) and applies perturbations across its morphological parameter space via scale, rotation, and pruning. This optimization-free regularizer preserves spatial consistency across views and eliminates per-scene 3DGS optimization loops from dataset curation.

Result: The method was evaluated on a lightweight video diffusion sandbox and scaled to a 14B-parameter video model via ControlNet. It maintains visual fidelity while reducing mean depth error by 12.5% over state-of-the-art image-to-image 3D artifact refiners, and boosts downstream robotics policy success rates by up to 8.0% across 3 of 4 manipulation tasks.

Conclusion: 3D Morphological Perturbations provides an effective optimization-free regularizer for 3D representations that preserves spatial consistency. It enables models to learn stronger geometric priors than sparse-view baselines while eliminating costly per-scene optimization loops, demonstrating significant improvements in both depth accuracy and robotics manipulation tasks.

Abstract: 3D scene representations like NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) suffer severe artifacts in sparse-view settings. Recent generative 3D artifact fixers attempt to address this, but rely on paired corrupted and clean renders requiring costly, per-scene reconstructions across varying view configurations. While 2D image augmentations act as instant regularizers, no explicit equivalents exist for 3D representations to preserve spatial consistency across views, an essential property for 3D-aware training. We propose 3D Morphological Perturbations as an optimization-free regularizer that preserves spatial consistency. Leveraging explicit 3DGS, we treat each Gaussian as a fundamental building block - analogous to a 2D pixel - and apply perturbations across its morphological parameter space via scale, rotation, and pruning. Our method eliminates per-scene 3DGS optimization loops from dataset curation while enabling models to learn stronger geometric priors than sparse-view baselines in diagnostic ablations conducted on a lightweight video diffusion sandbox. Scaled to a 14B-parameter video model via ControlNet, our approach maintains visual fidelity while reducing mean depth error by 12.5% over state-of-the-art image-to-image 3D artifact refiners, ultimately boosting downstream robotics policy success rates by up to 8.0% across 3 of 4 manipulation tasks.

</details>


### [50] [Cross-Dataset Transfer and Reliability of Explainable Artificial Intelligence for RhythmFormer Remote Photoplethysmography](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03663)
*Louis Chen,Torbjörn E. M. Nordling*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper quantifies explainability methods for remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) models, testing whether attention-based explanations transfer between datasets and correlate with model performance. The study trained RhythmFormer models on NCKU-rPPG under various conditions (illumination, motion) and evaluated explanation methods using skin coverage and Salience-guided Faithfulness Coefficient (SaCo).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current rPPG explanations rely on heatmap inspection rather than quantitative evidence. The authors aimed to determine whether explanations can transfer between datasets and whether they correlate with model performance metrics like heart-rate error, waveform correlation, and signal-to-noise ratio.

Method: Trained 8 condition-specific RhythmFormer models on NCKU-rPPG dataset under 3 illumination levels, speaking, rotation, and cycling conditions. Estimated one heart rate per 5.12-second clip. Compared with UBFC-rPPG reproduction. Assessed raw attention, rollout, attention flow, and Beyond Intuition methods using skin coverage and SaCo metrics.

Result: Beyond Intuition achieved highest rankings on both datasets (median coverage 0.789, SaCo 0.837 on Static level 3 vs 0.826 and 0.917 on UBFC-rPPG). Within-participant analysis showed no relationship between explanation metrics and heart-rate error, waveform correlation, or SNR in 186 of 252 coefficients. Only Beyond Intuition's coverage correlated with performance measures (ρ=-0.43, +0.57, +0.43). Attention-only methods' SaCo correlated inversely with performance. At 40 lux, coverage dropped to 0.180 and SaCo to -0.178.

Conclusion: Skin coverage and SaCo provide information complementary to performance metrics rather than serving as proxies. Attribution reveals where the model looks, not how faithfully the map is ordered. Accurate estimates are not guaranteed simply by attributing to skin regions.

Abstract: Background. Remote photoplethysmography estimates the cardiovascular pulse from facial video, and its explanations have rested on inspecting heatmaps rather than on quantitative evidence about where a model reads it. We quantified the explanations and asked whether such explanations transfer between datasets and track model performance. Method. We trained eight condition-specific RhythmFormer models on NCKU-rPPG, recorded under three illumination levels, speaking, rotation, and cycling, estimated one heart rate per 5.12-second clip, and set them beside a UBFC-rPPG reproduction. Raw attention, rollout, attention flow, and Beyond Intuition were assessed by skin coverage and the Salience-guided Faithfulness Coefficient (SaCo). Results. Beyond Intuition ranked highest on both datasets, at median coverage 0.789 and SaCo 0.837 on Static level 3 against 0.826 and 0.917 on UBFC-rPPG; lower ranks differed. Within one participant of one condition, neither measure was related to a clip's heart-rate error, waveform correlation, or signal-to-noise ratio on either dataset: 186 of the 252 coefficients fell below $|ρ|=0.10$ and 28 reached $p<0.05$ against the 13 expected by chance. Across the eight scenarios only Beyond Intuition's coverage followed the three performance measures, at $ρ=-0.43$, $+0.57$, and $+0.43$, while the attention-only methods' SaCo ran opposite to each. It failed at 40 lux alone, its median coverage falling to 0.180 and its median SaCo to $-0.178$, whereas motion degraded the estimates far more without such a drop. Conclusions. Skin coverage and SaCo carry information complementary to the performance measures rather than a proxy for them: attributing to the skin does not guarantee an accurate estimate. What an attribution reveals about a condition is where the model looks rather than how faithfully its map is ordered.

</details>


### [51] [ARCOS: Zero-shot Boundary Localization for Corneal Layer Segmentation Across Optical Coherence Tomography Devices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03668)
*Nuno Vivas Brás,Benjamin Memmi,Maëlle Bouhassane,Cristina Georgeon,Vincent Borderie,Karsten Plamann,Anatole Chessel*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ARCOS is a patch-based zero-shot boundary localization framework for automatic segmentation of corneal layers in anterior-segment OCT images. It predicts boundary heatmaps from overlapping patches and combines multi-scale feature fusion with self-conditioned refinement to achieve 95.1% off-by-one accuracy and 0.514 pixel mean absolute error on matched-device testing, with 84.3% accuracy in cross-device zero-shot evaluation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automatic corneal layer segmentation in OCT is challenging due to thin interfaces, speckle noise, and device variability. Accurate segmentation is essential for quantitative assessment of corneal morphology including thickness measurements and detecting disease or surgery-related changes.

Method: The method uses a patch-based approach that predicts boundary heatmaps for main corneal interfaces from overlapping native-resolution patches. Patch-level predictions are stitched across the full B-scan and converted into boundary locations. The network incorporates multi-scale feature fusion and a self-conditioned refinement module that uses intermediate boundary information to improve local predictions while preserving spatial detail. The approach is zero-shot, meaning it can generalize to unseen acquisition devices.

Result: On matched-device test set: 95.1% off-by-one boundary localization accuracy, 0.514 pixels mean absolute boundary error. In zero-shot cross-device evaluation: 84.3% average off-by-one accuracy, 0.855 pixels mean absolute boundary error. Thickness estimates showed low error across corneal regions.

Conclusion: ARCOS outperforms baseline models in both matched-device and cross-device evaluation, demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization capability across different acquisition devices. The method supports quantitative corneal OCT analysis with reliable thickness measurements.

Abstract: Accurate segmentation of corneal layers in optical coherence tomography (OCT) is essential for quantitative assessment of corneal morphology, including layer thickness and structural changes associated with disease or surgery. However, automatic segmentation remains challenging because corneal interfaces are thin, affected by speckle noise, and variable across acquisition devices. In this work, we propose ARCOS, a patch-based zero-shot boundary localization framework for corneal layer segmentation in clinical anterior-segment OCT images. Rather than performing conventional region classification, the method predicts boundary heatmaps for the main corneal interfaces from overlapping native-resolution patches. Patch-level predictions are stitched across the full B-scan and converted into boundary locations to obtain continuous, anatomically ordered layer segmentations. The network combines multi-scale feature fusion with a self-conditioned refinement module that uses intermediate boundary information to improve local heatmap predictions while preserving spatial detail. The method was evaluated on clinical OCT images acquired from multiple devices and compared with representative segmentation baselines using boundary localization and derived thickness metrics. The proposed method achieved an off-by-one boundary localization accuracy of 95.1% and a mean absolute boundary error of 0.514 pixels on the matched-device test set. In zero-shot cross-device evaluation, it maintained an average off-by-one accuracy of 84.3% and a mean absolute boundary error of 0.855 pixels across unseen acquisition devices, outperforming the baseline models. Thickness estimates derived from the predicted boundaries showed low error across corneal regions, supporting the method's use for quantitative corneal OCT analysis.

</details>


### [52] [Do Video Generators Track the World Across Segments? A Benchmark and Method for World-State Reasoning in Video Continuation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03673)
*Yingmao Miao,Pengfei Zhang,Chaoran Xu,Meng Yu,Jing Tang,Xiangxiang Chu,Chao Shen,Chenhao Lin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses video continuation by introducing Statebench, a benchmark testing three state categories (past-visible, occluded-process, complex-transition), and Stateagent, a method that maintains and updates entity-state representations. The method achieves state score improvement from 45.2 to 69.3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current video generators rely on historical observations (frames, key frames, memory banks) but fail to properly model world state transitions. The key insight is that some states must be inferred rather than directly observed, creating a gap in video continuation capabilities. The authors identify this as an overlooked question: given a previous video, its prompt, and a new prompt, can a model generate a continuation reflecting the state determined by both?

Method: The authors propose: (1) Statebench, a benchmark with three state categories: past-visible states (directly observable from history), occluded-process states (inferred from implicit changes), and complex-transition states (multi-step state changes); (2) Stateagent, which explicitly maintains an entity-state representation, updates it under the new prompt, grounds predicted post-action state as a future end frame, and renders the next video.

Result: Stateagent improves controlled video continuation significantly, raising the all-case state score (SCS-All) from 45.2 to 69.3. It also benefits story generation at the one-minute scale.

Conclusion: The proposed approach successfully addresses the state modeling gap in video continuation by explicitly maintaining and updating entity-state representations. Stateagent demonstrates substantial improvements in state consistency for video generation, particularly for scenarios requiring inference rather than direct observation.

Abstract: Video generators build long videos by composing shorter parts, either by generating segments one after another or by autoregressively extending chunks. Each new part usually depends on memories of historical observations, such as recent frames, selected key frames, memory banks, or cached features. These memories preserve visible evidence from the past, but current generators do not reliably turn such evidence into a world-state interface: what holds in the video world after previous actions and how it should change under the next prompt. A past frame remains valid history, but it may not describe the state needed by the next segment; some states must instead be inferred from occluded or implicit changes rather than copied from a directly observed frame. This creates a simple but overlooked question for video continuation: given a previous video, its prompt, and a new prompt, can a model generate a continuation that reflects the state determined by both the historical video and the new prompt? To answer this question, we introduce Statebench, a benchmark that targets this gap by testing continuations over three state categories: past-visible states, occluded-process states, and complex-transition states. We further propose Stateagent, which explicitly maintains an entity-state representation, updates it under the new prompt, grounds the predicted post-action state as a future end frame, and renders the next video. Experiments show that our method improves controlled video continuation by raising the all-case state score (SCS-All) from 45.2 to 69.3, and also benefits story generation at the one-minute scale. Code is avaliable at https://github.com/AMAP-ML/StateAgent.

</details>


### [53] [CoFiE: Coarse-to-Fine Evidence Selection for Efficient Streaming Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03675)
*Jing Jiang,Yiran Ling,Ruonan Li,Dimitrios Stamoulis,Jie Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CoFiE proposes a coarse-to-fine evidence selection framework for streaming video understanding that filters frames BEFORE expensive vision encoding (coarse, query-agnostic) and refines relevant frames AFTER semantic understanding is available (fine, query-specific). This approach achieves state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off with 78.86% on StreamingBench and 68.72% on OvO-Bench, while speeding up inference by 2.54x.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing token pruning and memory-bank methods reduce visual tokens AFTER visual encoding, meaning the expensive frame encoding cost has already been incurred. This limits end-to-end latency reduction. There is a need to remove redundancy BEFORE frame encoding to substantially reduce computational costs.

Method: CoFiE decouples evidence selection into two stages: 1) Novelty-Guided Frame Filtering (coarse, query-agnostic) - retains visually distinctive candidate frames before the vision encoder; 2) Query-Specific Evidence Refinement (fine, query-specific) - selects frames most relevant to the user query during LLM prefill. This design removes redundancy before encoding while preserving query-specific refinement once semantic information is available.

Result: Achieves 78.86% accuracy on StreamingBench and 68.72% on OvO-Bench, with improvements of up to 3.15% over prior methods. Even with up to 80% evidence-frame filtering, CoFiE outperforms strong open-source multimodal models. End-to-end inference latency improved by up to 2.54 times.

Conclusion: CoFiE establishes a new state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off for streaming video understanding by performing evidence selection before vision encoding. The coarse-to-fine approach effectively balances computational efficiency with query-specific relevance, demonstrating that early filtering combined with late refinement can achieve both better accuracy and significantly reduced latency.

Abstract: Streaming video understanding requires Vision Language Models (VLLMs) to process growing video streams and answer user questions under tight latency constraints. Existing methods improve efficiency through token pruning and memory-bank schemes, but mainly reduce visual tokens after visual encoding. Consequently, downstream token pruning alone cannot substantially reduce end-to-end latency because the expensive frame encoding cost has already been incurred. We propose CoFiE, a Coarse-to-Fine Evidence Selection framework that decouples evidence selection into a coarse, query-agnostic filtering stage before the vision encoder and a fine, query-specific refinement stage during LLM prefill. CoFiE introduces Novelty-Guided Frame Filtering to retain visually distinctive candidate frames and Query-Specific Evidence Refinement to select the frames most relevant to the user query. This design removes substantial redundancy before frame encoding while preserving query-specific refinement once semantic information becomes available. Experiments show that CoFiE establishes a new state-of-the-art accuracy-efficiency trade-off across multiple video understanding benchmarks, reaching 78.86% accuracy on StreamingBench and 68.72% on OvO-Bench, with improvements of up to 3.15% over prior methods. Even with up to 80% evidence-frame filtering, CoFiE outperforms strong open-source multimodal models while improving end-to-end inference latency by up to 2.54 times.

</details>


### [54] [Understanding Autonomous Driving Datasets by Describing Differences between Image Subsets in Natural Language](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03677)
*Julian Truetsch,Felix Hauser,Christoph Stiller,Frank Bieder*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces set difference captioning for autonomous driving datasets—given two image sets (target and reference), the method generates natural-language descriptions of differences between them. The approach uses object-centric patches from object detection to enable attribution of differences to specific object instances or categories. A new benchmark (AD-Diff Bench) is introduced to evaluate this task in-domain.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Domain shift between locations in autonomous driving can cause dangerous performance degradation when training data misaligns with the operating environment. Existing data analysis methods rely on limited metadata, predefined labels, or manual inspection, which lack scalable semantic insight. There is a need for practical, human-interpretable dataset introspection.

Method: The paper adapts a two-stage set difference captioning formulation to autonomous driving by focusing on object-centric patches derived from object detection. This simplifies aggregation and enables attribution of differences to specific object instances or categories. Experiments use open-weight models for reproducibility and ease of deployment. A new benchmark (AD-Diff Bench) is introduced for in-domain evaluation, with low-concentration experiments assessing suitability for sparse, real-world differences.

Result: The proposed benchmark and analysis provide a step towards practical, human-interpretable dataset introspection for autonomous driving datasets. The implementation and benchmark dataset are made publicly available.

Conclusion: This work represents a practical approach to dataset introspection for autonomous driving, using set difference captioning with object-centric patches. The AD-Diff Bench benchmark enables evaluation of methods assessing differences between dataset subsets, supporting safety and robustness analysis across different domains.

Abstract: Understanding the composition of large-scale autonomous driving datasets is essential for safety, robustness, and reliable operation across domains. For example, domain shift between locations could lead to the operating environment being misaligned with the training data, resulting in potentially dangerous performance degradation. Yet, existing data analysis pipelines largely rely on metadata, predefined labels, or manual inspection, which provide limited semantic insight or do not scale. This paper studies set difference captioning: given two subsets of images, the goal is to produce a natural-language hypothesis describing differences between the target and reference set. Building on a two-stage formulation, we adapt the method to autonomous driving by focusing on object-centric patches derived from object detection, which simplifies aggregation and enables attribution of differences to specific object instances or categories. To evaluate this setting in-domain, we introduce a new benchmark, AD-Diff Bench. Low-concentration experiments assess the suitability of set-difference-captioning approaches to sparse, real-world differences. We restrict our experiments to open-weight models to support reproducibility and ease of deployment. The proposed benchmark and analysis provide a step towards practical, human-interpretable dataset introspection for autonomous driving datasets. Our implementation and benchmark dataset are available at https://github.com/KIT-MRT/AD-Diff

</details>


### [55] [DropClick: Semi-Automated One-Click Segmentation for Agricultural Robotic Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03680)
*Patrick Zimmer,Michael Halstead,Chris McCool*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DropClick is a semi-automated click-guided segmentation tool for agricultural robotics that uses single-click inputs to generate pseudo-labels, reducing annotation effort. It achieves mIoU of 70.0 and 72.6 on SB20 and BUP20 datasets with only 5 training images, and maintains performance even when 50% of clicks are missing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Labelling vision datasets for segmentation tasks is laborious and costly, which hinders development in agricultural robotics. Existing methods require a click for every object, making annotation still time-consuming.

Method: DropClick uses single-click inputs on objects to generate pseudo-labels. It is trained on just 5 images from the original training data. The system can handle missing clicks (dropped clicks) while maintaining high performance. It can also serve as a pseudo-labeling approach to train other models like Mask2Former in a semi-supervised manner.

Result: DropClick achieves mIoU of 70.0 (SB20) and 72.6 (BUP20). With 50% clicks missing, it still maintains 68.9 and 71.3 mIoU respectively. When used for pseudo-labeling Mask2Former, it achieves 70.1 vs 70.7 AP50 for SB20 and 77.0 for both BUP20 models, while saving 46.3% (SB20) and 31.9% (BUP20) of user input.

Conclusion: DropClick significantly reduces annotation effort by requiring only minimal user input (single clicks) and can maintain high performance even with missing clicks. It effectively serves as a pseudo-labeling tool for training other segmentation models, achieving comparable performance to full manual annotation while saving substantial user input.

Abstract: Labelling vision datasets, especially for segmentation tasks, is a laborious and costly process that stymies novel developments in agricultural robotics. In this paper, we present DropClick, a click-guided segmentation tool that simplifies the annotation process. Our system utilises single-click inputs on objects to generate pseudo-labels, which can replace manual annotations. DropClick stands out as it is a semi-automated approach and does not require a click for every object in the scene. It can therefore further reduce the required amount of user input drastically. We evaluate our method on two challenging agricultural robotic datasets, SB20 and BUP20 for plant and fruit segmentation, respectively. DropClick is first trained on a small subset of just 5 images from the original training data. This DropClick model can then be deployed as a one-click segmentation system and achieves comparable or higher performance than other one-click methods achieving an mIoU of 70.0 and 72.6 points, for SB20 and BUP20 respectively. DropClick then excels at maintaining high performance when clicks are not given (e.g. dropped); when 50% of the clicks are missing it still maintains an mIoU of 68.9 and 71.3 points, for SB20 and BUP20 respectively. We validate DropClick as a pseudo-labelling approach by taking its outputs to train a Mask2Former instance-based segmentation model in a semi-supervised manner. In this process, partially removing user input from DropClick yields similar high performance when compared to providing all clicks, at 70.1 vs 70.7 points AP50 for SB20 and no difference for BUP20 at 77.0 for both models; at the same time saving 46.3% of total input for SB20 and 31.9% for BUP20.

</details>


### [56] [ToPO: Token-Conditioned Preference Routing for Attention-Based Latent Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03688)
*Juntao Xu,Shihong Li,Hoi Fan Au,Ning Zhu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ToPO (Token-Oriented Preference Optimization) is a new method for preference optimization in attention-based, noise-prediction latent diffusion models that outperforms Diffusion-DPO by constructing per-minibatch spatial-temporal routes from branchwise squared-residual contrast in a frozen reference denoiser, using preferred-branch cross-attention with content tokens and an auxiliary pixel-midpoint ordering term.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Diffusion-DPO applies pairwise preference labels over many spatial and denoising-time coordinates, which may be inefficient. ToPO aims to work at the token level for more targeted preference optimization in latent diffusion models.

Method: ToPO constructs a per-minibatch, detached, separable spatial-temporal route from branchwise squared-residual contrast in a frozen reference denoiser. Preferred-branch cross-attention uses content tokens to modulate the spatial factor, and an auxiliary pixel-midpoint ordering term is added without local labels or a learned reward model.

Result: ToPO has higher endpoint estimates than Diffusion-DPO on all five reported SD-1.5 metrics and on HPSv2, ImageReward, and CLIP for SDXL. It also receives larger raw win shares in an aggregate blind SDXL A/B study.

Conclusion: ToPO outperforms Diffusion-DPO in the reported equal-update U-Net protocols. However, this is not an equal-compute comparison, limiting the generalizability of the findings.

Abstract: Pairwise preference labels rank complete images, yet Diffusion-DPO applies their effect over many spatial and denoising-time coordinates. For attention-based, noise-prediction latent diffusion, ToPO (Token-Oriented Preference Optimization) constructs a per-minibatch, detached, separable spatial-temporal route from branchwise squared-residual contrast in a frozen reference denoiser. Preferred-branch cross-attention uses content tokens to modulate the spatial factor, and an auxiliary pixel-midpoint ordering term is added without local labels or a learned reward model. In matched three-seed retrainings with a shared update schedule, ToPO has higher endpoint estimates than Diffusion-DPO on all five reported SD-1.5 metrics and on HPSv2, ImageReward, and CLIP for SDXL. It also receives larger raw win shares in an aggregate blind SDXL A/B study. These findings are scoped to the reported equal-update U-Net protocols rather than an equal-compute comparison.

</details>


### [57] [Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model for WSI Classification in Histopathology](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03689)
*Feixing Chen,Hao Lu,Lin Luo,Yan Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes SASG-SSM, a novel framework for whole slide image (WSI) classification in histopathology. It addresses limitations of conventional patch-based methods that fragment irregularly shaped semantic tissue units and fail to preserve spatial organization. The framework uses Semantic-Aware Subgraphs (SASGs) to group spatially connected patches and a Subgraph State Space Module (SG-SSM) combining graph neural networks with Mamba-based state space modeling for efficient contextualization across subgraphs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Histopathological subtyping relies on recognizing characteristic histological patterns that span irregularly shaped tissue regions (semantic units). Conventional patch-based representations fragment these units and fail to preserve internal spatial organization, while modeling relationships among spatially separated units remains challenging.

Method: The framework consists of two key components: (1) Semantic-Aware Subgraphs (SASGs) that approximate irregularly shaped semantic units by adaptively grouping spatially connected patches guided by class-agnostic visual-semantic priors, representing patches as graph nodes with adjacency edges to preserve spatial organization; (2) Subgraph State Space Module (SG-SSM) combining a graph neural network encoder for intra-subgraph topology encoding with a Mamba-based state space encoder for efficient contextualization across large numbers of subgraphs.

Result: Extensive experiments across four WSI subtyping datasets demonstrate consistent advantages over representative state-of-the-art methods. Further evaluations under small-cohort and few-shot settings demonstrate robustness and data efficiency under limited training data.

Conclusion: SASG-SSM provides an effective solution for WSI classification by preserving spatial organization within semantic units while efficiently modeling relationships across spatially distributed regions. The method shows strong performance and robustness, particularly in data-limited scenarios.

Abstract: Histopathological subtyping relies on the recognition of characteristic histological patterns. These patterns may be expressed by individual tissue structures or by the spatial distribution and co-occurrence of multiple structures, and they often span irregularly shaped tissue regions, termed semantic units in this work. However, conventional patch-based representations may fragment such units and fail to explicitly preserve their internal spatial organization, while efficiently modeling relationships among numerous spatially separated units remains challenging. To address these limitations, we propose the Semantic-Aware Subgraph State Space Model (SASG-SSM), a flexible and efficient framework for whole slide image (WSI) classification. Semantic-Aware Subgraphs (SASGs) first approximate irregularly shaped semantic units by adaptively grouping spatially connected patches guided by class-agnostic visual-semantic priors. By representing patches as graph nodes with adjacency edges, SASGs preserve their internal spatial organization rather than treating them as an unordered set. A Subgraph State Space Module (SG-SSM) subsequently combines a graph neural network encoder for intra-subgraph topology encoding with a Mamba-based state space encoder for efficient contextualization across large numbers of subgraphs. This module integrates local structural information within semantic units with global contextual information arising from their distribution and co-occurrence across the WSI, while efficiently modeling a large number of spatially distributed regions. Extensive experiments across four WSI subtyping datasets demonstrate consistent advantages over representative state-of-the-art methods. Further evaluations under small-cohort and few-shot settings demonstrate robustness and data efficiency under limited training data. Code will be released at https://github.com/HLSvois/SASG-SSM.

</details>


### [58] [MetaStructAtlas: A Grounded 3D Vision-Language Dataset and Benchmark for Functional and Structural Reasoning in Whole-Body PET/CT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03690)
*Chenguang Zheng,Le Xue,Yichi Zhang,Wenbo Zhang,Zehui Ling,Gang Feng,Xin Gao,Yuan Qi,Yuan Cheng,Zixin Hu,Mei Tian*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: MetaStructAtlas is a large-scale dataset for grounded whole-body PET/CT interpretation that provides 490 co-registered 3D PET/CT volumes with 50,470 organ-level segmentation masks, grounded radiology reports, and a benchmark (MetaStructVQA) with 100,565 QA pairs for 3D grounded visual question answering in nuclear medicine.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current 3D medical vision-language models are limited to regional CT imaging, leaving a critical void in comprehensive whole-body PET/CT analysis. The joint interpretation of metabolic function (PET) and anatomical structure (CT) is essential for clinical diagnosis but lacks dedicated datasets and benchmarks.

Method: The dataset synthesizes multimodal imaging with integrated anatomical, metabolic, and semantic annotations. MetaStructVQA was developed as a standardized 3D grounded VQA benchmark containing QA pairs that explicitly link diagnostic queries to visual evidence across PET and CT modalities, encompassing anatomical, morphological, and metabolic characteristics.

Result: The study establishes a robust foundation for multimodal representation learning and integrated whole-body reasoning in nuclear medicine by evaluating state-of-the-art 3D medical VLMs on the MetaStructVQA benchmark.

Conclusion: MetaStructAtlas and MetaStructVQA address the gap in whole-body PET/CT analysis by providing comprehensive multimodal data and a standardized benchmark, enabling future research in grounded visual reasoning for nuclear medicine.

Abstract: The joint interpretation of metabolic function and anatomical structure is essential for clinical diagnosis in whole-body PET/CT. Although recent advances in 3D medical vision-language models have demonstrated remarkable progress, current efforts are limited to regional CT imaging, leaving a critical void in comprehensive whole-body PET/CT analysis. In this work, we introduce MetaStructAtlas, a large-scale dataset for grounded whole-body PET/CT interpretation that synthesizes multimodal imaging with integrated anatomical, metabolic, and semantic annotations. MetaStructAtlas provides 490 co-registered 3D PET and CT volumes with 50,470 organ-level segmentation masks and grounded radiology reports. To facilitate interactive reasoning, we further developed MetaStructVQA, a standardized 3D grounded visual question-answering benchmark containing 100,565 QA pairs. This framework explicitly links diagnostic queries to visual evidence across modalities, encompassing anatomical, morphological, and metabolic characteristics. Finally, we evaluate state-of-the-art 3D medical VLMs on MetaStructVQA, establishing a robust foundation for multimodal representation learning and integrated whole-body reasoning in nuclear medicine.

</details>


### [59] [Observation-Conditioned Latent Energy Priors for Sparse Implicit Neural Shape Completion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03694)
*Paul Büschl,Ezequiel de la Rosa,Julia Wolleb,Julian McGinnis,César Nombela-Arrieta,Bjoern Menze*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a post-hoc observation-conditioned latent energy prior to prevent latent code drift in frozen autodecoder-style implicit neural representations (INRs) when inferring 3D shapes from sparse SDF samples. The method uses a conditional energy score alongside an L2 prior, without requiring decoder retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Autodecoder-style INR models optimize latent codes from sparse off-grid SDF samples at test time. When samples underconstrain inference, the latent code can drift toward regions that fit observations but decode to implausible unobserved geometry. Existing latent priors (e.g., L2, GMM) are observation-agnostic and cannot prevent this drift.

Method: The proposed method adds an observation-conditioned latent energy prior to frozen INR decoders. The energy scores standardized latents conditioned on a permutation-invariant encoding of the sparse observation set. This conditional energy serves as a residual expert alongside an L2 latent prior, with the L2 prior selected on validation data.

Result: On the sparsest cell-nucleus SDF regimes, the L2 objective augmented with conditional energy consistently improves over a validation-selected L2 baseline. On MedShapeNet, the proposed method outperforms both L2 and a six-component GMM latent-density prior across all reported readouts. Shuffled-context ablation is consistently weaker than matched context, supporting an observation-specific contribution.

Conclusion: Lightweight conditional energies can make pretrained INR decoders more observation-aware without retraining, effectively preventing latent drift when inferring 3D shapes from sparse observations.

Abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) can model continuous 3D shapes with a shared coordinate decoder and per-instance latent codes. At test time, autodecoder-style models commonly freeze the decoder and optimize a new latent code from sparse off-grid SDF samples. When these samples underconstrain inference, the latent can drift toward regions that fit the observations but decode implausible unobserved geometry. We propose a post-hoc observation-conditioned latent energy prior for frozen INR decoders. The energy scores standardized latents conditioned on a permutation-invariant encoding of the sparse observation set and is used as a residual expert alongside an L2 latent prior selected on validation data. We evaluate on a controlled cell-nucleus SDF dataset and a public MedShapeNet-derived SDF completion dataset. The proposed L2 objective augmented with conditional energy improves consistently over a validation-selected L2 baseline in the sparsest cell-nucleus regimes and, on MedShapeNet, outperforms both L2 and a six-component GMM latent-density prior across all reported readouts. A shuffled-context ablation is consistently weaker than matched context, supporting an observation-specific contribution. These results suggest that lightweight conditional energies can make pretrained INR decoders more observation-aware without retraining.

</details>


### [60] [SignSeek: Learning Transferable Representations for Sign Dictionary Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03695)
*Sobhan Asasi,Ozge Mercanoglu Sincan,Richard Bowden*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SignSeek is a sign language retrieval system that uses contrastive learning with saliency-guided articulator masking to achieve signer-independent sign retrieval from dictionary queries. It addresses the challenge of natural variability between signers in open-set retrieval settings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Sign language dictionaries are essential resources for learners, but automatically retrieving signs from dictionaries given only a query video remains challenging due to natural variability between signers. Existing sign representation learning methods are built for closed-set recognition and produce embeddings that do not generalize to the open-set, signer-independent setting that retrieval demands.

Method: SignSeek uses contrastive learning to align same-gloss signs across signers. The Articulator Saliency-Guided Masking (ASGM) identifies the most critical articulator per sign, driving two complementary objectives: (1) Masked Contrastive Alignment (MAC) loss that sees the sign through a single articulator, and (2) Masked Prediction (MAP) loss that reconstructs the sign in latent space from surrounding spatio-temporal context. Pretrained on 266K samples (~5,700 glosses) across multiple sign languages.

Result: SignSeek achieves state-of-the-art performance in cross-corpus retrieval on ASL-Citizen, WLASL, and NMFs-CSL without downstream fine-tuning. It achieves zero-shot generalisation to unseen British Sign Language (BSL), surpassing methods explicitly trained on BSL. It also transfers to isolated sign recognition and subtitle alignment, outperforming prior skeleton-based methods.

Conclusion: SignSeek successfully bridges the gap between closed-set recognition and open-set retrieval by using contrastive learning with articulator masking. Its ability to generalize to unseen sign languages (zero-shot BSL) demonstrates the robustness and transferability of the learned representations, making it a significant advancement for sign language retrieval and related tasks.

Abstract: Sign language dictionaries are essential resources for sign language learners, yet automatically retrieving a sign from a dictionary, given only a query video, remains a challenging problem due to the natural variability between signers. Existing sign representation learning methods are built for closed-set recognition, producing embeddings that do not generalise to the open-set, signer-independent setting that retrieval demands. \textbf{SignSeek} closes this gap by contrastively learning sign representations with saliency-guided articulator masking. A contrastive objective aligns same-gloss signs across signers, while our Articulator Saliency-Guided Masking (ASGM) pinpoints the single most critical articulator per sign. This drives two complementary objectives, a masked contrastive alignment (MAC) loss that sees the sign through a single articulator and a masked prediction (MAP) loss that reconstructs it in latent space from the surrounding spatio-temporal context. Pretrained on 266K samples ($\sim$5,700 glosses) across multiple sign languages, \textbf{SignSeek} sets a new state-of-the-art performance in cross-corpus retrieval on ASL-Citizen, WLASL, and NMFs-CSL without any downstream fine-tuning. Strikingly, it achieves zero-shot generalisation to an entirely unseen British Sign Language (BSL), surpassing methods explicitly trained on BSL, and transfers seamlessly to isolated sign recognition and subtitle alignment, outperforming prior skeleton-based methods.

</details>


### [61] [Unfold The World: Factorize 4D Properties in Reinforcing Spatial Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03729)
*Yijun Yang,Shenghe Zheng,Wenbo Li,Jianhui Liu,Haoze Sun,Yanbing Zhang,Jiaxiu Jiang,Lin Song,Haoyang Huang,Nan Duan,Lei Zhu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: FactoSR addresses VLMs' inability to perform true spatial reasoning by decomposing the problem into three factorized sub-objectives: planar correspondence (XY), depth consistency (Z), and temporal reversibility (T), transforming ill-posed 2D projection recovery into tractable reasoning steps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vision-Language Models remain "flat" when reasoning about the physical world due to a fundamental dimensional mismatch - they interpret 2D projections but true spatial reasoning requires recovering latent 3D geometry and temporal continuity. The monolithic approach fails to capture this high-dimensional complexity.

Method: FactoSR uses a factorized reinforcement learning framework that explicitly interprets dimensions collapsed by visual projection. It decomposes world-consistent reasoning into three orthogonal, geometric sub-objectives: planar correspondence (XY), depth consistency (Z), and temporal reversibility (T). These verifiable constraints are optimized within a unified policy learning mechanism.

Result: Extensive evaluations on multi-view and video benchmarks show substantial gains in 3D and 4D reasoning: 5.9% boost on VSI-Bench and 4.5% on All-Angles-Bench.

Conclusion: Reinforcing explicit, factorized 4D consistency is a critical step toward evolving VLMs into robust, world-aware reasoners. The "divide and conquer" paradigm effectively transforms ill-posed projection recovery into tangible reasoning steps.

Abstract: Despite the remarkable prowess of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) in general multimodal tasks, they remain fundamentally ``flat'' when reasoning about the physical world. We argue that this spatial bottleneck stems from a profound dimensional mismatch: while VLMs are trained to interpret 2D projections, true spatial reasoning demands the recovery of latent 3D geometry and temporal continuity. To conquer this high-dimensional complexity, we advocate a shift from monolithic learning to a ``divide and conquer'' paradigm. We present FactoSR, a factorized reinforcement learning framework that explicitly interpret the dimensions collapsed by visual projection. At its core, FactoSR decomposes the monolithic problem of world-consistent reasoning into three orthogonal, geometric sub-objectives: planar correspondence ($XY$), depth consistency ($Z$), and temporal reversibility ($T$). By optimizing these verifiable constraints within a unified policy learning mechanism, we effectively transform an ill-posed projection recovery problem into a series of tangible reasoning steps. Extensive evaluations on multi-view and video benchmarks demonstrate that this elegant decomposition yields substantial gains in 3D and 4D reasoning, achieving a 5.9% boost on VSI-Bench and 4.5% on All-Angles-Bench. Our findings suggest that reinforcing explicit, factorized 4D consistency is a critical step toward evolving VLMs into robust, world-aware reasoners.

</details>


### [62] [Fill My Mirror: Geometry-Constrained Mirror Inpainting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03740)
*Ofek Basson,Shimon Vainer,Yacov Hel-Or,Ohad Fried*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses mirror inpainting in real-world images, where the goal is to generate geometrically consistent reflections in mirror regions. The key insight is that mirror content is largely geometrically constrained by the visible scene, so the authors estimate scene geometry and project visible content into the mirror to recover reflection regions. A two-mask diffusion strategy balances geometric constraints with learned priors to reduce projection artifacts. The method is training-free and works on complex real-world scenes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mirrors are common in real-world images but producing geometrically consistent reflections with generative models remains challenging. Unlike most objects, mirror appearance depends on scene geometry and viewpoint, making it hard to synthesize using learned appearance priors alone. Existing generative models struggle to produce reflections that are geometrically consistent with the observed scene.

Method: 1) Estimate scene geometry from the image
2) Project visible content into the mirror region to recover reflection regions determined by geometry
3) Use a generative model with a two-mask diffusion strategy that balances geometric constraints with the model's learned priors
4) This approach reduces projection artifacts and improves reflection consistency
5) The method is training-free and applicable to complex real-world scenes

Result: The method was evaluated on MirrorBench-V2 (synthetic) and real images. Using standard and geometry-aware metrics, the experiments show that explicitly using scene geometry improves consistency compared to methods that rely solely on learned priors.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that incorporating explicit scene geometry into the mirror inpainting process significantly improves reflection consistency. By combining geometric projection with a two-mask diffusion strategy, the method can produce more realistic and physically accurate mirror reflections in complex real-world scenes without requiring any training.

Abstract: Mirrors are common in real-world images, yet producing geometrically consistent reflections with generative models remains challenging. Unlike most objects, mirror appearance depends on scene geometry and viewpoint, making it hard to synthesize using learned appearance priors alone. We address this in the mirror inpainting setting, where the scene is fixed and only the mirror region is generated. Our key insight is that much mirror content is geometrically constrained by the visible scene and need not be hallucinated. We estimate scene geometry and project visible content into the mirror to recover reflection regions determined by geometry. A generative model then completes the mirror region via a two-mask diffusion strategy balancing geometric constraints with the model's learned priors, reducing projection artifacts and improving reflection consistency. The method is training-free and applicable to complex real-world scenes. We evaluate on MirrorBench-V2 (synthetic) and real images. Using standard and geometry-aware metrics, we show that explicitly using scene geometry improves consistency.

</details>


### [63] [KnowVis: Knowledge-Centric Visual Summarization for Video Lectures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03742)
*Yi Xu,Yifan Hou,Xiaoyu Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: KnowVis is a novel framework that transforms linear video lectures into pedagogically grounded visual narratives to reduce cognitive overload for novice learners. It extracts concept maps from multimodal video content to identify threshold concepts, constructs structured knowledge units, and synthesizes visual summaries. The framework is evaluated on a dataset of 125 educational videos across 10 disciplines with 1,079 visual summaries.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video lectures deliver information linearly and transiently, while human learning requires constructing interconnected cognitive networks. This fundamental pedagogical mismatch causes severe cognitive overload for novice learners who lack prior domain knowledge. Existing video summarization methods fail to address this as they produce text-heavy, linear condensations that still demand high cognitive effort.

Method: KnowVis employs a three-stage approach: (1) Extract detailed concept maps from multimodal video content to identify important and challenging threshold concepts; (2) Construct structured knowledge units; (3) Synthesize engaging visual summaries. The framework is evaluated through extensive automated evaluations and a human study.

Result: KnowVis generates more accurate and clear visuals compared to state-of-the-art baselines. The framework successfully reduces cognitive load and significantly improves student learning effectiveness and knowledge retention.

Conclusion: KnowVis effectively addresses the pedagogical mismatch in video lecture learning by transforming linear video content into visual narratives. The proposed framework, combined with the curated dataset, provides a promising solution for helping novice learners handle dense educational video content with reduced cognitive burden and improved learning outcomes.

Abstract: Video lectures are valuable educational resources, but their dense and lengthy formats often overwhelm novice learners. This difficulty stems from a fundamental pedagogical mismatch: while videos deliver transient information linearly, human learning requires constructing interconnected cognitive networks, a task that induces severe cognitive overload for novice learners lacking prior domain knowledge. Existing video summarization methods fail to resolve this mismatch, as they primarily produce text-heavy, linear condensations that still demand high cognitive effort. To bridge this gap, we propose KnowVis, a framework that transforms linear video lectures into pedagogically grounded visual narratives. KnowVis first extracts a detailed concept map from multimodal video content to identify important and challenging threshold concepts, then constructs structured knowledge units, and finally synthesizes engaging visual summaries. Alongside the framework, we introduce a curated dataset of 125 educational videos across 10 academic disciplines, paired with 1,079 generated visual summaries. Extensive automated evaluations and a human study demonstrate that, compared to state-of-the-art baselines, KnowVis generates more accurate and clear visuals that successfully reduce cognitive load and significantly improve student learning effectiveness and knowledge retention.

</details>


### [64] [ENEAS: Embedding-guided Neural Ensemble for Adaptive Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03756)
*Javier del Pino,Salvador Rodríguez,Alejandro Garabito,Javier Álvarez,Chema Garabito*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: ENEAS is a unified text-promptable method for instance tracking and semantic discovery that addresses limitations of foundation models like SAM, including temporal hallucinations, spatial fragmentation, and semantic misclassification (confusing statues, paintings, or reflections with real objects).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Text-promptable segmentation models (including SAM) suffer from three critical failures: (1) temporal hallucinations - failing to report target absence when objects leave view, (2) spatial fragmentation - segmenting local textures instead of complete objects during close-ups, and (3) semantic misclassification - prioritizing visual features over ontological reality, segmenting artifacts like statues or reflections as target entities. These issues are particularly damaging in 3D reconstruction where a single misclassified distractor corrupts the asset.

Method: ENEAS works in two modes: (1) For tracking: extends the SeC architecture (geometrically robust, previously point-based) with a text-prompting adapter and leverages temporal memory to maintain target through disappearance without drifting to distractors, and keep objects whole even when filling the entire view. (2) For discovery: uses a semantic verification layer combining high-speed visual embedding matching with conditional VLM refinement - only invoking semantic reasoning for ambiguous candidates to filter ontological errors while maintaining low latency.

Result: ENEAS enables high-quality semantic tracking and segmentation of video, broad libraries, and temporally/spatially unordered data collections, with the ability to discriminate true instances from "doppelgangers" (visually similar but ontologically different entities like statues or reflections).

Conclusion: ENEAS provides a unified solution that addresses the fundamental limitations of text-promptable segmentation models in both tracking and open-concept discovery scenarios, with particular value for 3D reconstruction applications where semantic accuracy is critical.

Abstract: We present ENEAS, a unified, text-promptable method for instance tracking and semantic discovery. Text-promptable segmentation models, including the latest foundation models such as SAM 3, still suffer from temporal hallucinations, spatial fragmentation, and semantic misclassification: they fail to report target absence when an object leaves the field of view, segment local textures instead of the complete object during extreme close-ups, and prioritize visual features over ontological reality, so that visually similar artifacts such as statues, paintings, or reflections are segmented as target entities.
  ENEAS works two ways from a single method: precise tracking and high-quality segmentation of a unique instance, and open-concept discovery of every instance a text query names, resolved by a semantic verification layer. For tracking, we extend the geometrically robust SeC architecture, previously limited to point interactions, with a text-prompting adapter and leverage its temporal memory, so that the target is held through disappearance without drifting to distractors and kept whole even when it fills the entire view. For discovery, the verification layer combines high-speed visual embedding matching with conditional VLM refinement, invoking semantic reasoning only for ambiguous candidates, which filters out the ontological errors that visual-only models cannot distinguish while keeping latency low. Designed with 3D reconstruction in mind, where a single misclassified distractor corrupts the asset, ENEAS unlocks high-quality semantic tracking and segmentation of video, of broad libraries, and of collections of temporally or spatially unordered data, together with the discrimination to tell true instances from their doppelgangers: things that look alike but are not the same. The code and models are available at https://github.com/speridlabs/eneas

</details>


### [65] [RealCADBench: Benchmarking Parametric CAD Modeling from Industrial Design Intents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03773)
*JoyIndustrial VisCAD Team,Linxin Cai,Qiuhe Hong,Zhichao Huang,Guanlin Li,Zongzhen Li,Hongsen Liu,Yichen Long,Wei Wang,Yuchen Wang,Dongyue Yang,Huimu Yu,Xianwen Zhong*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RealCADBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating intent-to-program CAD modeling from real industrial design intents, containing 12,632 tasks across 19 categories with multiple input modalities. It evaluates generated FreeCAD Python code using executability, Solid IoU, Surface IoU, and a visual-semantic Judge metric. The study reveals that no single frontier model excels across all metrics, with significant variations in performance across different evaluation criteria.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CAD benchmarks have limitations: they focus on synthetic or CAD-native settings, have limited input modalities, and rely primarily on executability and IoU metrics. This paper addresses the need for a more realistic and comprehensive benchmark that evaluates CAD modeling from real industrial design intents using multiple input types and evaluation metrics.

Method: The researchers created RealCADBench with 12,632 tasks from 19 factory-automation categories, spanning text descriptions, 2D engineering drawings, real product pictures, and rendered images for both Part and Assembly modeling. They evaluated nine frontier large models on a 1,770-task slice (1,745 Part tasks across four input regimes plus 25 assembly tasks). Each model generates FreeCAD API Python code, which is executed to export 3D models evaluated using executability, Solid IoU, Surface IoU, and a rubric-based visual-semantic identity Judge.

Result: Across six frontier-scale models, executability ranges from 0.565 to 0.812, Solid IoU from 0.2841 to 0.5379, and Surface IoU from 0.112 to 0.217. No single model leads all four metrics. The highest regime-balanced composite comes from a different model than leaders on component metrics. On assembly tasks, Codex with GPT-5.5 improves executability and IoU metrics over standalone GPT-5.5 but lowers Judge score by 6.98 percentage points. Key failure modes include missing fine structures, loss of part identity, and incorrect assembly placement.

Conclusion: Execution alone is insufficient to characterize realistic CAD modeling. Frontier models and agents differ substantially across executability, IoUs, and visual-semantic identity, highlighting the need for multi-metric evaluation approaches. The benchmark reveals that current large models still struggle with fine structural details, part identification, and assembly placement in industrial CAD modeling tasks.

Abstract: Parametric computer-aided design (CAD) modeling is difficult to evaluate with a single metric. Existing CAD benchmarks often emphasize synthetic or CAD-native settings, limited input modalities, or executability and IoUs alone. We introduce RealCADBench, a benchmark for intent-to-program CAD modeling from real industrial design intents. It contains 12,632 tasks from 19 factory-automation categories and spans text descriptions, 2D engineering drawings, real product pictures, and rendered images for both Part and Assembly modeling. We report results on a 1,770-task evaluation slice: 1,745 Part tasks across four input regimes and RCB-Assm25, a 25-task assembly study used in every reported assembly comparison. Each method generates FreeCAD API Python, which a shared runtime executes to export the 3D model. We evaluate the exported model using executability, Solid IoU, Surface IoU, and a rubric-based visual-semantic identity Judge. Among the nine standalone frontier large models evaluated, no model leads all four metrics. Across six frontier-scale large models, executability ranges from 0.565 to 0.812, Solid IoU from 0.2841 to 0.5379, and Surface IoU from 0.112 to 0.217 across the four Part regimes. The highest regime-balanced composite comes from a different model than the leaders on the four component metrics. On RCB-Assm25, Codex with GPT-5.5 improves executability and both IoU metrics over standalone GPT-5.5, but lowers the Judge score by 6.98 percentage points, leaving GPT-5.5 as the Judge leader. We also observe recurring failure modes, most notably missing fine structures, loss of part identity, and incorrect assembly placement. These results show that execution alone is insufficient to characterize realistic CAD modeling and that frontier models and agents differ substantially across executability, IoUs, and visual-semantic identity.

</details>


### [66] [A Reverse Sign Language Dictionary: Open-Vocabulary Sign Recognition from Continuous Signing via Video Captioning and Description Retrieval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03788)
*Santiago Poveda-Gutiérrez,Hideki Nakayama,Mayumi Bono*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel open-vocabulary approach to Isolated Sign Language Recognition (ISLR) that abandons traditional closed-set gloss classification in favor of a vision-language retrieval system. The method captions sign-level video clips into free-form procedural descriptions using a fine-tuned vision-language model, then retrieves the closest match from a target vocabulary using a multilingual sentence encoder. Applied to Japanese Sign Language (JSL), this approach achieves 49% top-10 retrieval on seen classes (vs 4.5% untrained) and 21% on unseen classes (vs 11.5% untrained), addressing the fundamental limitation of closed-set classifiers that cannot generalize to unseen signs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional ISLR methods rely on closed-set classification over gloss labels, which cannot generalize to signs unseen during training and require a gloss-annotated lexicon for every deployment. This limits practical applicability and requires expensive annotation for each sign. The authors seek an open-vocabulary approach that requires no gloss supervision and can recognize signs not seen during training.

Method: The proposed method consists of two stages: (1) Captioning sign-level video clips into free-form procedural descriptions using an open-weight vision-language model with fine-tuned language and vision towers; (2) Retrieving the closest entry from a target vocabulary of procedural descriptions using a multilingual sentence encoder. This creates a "reverse sign language dictionary" requiring no gloss supervision. The approach was evaluated on 1,300 sign-level segments from a JSL dialogue corpus with a 503-entry target vocabulary.

Result: Fine-tuning the captioner substantially improved retrieval performance: top-10 retrieval on seen classes increased from 4.5% (untrained) to 49%, becoming statistically indistinguishable from a standard supervised closed-set classifier (I3D) on two of three test sets. More importantly, unseen-class retrieval improved significantly from 11.5% to 21.0% top-10 (p=0.0094), a regime where closed-set classifiers cannot participate. An upper-bound analysis showed the sentence encoder recovers close to 100% of paraphrased gold descriptions, indicating the main gap lies in captioning quality.

Conclusion: This work presents the first description-based, open-vocabulary sign lookup from continuous signing without gloss supervision, and the first such system for Japanese Sign Language. The approach successfully generalizes to unseen signs, addressing a fundamental limitation of traditional closed-set classification. Future work will focus on improving captioning quality, as the sentence encoder already achieves near-perfect performance on paraphrased descriptions.

Abstract: Isolated Sign Language Recognition (ISLR) is conventionally cast as closed-set classification over gloss labels, which cannot generalize to signs unseen in training and ties every deployment to a gloss-annotated lexicon. We instead recognize signs extracted from continuous signing by (1) captioning a sign-level clip into a free-form procedural description of the articulation with an open-weight vision-language model, and (2) retrieving the closest entry from a vocabulary of target descriptions with a multilingual sentence encoder: a reverse sign language dictionary that needs no gloss supervision and admits an open vocabulary. On 1,300 sign-level segments from a Japanese Sign Language (JSL) dialogue corpus annotated with procedural descriptions (against a 2% top-10 chance floor over the 503-entry target vocabulary), fine-tuning the captioner substantially improves seen-class retrieval: language and vision tower fine-tuning raises top-10 retrieval on seen classes from 4.5% (untrained) to 49%, becoming statistically indistinguishable from a standard supervised closed-set classifier (I3D) on two of the three test sets where a closed-set classifier can be evaluated at all. More importantly, unseen-class retrieval also improves significantly over the untrained pipeline (11.5% -> 21.0% top-10, p=0.0094), a regime in which the closed-set classifier cannot participate. A matcher-side empirical upper-bound analysis shows the sentence encoder already recovers close to 100% of paraphrased gold descriptions, locating a gap in captioning quality that we aim to address in future work. To our knowledge this is the first description-based, open-vocabulary sign lookup from continuous signing without gloss supervision, and the first for JSL.

</details>


### [67] [LLaDA-Image: Building Strong Image Generators with Fully Open Training Recipes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03796)
*Chuyan Chen,Haoxing Chen,Kun Chen,Zhenglin Cheng,Long Cui,Ruishan Fang,Zhangxuan Gu,Zhicheng Huang,Zhenzhong Lan,Yuanting Lei,Haoquan Li,Jianguo Li,Rongchuan Li,Sidu Li,Tao Lin,Deyuan Liu,Jiacheng Liu,Lin Liu,Yuxuan Lou,Zhisheng Lu,Yuxin Ma,Shuheng Shen,Peng Sun,Chaoyang Wang,Hongjun Wang,Xiaomei Wang,Yongxin Wang,Chengzhang Wu,Hongru Wu,Jun Xie*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LLaDA-Image is a unified framework combining a 6B Diffusion Transformer with a frozen vision-language module built on LLaDA2.0-Mini, achieving state-of-the-art results on Qwen-Image-Bench with scores of 53.53 (English) and 53.38 (Chinese).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to avoid heavy reliance on paired image-text data from the beginning by first building a strong visual generative prior through image-only pre-training and mid-training, enabling the model to generate photorealistic images while accurately following fine-grained editing instructions.

Method: The framework uses a 6B Diffusion Transformer (DiT) trained from scratch, paired with a frozen vision-language understanding module based on LLaDA2.0-Mini. Training involves 220M samples (98% real images) with parameter-free RMSNorm and Muon optimizer. The model is then distilled into LLaDA-Image-Turbo for fast inference in 2-4 sampling steps.

Result: LLaDA-Image achieves overall scores of 53.53 and 53.38 on the English and Chinese tracks of Qwen-Image-Bench respectively, setting a new state-of-the-art among open-source models on both tracks. The model produces highly photorealistic images while accurately following fine-grained editing instructions.

Conclusion: The unified diffusion-based approach demonstrates that image-only pre-training followed by mid-training is effective for building capable generative models. LLaDA-Image-Turbo enables efficient inference in just 2-4 steps. The authors release model weights, training code, and detailed recipes to support further research on capable and efficient generative models.

Abstract: We introduce LLaDA-Image, a unified framework that pairs a 6B Diffusion Transformer (DiT) trained from scratch with a frozen vision-language understanding module built on the LLaDA2.0-Mini diffusion language model backbone. Instead of relying heavily on paired image-text data from the beginning, we first build a strong visual generative prior through image-only pre-training and mid-training. The generation pipeline comprises 220M samples, 98 of which are real images. For efficient and scalable optimization, we use parameter-free RMSNorm throughout the DiT together with the Muon optimizer. The resulting unified model produces highly photorealistic images while accurately following fine-grained editing instructions. We further distill LLaDA-Image into LLaDA-Image-Turbo, enabling fast inference in 2-4 sampling steps. On Qwen-Image-Bench, LLaDA-Image achieves overall scores of 53.53 and 53.38 on the English and Chinese tracks, respectively, setting a new state-of-the-art among open-source models on both tracks. To support further research on capable and efficient generative models, we release our model weights, training code, and detailed recipes.

</details>


### [68] [Urban Boundaries, Social Barriers: A Benchmark and Vision-Centric Framework for Mapping Gated Communities and Equity Implications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03804)
*Minwei Zhao,Weiming Zhang,Jiawang Du,Qiming Liu,Weiming Zhuang,Pei Nie,Cai Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces GBA-GCs, a large-scale multimodal benchmark for detecting gated and open residential communities in China's Greater Bay Area, containing 37,444 residential compounds with satellite imagery, metadata, and structured attributes. A vision-centric multimodal classifier (MCGC) is proposed that fuses imagery, text, and structured cues to outperform baseline methods. The validated model is applied for metropolitan-scale mapping revealing equity issues including spatial clustering, privatized green space, and reduced pedestrian connectivity.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Gated communities significantly impact urban form, mobility, access to public services, and equity. However, existing studies on Chinese fengbi xiaoqu (gated residential communities) remain largely qualitative or small-scale, limiting reproducible city-scale analysis. There is a need for a large-scale benchmark to enable systematic, reproducible research on gated community recognition.

Method: The authors created GBA-GCs, a metropolitan-scale multimodal benchmark with 37,444 residential compounds including aligned boundary polygons, high-resolution satellite imagery, Chinese metadata, and structured attributes with expert-verified labels. They proposed MCGC (Multimodal Classifier for Gated Community), a vision-centric multimodal framework based on DINOv3-SAT that fuses imagery, text, and structured cues via modality-aware cross-attention and adaptive gating to mitigate modality imbalance.

Result: MCGC consistently outperforms strong unimodal and multimodal baselines. The validated model was applied for metropolitan-scale mapping, revealing equity-oriented findings including spatial clustering of gated communities, privatized green space, and reduced pedestrian connectivity.

Conclusion: The GBA-GCs benchmark enables reproducible city-scale analysis of gated communities in China. The MCGC framework demonstrates effective multimodal fusion for this task. The urban equity analysis reveals significant spatial disparities associated with gated communities, providing valuable insights for urban planning and policy.

Abstract: Communities are fundamental spatial units that shape urban form and social life. Whether a residential compound is spatially open or enclosed affects mobility, access to public services, and equity, yet studies of Chinese fengbi xiaoqu remain largely qualitative or small-scale, limiting reproducible city-scale analysis. We address this gap by introducing GBA-GCs, a metropolitan-scale multimodal benchmark for locally grounded gated/open community recognition in China's Greater Bay Area, covering 37,444 residential compounds with aligned boundary polygons, high-resolution satellite imagery, Chinese metadata, and structured attributes, together with expert-verified labels, inter-annotator reliability, and official evaluation splits. Built on this benchmark, we present Multimodal Classifier for Gated Community (MCGC), a vision-centric multimodal framework based on DINOv3-SAT that fuses imagery, text, and structured cues via modality-aware cross-attention and adaptive gating to mitigate modality imbalance. MCGC consistently outperforms strong unimodal and multimodal baselines. Finally, we apply the validated model to metropolitan-scale mapping and report equity-oriented findings including spatial clustering of GCs, privatized green space, and reduced pedestrian connectivity.
