The benchmark, code, and release documentation are available at https://github.com/MinweiZhao/GBA-GCs.

</details>


### [69] [VisCAD: A Foundation Model Suite with Multimodal Industrial CAD Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03811)
*JoyIndustrial VisCAD Team,Linxin Cai,Qiuhe Hong,Zhichao Huang,Guanlin Li,Hongsen Liu,Ziqi Liu,Yichen Long,Luya Wang,Yuchen Wang,Wenxiang Wu,Huimu Yu,Ning Zhang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VisCAD is a foundation model suite for AI-assisted computer-aided design (CAD) of industrial products, featuring a 27B parameter model (VisCAD-M1) trained for part-level design generation and a domain-specific harness for assembly-level generation. It addresses the limitations of existing specialized CAD models (narrow input domains, poor generalization) and general-purpose frontier models (inconsistent CAD performance).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing CAD models face a trade-off: specialized models are trained on narrow input domains (renders, texts) and generalize poorly, while general-purpose frontier models cover broader inputs but perform inconsistently across CAD domains. Industrial CAD design involves two challenging phases: part-level generation (mapping diverse inputs to CAD programs) and assembly-level generation (handling interacting parts, mating relations, pose estimation).

Method: VisCAD uses a 27B parameter model (VisCAD-M1) trained through mid-training and post-training for part-level design generation. For assembly-level generation, it leverages frontier models with a domain-specific harness. The model reuses VisCAD-M1 as a test-time verifier to improve results.

Result: On PubCADBench and RealCADBench, VisCAD-M1 achieves the highest average part-level score of 0.5540, surpassing the previous best frontier model (0.5496). Using VisCAD-M1 as a test-time verifier further raises the score to 0.5797, representing approximately 5% relative improvement over the previous state of the art. The domain-specific harness also demonstrates advantages over general-purpose harnesses in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

Conclusion: VisCAD successfully provides both broad generalization and strong CAD capability for realistic industrial products. The combination of a large domain-specific model with test-time verification and a domain-specific harness for assembly generation offers a promising approach to bridging the gap between specialized CAD models and general-purpose AI systems.

Abstract: AI-assisted computer-aided design (CAD) for industrial products involves two challenging phases. Part-level generation maps diverse forms of user intent, including renders, text descriptions, 2D drawings, and real photographs, to executable programs in a CAD domain-specific language. Assembly-level generation must additionally handle interacting parts, plan mating relations, estimate poses, and place all parts correctly. Existing specialized CAD models are commonly trained on narrow input domains, such as renders or texts, and often generalize poorly, while general-purpose frontier models cover broader inputs but perform inconsistently across CAD domains. We present VisCAD, a foundation model suite designed to provide both broad generalization and strong CAD capability for realistic industrial products. At its core is VisCAD-M1, a 27B model trained through mid-training and post-training for part-level design generation. On PubCADBench and RealCADBench, VisCAD-M1 achieves the highest average part-level score among the evaluated models, reaching 0.5540 compared with 0.5496 for the strongest frontier model. Reusing VisCAD-M1 as a test-time verifier can further raise the score to 0.5797, an approximately 5 percent relative improvement over the previous state of the art. VisCAD also includes a domain-specific harness that leverages frontier models for complex assembly generation and demonstrates advantages over general-purpose harnesses in both quantitative and qualitative evaluations.

</details>


### [70] [SPARK: Input-Conditioned Sparse Activation Modulation for Frozen DiT-based Super-Resolution](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03813)
*Federico Putamorsi,Leonardo Zini,Marcella Cornia,Lorenzo Baraldi*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SPARK introduces a lightweight input-conditioned controller that predicts bounded per-channel affine transformations for dominant channels in frozen DiT-based SR models, achieving gains in fidelity and perceptual quality by modulating only 8 channels per stream and block.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: DiT-based SR models have internal activations dominated by a small number of massive channels, yet improving perceptual quality typically requires fine-tuning or additional adapters, leaving this structured activation space unexplored for adaptation.

Method: 1) Characterize dominant channel behavior in pretrained SR backbones through controlled interventions; 2) Identify dominant channels via online activation-ranking procedure; 3) SPARK predicts bounded per-channel affine transformations for only selected channels; 4) Keep SR backbone and VAE frozen; 5) Optimize a small predictor conditioned on low-resolution VAE latent.

Result: Experiments on three DiT-based SR backbones across DIV2K, RealSR, and DRealSR show consistent gains in both fidelity and perceptual quality while modulating only eight channels per stream and block. Controlled comparisons show gains cannot be explained by parameter budget or access to selected channels alone.

Conclusion: Dominant channels can serve as a compact adaptation interface for frozen DiT-based SR models, enabling efficient quality improvement without fine-tuning the backbone.

Abstract: Real-world image super-resolution (SR) increasingly relies on Diffusion Transformer (DiT) backbones, whose internal activations can be dominated by a small number of massive channels. Yet improving perceptual quality in these models still typically requires fine-tuning the network or attaching additional adapters, leaving this structured activation space largely unexplored for adaptation. We investigate whether dominant channels can instead serve as a compact adaptation interface for frozen DiT-based SR models. We first characterize their behavior in pretrained SR backbones and show through controlled interventions that they strongly affect reconstruction quality. Building on this observation, we introduce SPARK, a lightweight input-conditioned controller that predicts bounded per-channel affine transformations for only the selected channels, while keeping the SR backbone and VAE frozen. Dominant channels are identified through an online activation-ranking procedure, and only a small predictor conditioned on the low-resolution VAE latent is optimized. Experiments on three DiT-based SR backbones across DIV2K, RealSR, and DRealSR show consistent gains in both fidelity and perceptual quality while modulating only eight channels per stream and block. Controlled comparisons further show that these gains cannot be explained by parameter budget or access to the selected channels alone.

</details>


### [71] [Select, Compress, Reinvest: A Controlled Study of Visual-Token Allocation in Long-Video MLLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03820)
*Prakhar Khatri*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper investigates frame selection strategies for long-video language models, finding that selection is the most impactful decision. Query-selected frames outperform uniform sampling by 6.9 points, and a decades-old algorithm (Orthogonal Matching Pursuit) matches or beats purpose-built selectors. Compression is nearly free, and reinvesting saved tokens into more frames yields 2-3 additional points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Frame selection in long-video language models is typically treated as a preprocessing detail, but this paper investigates whether it should be a carefully considered design choice. The authors note that published selectors vary multiple factors simultaneously (frame scorer, prompt boundary, resolution policy, answering model), making comparison difficult.

Method: The authors isolate three decisions (selection, spatial compression, and reinvestment of savings) and test them one at a time while holding other factors fixed. They evaluate six training-free selection rules across three long-video benchmarks using two answering models.

Result: Selection is the largest single lever: eight query-selected frames beat sixteen uniformly spaced ones by 6.9 points on LongVideoBench's hour-long bin. Orthogonal Matching Pursuit matches or comes within a point of every purpose-built selector. Compression is nearly free (at most 0.44 points lost). Reinvesting saved tokens into more compressed frames yields 2-3 additional points.

Conclusion: Frame selection significantly impacts long-video language model performance and should not be treated as a minor preprocessing detail. Simple algorithms like OMP can outperform purpose-built selectors. Spatial compression is cheap, but its value is realized only when savings are reinvested into more frames. The authors also highlight the importance of controlled experimental harnesses, having discovered an implementation bug and significant cross-harness variance (0.07-3.74 points).

Abstract: Long-video language models cannot look at every frame: an hour sampled once per second is 3,600 images, and a system keeps only a small fixed slice of that pool. Which frames survive that slice is usually treated as a preprocessing detail; we test whether it should be. Published selectors make the comparison hard because they change the frame scorer, the prompt boundary, the resolution policy, and the answering model all at once. We hold each fixed and vary one decision at a time: selection, spatial compression, and reinvestment of the savings, across six training-free selection rules, three long-video benchmarks, and two answering models. Selection is the largest single lever: on LongVideoBench's hour-long bin, eight query-selected frames beat sixteen uniformly spaced ones by 6.9 points, and Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, an unmodified decades-old sparse-approximation algorithm, matches or comes within a point of every purpose-built selector we compare it against, across all three benchmarks. Compression is close to free: halving each frame's spatial budget at fixed timestamps costs at most 0.44 points. Reinvestment is where that budget turns back into accuracy: spending the freed tokens on twice as many compressed frames, at a measured cost no higher than the original eight, returns a further two to three points; compression only pays off once its savings are spent this way. Along the way, an implementation bug in our own AKS baseline and a 0.07 to 3.74 point gap between two harnesses running the same published rules at the same budget show why these comparisons need to happen inside one controlled harness rather than across papers.

</details>


### [72] [VI3: Grounding Pretrained 3D Foundation Models with Inertial Cues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03824)
*Ernesto Lozano,Alberto Jaenal,Javier Civera*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VI3 is a model-agnostic framework that uses IMU readings to recover metric scale for pretrained 3D foundation models (3DFMs) from monocular images, addressing the limitation that 3DFMs cannot observe absolute scale from single views.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: 3D foundation models excel at predicting camera poses and dense depth with zero-shot generalization, but they cannot observe metric scale from monocular images alone, resulting in inaccurate absolute scale predictions. IMUs, present in most devices, naturally complement cameras by observing scaled motion.

Method: VI3 initializes and preintegrates IMU readings to obtain a metric motion reference, which is then used to recover the scale of 3DFM outputs. The method includes adaptable anchoring strategies tailored to diverse 3DFM architectures.

Result: Experiments on synthetic and real aerial datasets demonstrate that VI3 recovers metric scale without ground-truth supervision while preserving geometric consistency. It acts as a fine refinement under well-conditioned motion and as a strong prior when motion is less informative.

Conclusion: VI3 successfully enables metric-scale predictions from 3DFMs by leveraging IMU data, providing a model-agnostic solution that works across different 3DFM architectures without requiring ground-truth supervision.

Abstract: 3D foundation models (3DFMs) excel at predicting camera poses and dense depth from multiple views of a scene, showcasing strong zero-shot generalization. However, as metric scale is not observable from monocular images, their absolute scale predictions are typically inaccurate. Inertial measurement units (IMUs), present in most devices, naturally complement monocular cameras by observing scaled motion. We introduce VI3, a model-agnostic framework that metrically anchors a pretrained 3DFM using only IMU readings. VI3 initializes and preintegrates the IMU to obtain a metric motion reference, which is then used to recover the scale of the 3DFM outputs. Our method includes adaptable anchoring strategies tailored to diverse 3DFM architectures. Experiments on synthetic and real aerial datasets demonstrate that VI3 recovers metric scale without ground-truth supervision while preserving geometric consistency, acting as a fine refinement under well-conditioned motion and as a strong prior when motion is less informative.

</details>


### [73] [The impact of phase information for few-shot fine-grained image classification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03829)
*Ruiling Liu,Linyue Zhang,Wenyi Zeng,Jiamiao Lu,Weichuang Zhang,Changming Sun,Zejun Zhang,Xiao Zhao*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes PSF-Net, a novel network with an amplitude-phase integration (API) module that leverages phase information for few-shot fine-grained image classification. The method adaptively fuses local and global frequency amplitude and phase information to create comprehensive feature descriptors.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Few-shot fine-grained image classification requires distinguishing similar images with limited labeled examples. While amplitude information has been widely used, phase information, which captures structural relationships within images, remains underutilized. This work aims to address this gap by integrating both amplitude and phase information for improved classification.

Method: The study introduces a plug-and-play amplitude-phase integration (API) module that combines local and global frequency amplitude and phase information. Additionally, PSF-Net is proposed to adaptively fuse phase-based spatial and frequency information. The network can be integrated into standard episodic training architectures for end-to-end training from scratch.

Result: Extensive experiments on five public datasets demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art benchmarks.

Conclusion: Phase information plays a critical role in few-shot fine-grained image classification, and effectively integrating amplitude and phase information leads to superior performance. The proposed API module and PSF-Net provide an effective solution for this task.

Abstract: Few-shot fine-grained image classification (FSFGIC) aims to classify similar images with limited labeled examples. This work highlights the critical yet underutilized role of phase information in capturing structural relationships within an image. This study introduces a novel plug-and-play amplitude-phase integration (API) module that effectively combines local and global frequency amplitude and phase information for obtaining more comprehensive feature descriptors. Additionally, a dedicated network, named PSF-Net, is proposed that adaptively fuses phase-based spatial and frequency information for FSFGIS. The designed PSF-Net can be easily integrated into standard episodic training architectures for end-to-end training from scratch. Extensive experiments on five public datasets demonstrate that the method outperforms existing state-of-the-art benchmarks.

</details>


### [74] [GraFT: A Training-Free Framework for Spatial Reasoning in Multimodal Large Language Models via 3D Scene Graphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03892)
*Junqing Du,Fernando Ropero,Erkin Turkoz,Yanfeng Zhang,Lu Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: GraFT is a training-free framework that enhances 3D spatial reasoning in multimodal large language models by supplying missing 3D structure through a compact 3D scene graph, providing symbolic geometry tools, BEV rendering, and egocentric visual grounding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current MLLMs struggle with 3D spatial reasoning: precise geometric measurement, viewpoint transformation between egocentric and allocentric frames, and fine-grained visual attribute grounding. Existing remedies require costly fine-tuning or backbone-specific encoders.

Method: GraFT uses a 3D scene graph (3DSG) to provide three spatial reasoning capabilities: (1) deterministic geometry via symbolic tools, (2) allocentric layout through bird's-eye-view (BEV) rendering, and (3) visual-attribute grounding through task-relevant egocentric frames. No training or fine-tuning required.

Result: On ScanQA: improves every metric over baseline, raising CIDEr by 27%. On VSI-Bench: improves frozen MLLMs by up to 65%, surpassing all proprietary and open-source baselines, and several prominent fine-tuned spatial models.

Conclusion: A training-free approach using 3D scene graphs can effectively enhance 3D spatial reasoning in MLLMs without costly supervision or backbone-specific modifications, demonstrating that structural 3D knowledge can be injected as symbolic tools rather than learned parameters.

Abstract: 3D spatial reasoning underpins understanding and acting in the physical world, yet it remains unreliable in current multimodal large language models (MLLMs). These models falter at precise geometric measurement, at transforming between egocentric and allocentric viewpoints, and at grounding fine-grained appearance. The most common remedies fine-tune the model on large-scale curated spatial-reasoning datasets or attach dedicated encoders for 3D geometry, which typically couples the solution to costly supervision and a specific backbone. We instead introduce GraFT, a training-free framework that supplies the missing 3D structure through a compact, easily maintained 3D scene graph (3DSG). From this 3DSG, GraFT provides three spatial reasoning capabilities: (1) deterministic geometry through symbolic tools, (2) allocentric layout through a bird's-eye-view (BEV) rendering, and (3) visual-attribute grounding through task-relevant egocentric frames. On ScanQA, GraFT improves every metric over the same-backbone baseline, raising CIDEr by 27%. On VSI-Bench, GraFT improves frozen MLLMs by up to 65%, surpassing every proprietary and general-purpose open-source baseline, and several prominent fine-tuned spatial models.

</details>


### [75] [Concept of a Sensor Test Environment for Dusty Agricultural Conditions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03895)
*Peter Buckel,Johannes Hermann,Jonas Wollmann,Thomas Dietmueller,Timo Oksanen*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper presents a proving ground concept for testing autonomous agricultural machinery under dusty conditions. The facility includes both indoor (laboratory test bench and test hall) and outdoor areas to enable reproducible testing with and without dust during real-world agricultural operations. All test setups are visualized in 3D.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dust in agriculture poses a significant challenge for autonomous agricultural machinery as it can impair the performance of sensors and algorithms, potentially compromising the reliability and safety of autonomous systems.

Method: The authors propose a proving ground concept with two main components: (1) An indoor area featuring a laboratory test bench with a closed dust circulation system and a test hall for life-size objects; (2) An outdoor area with dedicated test setups enabling reproducible data recording with and without dust during real-world agricultural work. The entire proving ground and test setups are visualized in 3D.

Result: A comprehensive proving ground concept has been developed that allows for controlled testing of autonomous agricultural machinery under dusty conditions, with both indoor laboratory environments and outdoor real-world test scenarios.

Conclusion: The proposed proving ground provides a systematic approach to evaluate and improve the dust robustness of sensors and algorithms used in autonomous agricultural machinery, enabling reproducible and controlled testing across different environmental conditions.

Abstract: Dust in agriculture presents a significant challenge for autonomous agricultural machinery. Dust can impair the performance of sensors and algorithms. This work, therefore, presents a concept for a proving ground consisting of an indoor and outdoor area. The indoor area comprises a laboratory test bench where dust circulates in a closed system and a test hall where life-size objects can be placed. The outdoor area features dedicated test setups that enable reproducible data to be recorded with and without dust during real-world agriculture work. The proving ground and the setups are visualized in 3D.

</details>


### [76] [OctWorld: Long-Range World-Consistent Video Generation with Octree-Based 3D Mapping](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03919)
*Zelong Lv,Sicheng Xu,Jianfeng Xiang,Ruicheng Wang,Yue Dong,Yu Deng,Guangzhong Sun,Jiaolong Yang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: OctWorld is a video diffusion framework with persistent 3D memory (OctMap) that generates explorable, world-consistent, high-fidelity visual scenes from a single image along user-specified camera trajectories, addressing long-range generation challenges.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-range generation with extended camera paths and wide viewpoint coverage faces significant challenges in preserving spatial consistency when previously generated regions are revisited. Existing methods struggle with maintaining geometric and appearance details across diverse scene scales.

Method: OctWorld introduces OctMap, an extensible and spatially adaptive 3D memory that progressively fuses generated visual observations and corresponding depth maps into a global representation. OctMap employs TSDF (Truncated Signed Distance Function) fusion within a dynamic sparse octree whose spatial resolution adapts to image evidence, preserving geometric and appearance details while maintaining low memory overhead.

Result: OctWorld generates long-range, spatially consistent videos and outperforms prior methods on both existing benchmarks and challenging long-range generation settings. OctMap provides clear advantages over point-based caches and fixed-resolution TSDF volumes.

Conclusion: The proposed OctWorld framework with OctMap 3D memory successfully addresses the challenge of maintaining spatial consistency in long-range visual scene generation, providing a practical solution for explorable, world-consistent video generation from single images.

Abstract: We present OctWorld, a video diffusion framework with persistent 3D memory for generating explorable, world-consistent, and high-fidelity visual scenes. Given a single image, OctWorld performs stable autoregressive world generation along user-specified camera trajectories. We focus on long-range generation, characterized by extended camera paths and wide viewpoint coverage, where preserving spatial consistency is particularly challenging when previously generated regions are revisited. To address this problem, we introduce OctMap, an extensible and spatially adaptive 3D memory that progressively fuses generated visual observations and their corresponding depth maps into a global representation. OctMap employs TSDF fusion within a dynamic sparse octree whose spatial resolution adapts to image evidence. This design preserves geometric and appearance details across diverse scene scales while maintaining low memory overhead. Experiments demonstrate that OctWorld generates long-range, spatially consistent videos and outperforms prior methods on both existing benchmarks and challenging long-range generation settings. OctMap also provides clear advantages over point-based caches and fixed-resolution TSDF volumes. Project page: https://maxtirerror.github.io/octworldpage/

</details>


### [77] [Sparse auto-regressive modeling for scene generation from multi-view images](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03931)
*Thomas Lucas,Maxime Pietrantoni,Philippe Weinzaepfel,Wonjune Cho,Bardienus Pieter Duisterhof,Vincent Leroy,Jerome Revaud*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: SPAR3S is a sparse voxel-aligned 3D latent generative model for conditional scene completion from sparse views, learning a compact latent space directly from multi-view images using photometric supervision via differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting, and using a masked autoregressive transformer to predict missing voxels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing feed-forward reconstruction methods are limited to content visible in input images, while 3D generative modeling suffers from high computational cost of dense volumetric representations and scarcity of large-scale 3D supervision. The goal is to generate complete 3D scenes from sparse, unconstrained views while remaining computationally tractable.

Method: 1) Formulate 3D scene generation in a structured, compact, voxel-aligned 3D latent space where only occupied voxels are represented. 2) Learn this sparse latent space directly from multi-view images using photometric supervision via differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. 3) Given partial observed voxels from sparse input views, train a masked autoregressive transformer that jointly models voxel occupancy and latent token values to predict missing latent tokens and their spatial support.

Result: Achieves higher novel-view quality than prior work on synthetic indoor scenes, and demonstrates generalization on RealEstate10k (real-world data).

Conclusion: The sparse voxel-aligned 3D latent approach enables efficient and spatially consistent generation of unseen regions without requiring ground-truth 3D supervision, making it applicable to real-world data.

Abstract: Generating complete 3D scenes from sparse, unconstrained views is a fundamental challenge in 3D vision which requires reasoning beyond observed content while remaining computationally tractable. Existing feed-forward reconstruction methods are inherently limited to content visible in the input images, while 3D generative modeling is hindered by the high computational cost of dense volumetric representations and the scarcity of large-scale 3D supervision. We introduce SPAR3S, a sparse voxel-aligned 3D latent generative model for conditional scene completion without requiring ground-truth 3D data for supervision. Our key insight is to formulate 3D scene generation in a structured, compact, voxel-aligned 3D latent space where only occupied voxels are represented. We learn this sparse latent space directly from multi-view images using photometric supervision via differentiable 3D Gaussian Splatting. Given a partial set of observed voxels encoded from sparse input views, scene completion reduces to predicting the missing latent tokens and their spatial support within the voxel grid. To this end, we train a masked autoregressive transformer that jointly models voxel occupancy and latent token values, enabling efficient and spatially consistent generation of unseen regions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on synthetic indoor scenes, achieving higher novel-view quality than prior work. We further validate its generalization on RealEstate10k, highlighting its applicability to real-world data.

</details>


### [78] [WorldReward: Reward Modeling for Camera-Conditioned World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03952)
*Yibin Wang,Zehan Wang,Junshu Tang,Zhimin Li,Yujie Zhou,Jiazi Bu,Pengyang Ling,Feng Han,Zhixiong Zhang,Long Xing,Shengyuan Ding,Ziang Li,Cheng Jin,Yuhang Zang,Jiaqi Wang,Tianyu Pang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: WorldReward is a VLM-based reward model that evaluates both action consistency and visual quality in camera-conditioned world models by decomposing videos into action-aligned chunks and aggregating decisions via voting. It outperforms GPT-5.5 on human-annotated benchmarks and improves RL post-training of world models.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing rewards for camera-conditioned world models are insufficient: geometry-based rewards estimate trajectory execution but cannot judge visual quality, while image-based rewards measure frame quality without capturing action execution or temporal dynamics. The paper proposes that a vision-language model (VLM) can provide shared reasoning to relate actions to visual outcomes, but judging complete long videos against action sequences creates noisy context where local action evidence may be missed.

Method: WorldReward is a VLM-based pairwise preference reward model that decomposes paired videos into action-aligned chunks, organizes each chunk into structured visual evidence, and aggregates chunk-level decisions by voting into separate video-level action and visual-quality preferences. Training uses a large-scale reasoning-augmented preference dataset generated by a frontier VLM, refined through tool-based agent auditing and targeted human review.

Result: WorldReward achieves the highest agreement on all three dimensions (action consistency, appearance quality, motion quality) on WorldReward-Bench, exceeding GPT-5.5 by 3.42, 1.45, and 3.56 percentage points respectively. When used for RL post-training of HY-WorldPlay 1.5, it consistently improves both action execution and visual quality across short- to long-term horizons.

Conclusion: WorldReward successfully unifies action-consistency and visual-quality evaluation for camera-conditioned world models through chunk-level decomposition and voting aggregation. The approach demonstrates superior human agreement and practical effectiveness in improving world model training.

Abstract: Camera-conditioned world models generate interactive videos in which commanded actions should induce the expected scene changes while appearance, geometry, and temporal dynamics remain coherent. Existing rewards assess these requirements separately: geometry-based rewards estimate trajectory execution but cannot judge the visual quality of the executed motion, whereas image-based rewards measure frame quality without capturing action execution or temporal dynamics. We posit that a vision-language model (VLM) offers a shared reasoning space for relating actions to their visual outcomes. However, judging a complete long video against its full action sequence creates a lengthy, noisy context in which short-lived local action evidence can be missed or diluted. We present WorldReward, a VLM-based pairwise preference reward model that unifies action-consistency and visual-quality evaluation for camera-conditioned world models. WorldReward decomposes paired videos into action-aligned chunks, organizes each chunk into structured visual evidence, and aggregates chunk-level decisions by voting into separate video-level action and visual-quality preferences. To train it, we construct a large-scale reasoning-augmented preference dataset using structured judgments generated by a frontier VLM and refined through tool-based agent auditing and targeted human review. We further introduce WorldReward-Bench, a human-annotated benchmark measuring reward-model agreement with human preferences across action consistency, appearance quality, and motion quality. WorldReward achieves the highest agreement on all three dimensions, exceeding GPT-5.5 by 3.42, 1.45, and 3.56 percentage points, respectively. When used for RL post-training of HY-WorldPlay 1.5, it consistently improves both action execution and visual quality across short- to long-term horizons.

</details>


### [79] [RARF: Region-Aware Rectified Flows for 3D Brain MRI Inpainting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03956)
*Tomas Guija-Valiente,Blanca Rodriguez-Gonzalez,Norberto Malpica,Angel Torrado-Carvajal*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: RARF is a task-agnostic region-aware rectified flow framework for 3D brain MRI inpainting, designed to reconstruct healthy tissue within pathological regions by restricting stochastic interpolation to the inpainting region while preserving observed voxels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Medical image inpainting has the potential to improve automated brain MRI analysis by reconstructing healthy tissue within pathological regions, which is important for the BraTS Inpainting Challenge 2026.

Method: RARF uses a 3D neural network that receives partially voided images with Gaussian noise in missing regions, combined with inpainting masks and timesteps. The model is trained using masked flow-matching and reconstruction-consistency objectives, with mask-aware preprocessing and data augmentation. During inference, the learned velocity field transports initial noise toward plausible tissue reconstruction.

Result: The approach produces competitive reconstructions while maintaining anatomical consistency under the BraTS evaluation protocol.

Conclusion: RARF demonstrates that region-aware rectified flow is an effective approach for 3D brain MRI inpainting, successfully preserving patient-specific anatomical context while generating plausible reconstructions within pathological regions.

Abstract: Medical image inpainting has the potential to improve automated brain MRI analysis by reconstructing healthy tissue within pathological regions. We introduce RARF, a task-agnostic region-aware rectified flow framework for masked data generation. We instantiate the framework for 3D brain MRI inpainting as our submission to the BraTS Inpainting Challenge 2026. RARF restricts the stochastic interpolation process to the inpainting region, while the observed voxels remain fixed and provide patient-specific anatomical context. A three-dimensional neural network receives the partially voided image, with Gaussian noise filling the missing region, together with the inpainting mask and the corresponding timestep. The model is trained using masked flow-matching and reconstruction-consistency objectives, combined with mask-aware preprocessing and data augmentation. During inference, the learned velocity field transports the initial noise toward a plausible reconstruction of the missing tissue, which is then combined with the unchanged observed anatomy. Experiments under the BraTS evaluation protocol show that the proposed approach produces competitive reconstructions while maintaining anatomical consistency. Source code is available at: https://github.com/TomasGuija/rarf.

</details>


### [80] [Sharpening the Ensemble: An SSIM-Aligned Residual Refiner for Brain-MRI Inpainting Post-Processing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03981)
*Kubilay Kağan Kömürcü,İlkay Öksüz*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper addresses the blur artifact problem in Brain-MRI inpainting by using a lightweight residual refiner trained on outputs from an ensemble of two top-performing 2025 models. The approach uses an L1 loss augmented with a structural-similarity term (λ), achieving modest but statistically significant SSIM improvements (0.8767→0.8780 on held-out, p=2.2×10^{-7}) without requiring large-scale retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from a limitation in current state-of-the-art Brain-MRI inpainting models: while they perform well on the BraTS local-synthesis benchmark (which evaluates SSIM, PSNR, and MSE jointly), they produce blurry synthesized regions. This blurriness is attributed to the mean-seeking behavior of ℓ1 and MSE loss terms during training. The authors seek a post-processing solution that can sharpen results without the computational cost of retraining large models.

Method: The method involves two key components: (1) Creating a deep ensemble of the two co-first-place 2025 models from the BraTS benchmark; (2) Training a lightweight residual refiner on the ensemble's outputs using an ℓ1 loss augmented with a structural-similarity term. The weight λ of this structural-similarity term is varied as a hyperparameter. The refiner learns to add residual details to the ensemble output rather than generating from scratch.

Result: At a moderate λ value, the refiner improves SSIM over the ensemble from 0.8767 to 0.8780 on a held-out reproduction of the official scorer and from 0.8555 to 0.8572 on the official validation leaderboard, with negligible change in MSE. The improvement is consistent across 62.6% of held-out cases with high statistical significance (signed-rank p=2.2×10^{-7}). However, over-weighting the structural term reverses the gains. Two ablations confirm the effect: (1) adding any third model to the ensemble degrades performance; (2) classical unsharp masking fails to improve SSIM (best 0.8765 vs 0.8767), confirming the gain comes from learned sharpening rather than generic enhancement.

Conclusion: The authors conclude that their residual refiner provides a cheap, reproducible post-processing stage that improves an already strong ensemble without requiring large-scale retraining. The approach is both computationally efficient and statistically validated, though the absolute gain is small. The method represents a practical contribution to the BraTS challenge pipeline, offering a simple way to squeeze additional performance from top models.

Abstract: Brain-MRI inpainting replaces a masked region of a scan with synthesized, anatomically plausible healthy tissue, so that analysis tools built for healthy brains can be applied to images they would otherwise reject. On the BraTS local-synthesis benchmark, which ranks submissions on the structural similarity index (SSIM), the peak signal-to-noise ratio, and the mean squared error (MSE) jointly, the strongest recent models are accurate, but several report blurry synthesized regions and attribute this to the mean-seeking behavior of the $\ell_1$ and MSE terms in their training losses. We address this in post-processing, forming a deep ensemble of the two co-first-place 2025 models and training a lightweight residual refiner on the ensemble's own outputs under an $\ell_1$ loss augmented with a structural-similarity term whose weight $λ$ we vary. At a moderate $λ$ the refiner improves SSIM over the ensemble, from $0.8767$ to $0.8780$ on a held-out reproduction of the official scorer and from $0.8555$ to $0.8572$ on the official validation leaderboard, with essentially no change in MSE. The gain is small but consistent, improving $62.6\%$ of the held-out cases with a signed-rank $p=2.2\times10^{-7}$, whereas over-weighting the structural term reverses it. Two ablations bound the effect. Adding any third model to the two-model ensemble degrades it, and classical unsharp masking fails to improve SSIM at any strength (best $0.8765$ against $0.8767$), so the gain reflects learned rather than indiscriminate sharpening. The result is a cheap, reproducible post-processing stage that improves an already strong ensemble without any large-scale retraining.

</details>


### [81] [IchthyoNoma: Nomenclature and Context Sensitivity of Zero-Shot Biological Vision--Language Models for Bangladeshi Freshwater Fish Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03985)
*Nazim-E-Alam,Tarek Rahman,Md Kishor Morol*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper audits zero-shot vision-language models (CLIP, BioCLIP, BioCLIP2, Jina CLIP v2) for freshwater fish species recognition in Bangladesh, revealing that model performance reflects multiple factors beyond visual knowledge, including multilingual alignment, nomenclature, and prompt formulation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Zero-shot VLMs are increasingly used as training-free species recognizers, but reported accuracy may not solely reflect visual species knowledge. The authors audit whether these models truly "see" species or rely on other cues like text alignment and naming conventions.

Method: Evaluated four VLMs on seven freshwater-fish categories from two Bangladeshi sources (10,321 images): BFF-15 (English common names) and SylFishBD (scientific names). Tested English vs. Bengali prompts, and conducted ablation experiments with blur, gray masking, and white masking interventions.

Result: BioCLIP2 achieved 72.36% on BFF-15 and 68.91% on SylFishBD, vastly outperforming generic CLIP (25.15% and 14.40%). Bengali prompts performed near chance (14.22-14.29%), while Jina partially recovered Bengali discrimination (21.89% and 16.36%). Interventions showed species-dependent effects: no significant weak-blur effect, modest losses from stronger blur/gray masking, and strong white-mask artifacts.

Conclusion: Zero-shot biological VLM scores jointly reflect biological specialization, multilingual alignment, nomenclature, prompt formulation, and context. Performance metrics alone cannot distinguish true visual species recognition from text-mediated discrimination. Users should interpret VLM-based species identification results with caution.

Abstract: Zero-shot vision-language models (VLMs) are increasingly used as training-free species recognizers, but reported accuracy can reflect more than visual species knowledge. We audit CLIP, BioCLIP, BioCLIP2, and a multilingual Jina CLIP v2 control on seven freshwater-fish categories from two Bangladeshi sources (10,321 images). BioCLIP2 reaches 72.36% on BFF-15 with English common names and 68.91% on SylFishBD with scientific names, versus 25.15% and 14.40% for generic CLIP. BioCLIP2 Bengali prompts are near chance in balanced accuracy (14.22-14.29%); Jina partially recovers Bengali discrimination to 21.89% and 16.36%, but bare Bengali names return to 14.29% on both sources. Paired SylFishBD interventions show no significant weak-blur effect, modest losses from stronger blur/gray masking, a larger white-mask artifact, and strong species dependence. Zero-shot biological VLM scores therefore jointly reflect biological specialization, multilingual alignment, nomenclature, prompt formulation, and context.

</details>


### [82] [Catalogue Photography as a Cold Start: Toward Deployable Carbide Burr Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03995)
*Abilash Philip Madavath,Chandra Yuvesh Aubeeluck,Augustin Raju,Nicolas Pyschny,Felix Hackelöer,Florian Zwanzig*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: The paper addresses automated quality assurance for milling tools/carbide rotary burrs using computer vision under cold-start constraints (no labeled field data). The authors investigate how well catalogue supervision transfers to field photographs, finding that metric learning works well on catalogue images but transfers poorly, and that simple domain-reducing techniques (grayscale conversion, Hungarian assignment) provide the largest transfer gains.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Automating verification of manufactured batches of milling tools remains a manual, error-prone task. Computer vision solutions face a cold-start problem since no labeled field imagery exists - only manufacturer catalogue photos are available as supervision source.

Method: The authors use metric learning with frozen feature extractors to investigate catalogue-to-field transfer. They systematically measure the gap between catalogue separability and field photograph performance, testing approaches including grayscale conversion and Hungarian assignment for constrained retrieval.

Result: Three key insights: (1) Off-the-shelf frozen feature extractors fail to reliably separate head shape and tooth profile attributes; (2) Metric learning achieves near-perfect unsupervised cluster discovery on catalogue images (ARI 0.94-0.97) but less than half transfers to field photos; (3) Largest transfer gains come from simple domain-reducing changes: grayscale conversion (+0.22) and Hungarian assignment (+0.11).

Conclusion: Catalogue photography should be treated as a useful cold start rather than deployment-ready training domain. The paper provides empirical baselines and an evaluation protocol for catalogue-to-field transfer in precision tool manufacturing, demonstrating that simple domain adaptation techniques outperform model scale or representation complexity.

Abstract: Verifying that manufactured batches of milling tools or carbide rotary burrs conform to production order sheets remains a largely manual and error-prone quality assurance task. Automating this process with computer vision faces a critical cold-start constraint since no labelled imagery is available, leaving manufacturer catalogue photography as the sole source of supervision. We investigate how far catalogue supervision can support an industrial recognition pipeline under domain shift, explicitly measuring the gap between catalogue separability and performance on held-out field photographs. Our findings reveal three key insights. First, off-the-shelf frozen feature extractors do not reliably separate the two task attributes, head shape and tooth profile, motivating targeted representation learning. Second, metric learning produces near-perfect unsupervised cluster discovery on catalogue images (adjusted Rand index 0.94--0.97), but less than half of this gain transfers to field photographs. Third, the largest transfer gains do not come from model scale or representation complexity, but from simple changes that reduce domain sensitivity: converting images to grayscale (+0.22) and constraining retrieval using the known order sheet via Hungarian assignment (+0.11). We therefore treat catalogue photography as a useful cold start rather than a deployment-ready training domain, and provide empirical baselines and an evaluation protocol for catalogue-to-field transfer in precision tool manufacturing.

</details>


### [83] [The Blind Spot in 2D Infants' Pose Estimation:Robust Learning from Noisy Annotations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04009)
*Emanuele Cardinale,Marco Proietti,Alessandro Cacciatore,Maria Francesca Spadea,Lucia Migliorelli,Sara Moccia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces REMIND (REliable keypoint selection via Memory of traINing Dynamics), a clustering-based method to identify and handle noisy annotations in preterm infant pose estimation. The approach uses keypoint-wise training dynamics to detect noisy labels without prior knowledge of the noise distribution, enabling noise-free model training for clinical applications.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Noisy annotations are a significant challenge for supervised deep learning in pose estimation, particularly in clinical settings like neonatology where labeling preterm infant images is inherently challenging due to keypoint self-occlusions and caregiver interference. While label noise robustness has been studied for classification, it remains underexplored for pose estimation, despite being critical for trustworthy clinical applications.

Method: REMIND is a clustering-based keypoint-selection strategy that exploits keypoint-wise training dynamics to identify noisy labels. The method does not assume any prior knowledge of the noise distribution. It was evaluated using three different pose estimation architectures on the NeoPose dataset.

Result: REMIND achieved up to 93% Area Under the Curve (AUC) in correctly identifying noisy annotations across multiple corruption scenarios when evaluated on the NeoPose dataset (46 videos of 46 preterm infants recorded in real clinical settings) with three different pose estimation architectures.

Conclusion: This is the first study to explicitly address label noise in preterm infants' pose estimation. REMIND effectively identifies noisy annotations without prior noise distribution assumptions, paving the way for trustworthy learning-based algorithms for infant monitoring support when data quality cannot be guaranteed.

Abstract: Noisy annotations pose a significant challenge for supervised deep learning, as neural networks rely on large-scale, high-quality labeled data whose corruption can severely impair model performance. Although robustness to label noise has been extensively studied for classification tasks, it remains relatively underexplored in Pose Estimation (PE). This limitation becomes critical in clinical contexts, including neonatology, where PE of preterm infants is used to support the assessment of spontaneous motility, a key indicator of neurodevelopmental trajectories. In such settings, infants' images labeling is further hindered by visual challenges (e.g., keypoint self-occlusions, caregiver interference), making the annotation process inherently susceptible to errors. To tackle noisy annotations in PE, we introduce REliable keypoint selection via Memory of traINing Dynamics (REMIND), a clustering-based keypoint-selection strategy that exploits keypoint-wise training dynamics to identify noisy labels without assuming any prior knowledge of the noise distribution, thus enabling noise-free model training. When evaluated on the proprietary NeoPose dataset, comprising 46 videos of 46 preterm infants recorded in real clinical settings, REMIND correctly identifies noisy annotations across multiple corruption scenarios, achieving up to 93\% Area Under the Curve (AUC) with three different PE architectures used in the relevant literature. To our knowledge, this is the first study to explicitly address label noise in preterm infants' PE, paving the way for the design of trustworthy learning-based algorithms for infants'monitoring support when data quality cannot be guaranteed.

</details>


### [84] [Stable and Scalable Bundle Adjustment of Holistic 3D Structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04026)
*Shaohui Liu,Rémi Pautrat,Daniel Barath,Richard Hartley,Viktor Larsson,Marc Pollefeys*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a unified framework that extends traditional point-based Bundle Adjustment (BA) to jointly optimize geometric features (points, lines) and higher-order relations (parallelism, coplanarity, wireframes). The key insight is modeling groups as camera-like entities and expressing group constraints through 2D reprojection measurements, preserving the sparsity structure of classical BA while avoiding direct 3D regularization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional bundle adjustment was developed for optimizing camera intrinsics, poses, and sparse 3D points. While extensions to lines and other primitives exist, integrating richer geometric structures like parallelism, coplanarity, or wireframes introduces significantly increased computational cost and reduced numerical stability. There was a need for a unified framework that can handle both geometric features and higher-order relations efficiently.

Method: The paper introduces a taxonomy distinguishing: (1) scalable geometric features with direct 2D measurements (points, lines), and (2) groups encoding higher-order relations (coplanarity, parallelism). The key approach models groups as camera-like entities within the BA framework. Both group constraints and cross-feature relations (point-line associations) are expressed through 2D reprojection measurements, preserving sparsity under Schur elimination while avoiding direct 3D regularization.

Result: Experiments on real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate runtime performance comparable to classical point-only bundle adjustment, while producing significantly richer 3D structures and improved geometric accuracy.

Conclusion: The proposed unified framework successfully extends bundle adjustment to handle higher-order geometric relations without sacrificing computational efficiency or numerical stability. It achieves comparable runtime to classical point-based BA while delivering richer 3D reconstructions and better geometric accuracy.

Abstract: Bundle Adjustment (BA) is a cornerstone of 3D computer vision and has benefited from decades of advances in sparse optimization and numerical methods. It was originally developed for jointly optimizing camera intrinsics, poses and sparse 3D points. While extensions incorporate lines and other primitives, integrating richer geometric structures such as parallelism, coplanarity, or wireframes often introduces significantly increased computational cost and reduced numerical stability. In this paper, we propose a unified framework that extends bundle adjustment to jointly optimize geometric features and higher-order relations. We first introduce a taxonomy that distinguishes scalable geometric features with direct 2D measurements (e.g., points and lines), from groups encoding higher-order relations (e.g., coplanarity, parallelism, etc.), where we show that groups can be modeled as camera-like entities within the bundle adjustment framework. Building on this formulation, we propose that both group constraints and cross-feature relations (i.e., point-line associations) can be expressed through 2D reprojection measurements. By formulating group-induced and cross-feature reprojection errors, we preserve the sparsity structure of classical point-based BA under Schur elimination, while avoiding direct 3D regularization that degrades the conditioning and stability. Experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets demonstrate runtime performance comparable to classical point-only bundle adjustment, while producing significantly richer 3D structures and improved geometric accuracy.

</details>


### [85] [DSAQuant: Denoising-Stage-Aligned Quantization-Aware Training for Video Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04031)
*Shuaiting Li,Zelin Gao,Haibin Shen,Yujun Shen,Haotong Qin,Yinghao Xu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: DSAQuant addresses visual quality degradation in quantized video diffusion models by aligning quantization training and inference with the stage-wise nature of video denoising. It uses Denoising-Stage Oriented Supervision during training and Denoising-Stage Gated Guidance during inference, achieving up to 6.60 improvement on VBench under aggressive W3A3 quantization.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video diffusion models (VDMs) have high memory and computational costs hindering practical deployment. While quantization-aware training (QAT) can compress these models, existing methods suffer from severe degradation in visual details, texture fidelity, and sharpness, despite preserving prompt semantics, global layout, and coarse motion.

Method: The root cause is traced to timestep-agnostic design that overlooks stage-wise functionality: early denoising steps establish global structure and motion, while middle and late steps refine local appearance and high-frequency details. DSAQuant proposes two techniques: (1) Denoising-Stage Oriented Supervision during training - preserves teacher distillation in early steps for stable structure planning, shifts later steps toward target-driven optimization for detail reconstruction; (2) Denoising-Stage Gated Guidance during inference - disables CFG in final denoising steps to prevent amplification of quantization-induced errors.

Result: Extensive experiments on Wan and CogVideoX families under W4A4 and W3A3 settings show DSAQuant consistently outperforms SOTA QAT baseline, improving VBench average score by up to 6.60 under aggressive W3A3 quantization while preserving strong text-video alignment.

Conclusion: Effective VDM quantization requires not only reducing quantization error, but also aligning quantization training and inference with the stage-wise nature of video diffusion. This is a novel insight that the denoising process has distinct functional stages that should be considered in quantization design.

Abstract: Video diffusion models (VDMs) have achieved impressive progress in text-to-video generation, but their high memory and computational costs hinder practical deployment. Quantization-aware training (QAT) is an effective solution for compressing and accelerating advanced generative models without runtime overhead at inference. However, existing QAT methods suffer from a distinctive challenge in VDMs: while they often preserve prompt semantics, global layout, and coarse motion, the quantized model severely degrades visual details, texture fidelity, and sharpness. In this paper, we trace this degradation to the timestep-agnostic design of conventional quantization pipelines, which overlooks the stage-wise functionality of video denoising. In VDMs, early denoising steps mainly establish global structure and motion, whereas middle and late steps refine local appearance and high-frequency details. Based on this insight, we propose DSAQuant, a Denoising-Stage-Aligned Quantization-aware training framework for VDMs. During training, Denoising-Stage Oriented Supervision preserves teacher distillation in early steps for stable structure planning, while shifting later steps toward target-driven optimization to enhance detail reconstruction. During inference, Denoising-Stage Gated Guidance disables CFG in the final denoising steps to prevent it from amplifying quantization-induced errors into high-frequency artifacts. Extensive experiments on the Wan and CogVideoX families under W4A4 and W3A3 settings show that DSAQuant consistently outperforms the SOTA QAT baseline, improving the VBench average score by up to 6.60 under aggressive W3A3 quantization while preserving strong text-video alignment. These results demonstrate that effective VDM quantization requires not only reducing quantization error, but also aligning quantization training and inference with the stage-wise nature of video diffusion.

</details>


### [86] [Editable Visual Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04034)
*Junyan Ye,Wei Liu,Dongzhi Jiang,Zichen Wen,HaoDong Li,Zhutao Lv,Jiaxin Lin,Jinhua Yu,Jun He,Zilong Huang,Rui Chen,Weijia Li*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes "Editable Visual Design," a new paradigm that combines vision-language models (VLMs) as creative decision-makers with diffusion-based image generators as visual simulators, enabling production-grade editable web designs through a "imagine first, then act" workflow.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors address a fundamental limitation: diffusion-based image generators produce flattened bitmaps that cannot be edited layer-by-layer, while code-based generation lacks aesthetic intuition and struggles with complex visual assets. This creates a gap between high-quality visual generation and practical editability.

Method: The proposed method uses a VLM as the "creative brain" for requirement understanding, task planning, and aesthetic judgment, paired with an image generation model as an on-demand "visual world simulator" to synthesize standalone visual assets. The system operates in a closed-loop "imagine first, then act" workflow where the agent generates isolated assets, writes native HTML/CSS, and iteratively refines designs based on visual rendering feedback. Additionally, "Agent Design Replay" is introduced to capture and reproduce the creative reasoning trajectory.

Result: The system delivers editable artifacts with decoupled layers and real text, enabling intuitive mouse dragging and layout adjustments through a graphical user interface. Validation on posters, infographics, and other scenarios demonstrates successful achievement of both refined aesthetics and production-grade editability.

Conclusion: The "Editable Visual Design" paradigm successfully bridges the gap between diffusion-based visual quality and code-based editability, providing a practical solution for professional design workflows that require both aesthetic excellence and post-production editability.

Abstract: While diffusion base models such as GPT-Image-2 and Nano-Banana exhibit remarkable visual expressiveness, their end-to-end generation inherently yields flattened bitmaps with error-prone text, precluding layer-wise post-editing. Conversely, code-based visual generation via Coding Agents provides precise layout control and decoupled layers, yet remains constrained by a lack of global aesthetic intuition and the difficulty of coding complex visual assets.
  To address this, we propose Editable Visual Design, a new paradigm driven by a Coding Agent. We designate the VLM as the ``creative brain'' for requirement comprehension, task planning, and aesthetic judgment, while utilizing the image generation model as an on-demand ``visual world simulator'' to synthesize standalone visual assets. Operating under an ``imagine first, then act'' closed-loop workflow, the agent generates isolated assets, writes native HTML/CSS, and iteratively refines the design against visual rendering feedback.
  Furthermore, Agent Design Replay faithfully reproduces the creative and reasoning trajectory akin to that of professional human designers. Ultimately, the system delivers editable artifacts with decoupled layers and real text, enabling users to perform intuitive mouse dragging and layout adjustments on a graphical user interface. Validations on posters, infographics, and other scenarios show that this paradigm successfully achieves both refined aesthetics and production-grade editability.

</details>


### [87] [Continuous Actions from Discrete Minds: Latent-Aligned Planning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04070)
*Ruoyu Yao,Yusen Xie,Qingzhao Liu,Pei Liu,Zewei Yang,Yipeng Zhu,Xiaolong Wang,Jun Ma*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LaPla introduces a unified Vision-Language-Action (VLA) framework for autonomous driving that uses latent-aligned planning to bridge the gap between discrete semantic reasoning and continuous physics-constrained motion execution. It employs a residual VQ-VAE-based action tokenizer that serves as a physical prior, eliminating quantization errors through continuous latent projection rather than discrete codebook lookups.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core challenge is bridging the gap between the discrete reasoning capabilities of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and the continuous, physics-constrained nature of autonomous driving. Existing VLA methods suffer from quantization errors when using discrete codebook lookups and time-consuming autoregressive generation.

Method: 1) Design an action tokenizer based on residual VQ-VAE capturing vehicle kinematics and trajectory features into a structured latent space. 2) Use the VQ-VAE representation as a physical prior to bridge modality gap between semantics and raw action space. 3) Incorporate concurrent action queries to attend to multimodal context (multi-view images, historical actions, textual instructions) in a single forward pass. 4) Project hidden states directly into pretrained VQ-VAE latent space. 5) Use frozen decoder to translate continuous latents into actions, eliminating quantization errors and bypassing autoregressive generation.

Result: - On nuScenes benchmark: competitive open-loop performance with 15.52% reduction in long-horizon L2 error compared to state-of-the-art VLA methods
- On NVIDIA AlpaSim simulator: 33.34 percentage points improvement in success rate with significantly reduced inference latency

Conclusion: LaPla successfully bridges semantic understanding and precise motion execution through latent-aligned planning. By repurposing VQ-VAE as a physical prior and eliminating discrete codebook lookups, it achieves superior performance in both open-loop (nuScenes) and closed-loop (AlpaSim) evaluations, demonstrating the effectiveness of continuous latent projection for physics-constrained autonomous driving.

Abstract: Bridging the gap between the discrete reasoning of Vision-Language Models and the continuous, physics-constrained nature of autonomous driving remains a significant challenge. In this work, we introduce LaPla, a unified Vision-Language-Action (VLA) framework featuring latent-aligned planning to seamlessly ground semantic understanding in precise motion execution. We first design an action tokenizer based on a residual vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE), capturing vehicle kinematics and encoding trajectory features into a structured latent space. Rather than discrete codebook lookups that inevitably introduce quantization errors, LaPla repurposes this representation as a physical prior to bridge the modality gap between high-dimensional semantics and the raw action space. Specifically, given multimodal inputs integrating multi-view images, historical actions, and textual instructions, LaPla incorporates concurrent action queries to causally attend to the multimodal context in a single forward pass, projecting hidden states directly into the pretrained VQ-VAE latent space. The frozen decoder then translates these continuous latents into actions, effectively eliminating quantization errors and ensuring physically plausible trajectories while bypassing time-consuming autoregressive generation. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that LaPla achieves competitive open-loop performance, reducing long-horizon L2 error by 15.52% compared to state-of-the-art VLA methods. Closed-loop evaluations on the NVIDIA AlpaSim simulator further confirm its superior capability in ensuring smooth driving progress, improving the success rate by 33.34 percentage points with significantly reduced inference latency.

</details>


### [88] [TAP-Path: Task-Adaptive Structural and Token Pruning for Efficient and Trustworthy Pathology Foundation Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04071)
*Mehedi Hasan,Ashfak Yeafi,Md Khairul Islam*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TAP-Path is a task-adaptive compression framework that reduces a large pathology foundation model (Virchow2) by retaining only 24 of 32 transformer blocks and 70% of patch tokens, achieving better accuracy than the full model while using 24.96% fewer parameters and 35.20% less compute.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Large pathology foundation models with hundreds of millions of parameters achieve state-of-the-art performance but incur high inference costs. This paper aims to improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off through task-adaptive structural and token sparsification.

Method: TAP-Path combines five techniques: (1) validation-driven transformer-block selection, (2) physical removal of redundant blocks, (3) input-adaptive patch-token pruning, (4) multi-depth feature recovery, and (5) a lightweight gated task head. The framework directly restructures the pretrained Virchow2 encoder rather than distilling it into a separate student.

Result: TAP-Path reduced encoder parameters by 24.96% (631.24M to 473.70M) and compute by 35.20% (340.13G to 220.40G FLOPs). Across three seeds, it achieved 87.98% test accuracy, 81.26% balanced accuracy, and 82.38% macro-F1 on a 32-class histopathology benchmark—outperforming full Virchow2 (86.89%) and UNI2-h (87.67%). It achieved Brier score of 0.1800 and failure-detection AUROC of 0.9047. On external CPTAC evaluation (433 samples), it achieved 91.22% accuracy and 91.10% balanced accuracy.

Conclusion: Task-adaptive structural and token sparsification can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of large pathology foundation models while preserving reliability under internal and external evaluation. The approach demonstrates that compression can actually improve accuracy while significantly reducing computational cost.

Abstract: Pathology foundation models improve transferable representation learning for histopathology, but recent gains often rely on encoders with hundreds of millions of parameters and high inference cost. We propose TAP-Path, a task-adaptive compression framework that directly restructures a pretrained Virchow2 encoder rather than distilling it into a separate student. TAP-Path combines validation-driven transformer-block selection, physical removal of redundant blocks, input-adaptive patch-token pruning, multi-depth feature recovery, and a lightweight gated task head. The final model retains 24 of 32 transformer blocks and 70% of patch tokens after pruning, reducing encoder parameters by 24.96% (631.24M to 473.70M) and analytical encoder compute by 35.20% (340.13G to 220.40G FLOPs). Across three task-head optimization seeds, TAP-Path achieved $87.98 \pm 0.067%$ test accuracy, $81.26 \pm 0.49%$ balanced accuracy, and $82.38 \pm 0.48%$ macro-F1 on a 32-class histopathology benchmark, compared with 86.89% for full Virchow2 and 87.67% for UNI2-h. TAP-Path achieved a Brier score of $0.1800 \pm 0.0005$ and failure-detection AUROC of $0.9047 \pm 0.0060$. A validation-only rare-aware objective improved rare-class balanced accuracy in a secondary operating analysis. Frozen external evaluation on 433 CPTAC samples yielded $91.22 \pm 0.83%$ accuracy and $91.10 \pm 0.81%$ balanced accuracy. These results show that task-adaptive structural and token sparsification can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off of large pathology foundation models while preserving reliability under internal and external evaluation.

</details>


### [89] [CORE: Improving Compositional Reasoning in MLLM Embedding via Reranker Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04083)
*Tingyu Song,Mingxin Li,Yanzhao Zhang,Dingkun Long,Chu Liu,Pengjun Xie,Yilun Zhao,Shu Wu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: CORE distills compositional reasoning from cross-attentive rerankers into embedding models using a Rank-KL objective that trains embeddings to reproduce the reranker's fine-grained rankings across five compositional matching levels. This achieves state-of-the-art results on compositional retrieval benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: MLLM-based embedding models struggle with compositional retrieval - they cannot distinguish scenes with same concepts but different attribute-object bindings. However, the same backbone can resolve these distinctions when used as a cross-attentive reranker, motivating knowledge distillation from reranker to embedding model.

Method: CORE synthesizes candidate lists spanning five compositional matching levels and introduces a Rank-KL objective that trains the embedding model to reproduce the reranker's fine-grained ranking. The paper compares three approaches under the same data and tuning budget: contrastive learning, pairwise CoSENT, and listwise Rank-KL.

Result: Rank-KL achieves strongest overall performance. CORE-RERANKER-8B achieves 82.7% total average, outperforming Jina-Reranker by 10.7 points on COLA, SUGARCREPE++, and NEGBENCH benchmarks. CORE-EMBED-8B achieves best total average (0.666) among all evaluated embedding models. Improvements transfer to MCMR benchmark without sacrificing retrieval performance on COCO and Flickr30K.

Conclusion: The Rank-KL objective effectively distills compositional judgments from the reranker into the embedding model. Both CoSENT and Rank-KL utilize multi-level supervision more effectively than contrastive learning, with Rank-KL achieving the best overall performance. The approach successfully transfers to other benchmarks while maintaining standard retrieval performance.

Abstract: MLLM-based embedding models remain limited in compositional retrieval, often failing to distinguish scenes containing the same concepts but different attribute-object bindings. Yet the same backbone can resolve such distinctions when used as a cross-attentive reranker, motivating us to distill its compositional judgments into the embedding model. We propose CORE, which synthesizes candidate lists spanning five compositional matching levels and introduces a Rank-KL objective that trains the embedding model to reproduce the reranker's fine-grained ranking. We further introduce a graded evaluation protocol and compare contrastive learning, pairwise CoSENT, and listwise Rank-KL under the same data and tuning budget. Our comparison shows that both CoSENT and Rank-KL use the multi-level supervision more effectively than contrastive learning, with Rank-KL achieving the strongest overall performance. Across three compositional reasoning benchmarks (COLA, SUGARCREPE++, NEGBENCH), CORE-RERANKER-8B achieves an 82.7% total average, outperforming Jina-Reranker by 10.7 points, while CORE-EMBED-8B achieves the best total average (0.666) among all evaluated embedding models. The improvements transfer to the MCMR benchmark without sacrificing retrieval performance on COCO and Flickr30K.

</details>


### [90] [Efficient Semantic Understanding from Digital Foveation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04088)
*Caterina Caccavella,Vittorio Fra,Andreas Ziegler,Giulia D'Angelo,Yulia Sandamirskaya*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes a lightweight active-vision pipeline for semantic segmentation using digital foveated perception, inspired by biological vision systems. The approach selectively allocates computational resources based on saliency, using high-resolution foveal observations for important regions and low-resolution context elsewhere. On ADE20K-Object, a single foveated observation achieves 95.9% Top-1 and 96.9% Top-3 accuracy while using only 4.7% of computation. Semantic accumulation recovers 90.6% object recall at 58.6% computation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Dense semantic segmentation wastes computational resources by processing all image regions uniformly, regardless of their complexity or task relevance. The authors seek a more efficient approach inspired by biological foveated vision, where attention is selectively focused on informative regions.

Method: The paper introduces a lightweight active-vision pipeline with five key components: (1) saliency-driven fixation selection to determine where to look, (2) high-resolution foveal observations for selected regions, (3) low-resolution contextual information for the broader scene, (4) semantic accumulation to combine observations over time, and (5) adaptive computation allocation. Evaluation uses both conventional dense prediction metrics and object-level metrics.

Result: On ADE20K-Object dataset: (1) A single foveated observation achieves 95.9% of baseline Top-1 accuracy and 96.9% of baseline Top-3 accuracy while requiring only 4.7% of computational cost. (2) Semantic accumulation recovers 90.6% of baseline object recall while using 58.6% of computation.

Conclusion: The results demonstrate that substantial semantic understanding can emerge from sparse observations when computation is allocated selectively. Active vision offers an efficient alternative to uniform dense processing, and the authors advocate for evaluation protocols beyond conventional pixel-wise segmentation metrics.

Abstract: Dense semantic segmentation allocates computational resources uniformly across the entire image, regardless of scene complexity or task relevance. Inspired by biological vision, we investigate whether semantic understanding can be achieved more efficiently through digital foveated perception. We introduce a lightweight active-vision pipeline that combines saliency-driven fixation selection, high-resolution foveal observations, low-resolution contextual information, semantic accumulation, and adaptive computation. Beyond conventional dense prediction metrics, we use object-level evaluation to measure semantic understanding under sparse observations. On ADE20K-Object, a single foveated observation achieves 95.9% of the baseline Top-1 accuracy and 96.9% of the baseline Top-3 accuracy while requiring only 4.7% of the computational cost. At the scene level, semantic accumulation recovers 90.6% of the baseline object recall while using 58.6% of the computation. These results suggest that substantial semantic understanding can emerge from sparse observations when computation is allocated selectively, highlighting active vision as an efficient alternative to uniform dense processing and motivating evaluation protocols beyond conventional pixel-wise segmentation metrics.

</details>


### [91] [The Shape of Time: Video-Token Contrast for Temporal Understanding in VideoLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04110)
*Yumeng Shi,Quanyu Long,Yin Wu,Wenya Wang*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: VT-Contrast is a representation-level temporal counterfactual objective for VideoLMs that supervises late-layer video tokens by contrasting order-preserving video views with reordered counterfactuals, improving temporal understanding without architectural changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern VideoLMs receive ordered video streams but their supervision acts on generated text rather than video-token representations where event dynamics should emerge. This mismatch allows models to learn temporal answers from shortcuts (objects, scenes, language priors) without requiring internal video representations to capture event progression.

Method: VT-Contrast supervises selected late-layer last-frame video tokens (where temporal information is integrated before language generation) and contrasts order-preserving views with same-video reordered counterfactuals graded by Kendall tau distance. It requires no architectural changes and is compatible with diverse VideoLM training tasks.

Result: Improves overall performance across temporal understanding benchmarks.

Conclusion: VT-Contrast provides a simple yet effective representation-level temporal supervision objective that addresses the supervision mismatch problem in VideoLMs, enabling better internal video representations without requiring architectural modifications.

Abstract: Seeing frames in order does not mean representing time. Modern VideoLMs receive ordered video streams, yet their main supervision acts on generated text rather than video-token representations where event dynamics should first emerge. This mismatch allows models to learn temporal answers from shortcuts such as objects, scenes, and language priors, without requiring internal video representations to capture event progression. To address this, we propose VT-Contrast, a representation-level temporal counterfactual objective for VideoLMs. Its design asks where temporal supervision should act and what temporal differences it should expose. VT-Contrast supervises selected late-layer last-frame video tokens, where temporal information is expected to be integrated before language generation, and contrasts order-preserving views with same-video reordered counterfactuals graded by Kendall tau distance. It requires no architectural changes, is compatible with diverse VideoLM training tasks, and improves overall performance across temporal understanding benchmarks. Our code is available at https://github.com/ANDgate99/VT-Contrast.

</details>


### [92] [BooM-VVT: Boosting Mask-Free Video Virtual Try-On with Image-Level Pseudo Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04120)
*Wei Zhang,Xin Li,Peishu Shi,Jialin Gao,Xuekang Peng,Zhichao Lian,Yeying Jin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: BooM-VVT is a mask-free video virtual try-on framework that addresses limitations of existing methods by using multi-stage training with image-level pseudo data, garment-sensitive keyframe sampling, and Frame-Shared 3D-RoPE, supported by a new large-scale multi-view dataset called OmniView.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing keyframe-driven VVT methods rely on masks for try-on region localization, making them vulnerable to large motions and severe occlusions.
