While mask-free image-based try-on exists, extending it to videos is prohibitively expensive. Additionally, coarse keyframe sampling and scarcity of multi-view data limit garment consistency and diverse try-on tasks.

Method: The proposed BooM-VVT framework includes: (1) Multi-stage training strategy leveraging image-level pseudo data for mask-free localization learning, reducing need for costly video-level pseudo data; (2) Garment-Sensitive Keyframe Sampling that selects keyframes based on garment-relevant body regions; (3) Frame-Shared 3D-RoPE to establish spatiotemporal correspondences between keyframes and target video frames; (4) Construction of OmniView, a large-scale multi-view try-on dataset.

Result: BooM-VVT achieves superior temporal consistency and garment fidelity over existing methods.

Conclusion: The mask-free approach combined with garment-sensitive keyframe sampling and spatiotemporal correspondence modeling effectively addresses the challenges of VVT, enabling high-quality try-on videos under complex camera viewpoints and diverse try-on tasks.

Abstract: Video virtual try-on (VVT) aims to generate realistic videos of a person wearing a target garment. Recent methods leverage a keyframe-driven video generation paradigm to improve in-the-wild performance, yet they still rely on masks to localize try-on regions, making them vulnerable to large motions and severe occlusions. Although mask-free image-based try-on methods have shown promising results by leveraging large-scale pseudo data, extending this paradigm to videos remains difficult, as constructing video-level pseudo data is prohibitively expensive. Furthermore, coarse keyframe sampling and the scarcity of multi-view try-on data limit existing keyframe-driven methods in maintaining garment consistency and handling diverse try-on tasks.
  To address these challenges, we propose BooM-VVT, a mask-free VVT framework built upon the keyframe-driven paradigm. To achieve mask-free VVT, we introduce a multi-stage training strategy that leverages image-level pseudo data for mask-free localization learning, substantially reducing the need for costly video-level pseudo data. To improve garment consistency, we propose Garment-Sensitive Keyframe Sampling, which selects keyframes based on garment-relevant body regions to better capture garment appearance. We further introduce Frame-Shared 3D-RoPE to establish spatiotemporal correspondences between keyframes and target video frames for accurate garment-detail transfer. Finally, we construct OmniView, a large-scale multi-view try-on dataset to support reliable try-on video generation under complex camera viewpoints and diverse try-on tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that BooM-VVT achieves superior temporal consistency and garment fidelity over existing methods. Project page: https://boomvvt.github.io/boomvvt.

</details>


### [93] [Beyond Retrieval: Progressive Latent Memory Evolution for Streaming Video Understanding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04131)
*Hongyu Qu,Guangming Yao,Ling Xing,Xiaobin Hu,Rongxing Ding,Guibin Zhang,Fan Zhang,Yi Yuan,Xiangbo Shu,Shuicheng Yan*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: LatentStream introduces a progressive latent working memory framework for streaming video understanding that shifts from store-and-retrieve to retrieve-and-internalize paradigm. It uses hierarchical memory organization with Jenks-guided consolidation, evolving latent memory tokens with expanding receptive fields, and confidence-guided optimization to achieve state-of-the-art results on video benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing streaming video approaches use store-and-retrieve paradigms that keep historical evidence as external visual context, preventing internalization into compact latent memory for continuous reasoning. This limits the model's ability to continuously guide streaming reasoning under strict causality and bounded memory constraints.

Method: Three coordinated components: (1) Query-agnostic Hierarchical Streaming Memory organizes visual history into short-, mid-, and long-term levels under fixed memory budget via Jenks-guided adaptive consolidation; (2) Hierarchical Latent Memory Evolution equips latent memory tokens with progressively expanding receptive fields to iteratively retrieve and internalize historical evidence; (3) Progressive Confidence-guided Latent Memory Optimization constructs hierarchical progression reward from group-wise predictive entropy to jointly refine latent memory tokens and retrieved evidence.

Result: Achieves new state-of-the-art results on existing online and offline video benchmarks.

Conclusion: The retrieve-and-internalize paradigm with progressive latent memory evolution effectively addresses streaming video understanding constraints, demonstrating the advantage of internalizing historical evidence into compact latent memory over external store-and-retrieve approaches.

Abstract: Streaming video understanding requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to process continuous visual inputs and respond to user queries under strict causality and bounded memory. Existing approaches typically compress historical observations into an external memory bank and retrieve query-relevant evidence as additional visual context. Though effective, this store-and-retrieve paradigm keeps historical evidence as external visual context, preventing it from being internalized into a compact, evolving latent memory that can continuously guide streaming reasoning. To bridge this gap, we introduce LatentStream, a progressive latent working memory framework that shifts streaming memory from store-and-retrieve to retrieve-and-internalize. Specifically, LatentStream comprises three coordinated components. First, Query-agnostic Hierarchical Streaming Memory organizes visual history into short-, mid-, and long-term levels under a fixed memory budget through Jenks-guided adaptive consolidation. Once a query arrives, Hierarchical Latent Memory Evolution equips groups of latent memory tokens with progressively expanding memory receptive fields, enabling them to iteratively retrieve historical evidence from their corresponding scopes and internalize it into a compact, fixed-length latent memory. Finally, Progressive Confidence-guided Latent Memory Optimization constructs a hierarchical progression reward from group-wise predictive entropy and jointly refines the latent memory tokens and retrieved evidence, encouraging increasingly confident streaming reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LatentStream achieves new state-of-the-art results on existing online and offline video benchmarks.

</details>


### [94] [Persistent Identity Preservation in Generative Image Models: A Benchmark and Evaluation System](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04151)
*Mengwei Ren,Xuaner Zhang,Zhihao Xia*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper benchmarks three paradigms for identity preservation in generative image models (input context, trainable parameters, and persistent identity layers) across generation, editing, restoration, and multi-subject tasks. The study finds that persistent identity layers significantly reduce identity degradation while maintaining image quality and instruction adherence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current generative image models struggle to preserve subject identity during generation/editing when pose, expression, appearance, viewpoint, or surrounding scene changes. Existing methods use fundamentally different approaches to represent identity, but systematic comparison is lacking.

Method: Systematic benchmark of three paradigms: (1) input context (GPT-Image-2, NB2), (2) trainable subject-specific parameters (LoRA), (3) persistent identity layer (PHOTA IDENTITY). Tests across subject-driven generation, editing, restoration, and multi-subject settings with increasing stress on identity preservation.

Result: Identity preservation remains a distinct limitation of current models; strong image quality and instruction following don't guarantee identity fidelity. Identity degradation worsens under iterative edits, small subject scales, severe degradation, and multi-subject composition. Persistent identity layers substantially reduce degradation across tasks while maintaining comparable instruction adherence and perceptual quality.

Conclusion: Identity does not simply emerge from increasingly capable generative models. Instead, identity can be represented as persistent subject knowledge that composes independently with the underlying generative model, suggesting a new architectural approach for subject-driven generation.

Abstract: Generative image models can now produce high-quality images, follow complex instructions, and support precise edits, but they still struggle to preserve who or what is being depicted. When generating or editing images of a specific subject, identity may drift as the pose, expression, appearance, viewpoint, or surrounding scene changes. Existing subject-driven methods make fundamentally different choices about where identity is represented: through the input context (GPT-Image-2, NB2), as trainable subject-specific model parameters (LoRA), or as a persistent identity layer (PHOTA IDENTITY) reusable across generations and edits. We systematically benchmark these paradigms across subject-driven generation, editing, restoration, and multi-subject settings, with tasks designed to increasingly stress identity preservation. Our results show that identity preservation remains a distinct limitation of current generative foundation models: strong image quality and instruction following do not necessarily imply strong identity fidelity, and identity degradation becomes more pronounced under iterative edits, small subject scales, severe image degradation, and multi-subject composition. Persistent identity substantially reduces this degradation across generation, editing, and restoration, consistently improving identity preservation when applied to different foundation models while maintaining comparable instruction adherence and perceptual image quality. These results suggest that identity does not simply emerge from increasingly capable generative models, but can instead be represented as persistent subject knowledge that is composed independently with the underlying generative model.

</details>


### [95] [Zero-Shot Novel Depth Synthesis Using 3D Foundation Models Scene Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04174)
*Denis M. Akola,David F. Fouhey*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper introduces Z3D, a method that leverages internal representations of 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs) like VGGT to predict depth maps for novel views through latent diffusion. The approach demonstrates that internal representations of 3DFMs contain sufficient 3D scene knowledge to decode hidden surfaces and generate realistic depth predictions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors investigate whether internal representations of 3D Foundation Models can be used to infer 3D structure from novel viewpoints. The hypothesis is that solving 3D reconstruction requires these models to learn general knowledge about 3D scenes, which should be encoded in their latent representations.

Method: The approach involves two key steps: (1) Demonstrating that hidden surfaces can be decoded from internal 3DFM representations, and (2) Proposing Z3D, which estimates pointmaps in unseen views by performing latent diffusion on 3DFM representations.

Result: Z3D can predict realistic depth maps for new views across multiple datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of using internal 3DFM representations for novel view synthesis.

Conclusion: Internal representations of 3D Foundation Models contain sufficient 3D scene knowledge to enable novel view synthesis. Z3D's success with latent diffusion on these representations opens promising directions for leveraging foundation models for 3D vision tasks.

Abstract: 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs) such as VGGT have recently pushed the boundaries of 3D vision by predicting rich unified representations with feed-foward transformers. The scene representations learned by these models enable strong performance on multiple 3D vision tasks. In this paper, we investigate using their internal representations to infer 3D in the scene from new views. Our hypothesis is that in order to solve the task of 3D reconstruction, these models need to learn a representation that includes a large amount of general knowledge about 3D scenes. After showing that it is possible to decode hidden surfaces from internal 3DFM representations, we propose a method, Z3D, that estimates pointmaps in unseen views by doing latent diffusion on 3DFM representation. We show that Z3D can predict realistic depth maps for new views across multiple datasets.

</details>


### [96] [Seeing Before Synthesizing: VLM-Guided Transition Event Discovery for Weakly-Supervised Dense Video Captioning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04183)
*Ye-Chan Kim,Seunghee Choi,SeungJu Cha,Si-Woo Kim,Hwiseon Kim,Hyungee Kim,Dong-Jin Kim*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: This paper proposes Seeing Before Synthesizing (SBS), a novel framework for weakly-supervised dense video captioning that addresses limitations in prior work by providing adaptive, visually grounded linguistic guidance for inter-event transitions in untrimmed videos.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Weakly-Supervised Dense Video Captioning aims to localize and describe multiple events in untrimmed videos given only event-level captions. Prior work synthesizes auxiliary transition captions via LLM, but these captions lack visual grounding and are rigidly assigned to every inter-event gap at fixed locations and durations, limiting effectiveness.

Method: The proposed SBS framework uses three key components: (1) A VLM generates frame-level narratives for inter-event gaps to provide visually grounded linguistic guidance; (2) Semantic variation across gaps is analyzed to detect transitions; (3) For identified transitions, inter-event temporal masks are refined by blending the temporal midpoint with the semantic change point and selecting the width that maximizes vision-language alignment.

Result: Experiments on ActivityNet Captions and YouCook2 datasets demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both captioning and localization tasks.

Conclusion: SBS achieves superior performance by adaptively providing visually grounded linguistic guidance only where warranted, rather than applying rigid captions to all inter-event gaps. The adaptive mask refinement approach based on semantic change points improves both event localization and captioning quality.

Abstract: Weakly-Supervised Dense Video Captioning aims to localize and describe multiple events in untrimmed videos given only an ordered set of event-level captions per video. Recent work synthesizes auxiliary transition captions via LLM to provide additional vision-language alignment, but these captions lack visual grounding and are rigidly assigned to every inter-event gap at a fixed location and duration. To address these, we propose Seeing Before Synthesizing (SBS), a framework that adaptively provides visually grounded linguistic guidance only where warranted. Leveraging a VLM, we generate frame-level narratives for the inter-event gaps and detect transitions from the semantic variation across them. For identified transitions, we then refine inter-event temporal masks by blending the temporal midpoint with the semantic change point and selecting the width that maximizes vision-language alignment. Experiments on ActivityNet Captions and YouCook2 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both captioning and localization.

</details>


### [97] [One Editor, Many Edits: A Unified Training-Free Framework for Diverse Video Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04190)
*Adheesh Sunil Juvekar,Onkar Kishor Susladkar,Kiet A. Nguyen,Muntasir Wahed,Nabeel Bashir,Xiaona Zhou,Tianjiao Yu,Vedant Shah,Ismini Lourentzou*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: EditVid is a training-free video editing framework that unifies instruction-guided and reference-guided editing, supporting style transfer, attribute modification, object insertion, part-level editing, and subject replacement. It achieves 78.16 FiVE-Acc on the FiVE benchmark, outperforming the strongest training-free baseline (58.95), and receives 51.8% preference in user studies over 7 competing methods.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video editing spans diverse paradigms, but achieving high-quality instruction-guided and subject-guided editing within a single unified framework remains challenging. Existing methods typically excel at one type of editing but fail to provide a unified solution.

Method: EditVid combines three key techniques: (1) sparse causal memory for local coherence, (2) correspondence-based post-attention token injection for long-range identity preservation, and (3) soft latent blending for edit locality. The framework is training-free.

Result: On FiVE benchmark, EditVid achieves 78.16 FiVE-Acc, compared with 58.95 for the strongest evaluated training-free baseline. Competitive results are obtained on IVEBench. A user study shows 51.8% overall preference for EditVid over 7 competing methods.

Conclusion: EditVid successfully provides a unified training-free framework for diverse video editing tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance among training-free methods and strong user preference.

Abstract: Video editing spans diverse editing paradigms, yet achieving high-quality instruction-guided and subject-guided editing within a single unified framework remains challenging. We introduce EditVid, a training-free framework combining sparse causal memory for local coherence, correspondence-based post-attention token injection for long-range identity preservation, and soft latent blending for edit locality. The same framework supports instruction-guided and reference-guided edits, including style transfer, attribute modification, object insertion, part-level editing, and subject replacement. On FiVE, EditVid achieves 78.16 FiVE-Acc, compared with 58.95 for the strongest evaluated training-free baseline, while obtaining competitive results on IVEBench. A user study further shows a 51.8\% overall preference for EditVid over 7 competing methods.

</details>


### [98] [Puffin-World: Scaling a Unified Multimodal Model with Native 3D World States](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04196)
*Kang Liao,Yihang Luo,Xiao-Ming Wu,Linyi Jin,Size Wu,Chunyu Lin,Yao Zhao,Fei Wang,Wei Li,Chen Change Loy*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Puffin-World is a unified multimodal architecture that integrates physical understanding, spatial simulation, and 3D world generation/reconstruction without external offline modules. It jointly models physics, geometry, and appearance states with an Omni-Camera representation, enables physically consistent world generation through grounded camera properties, and supports closed-loop applications like world exploration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for 3D world construction and interaction rely on external offline modules, which limits integration and flexibility. The authors aim to create a unified framework that can reliably construct and interact with 3D worlds by natively modeling physical dynamics, geometry, and appearance together.

Method: The framework jointly models three native world states: physics (gravity field and latitude), geometry (depth), and appearance (image). It uses a unified Omni-Camera representation supporting diverse tasks and flexible motions. A strategy for propagating physical dynamics across future frames is introduced. Absolute camera properties are grounded in the real world for physically consistent generation. Appearance and geometry are coupled within a single generative process for joint view synthesis and geometry reconstruction.

Result: Puffin-World enables physically consistent and visually stable world generation. The unified paradigm supports interleaved closed-loop applications requiring synergy across multiple tasks, including mimic and self-calibrated world exploration. The approach is validated on Puffin-16M, a dataset with 15 million vision-language-camera triplets and 1 million trajectories with challenging motions.

Conclusion: Puffin-World presents a unified paradigm for multimodal 3D world understanding, successfully integrating physical understanding, spatial simulation, and generation/reconstruction. The released code, models, and datasets provide a foundation for further research in this area.

Abstract: We propose Puffin-World, a unified multimodal architecture that integrates physical understanding, spatial simulation, and 3D world generation and reconstruction without relying on external offline modules. To reliably construct and interact with 3D worlds, our framework jointly models three native world states: physics (gravity field and latitude), geometry (depth), and appearance (image), together with a unified Omni-Camera representation that supports diverse tasks and flexible motions. Beyond modeling these states, we introduce a strategy for propagating physical dynamics across future frames. By grounding absolute camera properties in the real world, Puffin-World enables physically consistent and visually stable world generation. We further couple appearance and geometry within a single generative process, jointly synthesizing each future view and reconstructing its underlying geometry. This unified paradigm enables interleaved closed-loop applications requiring synergy across multiple tasks, including mimic and self-calibrated world exploration. To scale Puffin-World to complex scenarios, we construct Puffin-16M, comprising 15 million vision-language-camera triplets and 1 million trajectories featuring various and challenging motions. To foster further research in this area, we released the code, models, and datasets.

</details>


### [99] [Principia: Relational Physics Tests for Video Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04200)
*Varun Varma Thozhiyoor,Shivam Tripathi,Venkatesh Babu Radhakrishnan,Anand Bhattad*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Principia is a benchmark for evaluating physical reasoning in video models through relational consistency between paired objects, independent of camera calibration. It covers 8 physical phenomena across 4 dynamic types. Current video generators and VLMs perform poorly on this benchmark.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current evaluation methods for physical reasoning in video models are problematic because absolute motion measurements depend on ambiguous factors like frame rate, object scale, and camera calibration. The authors propose using relational consistency between objects obeying the same physical law, which remains independent of calibration.

Method: The authors introduce Principia benchmark with 8 physical phenomena (gravity, restitution, friction, rotational inertia, projectile motion, momentum, pendulum, mass-spring oscillation) across translational, rotational, collisional, and oscillatory dynamics. They propose a calibration-independent consistency score that quantifies physical violation directly in image space without needing camera calibration.

Result: Across thousands of generations from six state-of-the-art video generators, no model exceeds 0.42 on Principia despite all scoring around 0.8 on VBench. Vision-language models evaluated on detecting relational physics violations achieve only up to 67% accuracy, with most performing near chance level.

Conclusion: Current video generation models fail to capture physical laws correctly despite performing well on standard benchmarks like VBench. This suggests a significant gap in physical reasoning capabilities. Additionally, even vision-language models struggle to detect physical violations, indicating the benchmark effectively identifies a meaningful weakness in current AI systems.

Abstract: Evaluating physical reasoning in video models is difficult because absolute motion measurements depend on frame rate, object scale, and camera calibration, all of which are often ambiguous or unavailable in generated video. We propose a different approach. When two objects in the same scene obey the same physical law, their motions must satisfy predictable relationships, and these relationships hold independent of calibration. We introduce Principia, a benchmark that evaluates Newtonian physics through relational consistency between paired objects. Principia spans eight phenomena - gravity, restitution, friction, rotational inertia, projectile motion, momentum, pendulum, and mass-spring oscillation - across translational, rotational, collisional, and oscillatory dynamics, using real-world scenes recorded under controlled protocols. We also introduce a calibration-independent consistency score that quantifies physical violation directly in image space. Across thousands of generations from six state-of-the-art video generators, no model exceeds 0.42 on Principia despite all scoring around 0.8 on VBench. Vision-language models are evaluated on their ability to detect relational physics violations, with the best model achieving only 67% accuracy and most performing near chance level.

</details>


### [100] [Scal3R: Learning Efficient Multi-Relative Pose Query for Scalable Online 3D Reconstruction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04201)
*Chin-Yang Lin,Yang-Che Sun,Cheng Sun,Fu-En Yang,Min-Hung Chen,Yen-Yu Lin,Wei-Chen Chiu,Yu-Lun Liu*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: Scal3R addresses the problem of online 3D reconstruction failing on long videos by reformulating it as multi-reference relative pose querying. It uses lightweight learnable tokens (~1% parameters) injected into a frozen backbone via asymmetric attention, combined with online pose-graph optimization with loop closure to suppress long-range drift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Online 3D reconstruction models perform poorly on long videos because regressing poses relative to a fixed first-frame anchor forces extrapolation far beyond the training distribution. Small drifts accumulate and amplify into significant geometric collapse, though the backbone's local geometry remains intact while only the global pose head breaks down.

Method: Scal3R uses lightweight learnable tokens (about 1% of parameters) injected into a completely frozen backbone via asymmetric attention. This approach queries poses relative to multiple past keyframes rather than a single anchor. An online pose-graph optimization system with loop closure is employed to suppress long-range drift.

Result: Scal3R reaches convergence in 8 hours on a single GPU. It reduces the average ATE by over 60% on KITTI compared to the online baseline. It also achieves state-of-the-art performance across Virtual KITTI, Sintel, TUM-Dynamic, ScanNet, and 7-Scenes.

Conclusion: The decoupled nature of the problem (local geometry intact, global pose head fails) enables an effective solution through multi-reference relative pose querying with minimal parameter overhead. This approach successfully handles long video sequences where traditional online methods collapse.

Abstract: Online 3D reconstruction models perform poorly on long videos. This happens because regressing poses relative to a fixed first-frame anchor forces extrapolation far beyond the training distribution. Small drifts accumulate and amplify into significant geometric collapse. However, we observe that per-frame depth remains stable throughout this failure. The backbone's local geometry remains intact; only the global pose head breaks down. Motivated by this decoupling, we introduce Scal3R. This approach reformulates online reconstruction as multi-reference relative pose querying. We use lightweight learnable tokens, which make up about ~1% of the parameters, and inject them into a completely frozen backbone via asymmetric attention. This setup queries poses relative to multiple past keyframes. An online pose-graph optimization system with loop closure suppresses long-range drift. Scal3R reaches convergence in 8 hours on a single GPU. It reduces the average ATE by over 60% on KITTI compared to the online baseline. It also achieves state-of-the-art performance across Virtual KITTI, Sintel, TUM-Dynamic, ScanNet, and 7-Scenes. Project page: https://linjohnss.github.io/scal3r/

</details>


### [101] [TokenMatch: 3D Mesh Correspondence Transformer with Curvature-Guided Tokenisation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04202)
*Adeela Islam,Zorah Lähner,Vittorio Murino,Vladislav Golyanik*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: TokenMatch is a transformer-based model for 3D shape correspondence estimation that can handle partial observations and non-isometric deformations. It uses self- and cross-attention with curvature-guided patch tokenization to learn geometric descriptors, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks while running at sub-second inference speeds.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While data-driven 3D shape correspondence estimation has improved, robust matching under partial observations and strong non-isometric deformations remains challenging. Existing methods rely on hand-crafted descriptors or template-based representations, while generative models over functional maps suffer from high inference cost, limited interpretability, and poor generalization to partial shapes.

Method: TokenMatch uses a transformer-based architecture with self- and cross-attention mechanisms to learn patch-level and point-level relations. Meshes are adaptively tokenized into patches using shape curvature guidance, enabling effective learning of shape-specific geometric descriptors. The model is trained exclusively on BeCoS, a challenging non-isometric partial-to-partial shape-matching dataset.

Result: TokenMatch achieves consistently high performance on standard benchmarks (CP2P, PSMAL, BeCoS, FAUST, SCAPE, SHREC'19) for both partial and full shape matching, outperforming existing methods in mean geodesic error and intersection-over-union metrics while running at sub-second inference speeds.

Conclusion: TokenMatch demonstrates that training on partial-to-partial shape matching enables generalization to full shapes without retraining or fine-tuning. The curvature-guided tokenization and attention mechanisms enable effective learning of geometric descriptors for correspondence estimation across various challenging scenarios.

Abstract: While data-driven 3D shape correspondence estimation has recently seen substantial progress, robust matching under partial observations and strong non-isometric deformations remains challenging. Existing learning-based approaches often rely on hand-crafted descriptors or template-based representations, whereas recent generative models over functional maps suffer from high inference cost, limited interpretability, and poor generalisation to partial shapes. In response to these limitations, this paper introduces TokenMatch, a new transformer-based unified model for estimating 3D shape correspondences. Our feed-forward approach trained exclusively on BeCoS, a challenging non-isometric partial-to-partial shape-matching dataset, can generalise to matching full shapes without retraining or fine-tuning. TokenMatch uses self- and cross-attention mechanisms to efficiently learn patch-level and point-level relations as well as dense correspondences between shape pairs. Our core insight is that meshes can be adaptively tokenised into patches using shape curvature guidance, enabling effective learning of shape-specific geometric descriptors for correspondence estimation. We evaluate TokenMatch on standard benchmarks for partial and full shape matching, including CP2P, PSMAL, BeCoS, FAUST, SCAPE, and SHREC'19. Our method achieves consistently high performance, in most cases outperforming existing methods for partial and full shape matching in the mean geodesic error and intersection-over-union metrics, while also running faster at sub-second inference speeds.

</details>


### [102] [Temporal Self-Distillation: Learning Visual State Tracking in Videos Without Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04203)
*Shravan Venkatraman,Wenshuai Zhao,Mohammad Hassan Vali,Arno Solin*

Main category: cs.CV

TL;DR: S³T is the first fully self-contained framework for continuous video state tracking, using self-supervised self-distillation over time where a denser temporal view serves as teacher to train a sparse-view student model without any labels or external teacher.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Video state tracking aims to monitor continuous changes in video content over time, but existing methods require labels, separate teacher models, or reward signals. The key insight is that denser temporal views of the same clip provide richer information to recover running states more accurately than sparse views.

Method: The method treats temporal sampling density as privileged information. A denser view of a video clip serves as the teacher, while a sparse-view student with identical weights learns to match the teacher's next-token distribution. The model generates its own training targets, requiring no labels, separate teacher, or reward signal, and adds no inference cost.

Result: On LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B: VSTAT accuracy improved by +1.74 as single model, +2.38 with souping, and +2.70 with additional vision-encoder adaptation. Prior self-evolving methods left state tracking largely unchanged. Transfer to real videos: +7.95 on VSTAT-YouTube and +4.50 on MVBench Action Count.

Conclusion: S³T demonstrates that self-supervised self-distillation using temporal density as privileged information effectively improves video state tracking without external supervision, showing significant transfer capability from synthetic to real videos.

Abstract: We introduce S$^3$T (Self-Supervised Self-Distillation over Time), which, to the best of our knowledge, is the first fully self-contained framework for continuous video state tracking. Our method treats temporal sampling density as privileged information, based on the hypothesis that a denser view of the same clip recovers the running state more accurately. This view serves as the teacher, while a sparse-view student with the same weights learns to match its next-token distribution. The model generates its own target, so training requires no labels, separate teacher, or reward signal, and adds no inference cost. On LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B, S$^3$T improves VSTAT accuracy by $+1.74$ as a single model, $+2.38$ with souping, and $+2.70$ with additional vision-encoder adaptation, while prior self-evolving methods leave state tracking largely unchanged. The capability learned from unlabeled synthetic clips transfers to real videos, improving performance by $+7.95$ on VSTAT-YouTube state-tracking questions and $+4.50$ on MVBench Action Count.

</details>

### [103] [ReRoom: Blending Virtual and Physical Contexts for In Situ Room Planning in Mixed Reality](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03596)
*Hongliang Yang,Yanjing Xu,Anhang Zhang,Hui Ye,Pengfei Xu*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: ReRoom is a mixed-reality system for in situ room-layout authoring that allows users to evaluate, refine, and preserve layout decisions directly in the physical room using a virtual room proxy and a skill-guided layout agent.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for room layout planning either separate layout editing from the physical room or provide limited support for evaluating and refining whole-room proposals in situ. Users need to evaluate candidate layouts at true scale, refine their intent, and carry accepted decisions into later iterations - all grounded in the physical context.

Method: ReRoom presents a shared layout state through a virtual room proxy spatially registered to the target room. Users refine proposals through direct manipulation or language and preserve accepted placements. The system uses a skill-guided layout agent whose room-layout design skill operationalizes three principles synthesized from established interior-design guidance, grounded in a normalized representation of the scanned room and reusable geometric checks.

Result: ReRoom produces high-quality layouts for non-rectangular rooms, and its in situ workflow improves the room-planning experience over an otherwise equivalent off-site VR workflow.

Conclusion: The research demonstrates that mixed-reality systems with skill-guided agents can enable effective in situ room layout authoring, maintaining physical context throughout the design process while producing high-quality layouts.

Abstract: Planning a real domestic space is an in situ authoring process: users evaluate candidate layouts at true scale, refine their intent, and carry accepted decisions into later iterations. Existing approaches either separate layout editing from the physical room or provide limited support for evaluating and refining whole-room proposals in situ. We present ReRoom, a mixed-reality system for in situ room-layout authoring. ReRoom presents a shared layout state through a virtual room proxy spatially registered to the target room, allowing interaction and layout generation to remain grounded in the physical context. Users refine the current proposal through direct manipulation or language and preserve accepted placements, allowing each generated update to continue the same evolving design. To balance layout quality with generation efficiency, ReRoom uses a skill-guided layout agent whose room-layout design skill operationalizes three principles that we formulate by synthesizing established interior-design guidance for real-room layout generation. The skill grounds these principles in a normalized representation of the scanned room and reusable geometric checks. Evaluations show that ReRoom produces high-quality layouts for non-rectangular rooms, while its in situ workflow improves the room-planning experience over an otherwise equivalent off-site VR workflow. Code will be released upon acceptance of the paper.

</details>


### [104] [TileGS: Tile-Local Depth Binning for Gaussian Splatting Rasterization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03613)
*Wei Tan,Matias Turkulainen,Lauri Ilola,Hamed Rezazadegan Tavakoli,Juho Kannala*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: TileGS is a tile-local reorganization of 3D Gaussian Splatting that breaks long tile ranges into shorter depth-local ranges, rasterizes them in front-to-back order, and applies selective repair for compositing. It achieves 1.44x raster-kernel speedup on RTX 4090 and ~1.07x end-to-end frame speedups while matching baseline output quality (|Delta PSNR| < 0.001 dB).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard 3DGS rasterization traverses globally sorted tile streams creating long per-tile ranges and heavy geometry-attribute traffic, which limits rendering performance despite 3DGS's high visual quality.

Method: TileGS reorganizes Gaussian splatting at tile level by: (1) converting long tile ranges into shorter depth-local ranges, (2) rasterizing in front-to-back order, (3) applying selective repair where coarse ordering is insufficient. Profiled using Nsight Compute to understand performance characteristics.

Result: Mean 1.44x raster-kernel speedup on RTX 4090, 1.069x end-to-end frame speedup on RTX 4090, and 1.094x on RTX 1000 Ada over gsplat. Matches gsplat output within numerical noise (|Delta PSNR| < 0.001 dB, |Delta SSIM| < 0.001, |Delta LPIPS| < 0.001). Profiling reveals TileGS is faster despite lower SM throughput, lower active-warp occupancy, and higher DRAM traffic, with 1.26x reduction in total SASS thread instructions. Geometry attributes dominate remaining memory pressure (85.8% of total raster traffic).

Conclusion: TileGS improves raster performance by reducing effective raster traversal work, not by reducing byte volume, improving coalescing, increasing occupancy, or reducing warp divergence. The optimization focuses on minimizing traversal operations rather than memory bandwidth.

Abstract: Real-time 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high rendering quality, but standard rasterization still traverses a globally sorted tile stream that creates long per-tile ranges and heavy geometry-attribute traffic. We present TileGS, a tile-local reorganization of Gaussian splatting. TileGS turns each long tile range into a sequence of shorter depth-local ranges, rasterizes those ranges in front-to-back order, and applies selective repair where coarse ordering is insufficient to match baseline compositing. Across a 9-scene benchmark on desktop and laptop Ada GPUs, our default No-GW (No Geometry-Write) variant delivers a mean 1.44x raster-kernel speedup on RTX 4090 and mean end-to-end frame speedups of 1.069x on RTX 4090 and 1.094x on RTX 1000 Ada over gsplat--a widely used optimized open-source 3DGS implementation--while matching the gsplat output up to numerical noise (|Delta PSNR| < 0.001 dB, |Delta SSIM| < 0.001, |Delta LPIPS| < 0.001). Full-suite RTX 4090 Nsight Compute profiling reveals TileGS is faster despite lower SM throughput, lower active-warp occupancy, and higher DRAM traffic, while total SASS thread instructions fall by 1.26x. Source-attributed profiling confirms that geometry attributes dominate the remaining memory pressure (85.8% of total raster traffic and 88.6% of excess sectors). Together, these counters support the interpretation that TileGS improves raster performance by reducing effective raster traversal work, rather than by reducing byte volume, improving coalescing, increasing occupancy, or directly reducing measured warp divergence.

</details>


### [105] [Reparametrizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Palette-based Color and Luminance Editing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03897)
*Cheng-Kang Ted Chao,Yotam Gingold*

Main category: cs.GR

TL;DR: A real-time interactive color editing framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that enables palette-based recoloring, per-palette tone curves for luminance adjustment, and pixel-level color constraints through reparameterizing pretrained spherical harmonics with view-dependent palette weights.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Professional color editing requires precise, independent control over hue/saturation and lightness. Prior primitive-space methods suffer from alpha-blending issues causing edits to bleed into unintended regions. There was a need for view-space formulation with independent luminance control per palette color and view-consistent pixel-level constraints.

Method: Reparameterizes spherical harmonics of pretrained vanilla 3DGS to encode view-dependent palette weights. Solves for weights and palette colors simultaneously via image-space sparsity loss. Luminance editing achieved as per-pixel weight shift along achromatic axis (equivalent to per-pixel palette-aware luminance edit). Uses iteratively reweighted least squares and damped block-coordinate descent coupling tone curves and palette shifts under view-space sparsity.

Result: Achieves sparser, more localized edits than prior palette-based 3DGS methods. Enables independent luminance control per palette color and view-consistent pixel-level constraints. Edits run in tens of milliseconds. Representation can be efficiently baked back into vanilla 3DGS for standard viewer compatibility.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully addresses core limitations of prior primitive-space methods through view-space formulation, providing precise, independent control over color and lightness with real-time performance and compatibility with standard 3DGS viewers.

Abstract: Professional color editing requires precise control over both color (hue and saturation) and lightness, ideally through separate, independent controls. We present a real-time interactive color editing framework for 3D Gaussian Splatting that supports palette-based recoloring, per-palette tone curves for color-aware luminance adjustment, and pixel-level color constraints. Rather than training a new representation from scratch, we reparameterize the spherical harmonics of a pretrained vanilla 3DGS to encode view-dependent palette weights. We simultaneously solve for weights and palette colors via a loss based on image-space sparsity. Luminance editing is realized as a per-pixel weight shift along the achromatic axis, which we show is equivalent to a per-pixel palette-aware luminance edit. This view-space formulation addresses a core limitation of prior primitive-space methods, where alpha-blending breaks per-Gaussian sparsity and causes edits to bleed into unintended regions. Our edits run in tens of milliseconds via an iteratively reweighted least squares and damped block-coordinate descent that couples tone curves and palette shifts under view-space sparsity. Our representation can be efficiently baked back into a vanilla 3DGS, preserving compatibility with standard viewers. We demonstrate sparser, more localized edits than prior palette-based 3DGS methods, while enabling independent luminance control per palette color and view-consistent pixel-level constraints, capabilities previously unavailable for 3DGS.

</details>

# cs.LG [[Back]](#toc)

### [106] [The Geometry of Ignorance: LLMs Know When to Temper Bayesian Priors](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02959)
*Toni J. B. Liu,Jiajun Bao,Yizhou Liu,Gurbir Arora,Nicolas Boullé,Raphaël Sarfati,Christopher J. Earls*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper discovers that language models have a geometric structure in their unembedding matrix called the "direction of ignorance" - a single direction that encodes the unigram distribution of the training corpus. When models have little context, they fall back on this prior. The projection onto this direction yields a "prior loading factor" λ that decreases as context becomes more informative, and this can be interpreted as a tempered Bayesian update. The findings hold across four model families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Pythia) from 0.4B to 405B parameters, with larger models showing lower prior reliance in high-context scenarios.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper seeks to understand what language models predict when they have few clues about the context. This is a fundamental question about model uncertainty and how they handle lack of information.

Method: The authors examined the unembedding geometry of language models across four families (Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Pythia) ranging from 0.4B to 405B parameters. They identified a single direction in the unembedding matrix that encodes the unigram distribution (the Bayesian prior). They computed a prior loading factor λ by projecting the final prediction state onto this "direction of ignorance." They validated the causal role of this direction by experimentally raising/lowering λ to observe its effect on predictions.

Result: The direction of ignorance exists in all examined model families. The prior loading factor λ declines steadily as context becomes more informative. The geometric projection decomposes the prediction state into two orthogonal vectors corresponding to a tempered Bayesian update: a unigram prior raised to exponent λ and a context-driven likelihood. Larger models generally exhibit lower prior reliance in the high-context limit. The direction is causally active: manipulating λ steers predictions toward or away from the unigram prior in KL divergence.

Conclusion: Language models implement a Bayesian-like uncertainty mechanism through their unembedding geometry. The "direction of ignorance" provides a unified framework for comparing prior reliance across different model sizes and families. This geometric-probabilistic interpretation offers a meaningful way to calibrate and compare model uncertainty behavior, revealing that larger models rely less on the unigram prior when context is informative.

Abstract: What does a language model predict when it has few clues? The answer lurks in its unembedding geometry: a single direction of the unembedding matrix encodes the unigram distribution of the training corpus, which serves as the Bayesian prior the model falls back on when uncertain. This structure --- which we term the \emph{direction of ignorance} --- appears in all four model families examined (\texttt{Llama}, \texttt{Qwen}, \texttt{Gemma}, and \texttt{Pythia}), ranging from 0.4B to 405B parameters. Projecting the final prediction state onto this direction yields a per-token \emph{prior loading factor} $λ$, which, empirically, declines steadily as the context becomes more informative. Formally, the same projection decomposes the prediction state into two orthogonal vectors that correspond exactly to the two factors of a tempered Bayesian update: a unigram prior raised to the exponent $λ$ and a context-driven likelihood. This geometric-probabilistic interpretation calibrates $λ$, making it meaningfully comparable across model sizes and families, with larger models generally exhibiting lower prior reliance in the high-context limit. Finally, we show that the direction of ignorance is causally active: raising or lowering $λ$ at the final prediction state steers the prediction toward or away from the unigram prior in KL divergence.

</details>


### [107] [Equation Recast for Canonical Operator Learning Across Parametric PDEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02982)
*Qiyun Cheng,Valentin Duruisseaux,Cesar F. Clauser,Md Hossain Sahadath,Huihua Yang,Shaowu Pan,Nathaniel Ferraro,Anima Anandkumar,Wei Ji,Cristina Rea*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: Equation recast reformulates parametric operator learning as learning a single canonical operator by analytically deriving parameter-induced operator variations and absorbing them into effective sources, enabling zero-shot prediction across new parameter regimes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Learning solution operators across broad parameter ranges requires substantial coverage of input functions and physical parameters for purely data-driven parametric models. Additionally, these models may fail silently outside the training distribution.

Method: The method reformulates parametric operator learning as learning a single canonical operator. Parameter-induced operator variations are derived analytically from the governing equation and absorbed into effective sources. This enables zero-shot prediction across new parameter regimes, integration of sparse heterogeneous datasets in a shared canonical representation, and use of loss of convergence as an internal warning signal for failure.

Result: The framework demonstrates extrapolation capability across multi-parameter, nonlinear, and singular PDE settings. In high-fidelity tokamak simulations for nuclear fusion, it unifies electron-temperature data across four device geometries through canonical-domain mapping within one jointly trained operator.

Conclusion: Equation recast provides a route toward reusable neural PDE solvers combining equation-guided transfer, data efficiency, and monitorable inference.

Abstract: Learning solution operators across broad parameter ranges can require substantial coverage of both input functions and physical parameters, particularly for purely data-driven parametric models. In addition, the resulting models may fail silently outside the training distribution. We introduce equation recast, which reformulates parametric operator learning as the learning of a single canonical operator. Parameter-induced operator variations are derived analytically from the governing equation and absorbed into effective sources, enabling zero-shot prediction across new parameter regimes. Across multi-parameter, nonlinear, and singular PDE settings, equation recast supports extrapolation, integrates sparse heterogeneous datasets in a shared canonical representation, and uses loss of convergence as an internal warning signal for failure of the recast iteration. In high-fidelity tokamak simulations for nuclear fusion, the framework unifies electron-temperature data across four device geometries through canonical-domain mapping within one jointly trained operator. Equation recast provides a route toward reusable neural PDE solvers combining equation-guided transfer, data efficiency, and monitorable inference.

</details>


### [108] [From Euclidean to Graph-Structured Data: A Survey of Collaborative Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02984)
*Rémi Bourgerie,Šarūnas Girdzijauskas,Viktoria Fodor*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A comprehensive survey on collaborative learning that extends from traditional Euclidean data to graph-structured data, addressing challenges in scalability, privacy, and heterogeneity in distributed learning environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Conventional machine learning approaches face fundamental limitations in scalability and privacy. While collaborative learning approaches like federated learning have emerged, they primarily focus on Euclidean data (images, text). Graph-structured data, which represents relational patterns in many real-world applications, remains largely underexplored in collaborative settings despite being conceptually well-suited for message-passing mechanisms.

Method: The survey organizes research along three core dimensions for Euclidean data: learning effectiveness, efficiency, and privacy preservation. For graph-structured data, it introduces a taxonomy of graph distribution scenarios, characterizes statistical heterogeneities, and develops standardized problem formulations and algorithmic frameworks.

Result: The paper consolidates this emerging field by providing a comprehensive investigation, reviewing foundational principles, extending discussions to graph data with proper taxonomies and frameworks, and identifying open challenges and future research directions.

Conclusion: This survey bridges the gap between collaborative learning and graph learning, providing a systematic foundation for future research in graph-based collaborative learning, with identified open challenges and promising research directions.

Abstract: The conventional approach to machine learning, that is, collecting data, training models, and performing inference in a single location, faces fundamental limitations, including scalability and privacy, that restrict its applicability. To address these challenges, recent research has explored collaborative learning approaches, including federated learning and decentralized learning, where individual agents perform training and inference locally, with limited collaboration. Most collaborative learning research focuses on Euclidean data with regular, grid-like structure (e.g., images, text). However, these approaches fail to capture the relational patterns in many real-world applications, best represented by graphs. Learning on graphs relies on message-passing mechanisms to propagate information between connected nodes, making it conceptually well-suited for collaborative environments where agents must exchange information. Yet, the opportunities and challenges of learning on graph-structured data in collaborative settings remain largely underexplored. This survey provides a comprehensive investigation of collaborative learning from Euclidean to graph-structured data, aiming to consolidate this emerging field. We begin by reviewing its foundational principles for Euclidean data, organizing them along three core dimensions: learning effectiveness, efficiency, and privacy preservation. We then extend the discussion to graph-structured data, introducing a taxonomy of graph distribution scenarios, characterizing associated statistical heterogeneities, and developing standardized problem formulations and algorithmic frameworks. Finally, we systematically identify open challenges and promising research directions.

</details>


### [109] [Modern Transformers Are Implicit Hybrids: From Functional Differentiation to Principled Hybrid Architecture Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02986)
*Runlin Shi,Bojian Yin,Guoqi Li*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates hybrid attention architectures combining Full Attention (FA) and Linear Attention (LA) in RoPE-based Transformers, proposing two metrics (RFIS and RPD) to analyze head-level functional organization. The authors discover a taxonomy of retrieval vs positional heads separated by a "Global Positional Band" (GPBand), and instantiate these findings in Head-wise Hybrid Architecture (HwH) that achieves improved retrieval and zero-shot length extrapolation with FA:LA ratio below 1:3.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current hybrid FA/LA architectures rely on heuristic allocation rather than evidence-based design. The authors seek to understand head-level functional organization in RoPE-based Transformers to enable principled architecture design, since behavioral probes alone cannot provide a complete taxonomy of attention head functions.

Method: The authors propose two intervention metrics: (1) RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS) measures how each frequency affects a head's attention distribution; (2) RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD) isolates dependence on rotary positional modulation. Experiments are conducted on Qwen3-series and Llama3.1 models, with controlled Transformers to validate findings. The proposed Head-wise Hybrid Architecture (HwH) uses NoPE FA for global retrieval and LA for local positional modeling.

Result: RFIS suggests and RPD verifies a complete taxonomy of retrieval and positional heads separated by a salient mid-low-frequency band (GPBand). This boundary follows the training-length positional scale. HwH with FA:LA ratio below 1:3 retains strong language modeling and commonsense reasoning while improving retrieval and substantially strengthening zero-shot long-context extrapolation over Transformer, LA, and layer-wise hybrid baselines.

Conclusion: The paper yields two design principles: (1) positional modeling should operate only locally, with global access through position-independent retrieval; (2) both functions should be assigned at head granularity with layer-specific allocation. Principled hybrid architecture design is a promising route toward future foundation models, with HwH demonstrating the practical value of this approach.

Abstract: Hybrid architectures combining Full Attention (FA) and Linear Attention (LA) are increasingly prominent, yet their allocation remains heuristic. We seek an evidence-grounded basis in head-level functional organization learned by RoPE-based Transformers. Behavioral probes do not yield a complete taxonomy, so we propose two intervention metrics: RoPE Frequency Importance Score (RFIS), measuring how each frequency affects a head's attention distribution, and RoPE Positional Dependence (RPD), isolating dependence on rotary positional modulation. On Qwen3-series models and Llama3.1, RFIS suggests and RPD verifies a complete taxonomy of retrieval and positional heads separated by a salient mid-low-frequency band. Controlled Transformers show that this boundary follows the training-length positional scale; we term it the Global Positional Band (GPBand). The analysis suggests a potential cause of zero-shot length-extrapolation failure and yields two principles: positional modeling should operate only locally, with global access through position-independent retrieval; and both functions should be assigned at head granularity with layer-specific allocation. We instantiate them in Head-wise Hybrid Architecture (HwH), using NoPE FA for global retrieval and LA for local positional modeling. With an FA-to-LA ratio below 1:3, HwH retains strong language modeling and commonsense reasoning while improving retrieval and substantially strengthening zero-shot long-context extrapolation over Transformer, LA, and a layer-wise hybrid baseline. Ablations validate both principles and component roles, highlighting principled hybrid architecture design as a promising route toward future foundation models.

</details>


### [110] [Tail-Likelihood Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02987)
*Shrinivas Ramasubramanian,Daman Arora,Fahim Tajwar,Guanning Zeng,Qingyang Wu,Zhongzhu Zhou,Chenfeng Xu,Haiwen Feng,Yuda Song,Aarti Singh,Ruslan Salakhutdinov,J. Andrew Bagnell,Jeff Schneider,Andrea Zanette*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TailRL is a reinforcement learning method that optimizes for the probability of achieving high-reward outcomes (upper tails of the reward distribution) rather than just average reward. It maximizes the log-probability of exceeding randomly chosen reward thresholds, giving more weight to rare, high-reward rollouts. This simple modification to the advantage function makes it compatible with existing RL pipelines and helps avoid suboptimal solutions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard RL optimizes average reward, which can hide important differences between policies. Two policies can have the same mean reward but very different probabilities of achieving rare high-reward outcomes. This matters because the benefit of sampling during training and inference depends on retaining probability mass on high-reward outcomes.

Method: Tail-Likelihood Reinforcement Learning (TailRL) optimizes the upper tails of the reward distribution directly. For each reward threshold, it considers how likely the policy is to exceed it, turning continuous reward into binary success events. TailRL maximizes the log-probability of exceeding a randomly chosen reward threshold. Its gradient gives more weight to rare, high-reward rollouts and can be interpreted as a mixture of Best-of-(k) gradients. It requires only a simple modification to the advantage function.

Result: Across four domains—object localization, maze navigation, GUI grounding, and code optimization—TailRL leverages rare high-reward training samples to avoid suboptimal solutions and yields models that benefit more from additional samples at inference time.

Conclusion: TailRL provides a simple but effective way to optimize for high-reward outcomes rather than average performance. By modifying only the advantage function, it integrates easily with existing RL pipelines and successfully addresses the problem of hidden suboptimal policies that appear equal when only average reward is considered.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning typically optimizes average reward. For generative policies, the average can hide an important distinction: two policies can achieve the same mean reward while having very different chances of producing a rare but high-reward rollout. This matters as sampling increases during training and inference, since its benefit depends on retaining probability mass on high-reward outcomes. We propose to optimize this coverage directly. Rather than considering only expected reward, we consider all of its upper tails: for each reward threshold, how likely is the policy to exceed it? This turns a continuous reward into a family of binary success events. We introduce Tail-Likelihood Reinforcement Learning (TailRL), which maximizes the log-probability of exceeding a randomly chosen reward threshold. Its gradient gives more weight to rare, high-reward rollouts and can be interpreted as a mixture of Best-of-(k) gradients. TailRL requires only a simple modification to the advantage function, making it compatible with existing reinforcement learning pipelines. Across object localization, maze navigation, GUI grounding, and code optimization, TailRL leverages rare high-reward training samples to avoid suboptimal solutions and yields models that benefit more from additional samples at inference time.

</details>


### [111] [Mesh-Native Physics-Informed Graph Surrogates for TCAD-in-the-Loop Design Space Exploration](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02988)
*Leonid Popryho,Ayoub Sadeghi,Inna Partin-Vaisband*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a physics-informed graph attention network (GAT) surrogate model for high-fidelity TCAD simulation of FinFET devices. The model operates directly on tetrahedral meshes and predicts electrostatic potential and quasi-Fermi levels at each node, combining data loss with physics-based continuity residuals. It achieves size generalization and enables active learning for efficient design space exploration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional TCAD drift-diffusion simulation is computationally expensive, especially for 3D FinFET structures, limiting multi-objective design space exploration. Existing ML surrogates lack physics transferability across device geometries.

Method: Physics-informed GAT operating on tetrahedral TCAD mesh as a graph, predicting node-level electrostatic potential and electron/hole quasi-Fermi levels. Training combines data loss with finite-volume current-continuity residuals. Deep ensemble provides per-node uncertainty for active learning.

Result: Sub-volt RMSE per field, orders of magnitude higher throughput than full simulator. Inference under 1 second per device for large multi-fin arrays, enabling Pareto-front exploration across device scales infeasible for direct TCAD.

Conclusion: The physics-informed GAT surrogate achieves high-fidelity prediction with size generalization, dramatically accelerating FinFET design exploration while maintaining physical consistency through embedded transport physics.

Abstract: High-fidelity TCAD simulation of drift-diffusion transport remains the workhorse of emerging FinFET device design, but it is computationally expensive, especially for 3D structures where runtime escalates steeply with mesh complexity. This sharply limits multi-objective design space exploration. Existing machine-learning surrogates map a fixed set of design parameters to a few scalar device metrics, discarding the underlying physics and losing transferability across device geometries and families. A physics-informed graph attention network (GAT) surrogate is proposed. It operates directly on the tetrahedral TCAD mesh and predicts, at every mesh node, the electrostatic potential together with the electron and hole quasi-Fermi levels, the fundamental unknowns of the drift-diffusion system. Training combines a data loss with finite-volume current-continuity residuals, embedding carrier-transport physics into the objective. Operating on the mesh as a graph, the surrogate inherits size generalization: a model trained on few-fin meshes applies unchanged to substantially larger arrays, bounded at inference only by GPU memory. Per-node uncertainty from a deep ensemble drives an active-learning loop that screens large candidate pools in seconds and forwards only the most informative designs for full simulation. Benchmarked against Sentaurus Device on multi-fin tri-gate FinFETs, the surrogate reproduces the three drift-diffusion fields with sub-volt per-field RMSE and reaches a per-design throughput orders of magnitude higher than the full simulator. The advantage grows with device size: on large multi-fin arrays that are prohibitively slow to simulate directly, inference still completes in under a second per device, enabling Pareto-front exploration across device scales infeasible for direct TCAD sweeps.

</details>


### [112] [TRACE: Spatiotemporal Contact Memory Graph Network Simulator for Granular Dynamics](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02991)
*Changjian Zhou,Negin Yousefpour,Jie Qi,Junfeng Fang,Guillermo A. Narsilio,Hans Petter Jostad*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TRACE is a graph-network simulator for granular dynamics that stores contact history directly on edges rather than nodes, using attention-based message passing and GRU units. It predicts contact forces with physics constraints (Coulomb friction, equal-and-opposite forces) and achieves 31-62% lower long-rollout error and 58-89% lower final-deposit error compared to GNS and NMGNS, while being 8.9-12.2× faster than MPM solvers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Granular dynamics depend heavily on inter-granular contact history, which is difficult to preserve when contacts form, break, and rearrange. Existing simulators store temporal information in node features or node-level memory, but this approach is insufficient for capturing the complex contact history needed for accurate granular flow simulation.

Method: TRACE uses a graph-network architecture with edge-level persistent memory updated by attention-based message passing and gated recurrent units (GRU). An edge-identity dictionary preserves memory as the contact graph changes. A physics-structured decoder predicts normal and tangential contact forces, enforces Coulomb friction limits, and applies equal-and-opposite internal forces. Training involves single-step pretraining followed by autoregressive rollout fine-tuning.

Result: On 2D and 3D granular column-collapse benchmarks, TRACE produces stable, physically consistent long-horizon rollouts. It reduces long-rollout position error by 31-62% and final-deposit error by 58-89% compared to GNS and NMGNS, while using fewer parameters and maintaining near-zero particle interpenetration. Speedups of 12.2× (2D) and 8.9× (3D) over MPM reference solver are achieved.

Conclusion: Storing interaction history directly on contact edges rather than nodes enables more accurate and efficient granular dynamics simulation. TRACE successfully captures contact history that existing methods miss, leading to significant improvements in prediction accuracy while maintaining physical consistency and computational efficiency.

Abstract: Learned graph simulators provide an efficient alternative to high-fidelity solvers for granular dynamics. However, granular motion depends strongly on inter-granular contact history, which is difficult to preserve when particle contacts form, break, and rearrange. Existing simulators mainly store temporal information in node features or node-level memory. Here we introduce TRACE, a graph-network simulator that stores interaction history directly on contact edges. Each edge maintains a persistent memory updated by attention-based message passing and a gated recurrent unit, while an edge-identity dictionary preserves this memory as the contact graph changes. A physics-structured decoder predicts inter-granular normal and tangential contact forces, enforces the Coulomb friction limit, and applies equal-and-opposite internal forces. The model is trained with single-step pretraining followed by autoregressive rollout fine-tuning. We evaluate TRACE on 2D and 3D granular column-collapse benchmarks. In both cases, TRACE produces stable, physically consistent long-horizon rollouts, closely reproducing the final deposit geometry and the kinetic energy released during collapse. Compared with graph network simulator (GNS) and node-memory graph neural simulator (NMGNS), TRACE reduces long-rollout position error by 31-62% and final-deposit error by 58-89% across the two benchmarks, while using fewer parameters and maintaining near-zero particle interpenetration. TRACE also achieves 12.2$\times$ and 8.9$\times$ speedups over the material point method (MPM) reference solver in 2D and 3D, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/Data-Driven-Computational-Geotechnics/TRACE.

</details>


### [113] [No-Regret Bayesian Optimization with Finite-Library Input-Warped Kernels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02993)
*Edvin Ketabati Augustinsson,Robert A. Bridges*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: FLIWBO extends GP-UCB Bayesian optimization by selecting input warps from a finite library to adapt the kernel geometry to the problem structure. It retains high-probability convergence guarantees while improving sample efficiency when raw coordinates poorly match the underlying geometry, such as with log-scaled hyperparameters or localized peaks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard GP-UCB requires a fixed kernel, but raw coordinates often poorly match the geometry of the objective function (e.g., log-scaled hyperparameters, localized peaks). Input warping can improve sample efficiency, but existing GP-UCB proofs require a fixed kernel, limiting practical applicability.

Method: FLIWBO selects warps from a finite library of smooth input maps using any history-dependent rule. It adapts input geometry to accelerate learning while retaining high-probability convergence guarantees under mild hypotheses, with an explicit √(N_ε) library-size cost.

Result: FLIWBO-UCB outperforms raw-coordinate GP-UCB under misspecified geometry, escapes traps that defeat even oracle-warp expected improvement, and recovers much of the gain from manual log scaling. It leads tested methods with matching regret guarantees. A 20-dimensional MAS design study shows feasibility under costly noisy evaluations.

Conclusion: Finite-library input warping is a practical approach to adapt kernel geometry in GP-BO while maintaining theoretical guarantees. It effectively handles geometry mismatches in various applications including HPO, synthetic benchmarks, and multi-agent system design.

Abstract: Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization (GP-BO) excels at black-box optimization of costly functions, e.g., hyperparameter optimization (HPO) and multi-agent system (MAS) design. Convergence-rate guarantees exist for select methods, notably GP upper confidence bound (GP-UCB), but require a fixed kernel. Critically, the kernel encodes how input proximity affects objective value similarity. When raw coordinates poorly match this geometry - as with log-scaled hyperparameters or localized peaks - input warping can greatly improve sample efficiency, yet known GP-UCB proofs require a fixed kernel. We propose Finite-Library Input-Warped Bayesian Optimization (FLIWBO), which selects warps from a finite library of smooth input maps by any history-dependent rule. It adapts the input geometry to accelerate learning while retaining high-probability convergence guarantees under mild hypotheses, with an explicit $\sqrt(N_\varepsilon)$ library-size cost. Controlled diagnostics show that finite-library warping repairs planted geometry mismatches and identify FLIWBO failure cases. Across four repeated benchmarks - warped synthetic objectives, a confidence-fence trap, and Fashion-MNIST HPO - FLIWBO-UCB beats raw-coordinate GP-UCB under misspecified geometry, escapes traps that defeat even oracle-warp expected improvement, and recovers much of the gain from manual log scaling, while leading the tested methods that admit a matching regret guarantee. A 20-dimensional MAS design study further shows feasibility under costly noisy evaluations. Code for experiments is available: https://github.com/edvin-ketabati/bogp-paper-experiments.

</details>


### [114] [Evaluating Graph Neural Networks for Change-Criticality Classification in Maritime Navigation Charts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02996)
*Abhishek Potnis,Jacob Arndt*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes using Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) to classify changes in Electronic Navigational Charts (ENCs) as critical or non-critical risks to navigational safety. ENC vector datasets are represented as graphs where spatial objects are nodes and their relationships form edges. The task is framed as graph-pair classification comparing old and new ENC datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Maintaining ENC datasets is challenging, and categorizing changes to objects based on their significance to navigational safety is important but unclear which GNN message-passing operations, architectural configurations, and graph representations are best suited for this task.

Method: Represent ENC vector datasets as graph structures where spatial objects serve as nodes and spatial/semantic relationships form edges. Encode both old and new ENC datasets into a pair of graphs and frame the task as graph-pair classification. Train and evaluate several GNN architectures on ENC changes reviewed by maritime experts.

Result: Graph-based representations improve classification of ENC updates, providing a scalable approach for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.

Conclusion: GNNs can effectively classify ENC changes as critical or non-critical risks to navigational safety, offering a scalable solution for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.

Abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) are a class of neural networks suitable for learning on graph-structured data. Their application to spatial data is a natural extension, however its relatively unclear which message-passing operations, architectural configurations, and graph representation is best suited for classifying changes to objects in electronic navigational charts (ENCs)--geospatial vector datasets used for marine navigation. Maintaining these datasets is a challenge, and categorizing changes to objects in the ENC based on their significance to navigational safety is of particular importance. Here, we propose to represent these vector navigation datasets as a graph structure where the spatial objects serve as nodes and their spatial and semantic relationships form edges. We encode both the old ENC dataset and new ENC dataset into a pair of graphs and frame the task as a graph-pair classification problem. Building on this representation, we investigate the use of GNN architectures to classify whether the encoded graphs constitutes a critical or non-critical risk to navigational safety. We train and evaluate several GNN architectures and model configurations on ENC changes reviewed by maritime experts. Our results demonstrate that graph-based representations improve the classification of ENC updates, providing a scalable approach for automating or improving ENC maintenance workflows.

</details>


### [115] [Verify Before You Distill: Prompt-Level Teacher Gating for On-Policy Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02998)
*Zhiwei Zhang,Zechen Sun,Fei Zhao,Kang Peng,Bin Liang,Huayu Deng,Yao Hu,Kam-Fai Wong,Mu Chuan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TGOPD introduces a gating mechanism that verifies teacher reliability at the prompt level before applying dense token-level supervision, routing unreliable prompts to verifier-grounded GRPO instead. This approach outperforms Vanilla OPD across mathematics, code, and instruction-following tasks at both 4B and 35B scales while improving teacher GPU utilization from 9.8% to 78.9%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Vanilla on-policy distillation (OPD) applies uniform token-level supervision from a frozen teacher without verifying teacher reliability per prompt. Since reverse KL is mode-seeking, a confidently wrong teacher can induce strong but misleading updates. Existing distributional proxies (entropy, teacher-student agreement) measure uncertainty but don't verify outcome correctness directly.

Method: TGOPD uses small verifier-scored teacher probes to estimate reliability at the prompt level. Each prompt is routed exclusively to: (1) dense OPD when reliability check passes, or (2) verifier-grounded GRPO otherwise. This gating mechanism filters out unreliable teacher outputs before they can cause harmful updates.

Result: TGOPD outperforms Vanilla OPD in all six single-domain settings (mathematics, code, instruction following) at both 4B and 35B scales. Higher seven-benchmark averages achieved under multi-domain training. Teacher-side compute waste is reduced - GPU utilization increased from 9.8% to 78.9% in 4B single-domain run.

Conclusion: Prompt-level teacher reliability verification is crucial for on-policy distillation.
