We further find that the largest public Armenian corpora overlap web-derived evaluation panels heavily, including a train/test self-overlap inside FineWeb-2. We openly release all data, models, and code.

</details>


### [139] [Time Without Timesteps: Simulating Coupled Dynamical Systems via Self-Consistency](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03358)
*Liyu Zerihun,Mark Shinyoung Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a neural surrogate approach for simulating coupled dynamical systems, where instead of traditional time-stepping, a trained network maps full trajectories to outputs, and self-consistency is enforced via waveform relaxation, turning simulation into a fixed-point problem. The method shows 4-10 Newton iterations versus 1500 steps, with memory-independent gradients and a spectral radius predictor for convergence.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional numerical simulation of dynamical systems uses causal time-marching where each state is computed from the previous one. This approach becomes inefficient for coupled systems and suffers from vanishing gradients in backpropagation through long simulations. The authors seek an alternative formulation that treats entire trajectories as units rather than individual time steps.

Method: The authors train neural surrogates for each subsystem type that map full driving trajectories and initial conditions directly to full output trajectories. Following classical waveform relaxation, coupled systems are assembled by enforcing self-consistency among these trajectories. This transforms simulation from a stepwise rollout into a fixed-point problem over complete trajectories. The gradient is computed implicitly as a linear system solved by GMRES, avoiding time recursion. A spectral radius measure of the Jacobian predicts convergence behavior.

Result: On coupled van der Pol oscillators and Hodgkin-Huxley neuron networks, the method achieves 4-10 Newton iterations compared to 1500 steps in reference integrators. The gradient becomes memory-independent of solver depth. The spectral radius of the Jacobian accurately predicts convergence boundaries. Beyond these boundaries, unrolled backpropagation diverges and Neumann adjoint fails, while the implicit gradient remains accurate to 0.04%.

Conclusion: The proposed waveform relaxation approach with neural surrogates successfully transforms timestep-by-timestep simulation into a fixed-point problem over trajectories, achieving computational efficiency and stable gradient computation. The spectral radius serves as a reliable predictor of convergence. However, the approach has limitations where surrogate error degrades performance, and these failure modes are discussed in the paper.

Abstract: Numerical simulation of dynamical systems is usually organized as a causal march through time: each state is computed from the previous one. We explore a different formulation for coupled systems. For each subsystem type we train a neural surrogate mapping a full driving trajectory and initial condition directly to a full output trajectory; following classical waveform relaxation, coupled systems are assembled by enforcing self-consistency among these trajectories: simulation becomes a fixed-point problem over complete trajectories rather than a stepwise rollout. On coupled van der Pol oscillators and Hodgkin-Huxley neuron networks, sequential depth becomes the number of solver iterations: 4-10 Newton iterations where the reference integrator takes 1500 steps. The gradient likewise loses its time recursion: it becomes a linear system solved by GMRES at memory independent of solver depth. A single scalar measured from the learned operator, the spectral radius of its Jacobian, predicts in advance where the coupled solve will converge; past that boundary, unrolled backpropagation diverges and a Neumann adjoint fails, while the implicit gradient remains correct to 0.04%. We report where the approach succeeds and where surrogate error degrades it.

</details>


### [140] [SimpleDesign: A Joint Model for Protein Sequence and Structure Codesign](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03377)
*Jiarui Lu,Yuyang Wang,Yizhe Zhang,Jiatao Gu,Navdeep Jaitly,Joshua M. Susskind,Miguel Ángel Bautista*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: SimpleDesign is a multi-modal protein design model that trains end-to-end in data space (instead of latent space), using a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture to jointly generate protein sequences and structures with combined cross-entropy and regression objectives.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing protein co-design models require multi-stage training: first training autoencoders to tokenize data into latent representations, then training generative models in that latent space. This work hypothesizes that this multi-stage approach is unnecessary and proposes a single-stage end-to-end training directly in data space.

Method: SimpleDesign uses a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture enabling modality-specific processing while maintaining global self-attention over both sequence and structure modalities. It combines discrete cross-entropy loss for sequence generation with regression loss for structure prediction, trained end-to-end on over 2 million sequence-structure pairs.

Result: SimpleDesign achieves strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks, demonstrating that single-stage training in data space can match or exceed multi-stage latent space approaches.

Conclusion: Multi-stage training is not necessary for performant co-design models. SimpleDesign's single-stage end-to-end approach provides an effective alternative for multi-modal protein design, with implications for drug discovery and protein engineering applications.

Abstract: Proteins are fundamental to biological processes, with their function determined by the complex interplay between the amino acid sequence and the three-dimensional structure. Developing generative models capable of understanding this intrinsically multi-modal relationship is crucial for fields like drug discovery and protein engineering. Existing models often rely on a multi-stage training process where autoencoders that tokenize data into latent representations are trained in a first stage. Secondly, a generative model is trained on the latent representation of the autoencoder(s), i.e., generative modeling in a latent space. We hypothesize that this multi-stage training is not necessary to obtain performant co-design models and thus present SimpleDesign, an effective multi-modal protein design model trained directly in the data space. SimpleDesign leverages a single-stage end-to-end objective that combines discrete cross-entropy for sequences and a regression objective for structures. In order to effectively model the difference in sequence and structure modalities, we develop a Mixture-of-Transformer architecture that allows modality-specific processing while keeping global self-attention over both modalities. We train SimpleDesign on over 2M sequence-structure pairs achieving strong performance across co-design and unconditional sequence/structure generation benchmarks.

</details>


### [141] [RecurTrace: Adaptive Latent Reasoning with Loop-Time Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03379)
*Yuxiang Wang,Kunyu Feng,Yingda Shen,Haoning Xu,Junyu Wang,Zhizheng Wu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RecurTrace is a method that improves language model reasoning by allowing looped layers to attend to their own states from previous iterations (Loop Memory Attention) and adaptively deciding when to stop looping using a halting head with oracle supervision. This addresses two key limitations of prior latent recurrence methods: restricted access to earlier computations and fixed loop counts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Latent recurrence (repeating a small block of middle layers) increases effective inference depth without adding parameters or generating extra tokens. However, existing approaches suffer from two limitations: (1) each iteration only sees the previous output and cannot access earlier computations, and (2) a fixed loop count wastes depth on easy inputs while providing insufficient computation for hard ones.

Method: RecurTrace introduces two key innovations: (1) Loop Memory Attention - allows each looped layer to attend to its own states from previous iterations along the loop-time axis, enabling the model to revisit earlier computations instead of relying solely on the latest state; (2) A halting head that reads the loop state and predicts whether to continue, with supervision from an oracle that identifies when additional depth still reduces loss.

Result: On MathQA, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, exceeding the best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute. Compared to baselines: ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop; CALM reaches 54.1% with 5.6 loops; LoopUS-Conf achieves 55.3% at 3.2 loops; TaH-Mismatch achieves 55.7% at 2.1 loops. RecurTrace also improves generation accuracy over same-budget fine-tuned baselines at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B model sizes, with gains growing from 0.6 to 3.4 points as model size increases.

Conclusion: RecurTrace effectively addresses the limitations of prior latent recurrence methods by enabling access to earlier computations and adaptive halting. The method shows superior performance over multiple baselines across different compute budgets, with gains that scale positively with model size, demonstrating the approach's practical value for improving language model reasoning capabilities.

Abstract: Repeating a small block of middle layers increases a language model's effective inference depth without adding parameters or generating extra tokens, and recent work shows that this latent recurrence improves reasoning. However, two design choices limit these gains. Each iteration sees only the previous output and cannot directly access earlier computations. Moreover, a fixed loop count wastes depth on easy inputs while leaving hard ones with too little computation. We introduce RecurTrace, which addresses both limitations using the loop's own trajectory. Specifically, Loop Memory Attention lets each looped layer attend to its own states from previous iterations along the loop-time axis, so the model can revisit earlier computations instead of relying on the latest state alone. A halting head then reads the loop state and predicts whether to continue, with supervision from an oracle that identifies when additional depth still reduces loss. In a controlled MathQA comparison on the same looped backbone, RecurTrace achieves 56.9% accuracy with an average of 2.0 loops, exceeding the best fixed loop depth by 2.2 points at matched compute. By comparison, ACT and PonderNet collapse to one loop, and CALM reaches only 54.1% with 5.6 loops, while the stronger LoopUS-Conf and TaH-Mismatch baselines reach 55.3% at 3.2 loops and 55.7% at 2.1 loops. Finally, RecurTrace improves generation accuracy over same-budget fine-tuned baselines at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, and 8B, with the gain growing with model size from 0.6 to 3.4 points.

</details>


### [142] [TIGPO: Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization for Long-Horizon LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03383)
*Jinwei Gan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: TIGPO is a novel graph-based policy optimization method that maintains persistent transition graphs across policy updates to improve credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents, using a dual-slot rollout budget (Exploration and Revisit) to connect current exploration with historical experience.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing graph-based policy optimization methods construct graphs independently within each policy update, which discards transitions discovered by earlier policies and limits advantage estimation to small, batch-local rollout groups. This creates two key limitations: (1) historical transition knowledge is lost, and (2) advantage estimation is unstable due to small rollout groups.

Method: TIGPO maintains a persistent transition graph for each task across policy updates, allowing transitions discovered by different policy versions to jointly determine credit for current rollouts. It allocates a fixed rollout budget between Exploration slots (for ordinary task sampling) and Revisit slots (for delayed reattempts of previously explored tasks). For each revisit, the current rollout group is paired with its corresponding earlier Exploration group to construct a cross-temporal reference. Historical transitions serve only as structural references and are never replayed in the policy loss.

Result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.

Conclusion: TIGPO successfully extends graph-based credit assignment across policy updates by maintaining persistent transition graphs and using a dual-slot rollout mechanism. This approach stabilizes relative advantage estimation under small rollout groups while capturing policy improvement across training stages, leading to consistent performance improvements over existing methods.

Abstract: Graph-based policy optimization improves credit assignment for long-horizon LLM agents by organizing rollout trajectories into state-transition graphs. However, existing methods construct graphs independently within each policy update, discarding transitions discovered by earlier policies and limiting advantage estimation to small, batch-local rollout groups. We propose \emph{Temporal Instance-Graph Policy Optimization} (TIGPO), which extends graph-based credit assignment across policy updates. TIGPO maintains a persistent transition graph for each task, allowing valid transitions discovered by different policy versions to jointly determine credit for current rollouts. To actively reconnect current exploration with historical experience, TIGPO allocates a fixed rollout budget between Exploration slots for ordinary task sampling and Revisit slots for delayed reattempts of previously explored tasks. For each revisit, TIGPO pairs the current rollout group with its corresponding earlier Exploration group to construct a cross-temporal reference. The enlarged reference is designed to stabilize relative advantage estimation under small rollout groups, while comparison on the same task directly captures policy improvement across training stages. Historical transitions and scores serve only as structural and detached statistical references and are never replayed in the policy loss. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebShop demonstrate that TIGPO consistently outperforms prior group-based and graph-based policy optimization methods.

</details>


### [143] [Inferred Generative-Process Diversity Predicts Correlated Failure Across Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03422)
*Ross Tieman,Evan Markou*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "generative-process diversity" as a more fundamental measure of diversity in multi-language-model systems, using Normalised Compression Distance (NCD) between raw model outputs to capture differences in the underlying generative processes rather than just semantic similarity of outputs. This measure predicts correlated failure patterns across 38 models on ten benchmark families.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current assessments of language model populations use semantic similarity, which only captures differences in output meaning. However, different models may exhibit strongly correlated failures even when treated as independent components. The authors argue that a more fundamental notion of diversity is needed - generative-process diversity, which captures differences between the processes capable of generating observed outputs.

Method: The authors use Normalised Compression Distance (NCD) between raw model outputs, residualised against a permutation control, as a measure of inferred generative-process diversity. They tested this across 38 language models and compared it with semantic similarity measures.

Result: The NCD-based measure identifies population structure missed by semantic similarity. It predicts cross-task variation in chance-corrected correlated failure among model pairs across ten disjoint benchmark families, beyond semantic similarity and model-pair capability. The cross-benchmark partial rank association is -0.216 (95% CI: [-0.309, -0.122]), and the estimate is negative on all ten benchmarks.

Conclusion: Increased generative-process diversity is associated with reduced correlated failure in model pairs, beyond what can be attributed to semantic similarity or capability differences. This provides a novel and practical approach for investigating diversity of multi-model systems in safety-relevant contexts.

Abstract: Diversity is a widely observed factor in the resilient function of collective systems, yet the type of diversity that matters depends on the properties and failure modes of the system. This distinction is important for systems composed of multiple language models. Different models may be treated as independent components even when their behaviour and failures remain strongly correlated. Assessments of language-model populations using semantic similarity demonstrate limited semantic diversity, but this captures only differences in the meaning of observed outputs. We argue that a more fundamental notion of model diversity is generative-process diversity, the differences between processes capable of generating the observed outputs. Drawing from Algorithmic Information Theory, we use Normalised Compression Distance between raw model outputs, residualised against a permutation control, as a measure of inferred generative-process diversity. Across 38 language models, this measure identifies population structure missed by semantic similarity and predicts cross-task variation in chance-corrected correlated failure among model pairs across ten disjoint benchmark families, beyond semantic similarity and model-pair capability. The cross-benchmark partial rank association is $-0.216$ with a 95% interval of $[-0.309,-0.122]$, and the estimate is negative on all ten benchmarks. These results indicate that increased generative-process diversity is associated with reduced correlated failure in model pairs that is not attributable to semantic similarity or capability. Inferred generative-process diversity offers a novel and practical approach for investigating diversity of multi-model systems in safety-relevant contexts.

</details>


### [144] [TraveL: Transformer-based Multi-view Path Distributional Representation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03427)
*Fang He,Tao-yang Fu,Wang-chien Lee*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes TraveL, a Transformer-based Multi-view Distributional Representation Learning framework that learns distributional representations for paths in road networks by capturing varied traveler behaviors and regional correlations among road segments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing path representation learning methods only exploit co-occurrence relationships among road segments and paths, but they fail to explore varied traveler behaviors and regional correlations on paths, which are valuable for path-related applications.

Method: The proposed TraveL framework encodes a path along with travel starting time into a distributional representation using a Transformer architecture. It incorporates regional attention to encode regional correlations among road segments, and uses the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test to compare sampled traveler behavior against ground truth for training.

Result: TraveL outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets, achieving 14.7% improvement in Mean K-S distance for travel time distribution estimation, 16.7% improvement in MAE for path similarity prediction, and 3.97% improvement in MAE for destination prediction.

Conclusion: The TraveL model effectively captures varied traveler behaviors and regional correlations through its distributional representation learning approach, significantly outperforming existing path representation learning methods across multiple evaluation tasks.

Abstract: Path representation learning (PRL) for road networks has received increasing research attention, due to various path-related applications. Existing works on PRL typically exploit the co-occurrence relationship among road segments and paths to learn a vector as the path representation, without exploring the varied traveler behaviors and the regional correlation on the path. In this work, we propose to learn distributional representations, which provide valuable information for use in path-related applications, by capturing the varied traveler behaviors as well as the various dependencies within regions of road segments. We propose a novel Transformer-based Multi-view Distributional Representation Learning (TraveL) framework to encode a path along with a travel starting time to a distributional representation, which can be used to decode possible samples of on-path traveler behavior. Moreover, by analyzing the regional correlation which reveals various road segment relationships, we propose a regional attention to encode these correlations in a path. Also, we explore the idea of Kolmogorov-Smirnov (K-S) test to compare the sampled traveler behavior against the collected ground truth to facilitate training. Experimental results show that the proposed TraveL model outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets, by 14.7% in Mean K-S distance for travel time distribution estimation, 16.7% in Mean Absolute Error (MAE) for path similarity prediction, and 3.97% in MAE for destination prediction.

</details>


### [145] [It's the Problem, Not the Path: Budget and Difficulty Confounds in LLM Reasoning Trajectories](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03436)
*Yigit Utku Bulut*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges two common interpretations of LLM reasoning traces: (1) "breakthrough" moments where models suddenly succeed, and (2) early-legible fates where early tokens predict final outcomes. The authors supply counterfactual controls at the claim level through two experiments: (1) a restart-controlled truncation probe comparing continuation vs. restart solve rates, and (2) a pre-registered test for early-window internal signals. Both analyses find no evidence supporting these claims - high pooled probe AUROCs are explained by difficulty proxies, and within-problem evaluation shows chance-level performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors argue that previous claims about "breakthrough" moments and early-legible fates in LLM reasoning rest on measurements missing a counterfactual control at the level of the claim. They aim to provide these controls to properly evaluate these interpretations.

Method: Two methods: (1) Restart-controlled truncation probe - compares per-anchor continuation solve rates against from-scratch restart curves at matched total generated-token budget across 178 problem-model cells (89 MATH problems × 2 models); (2) Pre-registered difficulty-controlled test - evaluates outcome information in early-window internal signals, with two generation-free analyses: a trace-blind difficulty proxy and a reconstruction of published early-window positive probe.

Result: Experiment 1: Only 1/178 cells survives as prefix-limited; continuing the model's own prefix beats restarting in 9/9 cases - predominantly compute compression rather than expanded reachability. Experiment 2: No detectable outcome information in early-window signals beyond difficulty baseline; trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches AUROC 0.873 (within published probe range); within-problem evaluation shows chance-level performance at all ten anchors (0.496 at t=4).

Conclusion: High pooled probe AUROCs cannot by themselves establish within-attempt information; a question-only baseline or within-problem evaluation is required. The "breakthrough" and "early-legible fate" interpretations of LLM reasoning are not supported when proper controls are applied.

Abstract: Reasoning traces of large language models are widely read as containing "breakthrough" moments and early-legible fates. Both readings rest on measurements missing a counterfactual control at the level of the claim; we supply both controls. First, a restart-controlled truncation probe separates when a solution fits the continuation budget from when a prefix carries value that fresh computation cannot buy, comparing per-anchor continuation solve rates against from-scratch restart curves at matched total generated-token budget. Applied to 178 problem-model cells (89 MATH problems x two small open models, an outcome-blind but difficulty-targeted cohort), exactly 1 of 178 cells survives as prefix-limited; restart dose-response separates a compute-starved model from a capability-limited one; and wherever the matched budget lies inside the restart grid, continuing the model's own prefix beats restarting (9 of 9) -- predominantly compute compression rather than expanded reachability. Second, a pre-registered, difficulty-controlled test finds no detectable outcome information in early-window internal signals beyond a problem-difficulty baseline, and two generation-free analyses of public corpora show why this control is needed: a trace-blind difficulty proxy reaches AUROC 0.873 on 192K DeepSeek-R1 generations -- inside the published probe range -- and a closely matched reconstruction of the closest published early-window positive recovers a comparable pooled result (0.849) while within problem it is statistically indistinguishable from chance at all ten anchors (0.496 at t=4); a post-hoc within-targeted probe finds only a small average residual, concentrated in three low-failure problems. High pooled probe AUROCs cannot by themselves establish within-attempt information; a question-only baseline or within-problem evaluation is required.

</details>


### [146] [Guide, Not Bind: Why Defeasible Priors Fail in Augmented Lagrangian Causal Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03442)
*Sairam Sundararaman,Sara Girdhar,Manit Narasimha Murthy,Samrudh N,Bhaskarjyoti Das*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper identifies two fundamental failures in differentiable causal discovery methods that encode expert priors as forbidden-edge constraints using Augmented Lagrangian (ALM). First, sequential penalty-ramping ALM suppresses true edges before detection. Second, correlation-matching objective creates a tie between edge directions that covariance matching would resolve.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The "guide, not bind" approach assumes that data-adaptive relaxation will override rules that data consistently contradicts. The authors investigate why this assumption fails in practice.

Method: The authors provide theoretical analysis with propositions and lemmas, plus empirical validation across 3,072 training runs with graphs of 4-32 nodes. They introduce DADU as a test case for natural relaxation rules.

Result: Two independent failures: (1) Sequential penalty-ramping suppresses true edges before counterfactual detection can identify the error (87-97% failure rate); (2) Correlation-matching creates exact cost ties (2r²) between edges and their reverses, while covariance matching provides separation margin of at least w₀⁴.

Conclusion: The "guide, not bind" design fails for two independent reasons. The first requires any adaptive relaxation to satisfy three necessary conditions (Proposition). The second requires switching from correlation-matching to covariance-matching to restore identifiability.

Abstract: Differentiable causal discovery methods increasingly encode expert priors as forbidden-edge constraints enforced by an Augmented Lagrangian (ALM) penalty, on the assumption that a data-adaptive relaxation mechanism will discount and eventually override a rule the data consistently contradicts. We show this design, which we call \emph{guide, not bind}, fails for two independent, precisely characterized reasons, and that directly repairing both restores it only partially. First, sequential penalty-ramping ALM suppresses a wrongly-forbidden true edge before any counterfactual check can detect it: we give three necessary conditions any adaptive relaxation must satisfy to avoid this (Proposition~\ref{prop:conditions}), prove that DADU---the natural relaxation rule this paper introduces as the object of study---violates all three (Corollary~\ref{cor:dadu_failure}), and confirm the failure across 3{,}072 training runs spanning graphs from 4 to 32 nodes, where a single wrong prior suppresses a true edge in 87--97\% of trials under DADU. Second, and independent of any fix to the mechanism, we prove in closed form that the standard correlation-matching objective ties a true edge and its reverse to an identical cost of exactly $2r^2$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:tie}), not because the underlying equal-variance model is unidentifiable, but because normalizing to correlation discards exactly the variance information that would make it identifiable; covariance matching instead separates the two directions by a provable margin of at least $w_0^4$ (Lemma~\ref{lem:separation}).

</details>


### [147] [Beyond Straightness: Non-Crossing Flow Matching via Quantile AlignTree Coupling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03443)
*Junyi Lin,Mengyu Li,Jingxuan Hu,Kejun He,Cheng Meng*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: QAT-FM proposes a hierarchical quantile-aligned tree coupling for flow matching that achieves O(Nd log N) construction time and O(d) sampling complexity, addressing path crossings and velocity ambiguity issues while maintaining competitive generative performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Flow Matching suffers from path crossings and local velocity ambiguity with independent coupling, while OT-based couplings are computationally expensive. This work aims to develop an efficient structured coupling strategy that balances computational cost with path quality.

Method: Quantile AlignTree Flow Matching (QAT-FM) constructs a hierarchical coupling between Gaussian prior and target data via quantile-aligned tree structure, enabling efficient O(Nd log N) coupling construction and O(d) per-pair source sampling.

Result: QAT-FM achieves marginal consistency, induces non-crossing linear interpolation paths, and improves path separation at intermediate times compared to independent coupling. Experiments show competitive generative performance with substantially reduced coupling construction cost.

Conclusion: QAT-FM provides an efficient alternative to OT-based coupling that addresses path crossing issues while maintaining scalability for large-scale high-dimensional generative tasks, with natural extension to conditional generation.

Abstract: The performance of Flow Matching largely depends on the quality of the coupling between the source and target distributions. However, independent coupling often leads to path crossings and local velocity ambiguity, while OT-based couplings typically incur high construction costs. To address this challenge, we propose Quantile AlignTree Flow Matching (QAT-FM), an efficient structured coupling strategy that constructs a hierarchical coupling between a Gaussian prior and the target data distribution via a quantile-aligned tree structure. QAT-FM constructs the coupling in $\mathcal{O}(Nd\log N)$ time and supports per-pair source sampling with $\mathcal{O}(d)$ complexity, enabling scalable training for large-scale high-dimensional generative tasks. Theoretically, we prove that the QAT coupling satisfies marginal consistency, induces non-crossing linear interpolation paths, and consistently improves path separation at intermediate times compared with independent coupling, thereby alleviating local velocity ambiguity. QAT-FM further extends naturally to conditional generation, enabling structured conditional coupling while preserving global Gaussian alignment. Experiments across diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that QAT-FM achieves competitive generative performance while substantially reducing coupling construction cost.

</details>


### [148] [A Two-Stage Forecasting System for CPU Workload Prediction in Private Clouds](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03457)
*Ashir Javeed,Anton Borg,Håkan Grahn,Lars Lundberg,Dhyey Patel,Sogand Shirinbab*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a two-stage integrated forecasting model for cloud resource prediction that first forecasts customer service requests (TPS) then estimates CPU workload from TPS forecasts, using XGBoost with adaptive online retraining to handle concept drift.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing cloud resource forecasting approaches directly estimate CPU workload from historical traces without considering the relationship between customer service demand and resource consumption, leading to suboptimal predictions.

Method: Two-stage cascaded learning architecture: (1) XGBoost model for TPS forecasting, (2) XGBoost model for CPU workload prediction from TPS forecasts, with adaptive online retraining using expanding-window strategy to address concept drift.

Result: Achieved SMAPE below 7% for most applications; best results: MAE=0.7372, RMSE=1.1866, SMAPE=3.57%, R²=0.9185. Stable recursive forecasting across 60-step horizon with controlled error accumulation.

Conclusion: The two-stage integrated model outperforms conventional direct CPU forecasting in robustness, computational efficiency, and interpretability, making it suitable for proactive resource management and intelligent auto-scaling in cloud environments.

Abstract: Accurate cloud resource forecasting is essential for proactive resource provisioning, maintaining Quality of Service (QoS), and reducing operational costs in dynamic cloud environments. The existing forecasting approaches predominantly estimate future CPU workload directly from historical resource traces, which often overlook the relationship between customer service demand and subsequent resource consumption. This study proposes a two-stage integrated forecasting model that explicitly models this dependency by first forecasting customer service requests, expressed as Transactions Per Second (TPS), and subsequently estimating future CPU workload from the TPS forecast. Both the forecasting component and resource prediction component employed the XGBoost model within a cascaded learning architecture, complemented by adaptive online retraining using an expanding-window strategy to address concept drift in continuously evolving cloud workloads. The proposed work was evaluated using real-world traces collected from a private cloud environment comprising ten applications. Experimental results demonstrate robust forecasting performance by achieving Symmetric Mean Absolute Percentage Error (SMAPE) below $7\%$ for most applications, with the best-performing application achieving an MAE of $0.7372$, RMSE of $1.1866$, SMAPE of $3.57\%$, and an R2 of $0.9185$. Horizon-wise drift analysis confirmed stable recursive forecasting behavior with controlled error accumulation across a 60-step prediction horizon. Compared with the conventional direct CPU forecasting method, the proposed two-stage integrated model gives improved forecasting robustness, computational efficiency, and interpretability, making it well-suited for proactive resource management and intelligent auto-scaling in cloud computing environments.

</details>


### [149] [Mind the Gap: Robustness Risks in PII Detection Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03464)
*Adeel Zafar,Slawomir Nowaczyk*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper exposes a critical gap in PII detection systems: strong benchmark performance masks significant robustness failures under realistic distribution shifts. The authors stress-test three major PII detection architectures (encoder-based NER, rule-based, and LLM-based) across seven categories of natural distribution shift, revealing that each has distinct and complementary failure modes. They propose a hybrid pipeline with QA-driven feedback loop to address these weaknesses.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Modern PII detection systems achieve high accuracy on standard benchmarks, but these benchmarks do not reflect realistic deployment conditions where inputs are noisy, unstructured, and informal. Missed PII entities in deployment constitute direct privacy and security risks, yet current evaluation methodologies mask these weaknesses by focusing only on aggregate accuracy scores.

Method: The authors construct a stress test benchmark spanning seven categories of natural distribution shift and evaluate three representative systems from major architectural families: (1) encoder-based NER (SpaCy), (2) rule-based hybrid detection (Presidio), and (3) generative LLM extraction (Qwen2.5-3B). They analyze failure modes across these architectures.

Result: All three architectures exhibit significant performance degradation on out-of-distribution inputs, but with distinct failure profiles: encoder models primarily fail on unseen surface forms and boundary detection; rule-based systems fail on non-standard formats; and LLMs exhibit entity-type confusion and generation instability. No single architecture is uniformly reliable across all PII categories.

Conclusion: Aggregate benchmark scores obscure deployment-critical weaknesses in PII detection systems. The authors propose a hybrid detection pipeline with a QA-driven feedback loop for iterative risk mitigation. They release their benchmark to support out-of-distribution-aware evaluation of PII systems.

Abstract: Personally Identifiable Information (PII) detection is a foundational component of data protection infrastructure where missed entities constitute direct privacy and security risks. Although modern PII systems report strong performance on standard benchmarks, we show that these evaluations mask substantial robustness failures under realistic distribution shifts encountered in deployment. Rather than comparing state-of-the-art accuracy, we study how different PII detection paradigms fail under noisy, unstructured, and informal inputs. We construct a stress test benchmark spanning seven categories of natural distribution shift and evaluate representative systems from three widely deployed architectural families: encoder-based NER (SpaCy), rule-based hybrid detection (Presidio), and generative LLM extraction (Qwen2.5-3B).
  All three exhibit significant degradation on out-of-distribution inputs, but with distinct and complementary failure modes. Encoder models primarily fail on unseen surface forms and boundary detection, rule-based systems fail on non-standard formats, and LLMs exhibit entity-type confusion and generation instability. These results show that aggregate benchmark scores obscure deployment-critical weaknesses and that no single architecture is uniformly reliable across PII categories. Motivated by these findings, we propose a hybrid detection pipeline with a QA-driven feedback loop for iterative risk mitigation, and release our benchmark to support OOD-aware evaluation of PII systems.

</details>


### [150] [Spectral characteristics of autoencoder parameters as a vector representation of data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03495)
*Maria Nikitina,Anton Bishuk,Oleg Bakhteev*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates whether autoencoder model parameters can serve as dense vector representations of training data samples. By analyzing the spectral characteristics of parameter matrices, the authors demonstrate that singular values of these matrices relate to eigenvalues of the data covariance matrix, enabling model discrimination without original data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors seek to establish a theoretical connection between autoencoder parameters and the statistical properties of training data, testing the hypothesis that model parameters can represent data samples in a compressed form.

Method: The study combines theoretical analysis with experimental validation. Theoretically, the relationship between singular values of parameter matrices and eigenvalues of the data covariance matrix is derived. Experimentally, vector representations based on spectral characteristics are used to classify models trained on different data subsets.

Result: On CIFAR-10 and FashionMNIST datasets, the spectral-based vector representations achieve high accuracy in distinguishing between models trained on different data subsets, without requiring complex algorithms or access to original samples.

Conclusion: The parameters of trained autoencoders can effectively be viewed as sample representations, establishing a theoretical bridge between parameter space and data space through spectral analysis.

Abstract: This paper examines the relationship between the parameters of autoencoder models and the statistical properties of the data on which they are trained. Autoencoders are defined as models with an encoder-decoder architecture, trained to reconstruct input data through a compressed latent representation. It is proposed that the model parameters can be viewed as a dense vector representation of the corresponding sample. To test this hypothesis, a theoretical and experimental study is conducted in which a vector representation is formed based on the spectral characteristics of the autoencoder parameter matrices. Theoretical analysis shows that the singular values of the model parameter matrices are related to the eigenvalues of the covariance matrix of the training data, ensuring the transfer of information between the data space and the parameter space. Experimental results on the CIFAR-10 and FashionMNIST datasets confirm that the resulting vector representations allow for a high degree of accuracy in distinguishing between models trained on different data subsets, without resorting to complex vector generation algorithms or using the original samples. These results suggest that the parameters of trained autoencoders can be viewed as sample representations.

</details>


### [151] [Restricted Eigenvalues Beyond Gaussian Width: Threshold Occupancy under Heavy Tails](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03504)
*Shi Fu,Huibo Xu,Qixin Zhang,Dacheng Tao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper resolves the COLT 2015 open problem by showing that restricted eigenvalue (RE) bounds guaranteeing stable recovery, which hold for isotropic sub-Gaussian designs with sample size 1+w(A)², fail in general for heavy-tailed designs under only uniform small-ball conditions. The obstruction is "simultaneous threshold occupancy," where constant-width polyhedral descent cones exhibit zero empirical RE on every sample path up to half the ambient dimension.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The COLT 2015 open problem asked whether the same sample size law (1+w(A)²) that governs stable recovery for isotropic sub-Gaussian measurements would also hold for heavy-tailed designs using only a uniform small-ball condition. This question is fundamental to understanding the minimal assumptions needed for successful regularized estimation in high-dimensional statistics.

Method: The authors construct explicit counterexamples using constant-width polyhedral descent cones with fixed small-ball constants. They demonstrate that every finite range space admits exact threshold encoding in an arbitrarily narrow spherical cap, with a lift to a full polyhedral descent-cone section. The analysis involves threshold VC dimension and worst-case sample complexity bounds.

Result: The proposed law fails in its full dimension-free, arbitrary-set form. For threshold VC dimension d, as β↓0, the sharp worst-case sample complexity is Θ(β^{-1}[d log(1/β) + log(1/δ)]). On the same constant-width cone, Gaussian measurements succeed with O(1 + log(1/δ)) samples, while isotropic heavy-tailed designs fail pathwise for n ≲ √(p/log p). Under isotropy, a distribution-free fallback governed by affine dimension × squared enclosing radius is sharp on this family.

Conclusion: The sample complexity law that works for isotropic sub-Gaussian designs does not generalize to heavy-tailed designs under small-ball conditions alone. The key obstruction is simultaneous threshold occupancy. A distribution-free fallback bound exists but is suboptimal. This settles the COLT 2015 open problem in the negative, demonstrating fundamental differences in the behavior of sub-Gaussian versus heavy-tailed designs for regularized estimation.

Abstract: Restricted eigenvalue (RE) bounds govern stable recovery by norm-regularized estimators. For isotropic sub-Gaussian measurements, the benchmark sample size is $1+w(A)^2$, where $w(A)$ is the Gaussian width of the normalized descent cone. The COLT 2015 open-problem note (Banerjee et al., 2015) asked whether the same law follows for heavy-tailed designs from a uniform small-ball condition alone. We give an explicit and systematic negative answer to the general question as formulated there: the proposed law fails in its full dimension-free, arbitrary-set form, and the missing obstruction is simultaneous threshold occupancy. A constant-width polyhedral descent cone with fixed small-ball constants has zero empirical RE on every sample path up to half the ambient dimension. More generally, every finite range space admits exact threshold encoding in an arbitrarily narrow spherical cap and a lift to a full polyhedral descent-cone section. For every fixed threshold VC dimension $d$, as $β\downarrow0$, the sharp worst-case sample complexity is $Θ(β^{-1}[d\log(1/β)+\log(1/δ)])$. The separation persists under exact isotropy and all finite moments: on the same constant-width cone, Gaussian measurements succeed with $O(1+\log(1/δ))$ samples, whereas an isotropic heavy-tailed design fails pathwise for $n\lesssim\sqrt{p/\log p}$. Gaussian smoothing yields an everywhere-positive $C^\infty$ density while retaining arbitrarily poor RE. Under isotropy, a distribution-free fallback governed by affine dimension times squared enclosing radius is sharp on this family.

</details>


### [152] [An Adversarial Zero-Shot Learning Approach for Anomaly Detection in Multivariate IoT Traffic Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03505)
*Mahshid Rezakhani,Tolunay Seyfi,Fatemeh Afghah*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a novel multivariate time-series anomaly detection framework for IoT networks using a sequence-based VAE combined with adversarial learning and contrastive loss. The method enables zero-shot domain adaptation without labeled data or raw feature transfer, using encoder/decoder adaptor layers to handle domain heterogeneity and a destination-based segmentation strategy for IoT traffic modeling.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation stems from the unique challenges of anomaly detection in IoT networks: device diversity, lack of labeled data, and domain variability across different environments (industrial, enterprise, smart home, military, etc.). Existing methods struggle with zero-shot generalization across domains without requiring labeled data or direct feature transfer.

Method: The proposed framework combines: (1) Sequence-based VAE architecture for multivariate time-series modeling, (2) Adversarial learning for domain-invariant latent representations, (3) Contrastive loss for semantically structured embedding spaces, (4) Encoder and decoder adaptor layers for cross-domain feature distribution alignment while preserving contextual semantics, (5) Destination-based segmentation strategy to model real-world IoT communication structures.

Result: Evaluated on 6 datasets across 5 domains (industrial, enterprise, general-purpose, smart home, military automation) with 44 transfer scenarios. The method demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization in several cross-domain settings and achieves competitive performance against a contrastive domain-adaptation baseline under realistic, heterogeneous, and privacy-constrained IoT conditions.

Conclusion: The proposed framework successfully enables zero-shot domain adaptation for IoT anomaly detection without requiring labeled data or raw feature transfer. The combination of adversarial learning, contrastive loss, and adaptor layers effectively addresses domain heterogeneity while preserving semantic information, making it suitable for real-world IoT deployments with diverse device types and environments.

Abstract: Anomaly detection in Internet of Things (IoT) networks presents unique challenges due to the diversity of devices, lack of labeled data, and domain variability across environments. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for multivariate time-series anomaly detection that leverages adversarial learning and contrastive loss within a sequence-based Variational Autoencoder (VAE) architecture. Our method enables zero-shot domain adaptation by jointly optimizing domain-invariant latent representations and semantically structured embedding spaces, without requiring labeled data or raw feature transfer. To address the heterogeneity of IoT deployments, we introduce encoder and decoder adaptor layers that align feature distributions across domains while preserving contextual semantics. Additionally, we propose a destination-based segmentation strategy to better model real-world communication structures in IoT traffic. Our framework is comprehensively evaluated on six distinct datasets spanning industrial, enterprise, general-purpose, smart home, and military automation domains across 44 transfer scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization in several cross-domain settings and competitive performance against a contrastive domain-adaptation baseline under realistic, heterogeneous, and privacy-constrained IoT conditions.

</details>


### [153] [LongCounsel-8: A Benchmark Suite for Longitudinal Depression Tracking from Multi-Session Counseling Dialogues](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03507)
*Jiayi Li,Zhaomin Wu,Bingsheng He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LongCounsel-8 is a benchmark suite with 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories for tracking depression across sessions. It addresses the scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with standardized depression labels by combining profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization. Experiments reveal that existing methods struggle with trend identification, are less reliable on worsening trajectories, and can be hurt by additional session history.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Progress on tracking depression from multi-session counseling dialogues is constrained by the scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with standardized session-level depression labels. Existing resources typically provide either multi-session conversations without depression labels or labeled interviews in a single session.

Method: The authors combine profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization to address three challenges: maintaining longitudinal consistency and diversity, grounding symptom progression in empirical patterns, and expressing controlled depression states naturally without exposing target labels.

Result: Simulated self-reports closely recover the controlled states, supporting label fidelity. Experiments on existing depression tracking methods reveal three key findings: (1) lower single-session score error does not guarantee accurate identification of trend; (2) existing methods are consistently less reliable on worsening trajectories; and (3) additional session history may reduce the accuracy of trend prediction.

Conclusion: LongCounsel-8 establishes a foundation for advancing depression assessment from static, single-session prediction toward reliable longitudinal tracking of mental-health change. The benchmark reveals critical limitations in current approaches that must be addressed for effective depression monitoring across counseling sessions.

Abstract: Tracking depression from multi-session counseling dialogues requires estimating both current symptom severity and how it changes across sessions. Yet progress on this task is constrained by the scarcity of longitudinal counseling data with standardized session-level depression labels. Existing resources typically provide either multi-session conversations without depression labels or labeled interviews in a single session. Building such a benchmark poses three challenges: maintaining longitudinal consistency and diversity, grounding symptom progression in empirical patterns, and expressing controlled depression states naturally without exposing target labels. To address these challenges, we introduce LongCounsel-8, a benchmark suite of three independently generated datasets totaling 7,749 five-session counseling trajectories, grounded in real-world client profiles, depression trajectories, symptom compositions, and counseling patterns. We combine profile-grounded simulation, empirically informed state construction, and indirect behavioral realization to address these challenges. Across the benchmark, simulated self-reports closely recover the controlled states, supporting label fidelity. Experiments on existing depression tracking methods reveal three key findings: (1) lower single-session score error does not guarantee accurate identification of trend, i.e., improvement or worsening; (2) existing methods are consistently less reliable on worsening trajectories; and (3) additional session history may reduce the accuracy of trend prediction. Together, these findings establish LongCounsel-8 as a foundation for advancing depression assessment from static, single-session prediction toward reliable longitudinal tracking of mental-health change.

</details>


### [154] [LeanGRPO: Eliminating Redundant Recomputation in Diffusion RL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03528)
*Sijie Wang,Zhiqiang Tan,Xinrui Yang,Shaohuai Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LeanGRPO proposes two recompute-free training schedules for trajectory-logprob diffusion RL that eliminate redundant gradient computations in on-policy training settings, achieving up to 1.83x speedup over methods like DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing diffusion RL methods (DanceGRPO, FlowGRPO) recompute selected timesteps with gradient tracking after rollout, which is mathematically redundant when using the same backend for rollout and update. This redundancy creates unnecessary computational overhead.

Method: LeanGRPO restructures the data-parallel layout and introduces two training schedules: (1) LeanGRPO-Retain enables gradient tracking during rollout and directly reuses computation graphs and saved activations for backward; (2) LeanGRPO-Reweight enables gradients during rollout, backpropagates each selected step using provisional advantage, delays gradient synchronization, then corrects with true advantage after trajectory completion.

Result: LeanGRPO achieves up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup while preserving the original optimization objective, tested on FlowGRPO/DanceGRPO with FLUX.1-dev and Wan models.

Conclusion: The two schedules target different model scales and input sizes, successfully eliminating redundant computation in diffusion RL training without compromising optimization quality.

Abstract: Diffusion reinforcement learning (RL) has recently achieved significant success in post-training image and video generative models. However, most diffusion RL methods, including DanceGRPO and FlowGRPO, recompute selected timesteps with gradient tracking after rollout. Under on-policy training with the same backend for rollout and update, this recomputation is mathematically redundant. Intuitively, the rollout and policy update steps can reuse the same feed-forward backbone to avoid redundant computation, but doing so can incur a large memory overhead during rollout. To address the issue, we present LeanGRPO by restructuring the data-parallel layout and introducing two recompute-free training schedules for trajectory-logprob diffusion RL: (1) LeanGRPO-Retain enables gradient tracking during rollout and directly reuses the resulting computation graphs and saved activations for backward during update, requiring no recomputation; and (2) LeanGRPO-Reweight also enables gradients during rollout, but immediately backpropagates each selected step using a provisional advantage and delays gradient synchronization, then corrects the provisional gradients with the true advantage after the trajectory is completed. These schedules target different model scales and input sizes. Across FlowGRPO/DanceGRPO with FLUX.1-dev and Wan, LeanGRPO achieves up to 1.83x end-to-end speedup while preserving the original optimization objective.

</details>


### [155] [Coupled Scaling: A Representational Accessibility Framework for Neural Scaling Laws](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03533)
*Jie Wang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces "Coupled Scaling," a task-conditioned framework that explains how neural network scaling depends on the relationship between task structure and the geometry accessible to an architecture-optimization system. The framework derives scaling exponents from the interaction between data-model spectra and architectural support, rather than deriving them solely from data geometry.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing neural scaling theories derive scaling laws from data geometry or a specified data-model spectrum, but the authors observe that systems trained on the same data can scale differently when architecture or optimization changes the representations they can efficiently reach. This motivates a framework that accounts for how architecture and optimization affect the accessible representation geometry.

Method: The authors develop a solvable mode-truncation model where loss separates into: (1) target energy outside architectural support, and (2) an unresolved supported tail. They analyze the residual between the best-N supported tail and the tail beyond the largest completed high-value prefix. Using cumulative-tail and coverage log-rates (γ_{A,T} and ρ_{A,O,T}), they derive that the residual exponent lies in [ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T}, γ_{A,T}]. Under bounded off-prefix gain, they derive α_{A,O,T} = ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T} = ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T} - 1). A fixed-kernel specialization derives the training-time exponent from the near-zero tail of a task-weighted spectral measure.

Result: The framework establishes that the residual exponent lies in [ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T}, γ_{A,T}], with the completed prefix being rate-determining under bounded off-prefix gain. This yields α_{A,O,T} = ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T} - 1). The framework separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and motivates two validation tests: (1) static task-relevant geometry should track loss at common budget, and (2) multiscale geometry should track coupling-specific exponent ordering.

Conclusion: The Coupled Scaling framework provides a principled way to understand how architecture and optimization affect neural scaling. It separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and motivates specific experimental tests. The authors propose an audit of released emergence trajectories to identify controls needed for direct factorial tests that measure geometry separately from scaling fit.

Abstract: Existing theories derive neural scaling from data geometry or a specified data-model spectrum, but systems trained on the same data can scale differently when architecture or optimization changes the representations they can efficiently reach. We introduce Coupled Scaling, a task-conditioned framework in which finite-budget scaling depends on the relation between task structure and the geometry accessible to an architecture-optimization system. In a solvable mode-truncation model, loss separates into target energy outside architectural support and an unresolved supported tail. For an arbitrary priority order, the residual lies between the best-N supported tail and the tail beyond the largest completed high-value prefix. If the cumulative-tail and coverage log-rates are $γ_{A,T}$ and $ρ_{A,O,T}$, the residual exponent lies in $[ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T},γ_{A,T}]$. Under bounded off-prefix gain, the completed prefix is rate-determining and $α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}γ_{A,T}$; for $a_{A,T,j}\asymp j^{-b_{A,T}}$, this gives $α_{A,O,T}=ρ_{A,O,T}(b_{A,T}-1)$. A fixed-kernel specialization derives the training-time exponent from the near-zero tail of a task-weighted spectral measure defined independently of the loss fit. The framework separates architectural support from finite-budget acquisition and motivates two tests: static task-relevant geometry should track loss at a common budget, while multiscale geometry should track coupling-specific exponent ordering, including reversal across contrasting tasks. An audit of released emergence trajectories identifies the controls needed for a direct factorial test that measures geometry separately from the scaling fit.

</details>


### [156] [WeatherNext 3: Increasing resolution and performance of global weather models with raw observations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03582)
*Stephan Rasp,Boris Babenko,Dominic Masters,Andrew El-Kadi,Samier Merchant,Guy Shalev,Ilan Price,Fred Zyda,Remi Lam,Sasha Shysheya,Matthew Willson,Stratis Markou,Shreya Agrawal,Suhani Vora,Mohammed Alewi Hassen,Sunny Mak,Tom R. Andersson,Megan Bela,Akib Uddin,Nofar Peled Levi,Ben Gaiarin,Ferran Alet,Aaron Bell,Peter Battaglia,Alvaro Sanchez-Gonzalez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WeatherNext 3 is a new AI weather forecasting model that addresses limitations of existing AI models by ingesting real-time satellite data and achieving higher resolution (0.1 degree, hourly), enabling it to make predictions at any location using station data, establishing new state-of-the-art for probabilistic medium-range forecasting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI weather models suffer from two key shortcomings: (1) lower spatial and temporal resolution than physics-based models, and (2) inability to directly use observations as they are initialized with and trained on analysis data, inheriting any biases present in the analysis.

Method: WeatherNext 3 addresses these limitations through three key innovations: (1) generates hourly forecasts by ingesting low-latency geostationary satellite data (vs. traditional 6-hour intervals); (2) achieves temporal and spatial resolution on par with physics-based models (hourly time steps, 0.1 degree resolution for single-level variables including solar radiation and cloud cover); (3) learns to predict satellite-derived precipitation estimates, tropical cyclone and station observations, enabling 2m temperature and dewpoint predictions at any location conditioned on local geographical features.

Result: WeatherNext 3 establishes a new state-of-the-art for probabilistic medium-range forecasting skill. It achieves substantially lower error for 2m temperature and dewpoint predictions compared to competing global models, even when evaluated against unseen stations.

Conclusion: WeatherNext 3 moves operational AI-based weather forecasting beyond emulating the traditionally distinct stages of data assimilation, forecasting and post-processing, further pushing the frontier of performance and granularity for global weather prediction.

Abstract: State-of-the-art AI weather models have shown impressive medium-range forecast skill and computational efficiency, but suffer two key shortcomings: their forecasts have lower spatial and temporal resolution than the best physics-based models and they are exclusively initialized with and trained on analysis data. As a result, they cannot directly make use of observations, and any biases in the analysis are inherited by the forecast. WeatherNext 3 addresses these shortcomings and establishes a new state-of-the-art for probabilistic medium-range forecasting skill. First, WeatherNext 3 generates new forecasts every hour (rather than every 6 hours like traditional global models) by ingesting low-latency geostationary satellite data. Second, WeatherNext 3's temporal and spatial resolution are on par with physics-based global models, with hourly time steps and 0.1 degree resolution for single-level variables, including solar radiation and cloud cover. Third, WeatherNext 3 moves beyond traditional analysis variables by learning to predict satellite-derived precipitation estimates, as well as tropical cyclone and station observations. Modelling sparse station data allows WeatherNext 3 to make 2m temperature and dewpoint predictions at any location and time, conditioned on local geographical features, with substantially lower error than competing global models, even when evaluated against unseen stations. Together, WeatherNext 3's capabilities move operational AI-based weather forecasting beyond emulating the traditionally distinct stages of data assimilation, forecasting and post-processing, which helps to further push the frontier of performance and granularity for global weather prediction.

</details>


### [157] [Neural-Network Maxent: a general extension with learned nonlinearity, applied to time-series for Desert Locust distribution modelling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03603)
*Alessandro Grassi,Edoardo Kimani Bellotto,Wassim El Azami,Sabrina Outmani,Maximilien Houel*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RNN Maxent replaces Maxent's fixed feature transforms with a GRU neural network to capture temporal relationships in environmental time series for Desert Locust habitat modeling, improving AUC from 0.792 to 0.862 and F1 from 0.590 to 0.671.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard Maxent flattens time-series covariates into independent features, discarding sequential structure that carries critical signal for ecological monitoring. The Desert Locust's breeding dynamics are tightly coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions (precipitation, soil moisture, vegetation indices), requiring a method that captures nonlinear, temporal relationships.

Method: RNN Maxent replaces Maxent's fixed feature dictionary with a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) trained end-to-end via backpropagation. Preserves Maxent's presence-only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration. Uses 50-day environmental time series from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3 with a 7-day gap between covariates and presence records for forecasting behavior.

Result: RNN Maxent improves performance across metrics compared to standard Maxent: ROC AUC 0.862 (std 0.036) vs 0.792; F1 0.671 (std 0.056) vs 0.590.

Conclusion: The neural network approach successfully learns nonlinear temporal relationships from data rather than relying on fixed feature transforms, demonstrating significant improvements in habitat suitability mapping for Desert Locust forecasting.

Abstract: Species Distribution Modelling (SDM) is essential for understanding how environmental conditions shape biodiversity, particularly for destructive pests such as the Desert Locust (Schistocerca gregaria), whose breeding dynamics are tightly coupled to rapidly evolving environmental conditions. Maxent has become the dominant method for presence-only data, but its reliance on a linear combination of hand chosen feature transforms limits its ability to capture the nonlinear, temporal relationships common in ecological monitoring, where covariates such as precipitation, soil moisture, and vegetation indices evolve meaningfully over time. Standard implementations flatten time-series covariates into independent features, discarding sequential structure that carries critical signal. We introduce RNN Maxent, an extension of the Maxent framework that replaces the fixed feature dictionary with a neural network, specifically a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), trained end to end via backpropagation. The approach preserves Maxent's presence only statistical foundations, background normalization, and probability calibration, differing only in that the nonlinearity is learned from data rather than fixed in advance. We apply RNN Maxent to map suitable habitat for the Desert Locust using 50 day environmental time series derived from ERA5 Land, MODIS, and Sentinel 3, maintaining a 7 day gap between covariates and presence records to yield forecasting behavior. Compared against standard Maxent, RNN Maxent improves performance across metrics (ROC AUC 0.862 std 0.036 vs. 0.792; F1 0.671 std 0.056 vs. 0.590).

</details>


### [158] [On the Interaction Between Model Compression and Test-Time Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03604)
*Francesco Corti,Dong Wang,Young D. Kwon,Cecilia Mascolo,Olga Saukh*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper investigates how model compression affects test-time adaptation (TTA) performance. While compressed models maintain high accuracy under supervised adaptation, their TTA performance degrades significantly with increasing compression due to reduced representational diversity and structural constraints that limit recoverability.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Deep neural networks deployed in the wild require both efficiency (model compression) and adaptability (test-time adaptation). However, the interaction between these two techniques remains poorly understood, creating a need to systematically analyze how structured compression affects a model's ability to adapt under distribution shift.

Method: The authors use ResNet-18 and ViT-Base models on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C benchmarks. They evaluate multiple compression methods combined with standard TTA techniques. A diagnostic framework is introduced that examines representational expressivity and adaptation subspace compatibility.

Result: A consistent gap is revealed: compressed models retain high accuracy under supervised adaptation, but TTA performance degrades significantly with increasing compression. This degradation stems from reduced representational diversity and structural constraints that limit recoverability. The effects strongly depend on the compression method used.

Conclusion: The findings highlight the need to design compression strategies that preserve adaptability. Different compression methods have varying impacts on TTA performance, suggesting that compression technique selection should consider adaptation requirements alongside efficiency gains.

Abstract: Deep neural networks deployed in the wild must be both efficient and adaptable, requiring model compression and test-time adaptation (TTA). While both are well studied in isolation, their interaction remains poorly understood. We systematically analyze how structured compression affects a model's ability to adapt under distribution shift. Using ResNet-18 and ViT-Base on CIFAR-10-C and ImageNet-C, we evaluate multiple compression methods combined with standard TTA techniques. We introduce a diagnostic framework that examines representational expressivity and adaptation subspace compatibility. Our results reveal a consistent gap: although compressed models retain high accuracy under supervised adaptation, their TTA performance degrades significantly with increasing compression. We show that this stems from reduced representational diversity and structural constraints that limit recoverability. These effects strongly depend on the compression method, highlighting the need to design compression strategies that preserve adaptability.

</details>


### [159] [Local Updates, Global Learning (LUGL): Playing Games with non-incremental Learners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03660)
*David Milec,Spyridon Samothrakis,Michael Fairbank,Dennis J. N. J. Soemers*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: LUGL is a framework that enables gradient-boosted trees (LightGBM) to work in reinforcement learning settings by decoupling data collection from model fitting. It uses local updates (accumulating values in a table during self-play) and global learning (training a function approximator on the table before reset). This approach achieves competitive or superior performance compared to DQN and DeepCFR across nine benchmark games (Tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, Othello, Hex, Kuhn's poker, Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel, and Flop5 Hold'em).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neural Networks dominate RL in self-play training due to incremental learning capability. However, gradient-boosted trees (like LightGBM) are state-of-the-art for tabular data in supervised learning, often outperforming NNs. Game states are inherently tabular, making them ideal candidates for tree-based methods. The challenge is that non-incremental learners like GBTs fail in RL settings due to distributional shift.

Method: LUGL introduces a framework with two phases: (1) Local Updates phase - agent plays self-play games and accumulates tabular updates (Q-values, V-values, policies, or regret values) in a finite table; (2) Global Learning phase - the table is used to train a function approximator that generalizes to unseen states before the table is reset. This decouples data collection from model fitting, enabling non-incremental learners to operate in RL settings.

Result: Tested on four perfect-information games (Tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, Othello, Hex) and five imperfect-information games (Kuhn's poker, Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel, Flop5 Hold'em). LightGBM-based agents achieve competitive or superior performance compared to DQN and DeepCFR across all tested benchmarks.

Conclusion: The community's strong bias towards NNs in game-playing may be unwarranted. LightGBM-based agents using the LUGL framework achieve competitive or superior performance across all tested benchmarks, suggesting tree-based methods can be effective alternatives to NNs in RL for game-playing tasks.

Abstract: The dominance of Neural Networks (NNs) in RL is partially due to their incremental learning capability, which naturally suits the online, non-stationary nature of self-play training. However, gradient-boosted trees like LightGBM are widely recognised as the state of the art for tabular data in supervised learning, often outperforming NNs in accuracy and efficiency. Game states are inherently tabular---discrete actions, categorical card identities, structured board positions---which makes them an ideal candidate for tree-based methods. We introduce LUGL (Local Updates, Global Learning), a framework that decouples data collection from model fitting, enabling non-incremental learners such as GBTs to operate in RL settings where they would otherwise fail due to distributional shift. LUGL alternates between a local updates phase, where the agent plays self-play games and accumulates tabular updates (Q-values, V-values, policies, or regret values) in a finite table, and a global learning phase, where the table is used to train a function approximator that generalises to unseen states before the table is reset. We test our approach in four standard perfect-information games (Tic-tac-toe, Connect-4, Othello, and Hex) and five imperfect-information games (Kuhn's poker, Leduc Hold'em, Liar's Dice, Goofspiel, and Flop5 Hold'em), and show that our results are competitive with or superior to DQN and DeepCFR. Our experiments demonstrate that the community's strong bias towards NNs in game-playing may be unwarranted, since LightGBM-based agents achieve competitive or superior performance across all tested benchmarks.

</details>


### [160] [Extracting Forgotten Prompts from Targeted Unlearned Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03662)
*Au Ashley Hoi-Ting,Meghdad Kurmanji,William F. Shen,Nicholas D. Lane,Ligang He*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A new attack called Targeted Active Search (TAS) can extract forgotten prompts from unlearning models by identifying forgotten entities through selective querying using retained data and black-box model access, achieving 100% entity recovery and 95% prompt reconstruction with 99.7% fewer queries than naive probing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current unlearning methods (NPO, DPO, LUNAR) use refusal alignment to suppress forgotten data, but traces remain. While previous attacks assume forgotten prompts are known, this paper reveals a new vulnerability: forgotten prompts themselves can be extracted using only retained data and black-box model access.

Method: TAS attack works in two stages: (1) Identify forgotten entities by constructing canonical templates and entity pool, then selectively querying the model using the most informative template-entity pair under limited query budget; (2) Once entities are identified, instantiate prompt templates with those entities to probe the unlearned model and reconstruct the forgotten prompts.

Result: Experiments across three unlearning methods, three datasets, and three LLMs show that TAS recovers forgotten entities with 100% accuracy, reconstructs up to 95% of forgotten prompts, while using up to 99.7% fewer queries than naive probing.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates a significant security vulnerability in machine unlearning: adversaries can not only recover unlearned knowledge but also reconstruct the forgotten prompts themselves using only retained data and black-box model access, highlighting the need for more robust unlearning methods.

Abstract: Recent unlearning methods (e.g. NPO, DPO, LUNAR) make use of refusal alignment to suppress forgotten data. However, it has been shown that refusal responses might leave traces of unlearning, and recent attacks have been able to successfully recover some of the unlearned knowledge. In this paper, we uncover a new vulnerability. Existing attacks typically assume that the forgotten prompts are already known to the adversary and focus on recovering their answers. However, we show that the forgotten prompts themselves can be extracted by using the retained data and black-box access to the model. Our attack, Targeted Active Search (TAS), first identifies the forgotten entities by constructing canonical templates and entity pool, and selectively querying the model using the most informative template-entity pair under a limited query budget. Once the entities are identified, TAS instantiates prompt templates with those entities to probe the unlearned model and reconstruct the forgotten prompts. Experiments across three unlearning methods with three datasets and three LLMs shows that TAS recovers the forgotten entity with $100\%$ accuracy and reconstructs up to $95\%$ of forgotten prompts, all while using up to $99.7\%$ fewer queries than naive probing.

</details>


### [161] [Out-of-Distribution Generalisation with Sequence Models in Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03667)
*Oussama Hidaoui,Omer Ebead,Ulrich Armel Mbou Sob,Siddarth Singh,Juan Claude Formanek,Felix Chalumeau,Omayma Mahjoub,Sasha Abramowitz,Ruan John de Kock,Wiem Khlifi,Louay Ben Nessir,Simon Verster Du Toit,Daniel Rajaonarivonivelomanantsoa,Asim Awad Osman,Arnol Manuel Fokam,Refiloe Shabe,Arnu Pretorius*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses zero-shot task generalization in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) by extending sequence modelling architectures to handle multi-task settings with variable agent counts.
