The key finding is that scaling task diversity—not dataset size—is the dominant factor for achieving robust zero-shot transfer, with the approach achieving 3.2x improvement over single-task models across four environments.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning lacks principled analysis of zero-shot task generalization. A fundamental challenge exists in how to train MARL agents that can generalize to unseen tasks without additional fine-tuning, which is critical for real-world deployment where new tasks emerge frequently.

Method: Extended offline sequence modelling architectures to handle multi-task observation and action spaces alongside variable agent counts across tasks. Conducted large-scale experiments across four environments (Connector, RWARE, SMAX, LBF) investigating scaling behavior of task diversity, dataset size, and network capacity.

Result: Scaling task diversity is the dominant factor for zero-shot transfer, more important than dataset size. Multi-task approach achieves 3.2x mean improvement on held-out test tasks compared to single-task models and consistently outperforms strong behaviour cloning baselines.

Conclusion: Development of generalizable MARL agents should prioritize diversity of training distribution with varying numbers of agents rather than simply increasing dataset size. This provides a roadmap for scaling offline MARL effectively.

Abstract: Generalising to unseen tasks remains a fundamental challenge in offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). In this work, we present a principled analysis of zero-shot task generalisation in the offline setting and conduct an extensive empirical investigation into the scaling behaviour governing task diversity, dataset size, and network capacity. To facilitate this study, we extend offline sequence modelling architectures to handle multi-task observation and action spaces alongside variable agent counts across tasks. Our primary finding is that scaling task diversity---rather than sheer dataset size is the dominant factor in achieving robust zero-shot transfer. Through large-scale experiments across four challenging environments (Connector, RWARE, SMAX, and LBF), we demonstrate that our multi-task approach achieves a mean improvement of 3.2x on held-out test tasks compared to single-task models and consistently outperforms strong behaviour cloning baselines. These results suggest that the development of generalisable MARL agents should prioritise the diversity of the training distribution with varying numbers of agents, providing a roadmap for scaling offline MARL effectively.

</details>


### [162] [Resolution-Aware Experimental Design under Partial Identifiability](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03686)
*Sofianos Panagiotis Fotias*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Resolution-Aware Experimental Design (RAED), a novel framework for experiment selection under partial identifiability where nuisance uncertainty creates variable structural meanings for the same observation. The method selects experiments by minimizing expected nonempty structural candidate set size while controlling false exclusions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current experimental design frameworks choose experiments expected to provide the most information. However, under partial identifiability, persistent nuisance uncertainty causes the same observation to carry different structural meanings, making traditional information-based criteria potentially misleading.

Method: The authors propose RAED which selects experiments based on the smallest expected nonempty structural candidate set achievable subject to false-exclusion control. They prove an exact cross-nuisance aliasing separation showing experiments can be preferred by structural/full-latent information gain while having poorer valid structural resolution. They develop a learned score-based implementation with finite-sample nuisance-average and positive-tail calibration, with a rare-tail sample-complexity characterization.

Result: The paper demonstrates: (1) Theoretical separation between structural information gain and resolution - an experiment can be preferred by multiple information metrics while having arbitrarily poorer valid structural resolution; (2) Under constrained sensing, subsurface-flow benchmarks show genuine RAED-EIG disagreements with clearest/largest held-out resolution differences in WCA; (3) In fluvial benchmark, tail protection changes selected physical experiment and replaces hard-region false exclusions with explicit ambiguity; (4) In methane-oxidation benchmark, 5% false-exclusion tolerance yields nontrivial finite-sample population guarantee with 95% joint confidence across all three structural families.

Conclusion: RAED preserves expected ordering under genuine composite Blackwell comparison while addressing resolution limitations of traditional information-based approaches. The framework provides practical utility through tail-sensitive calibration and is applicable to real-world problems in subsurface flow, fluvial systems, and methane oxidation.

Abstract: Experimental design is commonly framed as choosing the experiment expected to provide the most information. Under partial identifiability however, persistent nuisance uncertainty can make the same observation carry different structural meanings. We introduce Resolution-Aware Experimental Design (RAED), which selects an experiment by the smallest expected nonempty structural candidate set achievable subject to false-exclusion control. We prove an exact cross-nuisance aliasing separation: an experiment can be preferred by structural and full-latent information gain, average classification, and nuisance-marginalized informativeness while having arbitrarily poorer valid structural resolution. RAED nevertheless preserves the expected ordering under a genuine composite Blackwell comparison. To make this criterion operational, we develop a learned score-based implementation with finite-sample nuisance-average and positive-tail calibration, and characterize a rare-tail sample-complexity obstruction. Under constrained sensing, two subsurface-flow benchmarks exhibit genuine RAED--expected-information-gain (EIG) experiment-selection disagreements, with the clearest and largest held-out resolution differences in WCA. In a fluvial benchmark, tail protection changes the selected physical experiment and replaces hard-region false exclusions primarily with explicit ambiguity. In a mechanistic methane-oxidation benchmark, a prospectively specified 5\% false-exclusion tolerance also yields a nontrivial finite-sample population guarantee for tail-sensitive nuisance risk, with 95\% joint confidence across all three structural families.

</details>


### [163] [Federated Causal Discovery via Regression-Directed Cumulants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03705)
*Pablo Torrijos,Fabio Stella,José A. Gámez,José M. Puerta*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses causal discovery in federated environments using Linear Non-Gaussian Acyclic Models (LiNGAM). The authors propose the FedRCD family of algorithms to overcome limitations of existing methods (DirectLiNGAM and FedISHC) that fail under near-symmetric noise or cannot be straightforwardly federated. A key finding is that cumulant-based federated methods actually rank variables by variance ladder (varsortability) rather than population asymmetry at zero, unlike scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Data scarcity in many domains makes centralized causal discovery challenging, while GDPR and other regulations prohibit centralizing data from different clients. The federated environment offers a solution to balance privacy and causal discovery accuracy, but existing federated LiNGAM methods have critical limitations.

Method: The authors use higher-order cumulant tensors that depend only on joint distributions and add across independent sample groups, enabling single-round communication for horizontal, vertical, and hybrid partitions. They propose the FedRCD family with three variants trading off communication rounds against algebraic noise, including exact federated counterparts of HC and HC-LiNGAM algorithms, with support for exact unlearning.

Result: At sample sizes typical of real deployments, cumulant-based federated methods do not rank variables by population asymmetry but by a variance ladder induced by the DAG along directed paths (cumulant counterpart of varsortability). Marginal standardization collapses every cumulant method to near-random ordering, while scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM remains unaffected but cannot be federated under this protocol.

Conclusion: The proposed FedRCD family provides federated causal discovery solutions with different trade-offs between communication efficiency and noise tolerance. However, a fundamental limitation was discovered: cumulant-based methods are susceptible to varsortability rather than true causal asymmetry, making them less reliable for causal discovery in practice compared to centralized DirectLiNGAM.

Abstract: In this paper we study linear non-Gaussian acyclic models (LiNGAM) when used in federated environments. These causal models allow one to go beyond Markov equivalence. However, in many domains data are scarce, and increasing the sample size by centralising data from different clients is not advisable due to regulations such as the GDPR. The federated environment offers an attractive option to balance privacy and causal discovery accuracy. Unfortunately, the standard centralised estimator in the LiNGAM setting, i.e., DirectLiNGAM, cannot be straightforwardly federated. Higher-order cumulant tensors offer a way around this obstacle: they depend only on the joint distribution of the variables involved and add exactly across independent sample groups, so a single communication round suffices in horizontal, vertical, and hybrid partitions.
  However, FedISHC, i.e., the current federated method along these lines, breaks down under near-symmetric noise. To overcome the above limitation, we introduce the FedRCD family of causal discovery algorithms, and investigate three variants that trade off communication rounds against algebraic noise; two of them are exact federated counterparts of the centralised high-order cumulant (HC) and HC-LiNGAM algorithms, and the single-round variants further effectively support exact unlearning at any granularity, from a single observation to a whole client. Numerical experiments show that at sample sizes typical of real deployments, the entire cumulant-based federated family does not actually rank variables by the population asymmetry that the scores encode at zero. It ranks them by a variance ladder induced by the DAG along its directed paths, the cumulant counterpart of varsortability. Marginal standardisation collapses every cumulant method to near-random ordering, while scale-invariant DirectLiNGAM, not federable under this protocol, is unaffected.

</details>


### [164] [Projected Riemannian Gradient Descent for the Bures-Wasserstein Barycenter: Dimension-Independent Linear Convergence at Unit Step Size](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03762)
*A. Afham*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper resolves a dichotomy in analyzing Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) for computing Bures-Wasserstein barycenters of positive definite matrices. Existing analyses showed either unit-step RGD with exponential dimension dependence or dimension-independent guarantees requiring small step sizes. The authors propose Projected RGD that achieves dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step size with rate (1 - κ^{-3/2}), improving iteration complexity from κ^{5/2} to κ^{3/2}. The key insight is a novel Projection Lemma showing eigenvalue clipping is the BW-metric projection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The existing analysis of RGD for BW barycenters presented a dichotomy: unit-step RGD (empirically fast) had worst-case exponential dimension dependence, while dimension-independent guarantees required small step sizes that lost empirical speed. The authors wanted to resolve this dichotomy without sacrificing the empirical performance of unit-step RGD.

Method: The authors propose a Projected RGD algorithm with unit step size. The key technical contribution is a novel Projection Lemma: clipping eigenvalues of a positive matrix to [α, β] is the closed-form, non-expansive (1-Lipschitz) BW-metric projection onto the set {S : αI ≤ S ≤ βI}. This projection reuses eigendecomposition needed for the next iteration, so computational cost remains unchanged.

Result: Projected RGD achieves dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step size with rate (1 - κ^{-3/2}), where κ is the condition number. This improves iteration complexity from κ^{5/2} (previous best small-step guarantee) to κ^{3/2}. The analysis also extends to the invariant matrix projection problem, identifying it as unit-step RGD on a totally geodesic submanifold.

Conclusion: The paper resolves the dichotomy between theoretical guarantees and empirical performance for RGD on BW barycenters. The proposed Projected RGD achieves the best of both worlds: dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step size. The Projection Lemma is the key technical insight that enables this result, and the same analysis applies to related problems like invariant matrix projection.

Abstract: The computation of the Bures-Wasserstein (BW) barycenter of an ensemble of positive definite matrices arises throughout machine learning, optimal transport, and quantum information. Riemannian gradient descent (RGD) at unit step size -- the fixed-point iteration used in practice -- converges rapidly, yet existing analyses present a dichotomy: unit-step guarantees carry worst-case exponential dependence on the dimension, while dimension-independent guarantees require small step sizes that forfeit the empirical speed. We resolve this dichotomy, not by improving the guarantees for unit-step RGD, but by proposing a Projected RGD algorithm that achieves dimension-independent linear convergence at unit step size. The achieved rate, $(1 - κ^{-3/2})$, where $κ$ is the condition number of the ensemble, also polynomially improves on the best small-step guarantee ($κ^{3/2}$ versus $κ^{5/2}$ iteration complexity). The crux is a novel Projection Lemma: clipping the eigenvalues of a positive matrix to an interval $[α, β]$ is the closed-form, non-expansive (1-Lipschitz) BW-metric projection onto the set $\{S : αI \leq S \leq βI\}$ -- a statement which, unlike its known one-sided counterpart, does not follow from convexity. The projection is moreover free: it reuses an eigendecomposition the next iteration must perform in any case, so the projected and unprojected iterations cost the same per step. The same analysis covers the invariant matrix projection problem of Brahmachari et al. (2025), whose fixed-point algorithm we identify as unit-step RGD on a totally geodesic submanifold, thereby extending the dimension-independent guarantee to that setting verbatim.

</details>


### [165] [From Nowcasting to Forecasting: Adapting a Reanalysis-Trained](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03763)
*Mikko Partio,Leila Hieta,Ossi Laine*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: CloudCast v2 is a machine-learning model for 12-hour cloud-cover forecasting that combines reanalysis data training with conditional flow matching for satellite cloud field adaptation, achieving 10% MAE improvement over its predecessor.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current short-range forecasting methods lose skill as clouds evolve through formation, dissipation, and deformation, while NWP forecasts may not accurately represent satellite-observed cloud states at initialization. The goal is to extend forecasts beyond the 1-3 hour nowcasting range while retaining spatial detail from satellite observations.

Method: CloudCast v2 uses a two-stage approach: (1) Training on Copernicus European Regional Reanalysis (Ridal2024) to learn cloud-evolution dynamics, then (2) Adaptation to satellite-derived cloud fields using conditional flow matching (Lipman2023), a generative method that transforms noise into forecasts conditioned on observed initial cloud fields and NWP inputs.

Result: CloudCast v2 reduces mean absolute error by 10% relative to CloudCast v1 over the 1-12 hour range. It also outperforms CloudCast v1 in fractions skill score (neighborhood-based spatial agreement) after approximately 3-6 hours, depending on cloudiness category.

Conclusion: Observation-initialized machine-learning forecasts can extend beyond the traditional 1-3 hour nowcasting range while retaining spatial detail from satellite cloud fields, demonstrating the potential of generative ML methods for medium-range cloud prediction.

Abstract: Accurate cloud-cover forecasts are important for temperature prediction, radiation forecasting, and solar-power operations. Short-range forecasting methods can preserve observed cloud placement during the first forecast hours, but their skill decreases when cloud fields evolve through formation, dissipation and deformation. Longer lead times require accounting for atmospheric evolution, but operational numerical weather prediction (NWP) forecasts may not accurately represent the satellite-observed cloud state at initialization. We develop CloudCast v2, a machine-learning model for 12-hour cloud-cover forecasting from observation-based initial conditions. The model is first trained on the Copernicus European Regional Reanalysis (Ridal2024) to learn cloud-evolution dynamics, and is then adapted to satellite-derived cloud fields using conditional flow matching (Lipman2023), a generative method that transforms noise into cloud-cover forecasts conditioned on the observed initial cloud fields and NWP inputs. CloudCast v2 reduces mean absolute error by 10% relative to its predecessor, CloudCast v1 (Partio2025), over the 1-12 h range. It also overtakes CloudCast v1 in fractions skill score, a neighborhood-based measure of spatial agreement, after approximately 3-6 h, depending on the cloudiness category. These results show that observation-initialized machine-learning forecasts can extend beyond the usual 1-3-hour nowcasting range while retaining spatial detail from satellite cloud fields.

</details>


### [166] [OBER+: Continuity-Aware Reporting and Traceable Continuous Improvement in Outcome-Based Education](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03770)
*Elakkiya Rajasekar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: OBER+ is an institutional attainment platform that computes the step from measured learning outcome shortfalls to evaluated corrective actions, with five connected stages that accumulate attainment, signal shortfalls, grade them on regulator cutoffs, record decisions against annotated practice catalogues, and quantify subsequent movement. When applied to real course data, it revealed that naive outcome tracking would have reported a 25-point collapse between non-comparable outcomes, identified computation defects, and detected patterns in outcome statement changes without requiring thresholds or labels.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Institutions practising outcome-based education routinely compute learning outcome attainment, but reviews of curriculum analytics report an absence of evidence on how that computation informs decisions. There was a need for a computational design that not only measures attainment but also tracks the corrective actions taken and their effectiveness.

Method: The study designed OBER+ with five connected stages: (1) accumulating attainment across course deliveries, (2) signaling shortfalls and persistent shortfalls, (3) grading shortfalls on regulator cutoffs, (4) recording decisions against a catalogue of practices annotated with evidence, and (5) quantifying subsequent movement in shortfalls. An additional rule compares successive statements of outcomes to ensure attainment is not read across outcome changes. The system was applied to live records of two real courses.

Result: Three findings emerged: (1) Every outcome of a core course was substantively redefined between consecutive deliveries, with subject matter moving between outcome numbers—a naive reading would have reported a 25-point collapse between quantities that do not refer to the same learning. (2) Recomputing the platform's figures using the documented rule showed 6 of 10 differed by more than rounding, revealing a defect since reported to the institution. (3) Across 15 statement pairs from three transitions, 5 were identical, and among the 10 that were not, the outcome carrying a given number was nearest to a differently numbered earlier outcome in 6 cases—a result requiring no threshold and no labelling.

Conclusion: The contribution is a computational design for outcome-based reporting, stated as rules any attainment platform can implement, with evidence of what they make visible in a live institutional record. The system reveals critical issues that naive tracking misses, including non-comparable outcomes across deliveries, computation defects, and patterns in outcome statement changes.

Abstract: Institutions practising outcome-based education compute learning outcome attainment routinely, while reviews of curriculum analytics report an absence of evidence on how that computation informs decisions. This paper presents OBER+, an extension of a deployed institutional attainment platform that computes the step from a measured shortfall to an evaluated corrective action. Five connected stages accumulate attainment across deliveries of a course, signal a shortfall and a persistent shortfall, grade it on cutoffs the regulator already uses, record the decision against a catalogue of practices annotated with their evidence, log the change, and quantify the subsequent movement in the shortfall. A further rule compares successive statements of an outcome, so attainment is never read as a series across a point at which the outcome changed. Applying the rules to the live record of two real courses produced three results. Every outcome of a core course was substantively redefined between consecutive deliveries, with subject matter moving between outcome numbers, so a naive reading would have reported a twenty-five point collapse between quantities that do not refer to the same learning. Recomputing the platform's figures from its documented rule showed six of ten differing by more than rounding explains, in a pattern that identified a defect since reported to the institution. Across fifteen statement pairs from three transitions, five were identical character for character, and among the ten that were not, the outcome carrying a given number was nearest to a differently numbered earlier outcome in six, a result resting on an ordering of similarities and requiring no threshold and no labelling. The contribution is a computational design for outcome-based reporting, stated as rules any attainment platform can implement, with evidence of what they make visible in a live institutional record.

</details>


### [167] [Landmark-Based Discrimination of Injury-Associated Athlete-Sessions from Minute-Resolution Multimodal Football Monitoring Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03790)
*Evangelos Chatzidimitriou,Konstantinos Tserpes*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses a mismatch in sports analytics where minute-by-minute athlete monitoring data must be modeled with only session-level injury labels. The authors propose a fixed-landmark approach that creates one representation per athlete-session at each landmark time point, avoiding the problem of assigning unsupported minute-level injury labels. Using data from 48 elite women's football athletes (3,743 sessions, 22 injury-associated), they evaluate various representations across different time landmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that athlete monitoring data is collected at minute-level granularity (e.g., GPS, heart rate, accelerometers), but injury outcome information is only available at the session level (the entire session was injury-associated or not). This temporal mismatch creates a modeling challenge: assigning the same session-level label to every minute implies knowing injury status at each exact time point, which is not actually known.

Method: The authors propose a fixed-landmark, one-representation-per-athlete-session formulation. Instead of labeling every minute, they construct one representation per athlete-session at each landmark (10, 20, 30 minutes) using only information observed up to that point. The target remains at the session level. They evaluated pre-session (PRE), cumulative (CUM), dynamic (DYN), and combined representations using Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost, with athlete-disjoint validation, bootstrap uncertainty, and sensitivity analyses.

Result: Primary CUM+DYN Logistic Regression achieved ROC-AUC ranging from 0.367 to 0.607 and PR-AUC from 0.0080 to 0.0150 across landmarks, with wide uncertainty intervals. PRE-containing representations showed higher point estimates at several landmarks but remained uncertain (overlapping confidence intervals).

Conclusion: The fixed-landmark approach successfully addresses the temporal mismatch problem in athlete monitoring. However, the results show substantial uncertainty, with ROC-AUC values suggesting performance near random or slightly below chance. The wide uncertainty intervals indicate the need for more data or better features. The study highlights the challenges of predicting injury from minute-level monitoring data when only session-level labels are available.

Abstract: Athlete monitoring data may be recorded minute by minute throughout a match or training session, while injury information may only indicate whether the entire session was injury-associated.
  This creates a modelling problem: assigning the same session-level label to every minute would imply that injury status is known at each exact time, even though within-session injury onset is unknown.
  Our novelty is a fixed-landmark, one-representation-per-athlete-session formulation that directly addresses this mismatch. Instead of labelling every minute, we construct one representation per athlete-session at each landmark using information observed up to that point. This keeps the target at the session level and avoids unsupported minute-level injury supervision.
  A landmark is a fixed time point within the same session, such as 10, 20, or 30 minutes. At each landmark, we assess whether the whole session is injury-associated or non-injury-associated and examine how discrimination changes as more within-session information becomes available.
  Using 2020 SoccerMon data, we analyse 3,743 athlete-sessions from 48 elite women's football athletes, including 22 injury-associated sessions from five athletes. We evaluate pre-session, cumulative, dynamic, and combined representations with athlete-disjoint validation, athlete-cluster bootstrap uncertainty, common-cohort sensitivity analysis, alternative negative-athlete fold allocations, equal-athlete weighting, and Logistic Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost benchmarks.
  Primary CUM+DYN Logistic Regression yields ROC-AUC 0.367-0.607 and PR-AUC 0.0080-0.0150 across landmarks, with wide uncertainty. PRE-containing representations show higher point estimates at several landmarks but remain uncertain.

</details>


### [168] [From Ordered Bernoulli Levels to Critical-Line Geometry: Integer Quantization, Bernoulli Residual Phase, and Prime-Power Spectra](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03801)
*Y. Kenan Yılmaz*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper investigates the ordered Bernoulli-word kernel f(p,n,k)=p^k(1-p)^(n-k) and its geometric properties under complex continuation, exploring connections to Riemann zeta function critical line zeros without claiming a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The study aims to examine the geometry generated by inverse-integer level sets of the Bernoulli kernel and their connections to critical-line zero ordinates of the Riemann zeta function, seeking to link Dirichlet-series and Euler-product assemblies through complex analysis.

Method: The analysis uses complement-preserving complex continuation, quadratic coordinate transformations Q(z)=z(1-z), decomposition of levels L_k into integer and periodic residual components, circularization via Z_k=exp(2πiδ_k), and unique factorization into prime-generator coordinates.

Result: The study identifies p=1/2 as a unique real split-independent anchor, produces a conjugation-symmetric vertical geometry through complex continuation, achieves exact integer quantization at the central point, and links the construction to Dirichlet atoms m^(-s) through a distinct complex exponent s.

Conclusion: The paper establishes connections between Bernoulli polynomials, complex geometry, and zeta function zeros through exact identities and classical zeta connections, while keeping numerical controls and open conditional Weyl tests separate. No proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is claimed.

Abstract: We study the ordered Bernoulli-word kernel f(p,n,k)=p^k(1-p)^(n-k) and the geometry generated by its inverse-integer level sets. The binary level 2^(-n) selects p=1/2 as the unique real split-independent anchor. Under complement-preserving complex continuation, the pair becomes z=1/2+iu and 1-z=1/2-iu, producing a conjugation-symmetric vertical geometry before any zeta-function input is introduced. The quadratic coordinate Q(z)=z(1-z)=1/4+u^2 has a sharp minimum at the central point and admits an exact integer quantization. For critical-line zero ordinates gamma_k, the induced levels L_k=1/4+gamma_k^2 are decomposed exactly as L_k=N_k+delta_k, where N_k is the nearest integer and delta_k is a periodic first-Bernoulli residual. Circularization gives Z_k=exp(2 pi i delta_k), isolating gamma_k^2 mod 1 as the residual phase variable. Unique factorization resolves the integer shells into prime-generator coordinates, while a distinct complex exponent s lifts the same construction to the Dirichlet atoms m^(-s), linking the Dirichlet-series and Euler-product assemblies. Exact identities, classical zeta connections, numerical controls, and open conditional Weyl tests are kept explicitly separate. No proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is claimed.

</details>


### [169] [Free Pause Tokens](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03807)
*John Langford,Nathan Godey,Giovanni Monea,Yoav Artzi,Harry Dong,Ying Fan,Gustavo de Rosa,Zheng Zhan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A "free pause token" mechanism provides extra compute for next-token prediction without adding sequence length or KV cache. It improves prediction by 2-3 centinats on a 1B model with minimal training cost (1.14x) and no inference overhead, achieving isoflop, isoparameter, and isotoken improvements over standard transformers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Standard "thinking" or "pause" tokens improve LLM predictions but come at the cost of extra context length, KV cache, and latency during inference. This paper seeks to retain the benefits of pause tokens while eliminating their inference overhead.

Method: The method introduces a "free pause token" that operates in a parallel prediction stream over a weight-shared backbone, rather than as an extra token in the sequence. This allows extra compute per prediction without increasing sequence length or memory requirements.

Result: The approach achieves 2-3 centinats improvement in next-token prediction on a 1B parameter model. Training compute overhead is reduced to as low as 1.14x compared to optimized pretraining. At inference, it adds no context length, no KV cache, and negligible latency.

Conclusion: The free pause token provides isoflop, isoparameter, and isotoken improvements over standard next-token trained transformers, making it a cost-effective way to enhance LLM predictions without sacrificing inference efficiency.

Abstract: A free pause token gives a language model extra compute to form each next-token prediction (as a pause, or thinking, token does) but carries that compute in a parallel prediction stream over a weight-shared backbone rather than as an extra token in the sequence. It improves next-token prediction by 2-3 centinats in practice on a 1B parameter model. Because the pause rides an existing position instead of adding one, it is free to use: at inference it adds no context length, no KV cache, and essentially no latency with the growth in inference flops typically irrelevant as it is not the active bottleneck on throughput. The only primary cost is in training, where additional training compute versus an optimized pretraining pipeline is reduced to as low as x1.14 while preserving most of the benefits. The result is an isoflop, isoparameter, and isotoken improvement over standard next token trained transformers.

</details>


### [170] [A Peer-Relative Representation Learning Framework for Energy Inefficiency Identification in Mobile Network Sites](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03809)
*Eliud Nyakweba Koto,Jaco du Toit,Adham Stoltz,Johan du Preez*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes an unsupervised method to detect energy inefficiencies in mobile network sites by using an energy-aware Minimum Distortion Embedding (MDE) approach. The method compares sites with similar characteristics to identify anomalies, enabling operators to prioritize field investigations for energy savings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mobile network operators face high energy costs, but site-level inefficiencies (faulty cooling, idle equipment, parasitic loads) often go undetected due to lack of ground-truth labels and the presence of embedded inefficiencies in historical data.

Method: The study introduces an energy-aware MDE formulation that extends standard MDE with an energy-based repulsion mechanism. This encourages sites with anomalously high energy consumption relative to comparable peers to be displaced from their local neighborhoods in the embedding space, creating a low-dimensional representation that preserves structural similarity while encoding energy-related deviations.

Result: The proposed approach outperforms conventional anomaly detection baselines, providing a robust method for large-scale energy-efficiency optimization in mobile networks.

Conclusion: The energy-aware MDE approach effectively identifies potentially inefficient sites through peer-relative comparison, enabling operators to prioritize engineering resources on sites most likely to yield energy savings.

Abstract: Energy consumption is one of the largest operational expenditure items for mobile network operators, yet site-level energy inefficiencies such as faulty cooling controllers, idle radio equipment, and parasitic auxiliary loads often remain undetected because no ground-truth inefficiency labels exist and historical measurements may already contain embedded inefficiencies. This study proposes an unsupervised peer-relative approach based on the premise that sites with similar structural and operational characteristics should exhibit comparable energy consumption. To capture these relationships, a novel energy-aware Minimum Distortion Embedding (MDE) formulation is introduced that extends the standard MDE objective with an energy-based repulsion mechanism. This encourages sites with anomalously high energy consumption relative to comparable peers to become displaced from their local neighbourhoods in the embedding space. The resulting low-dimensional representation simultaneously preserves structural similarity and encodes energy-related deviations, enabling the identification of potentially inefficient sites through peer-relative comparison. The derived anomaly scores provide a practical mechanism for prioritising field investigations, allowing mobile network operators to focus engineering resources on sites most likely to yield energy savings. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms conventional anomaly detection baselines and provides a robust foundation for large-scale energy-efficiency optimisation in mobile networks.

</details>


### [171] [Witnesses Explain Anomalies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03826)
*Lamine Diop*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: WAND is an unsupervised tabular anomaly detector that provides built-in explanations by using "witness directions" (feature space vectors) as attributions, achieving comparable accuracy to 16 baselines on 47 datasets while eliminating the need for expensive post-hoc explanation methods like SHAP/LIME.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current unsupervised anomaly detectors provide scores without explaining why points are flagged. When explanations are needed, they must be added post-hoc using SHAP or LIME, which require thousands of re-queries per point and only provide approximations. This creates a gap between scoring and explainability in anomaly detection.

Method: WAND organizes computation around directions on the unit sphere, scoring each point by how far its projection escapes a sub-Gaussian extreme-value baseline. The key innovation is that "witness directions" (vectors in feature space) that flag a point serve as its natural explanation, providing per-feature attribution at no extra cost. The score is differentiable, allowing explanations to be recovered via gradients. The method achieves linear time complexity in sample size, and a probe-efficiency bound guarantees every anomaly has a witness (explanation).

Result: Across 47 ADBench datasets, WAND achieves the best mean Friedman rank at ROC-AUC parity with 16 unsupervised baselines. Its native explanations are more accurate and faithful than post-hoc SHAP/LIME and ECOD at a fraction of the query cost.

Conclusion: WAND provides interpretability at no accuracy cost, making it a practical solution for explainable anomaly detection. It addresses the fundamental limitation of bolted-on explanations by integrating explainability into the core detection algorithm.

Abstract: Unsupervised anomaly detection scores each point of an unlabelled, contaminated sample in a single pass, and increasingly must also explain why a point is flagged. Yet the dominant detectors give a score with no account of which features drive it, and explanations are bolted on post-hoc with SHAP or LIME, which re-query the detector thousands of times per point and only approximate it. We introduce WAND, an unsupervised tabular anomaly detector that is explainable by design. WAND organises its computation around directions on the unit sphere, scoring each point by how far its projection escapes a sub-Gaussian extreme-value baseline. The originality of our approach is that the witness directions that flag a point, being vectors in feature space, are its explanation, a per-feature attribution obtained at no cost over scoring and, since the score is differentiable, recoverable by gradients. Scoring is linear in the sample size, and a probe-efficiency bound guarantees every anomaly a witness, hence an explanation. Across 47 ADBench datasets WAND attains the best mean Friedman rank at ROC-AUC parity with 16 unsupervised baselines, so the gain is interpretability at no accuracy cost; its native explanations are more accurate and faithful than post-hoc SHAP/LIME and ECOD at a fraction of the query cost. WAND is thus a practical, interpretable solution for explainable anomaly detection.

</details>


### [172] [Multi-step Proximal Policy Improvement in Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03842)
*Soohyun Choi,Seonvin Cho,Songnam Hong*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper proposes a geometric framework for offline reinforcement learning by modeling policies as a probability manifold. It introduces Single Proximal Policy Improvement (SPI) as a unifying interpretation of offline actor objectives, and Multi-step Proximal Policy Improvement (MPI) as a refinement mechanism that enables controlled policy improvement beyond dataset support while maintaining proximity constraints.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Offline RL faces a fundamental tension: policy updates must stay near dataset-supported actions for reliable value estimates, yet meaningful improvement often requires moving beyond the behavior distribution. Existing methods lack a unified geometric understanding of how different offline objectives achieve this balance.

Method: The paper develops a geometric view by modeling policies as a probability manifold with a chosen metric geometry. Under this lens, a broad class of offline actor objectives are interpreted as Single Proximal Policy Improvement (SPI) - an implicit discretization of manifold gradient flow induced by a critic-defined energy. MPI is proposed as a plug-in refinement mechanism that composes sequential re-centered proximal steps, enabling controlled policy improvement beyond dataset support while retaining proximal control at each refinement.

Result: Experiments on D4RL benchmarks show that small numbers of MPI refinements improve strong offline baselines (TD3+BC, ReBRAC, IQL) on many tasks. Focused diagnostics distinguish re-centered refinement from fixed-objective update scheduling and characterize limitations under critic error.

Conclusion: The geometric framework provides a unifying perspective on offline actor updates. MPI serves as a principled refinement mechanism that can enhance existing offline RL methods by enabling controlled exploration beyond the behavior distribution while maintaining stability through proximal constraints.

Abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) must reconcile two competing requirements: policy updates should stay near dataset-supported actions to keep value estimates reliable, yet meaningful gains often require moving beyond the behavior distribution. We develop a geometric view of offline actor updates by modeling policies as a probability manifold endowed with a chosen metric geometry. Under this lens, a broad class of offline actor objectives can be interpreted as a single proximal policy improvement step (SPI), i.e., an implicit discretization of a manifold gradient flow induced by a critic-defined energy. Building on this insight, we propose multi-step proximal policy improvement (MPI), a plug-in refinement mechanism that composes sequential re-centered proximal steps. MPI enables controlled policy improvement beyond dataset support while retaining proximal control at each refinement. The framework accommodates multiple policy geometries and admits practical instantiations for deterministic and diagonal-Gaussian policies. Experiments on D4RL benchmarks show that small numbers of MPI refinements improve strong offline baselines, including TD3+BC, ReBRAC, and IQL, on many tasks. Focused diagnostics further distinguish re-centered refinement from fixed-objective update scheduling and characterize limitations under critic error.

</details>


### [173] [Pushing the (Decision) Boundaries: Dynamically Calibrating Differentially Private Noise to Explainability in Federated Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03851)
*Michael Khavkin,Kichang Lee,Jaeho Jin,JeongGil Ko,Eran Toch*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: XCal-FL is a novel federated learning algorithm that dynamically calibrates differential privacy noise using three complementary explainability signals (prediction logit variations, counterfactual margins, saliency concentration) to improve both predictive performance and explanation fidelity in medical imaging applications, while maintaining formal DP guarantees.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that differential privacy noise in federated learning distorts learned representations and degrades explanation fidelity, which is critical for trust-critical applications like clinical diagnosis. Prior approaches used static noise calibration, limiting explainability to post-hoc analysis.

Method: XCal-FL uses a closed-loop approach with three dynamic explainability signals: (1) prediction logit variations measuring causal influence on model confidence, (2) counterfactual margins capturing decision-boundary sensitivity, and (3) saliency concentration quantifying spatial coherence of model attention. The method incorporates adaptive privacy accounting to maintain formal DP guarantees.

Result: Experiments on three medical imaging datasets show XCal-FL improves predictive performance by over 10% and explanation fidelity by up to 5× compared to static-noise FL, while achieving higher privacy-budget efficiency. A key finding is that explanation fidelity exhibits non-linear dynamics with privacy loss, unlike predictive performance which scales roughly linearly.

Conclusion: Explainability is a distinct dimension of the privacy trade-off that cannot be inferred from utility alone. This has significant implications for training and privacy-budget allocation in decision-critical applications where both accuracy and interpretability matter.

Abstract: Federated Learning (FL) with Differential Privacy (DP) is increasingly adopted to preserve data confidentiality in distributed machine learning. However, DP noise distorts learned representations and degrades explanation fidelity, limiting differentially private FL where trustworthy explanations are required, such as assistive clinical diagnosis. Prior work adapted DP noise with static feature-importance signals, restricting explainability to post hoc analysis and precluding noise calibration to explanation quality during training. We propose XCal-FL, a closed-loop, explainability-driven local training algorithm for image classification in cross-silo FL that dynamically calibrates DP noise from three complementary signals: (1) prediction logit variations, measuring causal influence on model confidence, (2) counterfactual margins, capturing decision-boundary sensitivity, and (3) saliency concentration, quantifying spatial coherence of model attention, while enforcing formal DP guarantees via adaptive privacy accounting. Experiments on three medical imaging datasets across varying FL configurations show that XCal-FL yields more accurate and interpretable global models, improving predictive performance by over 10\% and explanation fidelity by up to 5$\times$ over static-noise FL, and outperforming state-of-the-art adaptive DP methods in fidelity. XCal-FL also achieves higher privacy-budget efficiency, turning each unit of cumulative privacy loss into larger gains in both accuracy and explanation fidelity. Our analysis further reveals that, unlike predictive performance, which scales roughly linearly with privacy loss, explanation fidelity exhibits non-linear dynamics. These findings suggest explainability is a distinct dimension of the privacy trade-off that cannot be inferred from utility alone, with implications for training and privacy-budget allocation in decision-critical applications.

</details>


### [174] [High-Dimensional Learning Dynamics of Attention-Indexed Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03858)
*Yizhou Xu,Margarita Sagitova,Lenka Zdeborová,Florent Krzakala*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper studies the training dynamics of attention mechanisms in foundation models, particularly when attention matrices have extensive rank. The work introduces attention-indexed models and analyzes how different parameterizations (tied vs untied attention) affect learning dynamics, revealing that attention parameterization itself acts as an architectural implicit bias.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite the central role of attention mechanisms in modern foundation models, their training dynamics remain poorly understood, especially in high-dimensional settings with extensive rank attention matrices. The authors aim to bridge this gap by developing a theoretical framework to analyze these dynamics.

Method: The authors study attention-indexed models that can represent multi-layer and multi-head attention architectures. They analyze two limits: (1) population-loss landscape in high-dimensional limit using trace order parameters, and (2) online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) dynamics. They compare tied attention (S = WW^T) versus untied attention (S = UV^T) parameterizations.

Result: Key findings: (1) Population-loss landscape is characterized by finite trace order parameters, while online SGD exhibits infinite hierarchy of matrix moments that can be exponentially well-approximated by finite truncation. (2) Tied attention induces automatic symmetry-breaking yielding weak recovery in Θ(d²log d) samples. (3) Untied attention exhibits fast-slow mechanism where pre-activation mean evolves on fast timescale while overlaps evolve slowly. Weak recovery occurs when fast dynamics breaks initial symmetry.

Conclusion: Attention parameterization itself serves as an architectural implicit bias, determining whether models can escape uninformive states and achieve meaningful recovery. The work provides theoretical foundation for understanding how attention architecture influences training dynamics in large-scale models.

Abstract: Attention mechanisms are central to modern foundation models, yet their training dynamics remain poorly understood, especially when the attention matrices have extensive rank. In this work, we study attention-indexed models, a broad framework that can represent multi-layer and multi-head attention architectures. First, we show that, in a suitable high-dimensional limit, the population-loss landscape is characterized by a finite set of trace order parameters. In contrast, online stochastic gradient descent (SGD) is governed by an infinite hierarchy of matrix moments, which we show can be exponentially well-approximated by a finite truncated system. Second, this framework reveals that attention parameterization itself can act as an architectural implicit bias. Direct optimization of an attention matrix $S\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$ can remain trapped in an uninformative state. Tied attention ($S=WW^\top$) induces an automatic symmetry-breaking mechanism and yields weak recovery in $Θ(d^2\log d)$ samples. For untied attention, $S=UV^\top$, we uncover a fast-slow mechanism: the pre-activation mean first evolves on a fast timescale, while the overlaps evolve on a slower one. Weak recovery on the $Θ(d^2\log d)$ scale occurs when the state selected by the fast dynamics breaks the initial symmetry.

</details>


### [175] [Differentiable Interval Bottlenecks for Interpretable Anomaly Detection in Numerical Data](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03878)
*Lamine Diop,Marc Plantevit*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: DIFFINT is an interpretable autoencoder anomaly detector that uses soft axis-aligned interval memberships in its latent space, enabling human-readable feature range explanations while maintaining high accuracy on 48 ADBench benchmarks against 22 baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Reconstruction-based anomaly detectors are accurate but opaque - they flag anomalies without explaining which feature ranges caused the anomaly. There was a need for an interpretable yet accurate anomaly detection method.

Method: DIFFINT uses a latent bottleneck structured as soft, axis-aligned interval memberships learned end-to-end from raw numerical data without discretization/binarization. Each latent unit corresponds to a hyper-rectangle in feature space; instances are encoded by their membership strength in each interval, with reconstruction error serving as the anomaly score.

Result: DIFFINT achieves best mean rank on 48 ADBench benchmarks: 4.10 on ROC-AUC and 4.16 on AUPR, outperforming 22 baselines. It is the only interpretable detector in the statistically-tied leading cluster of seven methods.

Conclusion: DIFFINT successfully bridges the accuracy-interpretability gap in anomaly detection by providing inspectable internal structure (learned intervals) while maintaining competitive performance against both inlier-only and contaminated-data detectors.

Abstract: Reconstruction-based anomaly detectors are accurate but opaque: a deep autoencoder flags a sample without telling a practitioner which feature ranges made it anomalous. We propose DIFFINT, an autoencoder whose latent bottleneck is structured as a set of soft, axis-aligned interval memberships learned end-to-end directly from raw numerical data, without any discretization or binarization. Each latent unit corresponds to a human-readable hyper-rectangle in feature space; an instance is encoded by how strongly it falls inside each interval relative to the other units, and its reconstruction error is the anomaly score. This keeps the power of differentiable representation learning while exposing an inspectable internal structure. We make the inductive bias precise: a certified reconstruction-error lower bound for points that fall outside every active coordinate of the learned support (with a Lipschitz-enforced decoder), and a graded, empirically verified suppression mechanism for the usual case in which only a few features are abnormal; and we provide a closed-form, label-free importance that ranks each (unit, feature) pair from quantities the model already maintains, turning trained intervals into auditable candidate constraints without ever seeing an anomaly label. On 48 ADBench benchmarks against 22 baselines under a common [-1, 1]-normalized protocol, DIFFINT attains the best mean rank overall on both metrics (4.10 on ROC-AUC, 4.16 on AUPR); among inlier-only detectors it leads its regime clearly, and it is competitive with the strongest contaminated-data detectors (see the stratified and complete-case analyses). It is the only interpretable detector in the statistically-tied leading cluster of seven methods.

</details>


### [176] [Beyond Endpoint Scores: Time- and Capacity-Conditioned Evaluation of Continual Knowledge Updating](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03900)
*Heejin Choi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper challenges the common practice of evaluating continual knowledge-updating methods using a single checkpoint and one adapter rank. Through experiments on a 24-month Wikidata stream, the authors demonstrate that the apparent winner between a periodic hierarchy and cumulative replay can flip depending on evaluation timing and replay-side adaptation capacity. They propose a more rigorous evaluation protocol requiring trajectory reporting and capacity sweeps.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observed that continual knowledge-updating methods are often compared using just one final checkpoint and one conventional adapter rank. They suspected this is insufficient to identify the truly better method, as the ranking may change across different evaluation conditions.

Method: The authors compared a periodic hierarchy against cumulative replay over a 24-month Wikidata knowledge stream. They systematically varied three factors: (1) evaluation month, (2) replay LoRA rank, and (3) query formulation. Experiments were conducted on Qwen2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-1B, and held-out paraphrases.

Result: The authors found that the apparent winner changes across the evaluation region. On Qwen2.5-1.5B, the hierarchy's 5.0-point advantage over rank-8 replay becomes an 11.6-point deficit against rank-72 replay. At high ranks, a consolidation-aligned endpoint suggests a tie while time-averaged replay leads by 9-13 points. This rank-conditioned reversal appears consistently across different models and query formulations.

Conclusion: Method ranking in continual updating depends jointly on when performance is measured and how much replay-side adaptation capacity the baseline receives. The authors propose reporting trajectories and capacity sweeps, and declaring a robust winner only when the ordering is stable across the evaluation region. Otherwise, comparisons should report winner regions and retention-stability-cost frontiers. Under this protocol, the periodic hierarchy is characterized as a lower-update-cost operating point, not a quality winner.

Abstract: Continual knowledge-updating methods are often declared superior from one final checkpoint and one conventional adapter rank. We show that this can be insufficient to identify the better operating point. Holding a periodic hierarchy fixed, we compare it with cumulative replay over a 24-month Wikidata stream while varying evaluation month, replay LoRA rank, and query formulation. The apparent winner changes across this region: on Qwen2.5-1.5B, the hierarchy's 5.0-point advantage over rank-8 replay becomes an 11.6-point deficit against rank-72 replay, and at high ranks a consolidation-aligned endpoint can suggest a tie while time-averaged replay leads by 9-13 points. The same rank-conditioned reversal appears on Llama-3.2-1B and held-out paraphrases.
  These results show that method ranking in continual updating can depend jointly on when performance is measured and how much replay-side adaptation capacity the baseline receives. We therefore propose reporting trajectories and capacity sweeps, and declaring a robust winner only when the ordering is stable across the evaluation region; otherwise, comparisons should report winner regions and retention-stability-cost frontiers. Under this protocol, the periodic hierarchy is a lower-update-cost operating point, not a quality winner.

</details>


### [177] [RATL: Learning from Retrieved Residuals for Robust Multivariate Time-Series Forecasting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03937)
*Yuchen He,Yueyang Cang,Zhiyuan Ning,Ningyu Wang,Li Shi*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RATL is a plug-in method that improves multivariate time-series forecasting by retrieving and combining historical forecast residuals (prediction errors) from similar contexts, rather than retrieving target values. It uses a frozen base forecaster, builds a residual memory, and employs a set-aware router to select and combine residual trajectories for feedback correction.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional RAG approaches retrieve external evidence (target values) for regression tasks but are not robust when samples differ in output level, numerical scale, or local dynamics. Additionally, conventional forecasting pipelines use residuals for optimization but do not retain individual historical residual examples as accessible memory at inference time.

Method: RATL freezes a base forecaster to construct retrieval keys and turns its historical forecast residuals into a train-only memory. At inference time, it retrieves residual trajectories from similar historical contexts subject to causal availability constraints, then uses a set-aware router operating over forecast blocks and variables to select and combine these trajectories. The method includes validation-based correction-strength selection to limit residual over-injection.

Result: Experiments show that historical residuals matched to the current context contain reusable forecasting information. RATL improves frozen base forecasters in most experimental settings. Ablations demonstrate that learned routing strengthens raw residual feedback, while validation-based correction-strength selection limits residual over-injection. Using iTransformer as the primary base forecaster, RATL outperforms multiple strong forecasting baselines and shows transferability across backbones.

Conclusion: RATL shifts the retrieved object from historical target values to base-model-specific historical forecast errors, providing a plug-in, residual-memory-based paradigm for learned feedback correction in continuous-output forecasting. It can further improve base-forecaster performance in most settings.

Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) complements parametric models with retrieved external evidence. The same idea is attractive for continuous-output regression, but directly reusing retrieved target values is often not robust when samples differ in output level, numerical scale, or local dynamics. Moreover, conventional forecasting pipelines generally use residuals for model optimization and error diagnosis, but do not retain individual historical residual examples as memory that can be accessed at inference time.For multivariate time-series forecasting, we propose RATL, a plug-in residual-retrieval and feedback-correction method. RATL freezes a base forecaster to construct retrieval keys and turns its historical forecast residuals into a train-only memory specific to that base model. At inference time, RATL retrieves residual trajectories from similar historical contexts subject to causal availability constraints, then uses a set-aware router operating over forecast blocks and variables to select and combine these trajectories. Experiments show that historical residuals matched to the current context contain reusable forecasting information and that RATL improves frozen base forecasters in most experimental settings. Ablations further show that learned routing strengthens raw residual feedback, while validation-based correction-strength selection limits residual over-injection.On real-world benchmarks, we use iTransformer as the primary frozen base forecaster, compare against multiple strong forecasting baselines, and test transferability across backbones. The results show that RATL can further improve base-forecaster performance in most settings.Overall, RATL shifts the retrieved object from historical target values to base-model-specific historical forecast errors, providing a plug-in, residual-memory-based paradigm for learned feedback correction in continuous-output forecasting.

</details>


### [178] [Headroom-Drift Replay: A Primitive for Principled Replay Control in GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03941)
*Hyun Bin Park,Du-Seong Chang*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces Headroom-Drift Replay, a simple yet effective replay selection method for GRPO-based reinforcement learning training of reasoning models. It addresses the computational bottleneck of fresh rollout generation in agentic settings by intelligently selecting which past trajectories to reuse, without adding auxiliary generation or training machinery.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RL-based post-training for reasoning models is increasingly bottlenecked by repeated fresh rollout generation, especially in agentic settings where environment interaction dominates wall-clock cost. While replay can reduce this burden, existing methods embed it within larger training pipelines, making replay's own contribution difficult to isolate. The authors seek to answer: how far can principled replay selection alone go?

Method: The authors propose Headroom-Drift Replay, a group-level replay control primitive for GRPO that separates replay reuse into two decisions: (1) Headroom - ranks stored groups by remaining learning value, and (2) Drift - gates them by compatibility with the current policy. The fresh on-policy stream remains unchanged, and no auxiliary generation or training machinery is added.

Result: Across mathematical reasoning, multimodal reasoning, and Agentic Search benchmarks, this single intervention outperforms naive replay and matches or exceeds broader replay methods on Avg Mean@32. In Agentic Search, where environment interaction dominates cost, it delivers comparable quality at materially lower wall-clock time.

Conclusion: Principled replay selection alone can achieve significant improvements. The simple Headroom-Drift Replay method isolates the contribution of replay and demonstrates that careful selection of past trajectories can substantially reduce computational costs while maintaining or improving performance, particularly in agentic settings where environment interaction is expensive.

Abstract: RL-based post-training for reasoning models is increasingly bottlenecked by repeated fresh rollout generation, particularly in agentic settings where environment interaction dominates wall-clock cost. Replay can reduce this burden by reusing past trajectories, but existing methods typically embed it within larger training pipelines involving exploration, experience restructuring, or mixed-policy optimization. This makes replay's own contribution difficult to isolate. We ask a focused question: how far can principled replay selection alone go? We introduce Headroom-Drift Replay, a group-level replay control primitive for GRPO that separates reuse into two decisions. Headroom ranks stored groups by remaining learning value, while Drift gates them by compatibility with the current policy. The fresh on-policy stream remains unchanged, and the method adds no auxiliary generation or training machinery. Across mathematical reasoning, multimodal reasoning, and Agentic Search benchmarks, this single intervention outperforms naive replay and matches or exceeds broader replay methods on Avg Mean@32. In Agentic Search, where environment interaction dominates cost, it delivers comparable quality at materially lower wall-clock time.

</details>


### [179] [VestigeKV: The NoPE-MLA KV Cache Carries Its Own Eviction Signal in a Vestigial Branch](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03949)
*WenJie Fan*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: VestigeKV is a KV cache compression method for NoPE (No Position Embedding) models that uses a query-independent salience signal (64-dimensional decoupled branch from RoPE) to partition cache into an attended tier and GPU-resident archive. It achieves 1.00 retrieval accuracy under 8x and 0.92 under 32x compression from 8k to 65k context, with zero training or weight changes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current KV cache compression methods (H2O, SnapKV) rely on observed attention to select important tokens, but they fail when queries don't exist yet (0.00-0.33 needle retrieval on NoPE MLA models). The problem is that a token's importance has not yet been observed when compression must occur.

Method: VestigeKV uses the 64-dimensional decoupled branch (a vestige of RoPE that NoPE training repurposes into a salience channel) to partition the cache. It reads 11% of each row, keeps top-m rows in the attended tier, and moves every other row to a GPU-resident archive reachable per step by a certified trigger. No training, quantization, or weight changes required.

Result: Retrieval holds at 1.00 under 8x and 0.92 under 32x compression from 8k to 65k context, with zero gap to full-row selection. The attended tier is 0.25 KB of 8.1 KB per-token cache at 32x. The method only works on NoPE models (0.08 on RoPE MLA vs 0.42 for plain eviction).

Conclusion: VestigeKV provides effective query-independent KV cache compression for NoPE models by leveraging the salience channel from repurposed RoPE. The method does not work on RoPE models due to the absence of query-independent salience signals. The approach may extend to Kimi K3 if its cache layout matches, but this is not guaranteed.

Abstract: The problem. A long-lived KV cache must be compressed before the queries that will read it exist; selection by observed attention (H2O, SnapKV) collapses there (0.00-0.33 needle retrieval on a NoPE MLA model), because a token's importance has not yet been observed. The method. On Kimi Linear, VestigeKV evicts by a query-independent signal the cache already carries: the 64-dimensional decoupled branch, a vestige of RoPE that NoPE training repurposes into a salience channel. Reading 11% of each row, it partitions the cache: the top-m rows stay in the attended tier; every other row moves -- exactly, never deleted -- to a GPU-resident archive reachable per step by a certified trigger. No training, no quantization, no weight or kernel change. Cost. Nothing measurable: retrieval holds at 1.00 under 8x and 0.92 under 32x from 8k to 65k context, zero gap to full-row selection. The attended tier is 0.25 KB of Kimi Linear's 8.1 KB per-token cache at 32x; the archive stays bit-exact and GPU-resident, with host offload as the VRAM-reclaiming variant. The recall tier -- the standard configuration -- holds 128x at 1.00. Kimi K3 is reported to use a NoPE Gated-MLA variant; if its cache layout matches, the method plausibly extends there -- we make no claim beyond the measured model. NoPE exclusivity. The identical operator on a RoPE MLA collapses to 0.08 (plain eviction: 0.42); query-independent salience itself exists only without rotation (top-1 targets span 2.3-6.7% of tokens vs. 10.2-46.8%), and query-universal exact merging is provably impossible under RoPE. All thresholds were frozen before data; 20 archived verdicts and 8 closed routes accompany the paper.

</details>


### [180] [OSR: Output Space Redistribution for Adaptive Label Removal in Classification Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03972)
*Minyi Peng,Darian Gunamardi,Ivan Tjuawinata,Yongsen Zheng,Kwok-Yan Lam*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A novel method for handling label removal in classification systems with evolving taxonomies, using statistical redistribution in output space to approximate post-removal confidence vectors without requiring full retraining or access to original data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Label removal frequently occurs in classification systems with evolving taxonomies. Existing solutions (retraining-based and feature-space-adjustment-based) have significant limitations: reliance on original data, high computational/storage costs, inconsistent results, poor scalability, and model utility degradation. There is a need for a more efficient, privacy-preserving approach.

Method: The proposed method leverages statistical redistribution in the output space to approximate post-removal confidence vectors. It functions as a modular output filter that only requires existing labels and prior output confidences, bypassing the need for feature-space adjustments or loss-function convergence.

Result: Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive performance against full retraining, with improvements in computational efficiency and privacy preservation across several classification tasks.

Conclusion: The method successfully addresses the limitations of existing approaches by providing a data-independent, computationally efficient, and privacy-preserving solution for label removal in classification systems.

Abstract: Label removal occurs frequently in classification systems with evolving taxonomies, where categories must be dynamically updated or eliminated. To accommodate such changes, classification models must adapt accordingly. Existing solutions, broadly categorized as retraining-based and feature-space-adjustment-based, share common limitations despite their variations, including reliance on access to original data, substantial computational and storage costs, inconsistent results, poor scalability, and degradation of model utility. To address this, we propose a novel approach that leverages statistical redistribution in the output space to approximate the post-removal confidence vectors of a retrained model. Applicable as a modular output filter, our method bypasses the burden of feature-space adjustments or loss-function convergence, alleviating scalability limitations. Furthermore, by requiring only existing labels and prior output confidences, the method potentially mitigates privacy concerns inherent to data-dependent solutions. Extensive experiments demonstrate competitive performance against full retraining, with improvements in computational efficiency and privacy preservation across several classification tasks.

</details>


### [181] [RobustSeiz: An Open-Source Framework for Benchmarking the Robustness of EEG Seizure Detection Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04007)
*Mohammad Mohammadi,Alireza Zarei*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: RobustSeiz is an open-source, model-agnostic framework for stress-testing seizure detectors under clinically realistic distribution shifts (environment, noise, adversarial transforms) before deployment. It standardizes four public EEG corpora into BIDS-EEG format and evaluates subject-independent detectors using comprehensive metrics.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Despite strong performance on held-out EEG data, seizure detectors fail under real-world acquisition variability, artifacts, and adversarial inputs. There is a need for standardized, reproducible protocols to evaluate detector robustness under controlled, clinically motivated distribution shifts before deployment.

Method: The framework standardizes four public scalp-EEG corpora (CHB-MIT, TUSZ, Siena, SeizeIT1) into BIDS-EEG trees. It evaluates subject-independent detectors on held-out splits while sweeping environment, noise, and adversarial transforms over predefined hyperparameter grids. Each run reports sample- and event-level sensitivity, precision, F1, false positives per 24h, Lead/Lag onset timing, and Monte Carlo dropout predictive agreement. Includes Dockerized GPU pipeline, experiment registry, and full-evaluation/research-subset modes.

Result: The framework was demonstrated with a contemporary seizure detector on TUSZ across the complete shift grid. AWGN analysis showed how perturbation severity changes detection quality, onset timing, and predictive agreement, illustrating the framework's ability to quantify robustness degradation.

Conclusion: RobustSeiz provides a shared benchmarking standard for evaluating seizure-detector robustness under realistic clinical stressors, extending pre-deployment assessment beyond clean-data accuracy. It enables reproducible, standardized stress-testing of seizure detection systems.

Abstract: Despite strong performance on held-out electroencephalography (EEG) data, seizure detectors may fail under real-world acquisition variability, artifacts, and adversarial inputs. We introduce RobustSeiz, an open-source, model-agnostic framework that provides a standardized, reproducible protocol for stress-testing and comparing seizure detectors under controlled, clinically motivated distribution shifts before deployment. We standardize four public scalp-EEG corpora (CHB-MIT, TUSZ, Siena, and SeizeIT1) into BIDS-EEG trees and evaluate subject-independent detectors on held-out splits. Environment, noise, and adversarial transforms are swept over predefined hyperparameter grids. Each run reports sample- and event-level sensitivity, precision, F1, false positives per 24 h, Lead and Lag onset timing, and Monte Carlo dropout predictive agreement. RobustSeiz includes a Dockerized GPU pipeline, experiment registry, and full-evaluation and research-subset modes. We demonstrate the framework with a contemporary seizure detector on TUSZ across the complete implemented shift grid; an AWGN analysis illustrates how perturbation severity changes detection quality, onset timing, and predictive agreement. RobustSeiz provides a shared benchmarking standard for evaluating seizure-detector robustness under realistic clinical stressors, extending pre-deployment assessment beyond clean-data accuracy.

</details>


### [182] [Unlocking Lossless Speedups in LLMs via Discrete Diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04010)
*Subham Sekhar Sahoo,Lingjie Chen,Khiem Pham,Jonathan Geuter,Chaitanya Dwivedi,Varad Pimpalkhute,Yash Akhauri,Alexander Moreno,Mikhail Yurochkin,Zhenting Wang,Mostafa Elhoushi,Nolan Dey,Shane Bergsma,Joel Hestness,John Thickstun,Eric Xing,Zhengzhong Liu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper introduces "Uno" - diffusion-augmented LLMs that combine autoregressive modeling with parallel diffusion sampling to achieve up to 3× speedups over base AR models without sacrificing quality. It uses two parameter sets (AR weights + lightweight diffusion weights) learned via Diffusion Distillation, and introduces Ψ-Spec samplers for lossless acceleration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLMs rely on next-token prediction (NTP) but suffer from slow sequential token generation due to their autoregressive (AR) structure. Existing solutions like speculative decoding require separate draft models, while diffusion LLMs sacrifice quality. The authors aim to overcome this bottleneck while maintaining AR model quality.

Method: The method involves: 1) Decoupling parameters into AR weights (trained with standard NTP objective) and lightweight diffusion weights (trained to generate multiple tokens in parallel); 2) Learning diffusion weights through a Diffusion Distillation phase with negligible overhead; 3) Using Ψ-Spec samplers for lossless acceleration and inference-time scaling at fixed context length. Models can be trained from scratch or built by augmenting existing open-weight AR LLMs.

Result: Uno achieves higher throughput than leading speculative-decoding methods at every evaluated batch size. It delivers up to 3× speedups over the base AR model, including at the largest batch size supported by the device. The 8B Uno model outperforms the 26B DiffusionGemma and proprietary Mercury 2 across all evaluated benchmarks in agentic tool use, coding, and long-context reasoning.

Conclusion: Diffusion-augmented LLMs (Uno) successfully combine AR modeling with parallel diffusion sampling to accelerate LLM generation without sacrificing quality. This approach outperforms both speculative decoding and diffusion LLMs, offering a promising new direction for efficient LLM inference.

Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) owe much of their success to next-token prediction (NTP), but their autoregressive (AR) structure requires slow, sequential token generation. To overcome this bottleneck, we introduce diffusion-augmented LLMs, a new class of models that defines an AR model distribution while using diffusion to draw multiple tokens in parallel from that distribution. We decouple the parameters of these models into two sets: AR weights, trained using the standard NTP objective, and lightweight diffusion weights, trained to generate multiple tokens simultaneously. The diffusion weights are learned through a simple Diffusion Distillation phase that adds negligible overhead to existing LLM training pipelines. We also introduce $Ψ$-Spec, a family of samplers that enables lossless acceleration and inference-time scaling at a fixed context length. Unlike speculative decoding, our method requires no separate draft model. Unlike diffusion LLMs (d-LLMs), it accelerates generation without sacrificing the quality of the underlying AR model. The resulting models, called Uno, can be trained from scratch or built by augmenting existing open-weight AR LLMs. Uno achieves higher throughput than leading speculative-decoding methods at every evaluated batch size and delivers up to $3\times$ speedups over the base AR model, including at the largest batch size supported by the device. Notably, our 8B Uno model outperforms the leading open d-LLM, the 26B DiffusionGemma, and the proprietary Mercury 2 across all evaluated benchmarks in agentic tool use, coding, and long-context reasoning. We release code and checkpoints at: https://s-sahoo.github.io/uno/

</details>


### [183] [A location-invariant estimator of extremal quantile treatment effects for heavy-tailed distributions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04018)
*Xin Yu,Shuwei Huang,Jicheng Liu,Jielin Tang,Bolin Wang,Yunxiao Zhang,Tian Zhao*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses estimation of quantile treatment effects (QTEs) at extreme quantile levels for heavy-tailed potential outcomes.
