The authors propose a location-invariant QTE estimator by adapting the Fraga estimator of extreme value index to the causal setting using inverse propensity score weighting, and replacing extrapolation with a difference-based scheme that cancels location parameters.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing extremal QTE estimators rely on extrapolation combined with causal extreme value index (EVI) estimators, but they fail to be location-invariant—a property that the population QTE possesses. This lack of invariance under location shifts of potential outcome distributions is a critical methodological flaw that limits the practical applicability of these estimators.

Method: The proposed method consists of two steps: (1) Adapt the location-invariant Fraga estimator of the EVI to the causal setting using inverse propensity score weighting; (2) Replace the original extrapolation formula with a difference-based scheme where the location parameter cancels when quantile differences are taken. The resulting estimator is therefore location-invariant.

Result: The authors establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed extremal QTE estimators, and provide a consistent variance estimator for asymptotically valid inference. Simulation studies confirm the location invariance, stability with respect to the threshold, and proper coverage of the proposed methods.

Conclusion: The proposed methodology successfully resolves the location invariance issue in extremal QTE estimation for heavy-tailed potential outcomes, providing theoretically justified and practically reliable inference for treatment effects at extreme quantile levels.

Abstract: Quantile treatment effects (QTEs) measure the effect of a treatment on the distribution of an outcome, and their estimation at extreme quantile levels is of central interest in applications where the target quantiles lie far beyond the range of the data. For heavy-tailed potential outcomes, existing extremal QTE estimators rely on extrapolation combined with a causal extreme value index (EVI) estimator, but the resulting estimator is not invariant under a common location shift of the potential outcome distributions, even though the population QTE is. We address this issue in two steps. First, we adapt the location-invariant Fraga estimator of the EVI to the causal setting using inverse propensity score weighting. Second, we replace the original extrapolation formula with a difference-based scheme, under which the location parameter cancels when quantile differences are taken. The resulting QTE estimator is therefore location invariant. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the proposed extremal QTE estimators, and provide a consistent variance estimator, leading to asymptotically valid inference. A simulation study confirms the location invariance, the stability with respect to the threshold, and the coverage of the proposed methods.

</details>


### [184] [Subspace Inference Enables Efficient Active Reward Learning from Preferences](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04066)
*Yutai Zhou,Erdem Bıyık*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: PreferenceEKF is a sample-efficient approach for active preference learning in RLHF that uses sequential Bayesian filtering via an extended Kalman filter within a low-dimensional parameter subspace to track reward model uncertainty, enabling scalable acquisition function computation for active reward learning.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: RLHF has emerged as a powerful but sample-inefficient approach for learning reward models from human preferences. Effective uncertainty quantification required for active learning remains a key challenge for large neural network reward models, especially due to computationally prohibitive posterior inference over the full neural network parameter space.

Method: The paper frames active preference learning as a sequential Bayesian filtering problem. Instead of posterior inference over the full neural network parameter space, the method performs sequential inference via an extended Kalman filter within a low-dimensional parameter subspace. This enables scalable sampling of neural network parameters to efficiently compute acquisition functions for active reward learning.

Result: Experiments on D4RL and V-D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that the approach achieves better sample efficiency, runtime, scalability, and calibration compared to other Bayesian deep learning approaches. The learned reward models lead to competitive offline reinforcement learning policy performance.

Conclusion: The results highlight the potential of scalable Bayesian methods for preference-based reward modeling in RLHF. The approach successfully balances computational feasibility with accurate uncertainty quantification, enabling effective active learning in high-dimensional neural network reward models.

Abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a powerful yet sample-inefficient approach for learning reward models from human preferences, making active learning a critical component in synthesizing informative preference queries. However, effective uncertainty quantification required for active learning remains a key challenge for large neural network reward models. In this paper, we introduce PreferenceEKF, a sample-efficient approach that tracks reward model uncertainty by framing active preference learning as a sequential Bayesian filtering problem. Instead of relying on computationally prohibitive posterior inference over the full neural network parameter space, our method performs sequential inference via an extended Kalman filter within a low-dimensional parameter subspace, continuously updating the reward model posterior as new preference queries arrive. Our approach enables scalable sampling of neural network parameters to efficiently compute acquisition functions for active reward learning. Experiments on the D4RL and V-D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves better sample efficiency, runtime, scalability, and calibration compared to other Bayesian deep learning approaches, and the learned reward models lead to competitive offline reinforcement learning policy performance. This highlights the potential of scalable Bayesian methods for preference-based reward modeling in RLHF. Our code is available at https://github.com/yutaizhou/bnn_pref.

</details>


### [185] [Conditioning Degenerate Diffusion Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04090)
*Uğur Aydın,Tamer Başar*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses theoretical limitations in conditioned generative models (particularly diffusion-based models) when standard assumptions fail - specifically when the diffusion coefficient is singular or when underlying conditional densities don't exist or lack smoothness. The authors propose using causal optimal transport to define approximate loss functions that can identify minimum-entropy controls for guidance under minimal assumptions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current conditioned generative models rely heavily on score functions for guidance during training. However, this approach breaks down in practical scenarios where: (1) the diffusion coefficient becomes singular, and (2) the underlying conditional densities either do not exist or are not smooth. These are not edge cases but practical concerns in many real-world applications. The authors seek a framework that works under minimal assumptions.

Method: The approach relies on causal optimal transport theory and its characterization through the predictable representation property of (conditioned) diffusion processes. Specifically, the method uses the martingale problem approach "à la Üstünel" (referencing the work of Ali Süleyman Üstünel) to establish well-posedness of the associated martingale problem. This mathematical framework allows the definition of approximate loss functions that can handle the challenging cases where standard score-based methods fail.

Result: The paper provides a theoretical framework for defining approximate loss functions using causal optimal transport that can guide generative models even when densities don't exist or aren't smooth, and when diffusion coefficients are singular. The approach identifies a minimum-entropy control for guidance.

Conclusion: The proposed method offers a mathematically rigorous alternative to score-based guidance that works under minimal assumptions. By leveraging causal optimal transport and the predictable representation property, the framework extends the applicability of diffusion-based generative models to cases where traditional methods cannot be applied. This represents a theoretical advance that could enable more robust generative modeling in practical scenarios with non-smooth or non-existent densities.

Abstract: Current conditioned generative models heavily rely on score functions for guidance during training. When the generative model is a diffusion process with a singular diffusion coefficient and the underlying (conditional) densities either do not exist or are not smooth, we use causal optimal transport to define \emph{approximate} loss functions that identify a minimum-entropy control for guidance under minimal assumptions. Our approach relies on causal optimal transport and its characterization through the predictable representation property of (conditioned) diffusion processes whose associated martingale problem is well posed, à la Üstünel.

</details>


### [186] [Hardware-Aware FP4 FlashAttention-4](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04105)
*Robert Hu*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper addresses performance bottlenecks in using 4-bit floating-point (FP4) tensor cores for attention mechanisms in neural networks. The authors propose Direct-P for noncausal inference and a causal path that preserves forward quantization into backward pass, achieving significant speedups on NVIDIA GB200 hardware while identifying that MXFP4 probability/value training trajectories diverge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: FP4 tensor cores in NVIDIA's Blackwell architecture do not automatically deliver attention speedups because softmax conversion and on-chip dependencies become bottlenecks when matrix products shrink. This work aims to overcome these limitations while maintaining training accuracy.

Method: Two approaches: (1) Direct-P maps attention scores directly to FP4 probabilities without softmax conversion for noncausal inference; (2) A causal path reconstructs probabilities from saved quantized queries/keys during backward pass and uses FP8 gradient operands. The method also explores matched distributed training retaining FP8 probabilities and values.

Result: Direct-P achieves up to 2.13× the bfloat16 (BF16) forward throughput on NVIDIA GB200. The causal path accelerates a complete single-GPU 8-billion-parameter update by up to 1.14×. However, all tested MXFP4 probability/value training trajectories diverge.

Conclusion: Low-precision FP4 can accelerate attention inference and training on modern hardware, but requires careful design to avoid numerical instability. The divergence in MXFP4 probability/value training suggests that naive FP4 quantization for attention probabilities and values is not viable without specialized techniques like Direct-P or the causal path.

Abstract: Blackwell's 4-bit floating-point (FP4) tensor cores do not automatically make attention faster because softmax conversion and on-chip dependencies dominate once its matrix products shrink. We address this with \emph{Direct-P} for noncausal inference and a causal path that passes the forward quantization directly into backward. Direct-P maps scores directly to FP4 probabilities and reaches up to 2.13$\times$ the bfloat16 (BF16) forward throughput on an NVIDIA GB200. The causal path reconstructs probabilities from saved quantized queries and keys and uses 8-bit floating-point (FP8) gradient operands, accelerating a complete single-GPU 8-billion-parameter update by up to 1.14$\times$. Matched distributed training retains FP8 probabilities and values; every tested MXFP4 probability/value training trajectory diverges.

</details>


### [187] [Constant regret in general games via higher-order optimism](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04113)
*Omar Abbadi,Rida Laraki,Panayotis Mertikopoulos*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper introduces HOOD (Higher-Order Optimism with Discounting), an uncoupled learning algorithm for N-player normal form games with K actions per player that guarantees O(N³log²K) individual regret. It combines discounted (N+1)-th order predictors with entropic regularization over a lifted strategy space to mitigate oscillations in play.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The key motivation is to achieve constant (or near-constant) regret in general N-player games, which has been hindered by large oscillations in the induced sequence of play in previous attempts. The goal is to develop an uncoupled learning algorithm where players only need to know their own past payoffs, not the entire game structure or other players' actions.

Method: The proposed method HOOD is a variant of Optimistic Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (OptFTRL) that combines two key ingredients: (1) a discounted (N+1)-th order predictor for extrapolation, and (2) entropic regularization over a suitable "lifting" of the game's strategy space. This combination is designed to dampen large oscillations in a controlled manner.

Result: The algorithm guarantees O(N³log²K) individual regret, uniformly over the horizon of play. This is a significant improvement over the related work of Liu, Farina, and Ozdaglar (arXiv:2608.31166) which achieved O(N²¹log⁴K) regret bound.

Conclusion: The paper presents a novel approach to achieving low regret in general N-player games by addressing the oscillation problem through higher-order optimism and discounting. The approach is remarkably similar to but achieves better regret bounds than a concurrent independent work, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed techniques.

Abstract: We introduce an uncoupled learning algorithm which, when employed by all players of an arbitrary $N$-player normal form game with up to $K$ actions per player, guarantees $O(N^3\log^2 K)$ individual regret, uniformly over the horizon of play. The proposed algorithm - which we call higher-order optimism with discounting (HOOD) is a variant of optimistic follow-the-regularized-leader (OptFTRL) that combines a discounted $(N+1)$-th order predictor with entropic regularization over a suitable "lifting" of the game's strategy space. This combination of ingredients is purposefully designed to dampen large oscillations of the induced sequence of play in a controlled manner, removing in this way a key stumbling block of previous attempts to achieve constant regret in general games. Our approach bears several striking similarities to the concurrent - and completely independent - work of Liu, Farina, and Ozdaglar (arXiv:2608.31166), who very recently derived an $O(N^{21}\log^{4} K)$ regret bound through the use of higher-order optimism and an exponential moving average estimator.

</details>


### [188] [Prospective Coding Improves Learning in Deep Continuous-Time Recurrent Networks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04134)
*Shivang Rawat,Mirko Morello,Flaviano Morone,David J. Heeger*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: The paper addresses a fundamental problem in deep continuous-time recurrent networks where temporal integration delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors. The authors develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs) - biologically motivated complex-valued temporal filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models - and propose a parameter-free "prospective input" correction that makes each layer's bottom-up input predictive. This approach mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation, particularly under spatial-only backpropagation, and achieves strong results on raw-audio Speech Commands (96.09% accuracy with 31.9k parameters) and the long-sequence Path-X task (83.56% on 16,384 steps).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: In deep stacks of continuous-time recurrent networks, temporal integration provides memory but introduces two critical issues: (1) bottom-up signals are delayed due to the temporal processing at each layer, and (2) top-down error signals are attenuated as they propagate through layers. This creates a fundamental tension between the depth needed for hierarchical processing and the temporal dynamics needed for sequence modeling. The authors aim to address this failure mode by making each layer's bottom-up input "prospective" - i.e., predictive of future inputs rather than simply reflecting past information.

Method: The authors develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs) as a biologically motivated complex-valued temporal filter that is a special case of diagonal state-space models. Starting from an energy model, they derive RQF dynamics showing each RQF is a band-pass filter with learnable parameters controlling tuning frequency and bandwidth. They then introduce a parameter-free two-tap update to make each layer's bottom-up input prospective, which leaves the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged. This correction is extended to general diagonal SSMs. The intervention is evaluated in RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs (a nonlinear gated RNN) under both full backpropagation through time (BPTT) and spatial-only backpropagation (truncating temporal gradients).

Result: Under full BPTT, prospective variants match or outperform their non-prospective controls in every model and configuration. Specific results: (1) A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF achieves 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with only 31.9k parameters; (2) A width-64 six-layer RQF achieves 83.56% on the 16,384-step Path-X task. The prospective approach mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated (spatial-only backpropagation).

Conclusion: The paper identifies RQFs as a parameter-efficient recurrent substrate for sequence modeling and prospective-input coding as an effective input-side correction for deep continuous-time recurrent networks. The approach successfully addresses the delay and attenuation problems in deep hierarchical recurrent architectures, enabling strong performance on both audio classification and long-sequence modeling tasks with relatively few parameters.

Abstract: Temporal integration gives continuous-time recurrent networks memory, but in deep stacks it also delays bottom-up signals and attenuates top-down errors. We develop Recursive Quadrature Filters (RQFs), biologically motivated complex-valued temporal filters that are a special case of diagonal state-space models (SSMs), and ask whether this failure mode can be addressed by making each layer's bottom-up input prospective. Starting from an energy model, we derive the RQF dynamics and show that each RQF is a band-pass filter whose learnable parameters control its tuning frequency and bandwidth. We then make each layer's bottom-up input prospective using a parameter-free two-tap update that leaves the recurrent transition and parallel scan unchanged. We extend this correction to general diagonal SSMs and show that it mitigates depth-dependent gradient attenuation when temporal gradients are truncated, i.e., spatial-only backpropagation. We evaluate the intervention in RQFs, S5, and ORGaNICs (a nonlinear gated RNN) trained using full backpropagation through time (BPTT) and spatial-only backpropagation. Under full BPTT, prospective variants match or outperform their non-prospective controls in every model and configuration. A non-residual width-32 six-layer RQF reaches 96.09% accuracy on raw-audio Speech Commands with 31.9k parameters; a width-64 six-layer RQF reaches 83.56% on the 16,384-step Path-X task. These results identify RQFs as a parameter-efficient recurrent substrate and prospective-input coding as an input-side correction for deep continuous-time recurrent networks.

</details>


### [189] [A Low-Cost, Open Platform for End-to-End Autonomous Driving on a Miniature Ackermann Vehicle](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04147)
*Gustavo Claudio Karl Couto,Eric Aislan Antonelo,Gabriel George Zipperer*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: A low-cost, open experimental platform for end-to-end autonomous driving research using miniature Ackermann vehicles, combining physical vehicles with printed tracks and Webots digital twins. Implements command-conditioned behavior cloning and demonstrates sim-to-real transfer using synthetic data and learned image translation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Need for a practical, reproducible testbed that connects simulation-based autonomous driving methods to real-world execution, enabling controlled sim-to-real studies.

Method: 1) Physical platform with miniature Ackermann vehicle, printed urban track, data collection tools, and trajectory registration; 2) Webots digital twin for simulation; 3) Command-conditioned behavior cloning: neural policy receives onboard camera image + high-level navigation command → outputs steering and speed; 4) Sim-to-real transfer via synthetic data generation and learned image translator to reduce appearance gap.

Result: Real closed-loop: 6.1 cm mean cross-track error (vs 4.7 cm human demonstration). Digital twin: FOV significantly impacts performance—35.6 cm at 58° vs 3.3 cm at 120°. Only the higher-capacity policy trained on synthetic data + real demonstrations completes all four track routes in closed loop.

Conclusion: The open platform serves as a practical testbed for sim-to-real autonomous driving studies. Command-conditioned behavior cloning provides a functional baseline. The platform is released to support reproducible research.

Abstract: This paper presents a low-cost, open experimental platform for research in end-to-end autonomous driving with miniature Ackermann vehicles. The platform combines a physical vehicle, a printed urban track, data collection tools, trajectory registration, and a Webots digital twin, enabling controlled experiments that connect simulation-based autonomous-driving methods to real-world execution. As a first baseline, we implement command-conditioned behavior cloning, in which a neural policy receives an on-board camera image and a high-level navigation command and outputs steering and speed. The system is evaluated both on the physical vehicle and in simulation. In real closed-loop experiments, the learned policy follows lanes and executes commanded turns, reaching a mean cross-track error of 6.1 cm with respect to the reference route, close to the 4.7 cm observed in human demonstrations. In the digital twin, camera field of view has a strong effect on performance, reducing the mean cross-track error from 35.6 to 3.3 cm when widened from 58 to 120 degrees. Using the digital twin to generate synthetic driving data and a learned sim-to-real image translator to reduce the appearance gap, we further show that a higher-capacity policy trained on this synthetic data combined with real demonstrations is the only configuration that completes all four track routes in closed loop, whereas the compact baseline and the same network trained on real data alone complete fewer. These results establish the open platform as a practical testbed for sim-to-real studies and provide an initial command-conditioned imitation-learning baseline; we release it to support reproducible research.

</details>


### [190] [Robust PAC Learning of Concurrent Stochastic Games](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04189)
*Angel Y. He,David Parker*

Main category: cs.LG

TL;DR: This paper presents the first PAC learning framework for general-sum concurrent stochastic games (CSGs) with transition uncertainty. It addresses the challenge of Nash equilibrium (NE) existence by maintaining L¹ confidence sets over transition kernels and solving robust CSGs, with either returning an ε-approximate NE with near-optimal social welfare or providing a certificate that no exact NE exists.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address two key challenges in multi-agent reinforcement learning: (1) learning in stochastic games with transition uncertainty, and (2) the fundamental problem of Nash equilibrium existence in concurrent stochastic games. Existing frameworks lack principled methods for both transition learning and equilibrium existence verification.

Method: The method involves: (1) maintaining data-driven L¹ confidence sets over transition kernels, (2) solving a robust CSG to compute social-welfare optimal ε-NE, (3) using a robust MDP-based exploration mechanism to drive joint state-action coverage, and (4) introducing a Nash margin characterization for principled reasoning about equilibrium existence.

Result: Under a minimum reachability condition p_reach > 0 over relevant state-action pairs, the algorithm terminates after polynomial trajectory samples with sample complexity Ō(R_max² H⁴ |S|² |A| / (p_reach ε²)). Empirical results demonstrate near-optimal performance, correct handling of equilibrium (non-)existence, and sample complexity consistent with theory.

Conclusion: The framework provides a principled approach to PAC learning in general-sum CSGs with transition uncertainty, with the novel ability to either compute an ε-NE with near-optimal social welfare or provide a sound certificate of non-existence. This addresses a fundamental gap in multi-agent reinforcement learning theory.

Abstract: We introduce the first Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning framework for general-sum concurrent stochastic games (CSGs) with transition uncertainty, while addressing the challenge of Nash equilibrium (NE) existence. Our algorithm maintains data-driven $L^1$ confidence sets over transition kernels and solves a robust CSG to compute a social-welfare optimal $\varepsilon$-NE, using a robust MDP-based exploration mechanism to drive joint state-action coverage. Crucially, we introduce a Nash margin characterisation that enables principled reasoning about equilibrium existence: the framework either returns an $\varepsilon$-approximate NE whose social-welfare value is $\varepsilon$-close to optimal, or provides a sound certificate that no exact NE exists. Under a minimum reachability condition $p_{\mathrm{reach}}>0$ over relevant state-action pairs, the algorithm terminates after a polynomial number of trajectory samples, with sample complexity $\widetilde{O}\left( {R_{\max}^2 H^4 |S|^2 |A| / (p_{\mathrm{reach}} \varepsilon^2)} \right)$. Empirical results on benchmark CSGs demonstrate near-optimal performance, correct handling of equilibrium (non-)existence, and sample complexity consistent with theory.

</details>

### [191] [Structure and Implementation of New Practical English Textbooks Driven by Artificial Intelligence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02981)
*Ya Wang,Lei Zhang,Xueguang Yang,Bo Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes an AI-driven adaptive learning system for practical English education, featuring a five-layer architecture (knowledge mapping, learner profiling, task generation, feedback orchestration, and teacher-side governance) that was tested on 186 undergraduates over eight weeks, demonstrating significant improvements in learning outcomes and teaching efficiency.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Artificial intelligence is transforming applied English materials from static content to adaptive learning systems capable of diagnosing learners, recommending tasks, and providing formative feedback. This study addresses the need for personalized learning paths while maintaining curriculum stability in English language education.

Method: The researchers developed a five-layer architecture comprising: (1) knowledge mapping, (2) learner profiling, (3) task generation, (4) feedback orchestration, and (5) teacher-side governance. A prototype was tested on 186 non-English-major undergraduates over eight weeks of teaching and compared with a static digital textbook.

Result: The AI-driven system showed significant improvements compared to the static digital textbook: unit completion accuracy increased from 72.4% to 84.9%, average speaking task scores increased by 10.8 points, and teacher's correction time was reduced by 31.6%.

Conclusion: An AI-driven textbook can maintain curriculum stability while providing personalized learning paths, rich practice materials, and traceable classroom data. The system successfully combines adaptive learning capabilities with teacher governance, achieving both improved learner outcomes and reduced teacher workload.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the form of applied English materials from fixed paper sequences to adaptive learning systems that can diagnose learners, recommend tasks, and provide formative feedback. This paper studies the structure and application of a new practical English textbook driven by artificial intelligence. A five-layer architecture is proposed: knowledge mapping, learner profiling, task generation, feedback orchestration, and teacher-side governance. A prototype was tested on 186 non-English-major undergraduates for eight weeks of teaching. Compared with a static digital textbook, the proposed system increased the unit completion accuracy from 72.4% to 84.9%, raised the average score for speaking tasks by 10.8 points, and reduced the teacher's correction time by 31.6%. Therefore, an AI-driven textbook can maintain the stability of the curriculum while providing personalised learning paths, rich practice materials and traceable classroom data.

</details>


### [192] [MasterControl Seventeen Every Time](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03209)
*MasterControl AI Lab*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a governed approach to enterprise analytics where a language model interprets user questions while a deterministic policy selects and executes pre-approved analytical programs, ensuring deterministic, replayable results with evidence. The approach is tested across 440 runs comparing runtime planning agents against a policy-executed analyzer.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address reliability and governance challenges in enterprise analytics by AI systems. The authors aim to ensure that analytical results are deterministic, replayable, and come with evidence - addressing concerns about LLM-generated SQL and runtime planning that may fail to produce consistent, auditable results.

Method: The method involves a two-stage system: (1) an LLM interprets the user's question to determine intent, and (2) a deterministic policy selects and executes pre-approved analytical programs from a defined class of operations (relational operations, aggregation, comparison, windows, ranking, similarity). Three 8B parameter models were tested for runtime SQL generation and tool selection, while Qwen3-8B was used for intent interpretation only with policy-driven execution.

Result: The key finding is that none of the 330 runtime-planning episodes (across three 8B models) matched the full answer-and-evidence contract across all test datasets. In contrast, the policy-executed analyzer achieved 110 out of 110 matches. This demonstrates that the governed approach can ensure reliable, contract-compliant outputs.

Conclusion: The conclusion highlights that the governed approach with deterministic policy execution can achieve reliable, replayable results within a defined analytical class. However, the authors explicitly note this is a configuration-specific result and not general evidence that runtime agents cannot succeed under different designs. The approach emphasizes fixed meaning, policy, data, and execution rules for reproducibility.

Abstract: We study a governed approach to enterprise analytics: a language model interprets the question, while deterministic policy selects and runs a pre-approved analytical program that returns both results and evidence. We show that this restriction can remain expressive within a defined analytical class, using relational operations plus aggregation, comparison, windows, ranking, and similarity. Fixed meaning, policy, data, and execution rules also make results replayable. Across 440 runs, three 8B models generated SQL and selected tools at runtime, while Qwen3-8B interpreted intent only and policy executed the approved program. None of 330 runtime-planning episodes matched the full answer-and-evidence contract across all test datasets; the policy-executed analyzer matched 110 of 110. This is a configuration-specific result, not evidence that runtime agents cannot succeed under other designs.

</details>


### [193] [Speculative Macro Commit for Faster Tool-Using Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03236)
*Zeyu Liu,Souvik Kundu,Peter A. Beerel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Speculative Macro Commit (SMC) is a runtime mechanism for tool-using LLM agents that uses a two-tier system: a large authoritative actor model combined with a faster speculative drafter model that pre-executes future action chains. When the actor's next tool call matches the drafter's prediction, SMC commits the pre-executed steps to the official trajectory, reducing latency while maintaining accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Tool-using LLM agents experience significant latency not only from model inference but also from serial action-observation turns, where each tool call, environment transition, and observation delays subsequent decisions.

Method: SMC uses a two-tier agent system where a large authoritative actor model produces the official trajectory while a faster speculative drafter model continuously predicts and executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot. The system mines recurring multi-action skeletons from training traces and stores them in a macro library for runtime matching against action chains predicted by the drafter. When the actor's next tool call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the remaining pre-executed draft steps with their observations to the official trajectory.

Result: Using Qwen3.5-27B INT4 as the actor model and Qwen3.5-4B as the drafter, SMC matches sequential agent's overall accuracy on τ²-Bench Telecom subset while reducing latency by 10.23% over Speculative Actions baseline and 18.59% over sequential execution. On AppWorld, SMC reduces wall time by 7.7% over SA baseline and 44.9% over sequential execution, with a small reduction in task completion.

Conclusion: SMC provides a practical way to reuse multi-step speculative execution and reduce agent latency beyond single-step speculative actions, achieving significant latency reductions while maintaining comparable task completion rates.

Abstract: Tool-using LLM agents spend wall-clock time not only on model inference but also in serial action--observation turns, where each tool call, environment transition, and observation can delay subsequent decisions. We introduce \textbf{Speculative Macro Commit} (SMC), a runtime mechanism for a two-tier agent system: a large authoritative actor model produces the official trajectory, while a faster speculative drafter model continuously predicts and executes future action chains on an isolated environment snapshot. SMC mines recurring multi-action skeletons from training traces and stores them in a macro library used to match against action chains predicted by the drafter at runtime. When the actor's next tool call matches the first drafted action, SMC commits the remaining pre-executed draft steps, together with their observations, to the official trajectory. Using Qwen3.5-27B INT4 as the authoritative actor model and Qwen3.5-4B as the speculative drafter model, SMC matches the sequential agent's overall accuracy while reducing latency by 10.23\% over the Speculative Actions (SA) baseline and 18.59\% over sequential execution on the $τ^2$-Bench Telecom subset. On AppWorld, SMC reduces wall time by 7.7\% over SA baseline and 44.9\% over sequential execution, with a small reduction in task completion. Overall, SMC provides a practical way to reuse multi-step speculative execution and reduce agent latency beyond single-step speculative actions. Our code is publicly available \href{https://github.com/zeyuliu1037/speculative-macro-commit}{\textcolor{magenta}{here}}.

</details>


### [194] [Fresh Memory, Stale Plans: Dependency-Scoped Validation for Distributed LLM-Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03340)
*Evan Chen,Shiqiang Wang,Christopher G. Brinton*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: PlanFence addresses "stale-plan execution" in distributed LLM-agent teams, where agents may act on obsolete plans even when state appears fresh. It uses a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol where plans cite exact records used, and executors validate only relevant records before acting.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The problem is that in distributed LLM-agent systems, a planner may derive a plan from requirement r3, another agent commits r4, and an executor receives r4 without recognizing the plan from r3 is now invalid. State freshness alone doesn't guarantee plan validity - this is the fundamental issue being addressed.

Method: PlanFence uses a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol: (1) Plans cite exact public records they used, (2) Executors validate only the records that can affect the pending external action, (3) Replanning occurs once or blocks when validation is incomplete.

Result: In 30 controlled live workflows with post-plan revision: freshness-only executor acted on obsolete plan in every task (100% failure), while PlanFence completed all tasks without invalid action (100% success). Two conditional boundaries identified: (1) proactive synchronization yields lower coordination stall at low churn, (2) PlanFence avoids repeated update-path coordination as churn grows and avoids validating unrelated state as shared keyspace grows.

Conclusion: PlanFence effectively solves stale-plan execution through dependency-scoped validation. Results are specific to safety and systems-cost (coordination overhead), not general task-accuracy gains. The protocol shows conditional effectiveness: proactive sync works better at low churn, while PlanFence scales better at high churn and with large shared keyspaces.

Abstract: Distributed LLM-agent teams can read the latest shared facts and still act on an obsolete plan. A planner may derive an action from requirement $r_3$, another agent may commit $r_4$, and an executor may receive $r_4$ without replacing the plan derived from $r_3$. We call this \emph{stale-plan execution}: state freshness does not establish that the plan authorizing an action remains valid. We introduce PlanFence, a dependency-scoped action-validation protocol. Plans cite the exact public records they used, and an executor validates only the records that can affect the pending external action, replanning once or blocking when validation is incomplete. In 30 controlled live workflows with a post-plan revision, a freshness-only executor acts on the obsolete plan in every task, whereas PlanFence completes all tasks without an invalid action. Controlled replay reveals two conditional boundaries: proactive synchronization yields lower coordination stall at low churn, while PlanFence avoids repeated update-path coordination as churn grows and avoids validating unrelated state as the shared keyspace grows. These are controlled safety and systems-cost results, not general task-accuracy gains.

</details>


### [195] [A Prompt-Engineering Approach to Develop Scalable, Flexible, and Real-Time Hybrid Micro-Level Personalization in a General Purpose AI Teaching Assistant](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03402)
*Saptarshi Basu,Sandeep Kakar,Ashok Goel*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study presents a prompt-engineering framework to personalize LLM-based AI teaching assistants (like Jill Watson) across academic disciplines. The framework uses six learner dimensions to create 96 distinct profiles, integrates Bloom's Taxonomy for cognitive complexity assessment, and conditions the LLM through structured prompts without retraining. Evaluation via NLP metrics and a human study (n=5) shows measurable differences in response style and structure across personalization conditions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI teaching assistants powered by LLMs provide scalable educational support but lack personalization. There is a need to adapt AI responses to individual learner characteristics to improve educational effectiveness.

Method: The framework adapts LLM responses using six learner-specific dimensions: self-assessment, abstraction preference, verbosity preference, perceptual orientation, information processing style, and level of understanding. Student queries are analyzed using Bloom's Taxonomy to estimate cognitive complexity. Learner attributes and cognitive assessments are encoded in structured prompts to condition the LLM without requiring model retraining. Evaluation uses NLP metrics and a human study with five participants.

Result: Results show perceived differences in response style and structure across personalization conditions. Statistical analyses identified learner attributes associated with measurable response changes, providing preliminary evidence that prompt-based personalization can support adaptive behavior in LLM-powered educational agents.

Conclusion: Prompt-based personalization is a viable approach to enable adaptive behavior in LLM-powered educational agents without model retraining. The six-dimension framework and Bloom's Taxonomy integration offer a scalable method for personalizing AI teaching assistants across diverse learners and courses.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) teaching assistants powered by large language models (LLMs) offer scalable educational support but often provide limited personalization. This study presents a prompt-engineering-based framework for personalizing general-purpose LLM/RAG-based AI teaching assistants such as Jill Watson across academic disciplines and courses. The framework adapts responses using six learner-specific dimensions: self-assessment, abstraction preference, verbosity preference, perceptual orientation, information processing style, and level of understanding, yielding 96 distinct learner profiles. Student queries are additionally analyzed using Bloom's Taxonomy to estimate cognitive complexity at the interaction level. Learner attributes and cognitive assessments are encoded in structured prompts that condition the LLM without requiring model retraining. The framework is evaluated through experiments using NLP metrics and a human study with five participants. Results show perceived differences in response style and structure across personalization conditions, with statistical analyses identifying learner attributes associated with measurable response changes. These findings provide preliminary evidence that prompt-based personalization can support adaptive behavior in LLM-powered educational agents.

</details>


### [196] [Caught in the Story: Narrative Captivity in Multi-turn LLMs Conversation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03407)
*Yuhe Wu,Guangyu Wang,Yujie Chen,Jiatong Zhang,Yuran Chen,Yutong Zhang,Xiyin Cheng,Wenpeng Cao,Zhuang Liu,Guang Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces "narrative captivity," a failure mode where LLMs providing moral advice align with a one-sided narrator's account without seeking alternative perspectives. The authors built a benchmark of 5,078 interpersonal conflict scenarios across 6 moral dimensions and tested 17 LLMs, finding that multi-turn narration shifts end-state judgments by 25 percentage points on average compared to single-turn baselines. Preference optimization is identified as a major contributor, while inference-time strategies only partially mitigate this issue.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world moral guidance seeking differs from prior research assumptions (single-turn judgments or pressure-laden rebuttals). In actual consultations, one party often presents a self-justifying account over multiple turns, creating information asymmetry. The researchers aimed to study whether narration alone—without an explicit opposing position—can shift model judgments during multi-turn moral consultation.

Method: Built a benchmark of 5,078 interpersonal conflict scenarios spanning six moral dimensions. Tested 17 LLMs across both multi-turn narration conditions and matched single-turn baselines. Conducted stage-level analysis to identify contributing factors and evaluated four inference-time mitigation strategies.

Result: Narrative captivity is widespread across 17 LLMs. End-state judgments under multi-turn narration shift by 25 percentage points on average beyond the matched single-turn baseline. Preference optimization was identified as a major contributor. Four inference-time strategies provide only partial mitigation.

Conclusion: The findings reveal a significant limitation in current LLM moral advisors: they fail to preserve independent judgment when presented with one-sided narratives. The researchers hope this work fosters LLM advisors that maintain objectivity and seek missing perspectives in real-world consultation contexts.

Abstract: People increasingly turn to large language models (LLMs) for everyday advice, making ethically charged interpersonal problems a practical moral-advisory context. Most prior work has studied this context through single-turn judgments or pressure-laden rebuttals, assumptions that poorly match how guidance is sought in real-world contexts. These assumptions leave unclear whether narration alone, without an explicit opposing position, can shift model judgments during multi-turn moral consultation. Yet real-world moral-conflict conversation often elicits one party's self-justifying account, which can unfold over multiple turns and create information asymmetry. We introduce \textbf{narrative captivity}, a failure mode in which a model treats an unopposed one-sided account as complete and aligns with the narrator's interpretation without seeking missing perspectives. To measure this phenomenon, we build a benchmark of $5{,}078$ interpersonal-conflict scenarios spanning six moral dimensions. Across 17 LLMs, narrative captivity is widespread: end-state judgments under multi-turn narration shift by 25 percentage points on average beyond the matched single-turn baseline. Stage-level analysis identifies preference optimization as a major contributor, while four inference-time strategies provide only partial mitigation. We hope our project fosters LLM advisors that preserve independent judgment in real-world consultation.

</details>


### [197] [Dude: A Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for Paper-Code Discrepancy Detection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03416)
*Weijie Liu,Running Zhao,Wenhao Yuan,Jinfeng Xu,Zhanfeng Xu,Xiaoxi Zhang,Edith Cheuk-Han Ngai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Dude is the first Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for detecting discrepancies between research papers and their code implementations. It addresses granularity asymmetry between paper and code languages through granularity-aligned negotiation and two-stage salience-filtering, achieving up to 22.8% recall and 18.7% F1 score improvements over baselines.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing single-agent LLM paradigms for paper-code discrepancy detection suffer from limited context capacity and one-sided detection, leading to poor recall performance. The granularity asymmetry between paper-language and code-language creates over-interpretation and over-reporting challenges, increasing false positives.

Method: Dude employs a dual-detection multi-agent architecture with two novel mechanisms: (1) Granularity-aligned negotiation to address the asymmetry between paper and code languages, and (2) A two-stage salience-filtering mechanism to prevent false discrepancy reporting.

Result: Experimental results on real-world paper-code discrepancy datasets demonstrate significant improvements: up to 22.8% recall improvement, up to 18.7% F1 score improvement compared to baseline methods.

Conclusion: The proposed Dude system effectively addresses the granularity asymmetry challenge in multi-agent LLM-based discrepancy detection, achieving superior recall and precision through its dual-detection architecture and specialized filtering mechanisms.

Abstract: LLM-empowered paper-code discrepancy detection has received growing concern since the scaling of research submissions exceeds the manual review capability. However, the limited context capacity and one-sided discrepancy detection of existing single-agent LLM paradigms lead to an inferior recall performance in detecting discrepancies. In this paper, we propose Dude, the first Dual-Detection Multi-Agent System for paper-code discrepancy detection. We discover that the granularity asymmetry of the paper-language and code-language introduces over-interpretation and over-reporting challenges in a multi-agent system design for discrepancy detection, resulting in increasing false positives. To address this, we propose a granularity-aligned negotiation and a two-stage salience-filtering mechanism in Dude, which effectively prevents agents from falsely reporting discrepancies. Experimental results in real-world paper-code discrepancy datasets showcase Dude's significant recall and precision improvement by up to 22.8%, increasing F1 score by up to 18.7% compared to baseline methods.

</details>


### [198] [DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval: Evaluating Implicit Instruction Following in Full-Duplex Voice Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03423)
*Puneet Mathur,Dinesh Manocha*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval (DSB-IFEval), a benchmark for evaluating implicit instruction-following in real-time spoken interaction for full-duplex voice agents. It comprises 1,038 test cases across eight assistant roles and evaluates five conditioning protocols, revealing architecture-dependent trade-offs in how systems handle explicit vs. persona-implied instructions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks test turn-management behaviors through explicit instructions, but deployed agents often use roles/personas from which appropriate behavior must be inferred. This gap between explicit instruction following and persona-implied behavior is the key motivation.

Method: DSB-IFEval contains 1,038 test cases spanning eight diverse assistant roles. Five conditioning protocols are evaluated: default behavior, explicit behavioral instructions, persona-implied behavior, combined persona-rule conditioning, and instruction conflict. Two metrics are used: Instruction Adherence Score (IAS) for real-time floor management and LLM-judged Persona Adherence Score (PAS) for persona-consistent content. Six real-time speech systems were tested.

Result: Full duplex models (F-Actor, PersonaPlex) show 9.7% and 4.5% adherence drops respectively under persona-only conditioning vs. explicit instructions. GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, and Fun-Audio-Chat maintain persona-consistent content but don't adapt floor behavior across instruction types. Systems struggle to override persona instructions under safety conflicts even when reliably following conflicting directives to their prescribed persona.

Conclusion: Inferring behavior implied by a role, executing it at appropriate conversational moments, and resolving competing instructions remain distinct challenges for full-duplex voice agents. The field needs improvements in implicit instruction following and conflict resolution.

Abstract: Full-duplex voice agents must continuously decide when to listen, backchannel, interrupt, handle speech overlaps, take the floor, and yield. Existing benchmarks largely test these behaviors through explicit turn-management instructions, while deployed agents are often configured through roles or personas from which the appropriate conversational behavior must be inferred. We introduce DuplexSpeechBench-IFEval (DSB-IFEval) for evaluating implicit instruction-following in real-time spoken interaction. (DSB-IFEval) comprises 1,038 test cases spanning eight diverse assistant roles and evaluates five conditioning protocols for instruction-following: default behavior, explicit behavioral instructions, persona-implied behavior, combined persona--rule conditioning, and instruction conflict. We measure real-time floor management using a deterministic Instruction Adherence Score (IAS) and persona-consistent content using LLM-judged Persona Adherence Score (PAS). Across six real-time speech systems, we find architecture-dependent trade-offs. Full duplex models like F-Actor and PersonaPlex are more sensitive to whether conversational behavior is stated explicitly or must be inferred from a persona, with adherence dropping by 9.7% and 4.5%, respectively, under persona-only conditioning. In contrast, GPT-Realtime, MiniCPM-o, and Fun-Audio-Chat strongly adhere to persona-consistent content, but their floor behavior does not adapt across explicit and persona-only instructions and remains constrained on several proactive actions. We further find that even if systems reliably follow conflicting directives to their prescribed persona, they still struggle to override them under safety conflict. These results show that inferring the behavior implied by a role, executing it at the appropriate conversational moment, and resolving competing instructions remain distinct challenges for full-duplex voice agents.

</details>


### [199] [Do GUI Agents Know When Not to Act? Enabling Conflict-Aware Termination for Multimodal GUI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03438)
*Zhaoyuan Huang,Tianjie Ju,Pengzhou Cheng,Zheng Wu,Yansi Li,Chuanbiao Song,Jun Lan,Huijia Zhu,Weiqiang Wang,Zhuosheng Zhang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the problem of GUI agents that over-comply with infeasible or conflicting instructions. The authors introduce CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark for evaluating conflict-aware termination, and CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework that helps agents recognize when not to act. The framework combines feasibility verification with conditional action modulation to reduce over-compliance while maintaining normal task performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GUI agents are increasingly used to execute natural-language instructions on user interfaces. However, real users may issue infeasible instructions due to benign mistakes. Current agents continue executing blindly under conflicting instructions, demonstrating "execution-biased overcompliance." The authors argue that reliable agents should know not only how to act but also when not to act.

Method: The authors propose two key contributions: (1) CONFLICTGUI benchmark covering instruction-internal conflicts and instruction-GUI context conflicts; (2) CONFLICTGUARD inference-time framework with two components: (a) feasibility verification protocol that guides agents to assess instruction logic and GUI-side evidence before acting, and (b) conditional action modulation mechanism that steers agents from over-compliant execution into termination-oriented behavior.

Result: Experiments across five widely-used agents demonstrate that CONFLICTGUARD significantly improves average conflict task success rate while preserving normal GUI-task performance. The results validate that a lightweight inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI agents' competence to identify inappropriate execution scenarios.

Conclusion: The paper demonstrates that a lightweight inference-time intervention (CONFLICTGUARD) can substantially improve GUI agents' ability to recognize conflicting instructions and refrain from unnecessary actions. This work highlights the importance of conflict-aware termination in practical GUI agent deployments.

Abstract: Graphical user interface (GUI) agents are increasingly used to execute natural-language instructions on user interfaces, yet real users may issue infeasible instructions due to benign mistakes. A reliable agent should not only know how to act, but also when not to act. In this work, we introduce CONFLICTGUI, a benchmark covering instruction-internal conflicts and instruction-GUI context conflicts to study conflict-aware termination. Our evaluation reveals severe execution-biased overcompliance: agents that perform well on feasible tasks often continue to execute blindly under conflicting instructions. To mitigate this behavior, we propose CONFLICTGUARD, an inference-time framework that aligns an agent's feasibility awareness with its action generation. CONFLICTGUARD contains two coupled components: a feasibility verification protocol that guides the agent to assess instruction logic and GUI-side evidence before acting, and a conditional action modulation mechanism that steers agents from over-compliant execution into termination-oriented behavior. Experiments across five widely-used agents demonstrate that CONFLICTGUARD improves average conflict task success rate significantly, while preserving normal GUI-task performance. These results validate that a lightweight inference-time intervention can substantially boost GUI Agent's competence to identify inappropriate execution scenarios and refrain from unnecessary actions.

</details>


### [200] [Beyond "Made with AI": Visualizing Provenance Density to Mitigate the Transparency Penalty](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03460)
*Qing Zhang,Yifei Huang,Juyoung Lee,Thad Starner,Jun Rekimoto*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: As AI-generated text becomes indistinguishable from human writing, users fall into a "Fluency Trap" - trusting fluent hallucinations while discounting accurate AI content. The paper proposes "Provenance Density," an evidence-visualization interface showing the density of verified claims in text, which significantly improves users' ability to discern truth from fabrication.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address a critical problem in the AI era: users cannot rely on fluency as a proxy for truth. Binary "Made with AI" labels only disclose authorship but don't show what supports a claim. This creates a need for evidence-based transparency rather than simple authorship disclosure.

Method: The study used two methods: (1) A user study with 81 participants testing an idealized Provenance Density interface, and (2) A technical audit with 200 samples evaluating retrieval density and Consistency Veto.

Result: The Provenance Density interface produced a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication (+4.15 points, d=1.82), while participants given no signal showed no detectable discrimination. Technical audit revealed that retrieval density alone is insufficient, and unexpectedly, the Consistency Veto carries most of the discriminative signal on dynamic queries.

Conclusion: As AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from human writing, effective transparency must move from authorship disclosure toward evidence visualization. The Consistency Veto (rather than retrieval density) is the key discriminative factor.

Abstract: As generative AI makes polished prose cheap to produce, users can no longer rely on fluency as a proxy for truth. We call this failure mode the Fluency Trap: users trust fluent hallucinations while also discounting accurate content once it is disclosed as AI-generated. Binary ``Made with AI'' labels respond with authorship disclosure, but they do not show what supports a claim. We propose Provenance Density, an evidence-visualization interface that shows the density of verified claims in a text. In a user study with 81 participants, an idealized Provenance Density interface produced a large discernment gap between truth and fabrication ($+4.15$ points, $d=1.82$), whereas participants given no signal showed no detectable discrimination. A technical audit with 200 samples shows that retrieval density alone is insufficient; unexpectedly, the Consistency Veto carries most of the discriminative signal on dynamic queries. As AI-generated content becomes indistinguishable from human writing, effective transparency must move from authorship disclosure toward evidence visualization.

</details>


### [201] [AutoGraphForge: Towards Automated Graph Theory Discovery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03478)
*Ján Pastorek*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: AutoGraphForge is an automated pipeline for graph-theoretic conjecture generation, refutation, formalization, and proving, using Graffiti3 for conjecture generation, testing against ~348,000 graphs, and formalizing surviving conjectures in Lean 4 with neural prover integration.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The project aims to automate the mathematical discovery process in graph theory, addressing the challenges of conjecture generation, systematic refutation, formal verification, and proof assistance using modern AI and computational tools.

Method: The pipeline uses: (1) Graffiti3-based conjecture generation with counterexample-guided evolution; (2) novelty filter with 559 classical/folklore relations using linear programming; (3) refutation against ~348,000 graphs from House of Graphs, exhaustive census (n≤9), extremal families, and random models; (4) counterexample search algorithms; (5) Lean 4 formalization with kernel verification; (6) integration of neural provers DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B and OProver-32B.

Result: After several rounds on HPC cluster, the pipeline yielded 6,522 conjectures surviving refutation, novelty filter, and active search. This includes nontrivial relations between annihilation number and edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs, which were proven by hand.

Conclusion: The full pipeline is implemented end-to-end, passes initial sanity checks, and is currently running on the cluster. It demonstrates a novel approach to automated mathematical discovery combining symbolic computation, AI-based proving, and formal verification.

Abstract: We report on our ongoing project to develop a computational pipeline, AutoGraphForge, for an automated graph-theoretic conjecturing-refuting-formalizing-proving system. Conjecture generation is counterexample-guided and runs in rounds: a Graffiti3 generator proposes conjectures over a small, evolving snapshot table $T$ (initially a few hundred graphs with their computed invariants) that grows only by counterexamples to its own conjectures. A novelty filter of $559$ classical and folklore relations, closed under transitive composition and linear identity substitution, decides via a linear program whether a candidate is already implied by known results. Surviving candidates are tested against a dataset of about $348,000$ graphs, unioning the complete House of Graphs invariant export, the exhaustive census of all connected graphs on at most nine vertices, several extremal families (strongly regular, minimal Ramsey, Cayley, cages, barbells, lollipops, spiders), and random models. Counterexample-search algorithms then attack the remainder. Run for several rounds on an HPC cluster, the loop yields $6,522$ conjectures that survived the refutation dataset, the novelty filter and every active-search run -- among them nontrivial relations between the annihilation number and the edge-cover number for bipartite and regular graphs, which we prove by hand. A subsequent formalization and proving stage deterministically translates each surviving conjecture into a Lean 4 statement skeleton; every candidate proof is kernel-verified against a pinned mathlib4 and our custom invariant preamble. This stage integrates two neural provers -- DeepSeek-Prover-V2-671B (served with vLLM) and the Lean-specialised OProver-32B -- behind the independent kernel check. It is implemented end-to-end and passes initial sanity checks, with the full pipeline currently running on the cluster.

</details>


### [202] [DRACO: Fine-Grained Credit Assignment with Dynamic Rubrics for Long-Horizon Agent Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04094)
*Shubham Gandhi,Saurabh Goyal,Kiran Kate,Yara Rizk*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DRACO is a reinforcement learning method that handles the outcome-blind setting where ground-truth success signals are unavailable. It dynamically generates rubrics during training, scores them once per trajectory, and redistributes these judgments to step-level advantages for GRPO, without requiring trained attribution modules.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper addresses a key limitation in reinforcement learning: most long-horizon agent domains lack programmatic checkers (verifiers). Existing multi-criteria rubrics are scored once per trajectory, but a single scalar reward provides poor signal across tens of steps in complex tasks.

Method: DRACO generates rubrics dynamically during training to track the policy's evolving capability, scores those rubrics once per completed trajectory, and redistributes that judgment over the steps responsible for annotated rubrics to produce differentiated per-step advantages in GRPO. The redistribution is closed-form and does not introduce any trained attribution module.

Result: On AppWorld, DRACO gains 15.9 points over the base model and 5.3 points over GRPO trained with sparse ground-truth reward, despite not using any verifiers. On out-of-domain Tau-Bench, it gains 5.3 points over the base model, beating both ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based training settings.

Conclusion: DRACO successfully handles the outcome-blind setting by dynamically generating rubrics and redistributing trajectory-level judgments to step-level advantages. It outperforms both ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based approaches, demonstrating strong generalization to out-of-domain tasks without requiring verifiers.

Abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards works well when a task has a programmatic checker, but most long-horizon agent domains have none. We work in the outcome-blind setting, where ground-truth success signals are not available. Multi-criteria rubrics are a popular way to supply such a reward; they are scored once per trajectory, but a single scalar is a poor signal across tens of steps. We propose DRACO: Distributing Rubric-based Advantage for Credit Optimization. It generates rubrics dynamically during training to track the policy's evolving capability, scores those rubrics once per completed trajectory, and redistributes that judgment over the steps responsible for annotated rubrics to produce differentiated per-step advantages in GRPO. The redistribution is closed-form and does not introduce any trained attribution module. On AppWorld, DRACO gains 15.9 points over the base model and 5.3 points over GRPO trained with a sparse ground-truth reward, despite not using any verifiers itself. On out-of-domain Tau-Bench, it gains 5.3 points over the base model even without a frontier judge, beating both ground-truth-reward training and other rubric-based training settings. The code for DRACO is available at https://github.com/IBM/draco.

</details>


### [203] [Making Every Tool Call Count: Necessary Tool-Evidence Path Rewards for Agentic Vision-Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03493)
*Xingming Long,Yu Liu,Zhiwei Yang,Hanqi Feng,Shaojie Zhang,Barnabas Poczos,Chao Jiang,Zhenbo Luo,Lei Jiang,Pei Fu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses limitations in training agentic vision-language models (VLMs) that use tools (image cropping, image search, text search) to answer complex image-grounded questions. The authors propose NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), an annotation scheme specifying essential evidence and tool calls, along with NTEP-R, a supervision mechanism that rewards proper evidence acquisition and utilization. Their 8B-parameter model NTEP-8B significantly improves accuracy and efficiency on seven benchmarks.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing training paradigms for agentic VLMs only evaluate final answer correctness, leading to two critical problems: (i) models make redundant or off-target tool calls that fail to gather necessary evidence, and (ii) models fail to extract necessary information from tool observations even when appropriate tools are called.

Method: The authors introduce NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), an annotation scheme that explicitly specifies essential external evidence and corresponding tool calls for each query. Based on NTEP, they propose NTEP-R, a supervision mechanism with three components: (1) rewards alignment between pre-call intent and necessary evidence-seeking goal, (2) rewards post-call observation summaries that align with necessary evidence, and (3) a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant tool calls that revisit satisfied goals.

Result: NTEP-8B, an 8B-parameter model instantiation, significantly improves both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency within a unified three-tool framework (image cropping, image search, text search) across seven image-grounded benchmarks.

Conclusion: Fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision is critical for training robust agentic VLMs. The NTEP approach provides a novel framework for explicitly supervising evidence acquisition and utilization, leading to substantial improvements in both accuracy and efficiency.

Abstract: Modern vision-language models (VLMs) can directly answer many image-grounded questions, yet they often struggle with complex queries requiring fine-grained visual details or external knowledge. To acquire this missing evidence, agentic VLMs invoke tools such as image cropping, image search, and text search. However, existing training paradigms primarily evaluate tool-use based on final answer correctness, leaving evidence acquisition and utilization insufficiently supervised. This leads to two critical shortcomings: (i) models frequently issue redundant or off-target tool calls that fail to gather necessary evidence, and (ii) even when appropriate tools are called, models often fail to extract the necessary information from the resulting observations. To address these limitations, we introduce the NTEP (Necessary Tool-Evidence Path), a novel annotation scheme that explicitly specifies the essential external evidence and corresponding tool calls for each query. Building upon this, we propose NTEP-R (NTEP Reward), a supervision mechanism ensuring that each tool invocation strictly advances the reasoning process toward the final solution. Specifically, our approach rewards the agent for aligning its pre-call intent with a necessary evidence-seeking goal, and for ensuring the information summarized from the post-call observation aligns with the necessary evidence. Furthermore, we introduce a non-repeated-goal regularizer to penalize redundant calls that revisit satisfied NTEP goals. Extensive evaluations on seven image-grounded benchmarks demonstrate that our 8B-parameter instantiation, NTEP-8B, significantly improves both search-oriented accuracy and tool-use efficiency within a unified three-tool framework. These results highlight the critical value of fine-grained tool-evidence path supervision for training robust agentic VLMs.

</details>


### [204] [GrowPage: On-Demand KV Budgeting for Efficient LLM Reasoning Serving](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03494)
*Qiankun Ma,Yanjiang Zhou,Zinan Xiong,Haofei Wang,Zhen Song,Yang Xiang,Ziyao Zhang,Hairong Zheng*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GrowPage is an on-demand KV cache budgeting framework for efficient LLM serving that dynamically adjusts KV capacity based on runtime demand, using dual-timescale query summaries to track attention patterns and integrating with PagedAttention for continuous batching.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Long-output reasoning tasks create variable KV cache demands that existing methods cannot handle effectively, as they use fixed per-request budgets throughout decoding despite substantial demand variation across requests and during generation.

Method: GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture both recent and long-term attention behaviors, using their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution. At each capacity boundary, it either compresses KV states within the current allocation or acquires an additional physical page when broader demand emerges. The system integrates with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction.

Result: Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves a superior performance-throughput trade-off over existing approaches.

Conclusion: GrowPage effectively addresses the variable KV cache demands in reasoning workloads by dynamically adjusting capacity at runtime, preserving continuous batching and prefix caching while delivering better performance-throughput trade-offs.

Abstract: Long-output reasoning has made the key--value (KV) cache a critical memory bottleneck for efficient LLM serving. Existing KV compression methods usually rely on a predefined per-request budget and adjust only which KV states are retained, leaving the total capacity fixed throughout decoding. However, reasoning workloads exhibit substantial demand variation: different requests require different KV capacities, and the attention demand of an individual request evolves during generation. We introduce \textbf{GrowPage}, an on-demand KV budgeting framework that treats KV capacity as a runtime resource. GrowPage maintains lightweight dual-timescale query summaries to capture recent and long-term attention behaviors, and uses their relative attention working sets to estimate demand evolution. At each capacity boundary, GrowPage either compresses KV states within the current allocation or acquires an additional physical page when broader demand emerges. By integrating with PagedAttention's page-level memory abstraction, GrowPage preserves continuous batching and prefix caching. Experiments on reasoning benchmarks across multiple models show that GrowPage achieves a superior performance--throughput trade-off over existing approaches.

</details>


### [205] [PPO-STGNN: A Proximal Policy Optimization Approach with Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks for DAG Task Scheduling in Cloud-Edge-End Computing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03503)
*Yangshuo Qi,Chenwei Wang,Zihan Shen,Songlin Sun*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the NP-hard problem of scheduling computation-intensive DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) tasks in heterogeneous cloud-edge-end collaborative environments. The proposed PPO-STGNN algorithm combines Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with Spatio-Temporal Graph Neural Networks (STGNN) to learn scheduling policies that minimize makespan and Schedule Length Ratio (SLR) while improving CPU and memory load balancing.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement-learning methods fail to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources in heterogeneous cloud-edge-end environments. The heterogeneity of computing capacity, network bandwidth, and energy consumption across cloud, edge, and end nodes makes efficient DAG task scheduling a challenging NP-hard problem.

Method: The proposed method uses an STGNN to extract features from both the DAG task topology and the physical cloud-edge-end resource graph. A PPO algorithm then optimizes the scheduling policy to minimize makespan and SLR while improving CPU and memory load balancing. A multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism is introduced for pretraining to accelerate convergence.

Result: Experimental results show that PPO-STGNN significantly improves load balancing while maintaining a low completion time, making it suitable for dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge-end DAG scheduling scenarios.

Conclusion: PPO-STGNN successfully integrates STGNN with PPO for DAG task scheduling in cloud-edge-end environments. The multi-teacher behavior-cloning pretraining accelerates convergence. The algorithm achieves a good balance between load balancing and completion time, demonstrating its suitability for dynamic and heterogeneous scenarios.

Abstract: With the rapid development of the Internet of Things, computation intensive directed acyclic graph (DAG) tasks have become increasingly common in cloud-edge-end collaborative environments. However, cloud, edge, and end nodes are highly heterogeneous in computing capacity, network bandwidth, and energy consumption, which makes the efficient scheduling of tasks with complex dependencies an NP-hard problem. Traditional heuristic algorithms and conventional reinforcement-learning methods often fail to capture the spatio-temporal dynamics of system resources. This paper proposes PPO-STGNN, a DAG task-scheduling algorithm that integrates proximal policy optimization (PPO) with spatio-temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs). The method uses an STGNN to extract features from both the DAG task topology and the physical cloud-edge-end resource graph, and then optimizes the scheduling policy through PPO to minimize makespan and schedule length ratio (SLR) while improving CPU and memory load balancing. To accelerate convergence, a multi-teacher behavior-cloning mechanism is introduced for pretraining. Experimental results show that PPO-STGNN significantly improves load balancing while maintaining a low completion time, making it suitable for dynamic and heterogeneous cloud-edge- end DAG scheduling scenarios.

</details>


### [206] [What Matters for Aggressive Decoding-Time KV Eviction? Temporal Aggregation and Ranking Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03515)
*Bo Zeng,Yu Zhao,Yefeng Liu,Zhihong Lu,Xuanfan Ni,Xintong Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper reveals that under aggressive KV cache compression, the temporal aggregation rule (EMA) matters more than scorer modifications—different token scoring functions produce nearly identical retention sets when combined with EMA aggregation. The authors introduce InertiaKV (and InertiaKV-Lazy variant) achieving 1.34-1.46x throughput improvement, and Score-Free decoding which eliminates subsequent scoring with minimal quality impact (+0.03).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Decoding-time KV cache compression research focuses on designing better token scoring functions while treating temporal aggregation as an implementation detail. The authors investigate whether this neglect is warranted by examining how different aggregation methods interact with various scoring functions under aggressive compression.

Method: The authors evaluate multiple scoring functions (value-norm, entropy, KeyDiff, key norm, recency, learned scorer) combined with different temporal aggregation rules on six open-weight backbones across LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks. They propose InertiaKV (EMA-based eviction) and InertiaKV-Lazy (periodic refresh variant), and separately study Score-Free decoding which freezes rankings after the first step.

Result: EMA aggregation makes different scorer modifications largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level.
