Value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce unchanged retention sets, while KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and learned scorer alter rankings and degrade performance. InertiaKV achieves 1.34-1.46x decode throughput; Score-Free decoding incurs only +0.03 average quality change while removing all subsequent scoring.

Conclusion: Temporal aggregation and ranking preservation are distinct, consequential design factors in KV cache compression. This does not imply scoring quality is irrelevant in general, but highlights that aggregation choices can dominate scorer differences under aggressive compression.

Abstract: Decoding-time KV cache compression research focuses heavily on designing better token scoring functions, while the temporal rule that aggregates scores across decode steps is often treated as an implementation detail. Under aggressive KV compression, we find that exponential-moving-average (EMA) aggregation makes approximately order-preserving scorer modifications largely indistinguishable at the eviction-set level. Value-norm and entropy variants remain highly correlated with attention and produce nearly unchanged retention sets, whereas KeyDiff, key norm, recency, and a learned scorer alter the ranking and degrade substantially. We associate this stability with the evaluated aggregation, which couples layer weighting and temporal retention. Building on this observation, we introduce InertiaKV, an EMA-based decoding-time eviction method, and InertiaKV-Lazy, its periodic-refresh variant, which yields 1.34-1.46x decode throughput relative to full refresh InertiaKV. We also study Score-Free decoding as a separate empirical operating point: it scores the full context once at the first decode step, freezes that ranking, and incurs an average quality change of +0.03 while removing all subsequent scoring. Across six open-weight backbones and the LongBench, LongBench-v2, and RULER benchmarks, the results identify temporal aggregation and ranking preservation as distinct, consequential design factors; they do not imply that scoring quality is irrelevant in general.

</details>


### [207] [CulturalMenuBench: Probing the Knowledge-Application Gap in Multimodal Culinary Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03526)
*Bo Zeng,Linfeng Gao,Peiqin Lin,Yu Zhao,Mingyan Zeng,Yu Tong,Xintong Wang,Linlong Xu,Longyue Wang,Weihua Luo,Qinggang Zhang,Jinsong Su*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: The paper introduces CulturalMenuBench, a benchmark testing whether multimodal language models possess genuine cultural understanding of food or merely perform visual matching. Despite achieving near-perfect scores (94%+) on standard food recognition, models drop to at most 56% on Chinese regional cuisine attribution tasks, revealing a substantial knowledge-application gap.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to investigate whether multimodal language models' success on food recognition benchmarks reflects genuine cultural understanding or merely visual pattern matching. The researchers note that high benchmark scores may conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge, which is a critical distinction for AI systems operating in cultural contexts.

Method: The researchers created CulturalMenuBench with 4,870 items across 10 languages and 18 regions. The benchmark includes 10 tasks pairing final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels. They evaluated 12 models using diagnostic analyses including error pattern analysis, correlation with visual distinctiveness vs. cultural structure, and comparison of text-only vs. image-based classification. They also conducted ablation studies removing sequential cooking images.

Result: Key findings: (1) Models scoring >94% on standard tasks drop to at most 56% on Chinese regional cuisine attribution despite identical format; (2) Error patterns are consistent with random guessing; (3) Accuracy correlates with visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure; (4) Models classify cuisines more accurately from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points); (5) Ablation confirms process-grounded tasks genuinely require procedural evidence - removing sequential cooking images selectively degrades those tasks while others remain stable.

Conclusion: The study demonstrates that cultural knowledge is present in models but cannot be activated through visual input alone. Near-perfect recognition benchmarks can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge. This motivates the need for training approaches that explicitly connect perception, procedure, and cultural context. The benchmark and code are publicly available.

Abstract: Multimodal language models achieve near-ceiling scores on food recognition benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether this success reflects genuine cultural understanding or mere visual matching. To probe this distinction, we introduce CulturalMenuBench, a benchmark of 4,870 items in 10 languages across 18 regions; its 10 tasks pair final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels, spanning basic recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. Evaluating 12 models exposes a substantial knowledge-application gap: models exceeding 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks drop to at most 56% when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines, despite an identical four-way format. Diagnostic analyses explain why: error patterns are consistent with random guessing, accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models classify cuisines more accurately from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points). The knowledge is thus present but cannot be activated through visual input. An ablation confirms these tasks genuinely require procedural evidence: removing sequential cooking images selectively degrades process-grounded tasks while others remain stable. Overall, CulturalMenuBench shows that near-perfect recognition can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge, motivating training that explicitly connects perception, procedure, and cultural context. Code and data are publicly available.

</details>


### [208] [NeoRed: A Knowledge-Logic-Alignment Multimodal Large Language Model for Neonatal Respiratory Disease Diagnosis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03527)
*Yinan Liu,Hongtai Xia,Haoran Xu,Jiankang Hong,Jingkuan Song,Ye Luo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NeoRed is the first Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) specifically designed for neonatal respiratory disease diagnosis, addressing domain gaps and insufficient clinical context integration in existing models. It uses a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework with three components: Knowledge Prior Injection, Diagnostic Logic Constraint, and Visual Semantic Alignment.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, but existing MLLMs face two key limitations: (1) domain gap from predominantly adult training data, and (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis.

Method: The authors collected two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and proposed the KLA framework with three components: (1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) - incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations, guiding disease-specific attention; (2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) - aligns generated report semantics with multimodal diagnostic logic; (3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) - establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions.

Result: NeoRed achieves ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. It also preserves competitive performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray).

Conclusion: NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic report generation and represents a significant advancement in neonatal healthcare AI, filling the gap in neonatal diagnostic reports generation.

Abstract: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, posing substantial challenges in clinical practice. Despite recent advances, existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face two key limitations in neonatal diagnosis: (1) domain gap arising from predominantly adult training data; (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis. To address these challenges, we collect two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and propose NeoRed, to the best of our knowledge, the first MLLM tailored for neonatal respiratory disease, filling the gap in neonatal diagnostic reports generation. To enhance joint diagnosis from heterogeneous clinical context and chest X-rays, we design a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework which constrains model behavior from three perspectives: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations, guiding disease-specific attention across modalities; 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) aligns the semantics of generated reports with multimodal diagnostic logic; and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic reports generation, achieving ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. NeoRed also preserves competitive report generation performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray). Datasets will be available upon application.

</details>


### [209] [Feature Reconfiguration With Visual Prior for Medical Lesion Segmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03535)
*Yinan Liu,Jiankang Hong,Zhen Gao,Ye Lu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FreNet is a feature reconfiguration framework for medical lesion segmentation that addresses complex background interference and diverse lesion morphology through visual priors and dual-domain feature reconfiguration. It consists of IPNN for input preprocessing and DFR module (with FDM and SLM) for feature enhancement during encoding.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing encoder-decoder methods lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during encoding, limiting their effectiveness in handling complex background interference and diverse lesion morphology in medical image segmentation.

Method: FreNet employs two key components: (1) Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN) - models continuous spatial field and leverages visual prior from SAM to reconfigure input image before encoding; (2) Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module - uses Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) to decouple features in frequency domain for enhanced foreground-background discriminability, and Spatial Localization Module (SLM) for spatial relocation and stability improvement.

Result: FreNet significantly outperforms SOTA methods on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities. On the challenging ETIS dataset, it achieves 5.0% Dice improvement over SOTA and 7.2% over SAM.

Conclusion: The proposed feature reconfiguration framework with visual priors effectively addresses the challenges of lesion segmentation by incorporating early prior guidance and progressive feature reconfiguration, demonstrating superior performance across diverse medical imaging datasets.

Abstract: Lesion segmentation in medical images plays a critical role in clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. Despite significant advances, lesion segmentation remains challenging due to two major factors: (1) complex background interference; (2) diverse lesion morphology. Existing encoder-decoder based methods mainly focus on enhancing feature extraction or redesigning decoding strategies. However, they lack early prior guidance and feature reconfiguration during the encoding stage, limiting their effectiveness in handling these challenges. To address these limitations, we propose FreNet, a feature reconfiguration framework with visual priors, which performs pixel-level reconfiguration before encoding and feature-level reconfiguration during encoding for precise medical lesion segmentation. To suppress background responses, we propose an Implicit Prior Neural Network (IPNN), which models a continuous spatial field and leverages visual prior from SAM to reconfigure input image before encoding stage. To better handle diverse lesion morphology, we design a Dual-domain Feature Reconfiguration (DFR) module to progressively reconfigure backbone features during encoding stage. Within DFR, the Frequency Decoupling Module (FDM) decouples backbone features in frequency domain to enhance foreground-background discriminability, while the Spatial Localization Module (SLM) spatially relocates and improving spatial stability after frequency decoupling. Extensive experiments on 9 medical image segmentation benchmarks across three imaging modalities demonstrate that FreNet significantly outperforms state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods. On the challenging ETIS dataset, our method achieves Dice improvements of 5.0% over SOTA method and 7.2% over SAM.

</details>


### [210] [Dalek: A Constructive Agent Machine](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03546)
*Wanpeng Xie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Dalek is a closed machine for agents that achieves self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization using three primitives (actors, messages, channels) and four obligations (host boundary, construction language, admissible transitions, rule heredity). It combines von Neumann's self-reproducing automaton concept with a large language model and compiler to produce new capabilities that can be inherited by descendants.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The paper aims to create a general-purpose self-reproducing and self-evolving machine that can operate on any substrate satisfying a host contract. It extends von Neumann's 1948 self-reproducing automaton with explicit structures for boundary, identity, history, and growth, enabling autonomous machine evolution.

Method: The design combines three primitives (actors, messages, channels) with four obligations (host boundary, construction language, admissible transitions, rule heredity). It uses von Neumann's hereditary constructional core (self-description, constructor, copier, controller) as the foundation, and employs a large language model and compiler as the payload for capability production. New capabilities are authored, compiled, installed into the description, and inherited by descendants.

Result: The machine achieves closed heredity and evolution - it can produce its own organs and runtime, enabling self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization on any compliant substrate.

Conclusion: The paper presents a theoretical framework for creating autonomous, self-evolving machines that combine computational heritage with modern AI capabilities, enabling machines to author, compile, and inherit new capabilities across generations.

Abstract: We present Dalek, a closed machine designed for agents that realizes self-maintenance, self-evolution, self-reproduction, and self-organization on any substrate satisfying a general host contract. The machine is built from three primitives---actors, messages, and channels. Four obligations---a host boundary, a construction language, admissible transitions, and rule heredity---give its boundary, identity, and closure a structural basis.
  Von Neumann's 1948 self-reproducing automaton supplies a hereditary constructional core: a self-description together with a constructor, a copier, and a controller. Dalek combines this core with the four obligations and rederives its medium for a text-and-message agent substrate, adding explicit structures for boundary, identity, history, and growth. A large language model and a compiler occupy the payload position and form a general capability producer. New capabilities are authored, compiled, installed into the description, and inherited by descendants. The same path produces the machine's own organs and even its runtime, closing heredity and evolution within the machine.

</details>


### [211] [GPS-Bench: A Governance Policy Benchmark for Automating Policy Analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03553)
*Linh Le,Melanie Bui,My Chiffon Nguyen,Zachary Schlosser,David Williams-King*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GPS-Bench is an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that links policies to actors, actions, and downstream impacts using public records. It enables controlled comparisons of different LLM-based simulation approaches (joint reasoning, independent agents, communicating agents, graph-based methods, fine-tuning) over the same grounded policy state.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: LLM-based policy simulations lack validity when plausible behavior is never compared with observed outcomes. Current methods model actors at scale but fail to establish whether predictions align with real-world policy processes. There is a need for an evidence-grounded benchmark that links policies to actual actors, their actions, and verifiable impacts from public records.

Method: GPS-Bench constructs actors from dated legislative records rather than prompting archetypes, creating evidence objects with provenance. It uses Gold evaluation set (human-annotated) and Silver supervision (LLM-labelled from retrieved evidence, never used as test labels). The benchmark compares multiple inference modes: joint reasoning, independent agents, communicating actor agents, graph-based methods, and weight-level fine-tuning—all reading the same grounded state and emitting the same schema. Agents hold private, non-identical evidence, address named partners with concrete joint proposals, and coalitions can be checked against recorded commitments.

Result: Fine-tuning on the grounded record yields the strongest actor-level impact prediction. Decomposition methods do not outperform fine-tuning; however, they add value through mechanism interpretation. The multi-agent setup with private evidence, exposure clauses, and named partner interactions enables verification of coalition formation against actual commitments in the record.

Conclusion: GPS-Bench provides a common empirical setting for systematically studying when evidence, actor modeling, and multi-agent interaction improve prediction and interpretation of policy outcomes. It transforms the question "does multi-agent simulation help?" into a controlled empirical comparison rather than a speculative one.

Abstract: Policy analysis requires more than predicting whether a proposal will pass: it requires identifying who will be affected, how those actors respond, and what follows. LLM-based policy simulations model these processes at scale, but their validity is hard to establish when plausible behaviour is never compared with observed outcomes. We introduce GPS-Bench, an evidence-grounded benchmark for governance policy simulation that links policies to relevant actors, actor actions and downstream impacts using legislative records, lobbying disclosures, regulatory documents, corporate filings, economic data and other public evidence. Actors are reconstructed from the dated record rather than prompted as archetypes, so a persona is an evidence object with provenance; a human-annotated pool forms the Gold evaluation set, while cases labelled by a separate LLM from retrieved evidence are treated as Silver supervision and never as test labels. Because every inference mode reads the same grounded state and emits the same schema, GPS-Bench turns "does multi-agent simulation help?" into a controlled comparison: we contrast joint reasoning, independent and communicating actor agents, graph-based methods and weight-level fine-tuning over one policy state. Fine-tuning on the grounded record gives the strongest actor-level impact prediction, and decomposition does not beat it; what decomposition adds is mechanism. Agents hold private, non-identical evidence, each seeing its own exposure clause, and address named partners with concrete joint proposals, what they offer, what they need in return, and why acting together beats acting alone, so the coalitions that form can be checked against the commitments the record holds. GPS-Bench therefore gives a common empirical setting for studying when evidence, actor modelling and multi-agent interaction improve the prediction and interpretation of policy outcomes.

</details>


### [212] [HalluPeer: A Taxonomy-driven Benchmark for Detecting Hallucinations in Scientific Peer Reviews](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03580)
*Tzu-Ling Lin,Dong-Ting Yao,Teng-Fang Hsiao,Wei-Chih Chen,Hong-Han Shuai*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: HalluPeer is a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews generated by LLMs. It provides aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews, addressing the gap that existing hallucination benchmarks don't fit the peer review context where claims must be grounded in long technical papers.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The growing scale of academic peer review has motivated the use of LLMs as review assistants, but LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review verification which requires grounding claims in long, technical papers.

Method: The pipeline induces a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identifies review contexts, and injects hallucinations with automated filtering. Experiments conducted on 12K papers and 38K reviews.

Result: Existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique. Evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the critical need for source-aware verification.

Conclusion: There is a critical need for source-aware verification in peer review hallucination detection. HalluPeer provides a benchmark that addresses this need by offering aligned data for detection, classification, and localization of hallucinations in peer reviews.

Abstract: The growing scale of academic peer review has motivated the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as review assistants, yet LLMs can generate fluent but unsupported claims that undermine review reliability. Existing hallucination benchmarks are not designed for peer review, where verification requires grounding claims in long, technical papers. We introduce HalluPeer, a benchmark for detecting hallucinations in scientific peer reviews, providing aligned triples of paper content, human-written reviews, and hallucination-injected reviews, annotated for detection, classification, and localization. Our pipeline induces a peer-review-specific hallucination taxonomy, identifies review contexts, and injects hallucinations with automated filtering. Experiments on 12K papers and 38K reviews show that existing detectors struggle to separate hallucinations from legitimate critique, while evaluation on authentic reviews demonstrates that HalluPeer-defined hallucination patterns occur in real peer reviews, highlighting the critical need for source-aware verification. Our project page can be found in https://github.com/Lin-TzuLing/HalluPeer.git

</details>


### [213] [The Attention Triangle in Audio-Video Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03586)
*Sagi Polaczek,Noa Kraicer,Gal Metzer,Zhuo Ning,Ali Mahdavi-Amiri,Daniel Cohen-Or,Raja Giryes*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates semantic leakage in audio-video diffusion models caused by cross-modal attention mechanisms. The authors analyze the "attention triangle" - three cross-attention edges connecting text, audio, and video streams - and discover that the audio-video edge operates bidirectionally, routing semantic information based on model biases. These biases can override intended conditioning when prompts conflict with learned priors, leading to visually canonical but incorrect outputs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Audio-video diffusion models use cross-modal attention to coordinate text, sound, and visual content, but this mechanism can introduce subtle and systematic semantic leakage. Understanding how semantic information is routed across modalities during generation is crucial for improving model reliability and preventing artifacts.

Method: The authors analyze the "attention triangle" comprising three cross-attention edges (text-audio, text-video, audio-video) to examine cross-modal semantic routing. They extract attention-derived signals as diagnostic tools to analyze and deliberately induce leakage under controlled conditions. These signals are then used to guide inference-time interventions that encourage more consistent cross-modal alignment.

Result: The audio-video edge exhibits bidirectional routing where audio influences video generation and vice versa. This edge is shaped by parameter-encoded biases and emerges as a major contributor to semantic leakage. When prompts conflict with learned priors, cross-modal interactions can override intended conditioning and reroute semantics toward visually canonical but incorrect outcomes. The method enables probing internal dynamics of cross-modal routing and isolating individual interaction roles.

Conclusion: Semantic artifacts arise from structured, bias-driven interactions along specific attention pathways rather than mere attention spreading. Attention-derived signals serve as effective diagnostic tools for analyzing and deliberately incurring leakage. Inference-time interventions based on these signals improve semantic grounding while preserving generation quality.

Abstract: Audio-video diffusion models rely on cross-modal attention to coordinate text, sound, and visual content, yet this same mechanism can introduce subtle and systematic semantic leakage. We study these models by probing and analyzing the ``attention triangle,'' comprising the three cross-attention edges connecting the text, audio, and video streams, and examine how semantic information is routed across modalities during generation. Our analysis reveals that routing along the audio-video edge is bidirectional: audio can influence video generation, while video can influence audio generation. This edge is shaped by biases encoded in the model's parameters and emerges as a major contributor to leakage: when prompts are in tension with learned priors, cross-modal interactions may override the intended conditioning and reroute semantics toward visually canonical but incorrect outcomes. These effects suggest that semantic artifacts arise not merely from attention spreading beyond its intended target, but from structured, bias-driven interactions along specific pathways. Building on this perspective, we extract attention-derived signals that expose how semantics are distributed and grounded across modalities, and use them as a diagnostic tool to both analyze and deliberately incur leakage under controlled conditions. This enables us to probe the internal dynamics of cross-modal routing and isolate the role of individual interactions. We further leverage these signals to guide inference-time interventions that encourage more consistent cross-modal alignment. Extensive experiments support our analysis and demonstrate improved semantic grounding while preserving generation quality.

</details>


### [214] [KC-Bench: A Dynamic Interactive Benchmark for Evaluating Knowledge Conflicts in LLM Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03588)
*Yaxing Lyu,Shengjie Zhou,Binbin Toh,Pengyu Zhu,Lijun Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: KC-Bench is a controlled multi-turn benchmark designed to evaluate LLMs' capability to reconcile conflicts between user instructions, parametric knowledge, and dynamic environmental observations when acting through tools. It contains 238 manually screened tasks covering world-knowledge conflicts, input inconsistencies, and multi-source temporal conflicts.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs increasingly act through tools, they face situations where user instructions conflict with their parametric knowledge or with dynamic environmental observations. Currently, there is no systematic way to measure how well models handle these conflicts. Existing benchmarks do not adequately isolate this specific capability across different conflict types.

Method: The benchmark was constructed by manually screening 238 tasks from over 1,000 generated candidates. It combines: (1) a user simulator, (2) stateful tools, (3) deterministic environment assertions, (4) an open-source natural-language evaluator, and (5) human trajectory verification. The benchmark evaluates nine models including DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3.

Result: Evaluation reveals substantial cross-domain variation among models. No model reliably handles factual correction, identity consistency checking, and temporal conflict resolution across all settings. In simulated environments, missed conflicts can propagate to tool calls or synthetic protected-data flows.

Conclusion: KC-Bench successfully isolates model-level behavior rather than ranking complete agent frameworks. It provides a reproducible diagnostic tool for developing conflict-aware reasoning and execution safeguards in LLMs.

Abstract: As LLMs increasingly act through tools, they must reconcile user instructions, parametric knowledge, and dynamic environmental observations before taking actions. We introduce KC-Bench, a controlled multi-turn benchmark for measuring this capability across world-knowledge conflicts, input inconsistencies, and multi-source temporal conflicts. Its 238 tasks are manually screened from more than 1,000 generated candidates and combine a user simulator, stateful tools, deterministic environment assertions, an open-source natural-language evaluator, and human trajectory verification. Evaluation of nine models, including DeepSeek-V4-Flash, GLM-5.2, and MiniMax-M3, shows substantial cross-domain variation: no model handles factual correction, identity consistency checking, and temporal conflict resolution reliably across all settings. In the simulated environments, missed conflicts can propagate to tool calls or synthetic protected-data flows. KC-Bench isolates this model-level behavior rather than ranking complete agent frameworks, and provides a reproducible diagnostic for developing conflict-aware reasoning and execution safeguards.

</details>


### [215] [A computable representation of the physical laboratory enables verifiable workflows](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03621)
*Xiaobo Li,Luyao Ge,Xiaohui Li,Lulu Guo,Ming Mao,Jiwang Zheng,Wenting Guan,Xin Yang,Yi Luo,Jun Jiang,Linjiang Chen*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents a computational framework for representing physical laboratories to enable autonomous scientific discovery. The approach combines typed research objects, capability-bound operations, and a compositional workflow algebra to create a computational interface between agent reasoning and physical laboratory transformations. The system was implemented in a modular agentic robotic laboratory using Function Skills.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Making science computable requires representations of both scientific knowledge and the physical world where scientific claims are tested. While machine-readable knowledge exists, there was a need for a computable representation of the physical laboratory that can express workflows as programs over evolving laboratory states.

Method: The research established a computable representation through: (1) typed research objects, (2) capability-bound operations, and (3) a compositional workflow algebra. This was implemented in a modular agentic robotic laboratory by binding formal operations to executable Function Skills. Capability-relative workflows were generated for diverse scientific intents, with stateful simulation propagating object transformations and verifying operation preconditions and laboratory constraints before dispatch.

Result: The proposed representation and engineering framework establish a general computational interface between agent reasoning and capability-bound physical transformations, providing a foundation for end-to-end autonomous scientific discovery.

Conclusion: The framework successfully bridges the gap between computational reasoning and physical laboratory operations, enabling autonomous agents to execute scientific workflows with proper state management, precondition verification, and constraint checking.

Abstract: Making science computable requires representations of both scientific knowledge and the physical world in which scientific claims are tested. A computable representation of the physical laboratory is established through typed research objects, capability-bound operations and a compositional workflow algebra. It provides the physical-world counterpart to machine-readable knowledge, expressing workflows as programs over evolving laboratory states with explicit dependencies, decisions, iteration and concurrency. The representation was implemented in a modular agentic robotic laboratory by binding formal operations to executable Function Skills. For diverse scientific intents, capability-relative workflows were generated, while stateful simulation propagated object transformations and verified operation preconditions and laboratory constraints before dispatch. The proposed representation and its engineering framework jointly establish a general computational interface between agent reasoning and capability-bound physical transformations, providing a foundation for end-to-end autonomous scientific discovery.

</details>


### [216] [Analysis of Prompt Engineering for Drug Toxicity Prediction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03635)
*Mia MacGregor,Aakash Welgamage Don,Mark Bartlett*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates prompt engineering for drug toxicity prediction using LLMs. The authors found that natural variance in LLM outputs outweighs benefits from prompt optimization, and that using chemoinformatic code for feature extraction outperforms LLM-generated values.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to address the high cost (£1.3M) and failure rate (~90%) of clinical trials, with toxicity being a major cause. While LLMs are increasingly used for drug toxicity prediction, their sensitivity to prompt variations raises concerns about reliability. The paper aims to investigate the importance of prompt phrasing for drug toxicity prediction.

Method: The authors proposed a method to analyze prompt engineering for drug toxicity prediction. They prompted LLMs to identify chemical properties significant for toxicity prediction, testing different job roles, prompt structuring, and rule interpretations. The identified features were used to generate datasets, which were then passed to machine learning algorithms for performance evaluation.

Result: The experiments revealed two key findings: (1) Natural variance occurring in LLMs outweighs any benefits from fine-tuning prompts, suggesting prompt optimization may not be worthwhile; (2) Substantial improvements in model performance were achieved when using chemoinformatic code to extract features instead of relying on LLM-generated values.

Conclusion: The proposed analysis methodology for evaluating prompt engineering is applicable across different prompt types in bioinformatics. The study concludes that while LLMs can assist in identifying relevant features, using domain-specific tools (chemoinformatic code) yields better results than LLM-generated feature values.

Abstract: Clinical trials in the UK can cost up to £1.3 million, with approximately 90% drug failure rate. Toxicity is a major contributing factor in drug failure. Testing is time and cost intensive. In recent years, the use of artificial intelligence has been increasingly explored to aid in the prediction of drug toxicity, with extensive use of large language models (LLMs). However, LLMs can show considerable variation when minor changes are made to prompts, which raises concerns about their sensitivity to prompt engineering. Prompt engineering is used to optimise a prompt given to an LLM to generate the desired output. This paper proposes a method to analyse prompt engineering for drug toxicity prediction. The aim of the paper is to investigate the importance of prompt phrasing for drug toxicity prediction. LLMs were prompted to identify chemical properties of significance when predicting drug toxicity. Prompts were constructed to investigate; job role, prompt structuring, and rule interpretation. LLMs were then used to generate datasets, using the identified features from initial prompting, which were then passed to machine learning algorithms. The experiments show that the natural variance which occurs in LLMs outweighs any fine-tuning of prompts. There were, however, substantial improvements in model performance when using chemoinformatic code to extract features instead of using LLM-generated values. The proposed analysis methodology is applicable to a wide range of prompt types across different areas of bioinformatics.

</details>


### [217] [Synthetic Semantic Supervision for Contrastive Code Representation Learning in Small Transformers: An Empirical Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03702)
*Kenneth Paulsen,Florian Tambon,Mike Papadakis,Shin Yoo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes using contrastive pretraining with synthetically generated natural-language descriptions to create compact code embeddings. The method pairs code with AI-generated descriptions emphasizing functionality and intent, using a dual-encoder framework at training that is discarded at inference.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing approaches for code embeddings rely on either labor-intensive human-written docstrings or setting-specific execution traces. The authors seek a more scalable alternative that doesn't require expensive structural signals or manual annotation while still achieving high-quality code representations.

Method: Contrastive pretraining of small transformer encoders in a dual-encoder framework, using synthetically generated natural-language descriptions that emphasize code functionality and intent. The descriptions are used during training but discarded at inference time.

Result: Synthetic semantic supervision yields statistically significant gains over pretraining baselines of the same inference-time size on 5 of 8 tasks, with parity on 2 more. Once fine-tuned, it matches or exceeds zero-shot models two orders of magnitude larger on classification tasks. It also stays on par with execution-aware supervision at matched pretraining data.

Conclusion: Synthetic semantic supervision offers a scalable, effective alternative to existing code-representation paradigms, achieving competitive performance without requiring human annotations or execution traces while matching much larger zero-shot models after fine-tuning.

Abstract: General-purpose code embeddings power tools for code search, classification, and retrieval. Compact transformer encoders for code typically rely on either human-written docstrings (labor-intensive and inconsistent) or mined structural signals such as execution traces (setting-specific and costly to collect). We empirically study an alternative: contrastive pretraining of small encoders with synthetically generated natural-language descriptions emphasizing code functionality and intent, paired with code in a dual-encoder framework at training and discarded at inference. We benchmark this approach against pretraining-based baselines, generalist LLMs, and embedding-specific models on eight retrieval, classification, and generation tasks across C, C++, and Java. Synthetic semantic supervision yields statistically significant gains over pretraining baselines of the same inference-time size on five of eight tasks, with parity on two more; once fine-tuned, it matches or exceeds zero-shot models two orders of magnitude larger on classification, and it stays on par with execution-aware supervision at matched pretraining data, suggesting a scalable, effective alternative to existing code-representation paradigms.

</details>


### [218] [Counterfactual Routing Using Integer Programming with Constraint Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03707)
*Daniël Vos,Sterre Lutz*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: A competition submission to IJCAI 2025 Counterfactual Routing Competition that uses integer programming to find minimal network changes making a user's route optimal. Ranked 4th in solution quality but was fastest (9.0s avg vs 118.8s for next fastest).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The competition aims to provide explainable routing recommendations by identifying minimal changes to road networks (e.g., "road X would need to not be a bicycle path") that would make a user's suggested route become the optimal path.

Method: Integer programming formulation with iterative constraint incorporation to find exact solutions.

Result: Fourth place in solution quality on held-out test instances. Achieved fastest runtime on every instance with average 9.0 seconds, compared to 118.8 seconds for the next-fastest submission.

Conclusion: The integer programming approach provides an efficient exact method for counterfactual routing explanations, demonstrating strong performance in both solution quality and computational speed.

Abstract: We present our submission to the IJCAI 2025 'Counterfactual Routing Competition' (CRC 25). The goal of the competition is to find counterfactual explanations for the shortest path problem. This requires deciding what the minimal changes to a road network would make a route chosen by the user the optimal route. This enables explanations such as "Your suggested route would indeed have been optimal, if road X were not a bicycle path." Our solution models the problem as an integer program, iteratively incorporating constraints until an exact solution is found. In the final evaluation on held-out test instances, our method ranked fourth in solution quality and obtained its solution fastest on every instance, with an average runtime of 9.0 seconds compared to 118.8 seconds for the next-fastest submission.

</details>


### [219] [Artificial Intelligence for Energy Optimization in Data Centers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03716)
*Mohammed Basharath Ullah,Summaiya Unnisa Begum,Mohammed Nadeem Ullah*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper analyzes the literature on AI-driven energy optimization in data centers, revealing a critical gap: existing studies treat AI optimization and AI workload as separate problems. Through systematic review of 194 papers (63 coded), the authors identify 10 recurring gaps and propose CLEAR-DC, a framework that couples control-policy and workload-demand branches through an explicit elasticity term.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The literature treats AI optimization of data centers and AI's increasing workload as two unrelated problems. Control studies model workload as exogenous arrival processes, while sustainability studies model infrastructure as fixed multipliers. This conceptual separation leads to incomplete solutions that don't account for the full environmental impact.

Method: Systematic literature review: screened ~194 papers using a documented protocol, coded 63 papers, analyzed 28 primary control-oriented studies

Result: 18/28 studies validated in simulation alone; 5 reached physical hardware/production; none accounted for water withdrawal or embodied carbon; reported savings intervals across four technique families overlap completely, preventing ranking of methods

Conclusion: The field cannot presently rank its own methods. CLEAR-DC framework is proposed as an architectural and methodological proposal that couples control-policy branch to workload-demand branch through explicit elasticity term, reads out net rather than direct benefit, and emits schema-conformant records covering energy, carbon, water, embodied share, and validation venue. The main empirical contribution is the corpus analysis and reporting schema.

Abstract: Data centers are increasingly optimized by artificial intelligence and, at the same time, increasingly loaded by it. The literature treats these as two unrelated problems: control studies model workload as an exogenous arrival process, while sustainability studies model infrastructure as a fixed multiplier. We screen roughly 194 papers retrieved through a documented protocol, code 63 of them, and report what the coding shows. Of 28 primary control-oriented studies, 18 are validated in simulation alone and 5 reach physical hardware or a production facility; none account for water withdrawal, and none account for embodied carbon. Reported savings intervals across four technique families overlap almost completely, which means the field cannot presently rank its own methods. Ten recurring gaps are scored for consequence and tractability, and we set out CLEAR-DC, a framework coupling a control-policy branch to a workload-demand branch through an explicit elasticity term, reads out net rather than direct benefit, and emits a schema-conformant record covering energy, carbon, water, embodied share and validation venue. The framework is an architectural and methodological proposal, not a trained system; the contribution we defend empirically is the corpus analysis and the reporting schema derived from it. Coding sheet, derived statistics and all result artifacts: https://github.com/Kimalice/AI-for-Energy-Optimization-in-Data-Centers-Closing-the-Optimizer-Load-Loop

</details>


### [220] [Proactive Service Agents: A Unified Decision Framework, Methods, and Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03727)
*Yan Tang,Tingyu Cao,Yuanbo Tang,Huaze Tang,Keer Hu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This survey paper defines proactive service in LLM agents as the ability to infer service opportunities from incomplete environmental and user signals, rather than waiting for explicit user instructions. It formulates the problem as a partially observable sequential decision process and organizes existing methods along a decision pipeline.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Most current LLM agent systems still require explicit user instructions as a starting point. The authors argue that moving to proactive service requires agents to make decisions about when to take initiative (remaining silent, asking, assisting, or acting) while accounting for interruption, misunderstanding, overreach, and privacy costs.

Method: The paper provides an operational definition centered on initiative, formulates the problem as a constrained partially observable sequential decision process, and organizes existing methods into a decision pipeline with four stages: state and need estimation, intervention gating, action construction, and feedback adaptation. It also normalizes decision units across different domains (dialogue, screen, video, software engineering, human-agent collaboration).

Result: The synthesis identifies key requirements for reliable proactive service: calibrated incremental intervention value, verifiable authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence. It also clarifies why offline classification performance alone doesn't predict deployment benefit and why long-term memory isn't a defining condition of proactivity.

Conclusion: Proactive service requires balancing multiple factors including timing, content, delivery, option value of waiting, decision value of questions, and feedback-induced state changes. The paper formalizes metrics for triggering, timing, calibration, user burden, safety, and policy value to evaluate proactive systems.

Abstract: Large language model agents can plan, invoke tools, and modify external states, yet most systems still take an explicit user instruction as a fixed starting point. Proactive service moves the decision upstream: an agent must infer service opportunities from incomplete environmental and user signals, choose among remaining silent, asking, assisting, and acting, and account for interruption, misunderstanding, overreach, and privacy costs. This survey gives an operational definition centered on initiative and formulates the problem as a partially observable sequential decision process constrained by authorization and risk. The formulation represents timing, content, and delivery within one structured action, while making explicit the option value of waiting, the decision value of questions, and feedback-induced state changes. On this basis, we organize existing methods along one decision pipeline (state and need estimation, intervention gating, action construction, and feedback adaptation) and describe prescribed, predictive, model based, and return optimizing mechanisms as nonexclusive policy-construction components. We further normalize decision units and three-axis evidence descriptors across streaming dialogue, screen, video, software-engineering, and human-agent collaboration resources, and formalize metrics for triggering, timing, calibration, user burden, safety, and policy value. The synthesis shows why offline classification performance alone does not predict deployment benefit and why long-term memory is not a defining condition of proactivity. Reliable proactive service instead requires calibrated incremental intervention value, verifiable authorization, recoverable execution, and counterfactual evidence.

</details>


### [221] [SimSkill: A Lifelong Learning AI Agent for Autonomous Mastery of Traffic Simulation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03753)
*Qi Liu,Qinzheng Wang,Yiming Bie*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: SimSkill is a self-evolving AI agent that uses SUMO traffic simulator to autonomously identify capability gaps, generate tasks, verify solutions, and consolidate experience into memory without updating the backbone model. It improves verified completion by up to 25 percentage points.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: As LLMs become more capable, their long-term value depends on transforming experience into durable, reusable competence rather than just solving individual requests. Current approaches lack mechanisms for accumulating and reusing knowledge across tasks.

Method: SimSkill uses a self-evolving paradigm: (1) identifies capability gaps, (2) generates environment-grounded tasks using SUMO simulator, (3) verifies solutions through an action-critic loop, (4) consolidates experience into episodic, procedural, and semantic memory without updating the backbone model. Uses autonomous exploration to build a reusable library.

Result: SimSkill improves verified completion by up to 25 percentage points on two held-out benchmarks with three backbone LLMs. Ablations show complementary contributions from procedural and semantic memory. Benefits are backbone- and budget-dependent: memory does not improve every model or uniformly reduce inference cost.

Conclusion: SimSkill demonstrates a design paradigm where natural language preserves computational capabilities while executable tools provide precise execution. The approach shows that memory consolidation can enhance LLM capabilities without model modification, though benefits vary across models and computational budgets.

Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) become increasingly capable, the long-term value of AI systems depends not only on solving individual requests, but also on transforming experience and accumulated knowledge into durable, reusable competence. We introduce SimSkill, a self-evolving agent built around the Simulation of Urban MObility (SUMO) traffic simulator. SimSkill identifies capability gaps, generates and solves environment-grounded tasks, verifies solutions through an action--critic loop, and consolidates experience into episodic, procedural, and semantic memory without updating the backbone model. Through autonomous exploration, it builds a reusable library spanning the traffic-simulation workflow. We evaluate SimSkill on two held-out benchmarks with three backbone LLMs and independent artifact-based verification. SimSkill improves verified completion by up to 25 percentage points, while ablations show complementary contributions from procedural and semantic memory. Its benefits remain backbone- and budget-dependent: memory does not improve every model or uniformly reduce inference cost. More broadly, SimSkill illustrates a design paradigm in which natural language preserves and composes computational capabilities, while executable tools and code provide precise and reproducible execution. All code and experimental data are publicly available at https://github.com/qiliuchn/SimSkill-V1.

</details>


### [222] [Rethinking World Models for Safety-Critical Embodied Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03774)
*Kailang Ma,Heye Huang,Inhi Kim,Kitae Jang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This perspective paper argues that current world models for embodied AI systems fail to preserve safety-critical evidence despite high predictive likelihood and visual fidelity. The authors propose Risk-Informed World Model (RIWM) as a decision-centric framework organized around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability, moving from predicting likely futures toward identifying which futures matter.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current world models prioritize predictive likelihood and visual fidelity but fail to preserve evidence required for safe decision-making in safety-critical embodied systems. Three structural mismatches exist: likelihood vs risk, prediction vs intervention, and finite-horizon vs accumulated consequences.

Method: The paper proposes RIWM integrating four interdependent capabilities: (1) decision-relevant representation, (2) counterfactual reasoning, (3) safety-critical episodic memory, and (4) runtime safety assurance. It distinguishes physical, social, and operational consequences while using epistemic uncertainty to qualify action-supporting evidence.

Result: The paper presents a conceptual framework rather than empirical results, proposing a research agenda for risk-informed world modeling that addresses safety-critical decision-making in embodied systems.

Conclusion: Future world models should move beyond predicting likely futures toward identifying consequential futures, revising judgments through experience, and recognizing when to act, revise, sense, defer, or abstain. Five open challenges are identified: identifying consequential futures, validating counterfactual reasoning, maintaining revisable safety memories, translating learned consequences into executable constraints, and determining evidence sufficiency for action.

Abstract: World models have progressed from compact latent dynamics to generative, controllable, and interactive simulators of embodied environments. However, high predictive likelihood and visual fidelity do not necessarily ensure that a model preserves the evidence required for safe decision-making. This perspective identifies three structural mismatches in current world modeling: likelihood versus risk, prediction versus intervention, and finite-horizon prediction versus accumulated consequences. We propose the Risk-Informed World Model (RIWM) as a decision-centric research direction for safety-critical embodied systems. RIWM organizes world modeling around consequences, intervention, epistemic uncertainty, and recoverability, and integrates four interdependent capabilities: decision-relevant representation, counterfactual reasoning, safety-critical episodic memory, and runtime safety assurance. It distinguishes physical, social, and operational consequences while using epistemic uncertainty to qualify the evidence supporting action. We further discuss open challenges in identifying consequential futures, validating counterfactual reasoning, maintaining revisable safety memories, translating learned consequences into executable constraints, and determining when evidence is sufficient to act. This perspective argues that future world models should move beyond predicting likely futures toward identifying which futures matter, revising judgments through experience, and recognizing when to act, revise, sense, defer, or abstain.

</details>


### [223] [DNative-Twin: Decision Graphs and Digital Twins for Reconstructable Agentic Decisions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03787)
*Junjie Pang,Zhenzhen Xie,Haoke Han,Ying He,Jing Wang,Gang Liu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: DNative-Twin is a graph-native digital twin framework that records AI agent decisions as typed trajectories and re-executes decision mechanisms under declared conditions to enable audit and verification of agentic decisions.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents increasingly make decisions that people or software commit to action, but the final output alone cannot reveal which evidence, tool state, rule, authorization, or action path produced it, creating a critical auditability gap.

Method: The framework uses a graph structure that links the state observed by the agent, the path it followed, and the authority behind the resulting action. It synchronizes information, replays the mechanism in isolation, and compares outputs under controlled changes. Validated using three public process logs and controlled replay suites with 300 injected instances across three conditions, plus 500-5,000 BPI 2020 cases.

Result: A specific failure was identified: graph structure localizes represented changes but cannot determine the consequence of unobserved tool state. In a three-condition controlled experiment, unresolved-divergence recall increased from 0 to 0.667 when replay-contract state was added and to 1.0 when verification results were also available. Median end-to-end time increased from 0.794 to 8.889 seconds across 500-5,000 BPI 2020 cases.

Conclusion: The results separate the roles of graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence in reviewing decision mechanisms. Graph structure alone is insufficient; combining replay context and verification evidence achieves perfect recall (1.0) for detecting decision failures.

Abstract: AI agents increasingly gather evidence, invoke tools, apply constraints, and produce decisions that people or software may commit to action. A final output alone cannot show which evidence, tool state, rule, authorization, or action path produced it. We present DNative-Twin, a graph-native digital twin that records a committed agentic decision as a typed trajectory and re-executes its decision mechanism under declared conditions. The graph links the state observed by the agent, the path it followed, and the authority behind the resulting action. The twin synchronizes this information, replays the mechanism in isolation, and compares it under controlled changes. We instantiate the framework in enterprise decision processes using three public process logs and controlled replay suites. The experiments identify a specific failure: graph structure localizes represented changes but cannot determine the consequence of an unobserved tool state. In a three-condition controlled experiment with 300 injected instances, unresolved-divergence recall increased from 0 to 0.667 when replay-contract state was added and to 1.0 when verification results were also available; the held-out set contained no critical-class instance. Across 500--5,000 BPI 2020 cases, median end-to-end time increased from 0.794 to 8.889 seconds on the reported platform. These results separate the roles of graph structure, replay context, and verification evidence in reviewing a decision mechanism.

</details>


### [224] [Transfiver: Human-AI Co-Inference through a Shared Editable State](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03797)
*Minji Park,Seunghyun Yoon,Hyuk Lim*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Transfiver is a novel architecture for human-AI co-inference that maintains a shared editable persistent state (S_t) accessible to both the model and human users, enabling inspectable and controllable interaction-specific information without requiring parameter retraining.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that long-term human-AI interaction is difficult because information guiding inference is updated implicitly by the model and is not directly inspectable or controllable by users. This lack of transparency and editability limits human oversight and collaboration.

Method: Transfiver uses a shared persistent state (S_t) with two update modes: (1) implicit stream updates where the model autonomously decides whether new information revises existing state items or creates new ones, and (2) explicit directed edits where humans inspect and modify addressed items. The architecture separates pre-trained shared parameters (θ) from the deployment-time persistent state (S_t).

Result: The framework enables human-AI co-inference through a shared editable state where human corrections directly modify the state that subsequent computation reads, rather than adding separate instructions or records.

Conclusion: Transfiver provides a promising architecture for transparent, verifiable, and editable human-AI interaction. Future work includes extending the framework to rich natural-language, relational, and large-scale shared states.

Abstract: Long-term human-AI interaction is difficult because the information that guides inference is updated implicitly by the model and is not directly inspectable or controllable by the user. We introduce the TRANSparent Framework for Interactive, Verifiable, Editable Representation (Transfiver), an architecture for human-AI co-inference through a shared editable state. Its central idea is that interaction-specific information is maintained in a single persistent state $(S_t)$ that both the model and the human update.
  Transfiver distinguishes two modes of state evolution. In an implicit stream update, the model interprets ongoing interaction and decides whether new information revises an existing state item or creates a new one. In an explicit directed edit, a human inspects and modifies an addressed item. Both act on the same underlying state, so a human correction changes the state that subsequent computation reads, rather than adding another instruction or separate record.
  The architecture separates shared parameters $(θ)$, learned before ordinary use, from the persistent state $(S_t)$, which evolves during deployment without parameter retraining. Extending Transfiver to rich natural-language, relational, and large-scale shared states remains open.

</details>


### [225] [Govern the Model, Not Only the Data: Storage, Circulation, and Learning in Creative AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03800)
*Phoenix Perry,George Simms,Elizabeth Wilson,Yasmine Boudiaf,Nick Bryan-Kinns,Tega Brain,R. Luke DuBois,Alix Rule,Rachel Meade Smith,Kelani Nichole,Atharva Pravin Pawar,Rebecca Fiebrink*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Federated learning is presented as privacy-preserving but actually inverts the federated social web logic—distributing computation while keeping the resulting model with the convener. The paper argues that federation alone doesn't remedy extractive AI; outcomes depend on who governs data and models. Examining three layers (storage, circulation, learning), the authors find creator governance exists at storage and circulation but stops at learning. Four design principles are proposed for a creative data commons that governs models and their federation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the assumption that federated learning inherently protects creator interests, and to highlight that current implementations fail to give contributors governance over the resulting models or their federation—essentially continuing extractive AI practices under a decentralized guise.

Method: Conceptual analysis examining artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures across three layers of community work: storage, circulation, and learning. The authors map technical open problems alongside human questions they raise.

Result: Creator governance is established at storage and circulation layers but stops at the learning layer—contributors can consent to training but have little say over the resulting model or its federation. This reveals a critical gap in how federated learning is currently implemented for creative communities.

Conclusion: Four design principles are proposed for a creative data commons: (1) govern the model, not only the corpus; (2) make the terms legible at the moment of contribution; (3) design for refusal as a first-class state; (4) decide stewardship in the open and account for it. The paper opens a research space pairing technical challenges with human governance questions.

Abstract: Federated learning is increasingly presented as a privacy-preserving advance: personal data remain on the device, and only model updates are shared. It borrows the vocabulary of the federated social web, yet inverts its logic, distributing computation while the resulting model stays with whoever convened the training. We argue that federation is not in itself a remedy for extractive AI, because outcomes depend on who governs the data and the model and who has agency over the practices that shape them. We describe three layers at which a creative community can hold its work: storage, circulation, and learning. Examining artist-governed trusts, cooperatives, and consent infrastructures, we show that creator governance is established at storage and circulation but stops at learning: contributors can consent to training, yet have little say over the resulting model or its federation. We map the research space this opens, pairing technical open problems with the human questions from which they unfold. We propose four design principles for a creative data commons that governs models and their federation, not only datasets: govern the model, not only the corpus; make the terms legible at the moment of contribution; design for refusal as a first-class state; and decide stewardship in the open and account for it.

</details>


### [226] [SVG-Score: Human-Aligned Evaluation of Text-to-SVG Generation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03806)
*Marco Cipriano,Leonardo Zini,Alexandra Schild,Valentin Teutschbein,Afsana Mimi,Marcella Cornia,Lorenzo Baraldi,Gerard de Melo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the lack of proper evaluation metrics for text-to-SVG generation by introducing a human-aligned evaluation framework called "Ours" (the name appears to be placeholder). The authors demonstrate that existing CLIP-based metrics fail to detect SVG-specific errors, and develop two complementary evaluators: adapted CLIP scorers and a trained VLM judge.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The lack of domain-specific evaluation protocols for SVG generation. Current metrics like CLIPScore were designed for natural images and don't align with human judgment when evaluating vector graphics, holding back progress in the field.

Method: 1. Conducted controlled caption and image perturbations to analyze how existing metrics respond to SVG-specific errors (wrong colors, counts, spatial relations). 2. Created a human-annotated dataset for Semantic Alignment. 3. Developed two evaluators: (a) CLIP scorers adapted to vector graphics and aligned to human preferences for fast evaluation, and (b) a VLM judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning for more expressive assessment. 4. Benchmarking major SVG generators on an independent caption set.

Result: CLIP-based scores barely react to SVG-specific errors like wrong colors, counts, and spatial relations. Off-the-shelf VLM judges are more sensitive but respond unevenly across error types and SVG styles. The developed evaluators provide better alignment with human judgment.

Conclusion: The proposed evaluation framework (CLIP scorers adapted to vector graphics + trained VLM judge) provides more human-aligned evaluation for text-to-SVG generation, addressing the limitations of existing metrics designed for natural images.

Abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) generation is attracting increasing attention as generative models improve in expressiveness and controllability. Progress, however, is held back by the lack of domain-specific evaluation protocols: current practice relies on metrics designed for natural images, most notably CLIPScore, which was never trained on vector graphics and aligns only partially with human judgment. We introduce \textbf{\ours}, a human-aligned evaluation framework for text-to-SVG generation. Through controlled caption and image perturbations, we first show that CLIP-based scores barely react to the errors SVG generators actually make, such as wrong colors, counts, and spatial relations, and that off-the-shelf Vision-Language Model (VLM) judges, while more sensitive, respond unevenly across error types and SVG styles. We then introduce a human-annotated dataset for \textit{Semantic Alignment}, measuring how faithfully a generated SVG reflects its caption. Building on it, we develop two complementary evaluators: CLIP scorers adapted to vector graphics and then aligned to human preferences, for fast large-scale evaluation, and a VLM judge trained with supervised fine-tuning and reward-shaped reinforcement learning, for more expressive and interpretable assessment. Using both, we benchmark major open-source, commercial, and optimization-based SVG generators on an independent caption set.

</details>


### [227] [CauseCollab: Causal Unified and Modality-Agnostic Network for Heterogeneous Collaborative Perception](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03818)
*Weize Li,Yang Li,Quan Yuan,Xiaoyuan Fu,Guiyang Luo,Jinglin Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CauseCollab addresses heterogeneous modality fusion in collaborative perception by using causal metric learning to disentangle semantic factors from modality-specific confounders, achieving state-of-the-art performance on OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing protocol-based two-stage methods for collaborative perception suffer from semantic inconsistency and error accumulation due to independently trained modality-specific converters generating heterogeneous pseudo-protocol distributions, especially problematic in scenarios with large modality discrepancies.

Method: CauseCollab proposes: (1) Causal metric learning to explicitly disentangle semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders in the protocol space; (2) Context-guided Unified Converter to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency for heterogeneous modalities; (3) Adapter-based architecture allowing new modalities to be integrated with minimal parameter training.

Result: CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance on OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.

Conclusion: The causal perspective on representation learning effectively addresses the heterogeneity challenge in collaborative perception, providing a unified and modality-agnostic framework that scales well to new modalities through lightweight adapters.

Abstract: Collaborative perception enhances environment understanding through multi-agent information sharing, but its performance in real-world scenarios is constrained by heterogeneous sensor modalities and model architectures. Recent protocol-based two-stage methods alleviate this problem by mapping heterogeneous features into a shared protocol space; however, independently trained modality-specific converters often generate modality-specific pseudo-protocol distributions, leading to semantic inconsistency and error accumulation, which is particularly pronounced in scenarios with large modality discrepancies. To address this issue, we propose CauseCollab, a causal unified and modality-agnostic network. CauseCollab formulates representation learning in the protocol space from a causal perspective, explicitly disentangling semantic factors from modality-specific statistical confounders via causal metric learning. Meanwhile, CauseCollab adopts context-guided Unified Converter for heterogeneous modalities to ensure cross-modal semantic consistency. In addition, integrating new modalities only requires training adapters with minimal parameters. Extensive experiments on the OPV2V and DAIR-V2X datasets demonstrate that CauseCollab achieves state-of-the-art performance, with more significant gains in scenarios involving large modality gaps.

</details>


### [228] [Semantic Bayesian World Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03834)
*Tommaso Soru*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs) as a solution to the fundamental mismatch between knowledge graphs (crisp factual assertions) and modern AI systems (foundation models and autonomous agents that reason probabilistically). The authors envision a web described as beliefs over knowledge graphs rather than facts, where ontological axioms constrain priors, Bayesian conditioning updates beliefs from observations, and actions can intervene on the world.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The core problem is that knowledge graphs represent reality as crisp factual assertions, while modern AI systems (foundation models and autonomous agents) reason natively in probabilities. This mismatch causes integration to remain a "data-feeding pipeline" rather than a unified reasoning architecture. The authors argue this is a fundamental architectural limitation that needs addressing.

Method: The paper is a conceptual/vision paper that works through specific examples to demonstrate what an agent gains from SBWMs: (1) a home-security agent reasoning about whether a figure is a courier or burglar, (2) actuarial estimates aggregated by entailment rather than string frequency, (3) a planning task that LMs reliably fail, and (4) estimation of quantities never stated in documents. The authors then outline required infrastructure: belief annotation over RDF, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and protocols for agents to exchange calibrated beliefs.

Result: Four concrete use cases demonstrating SBWM benefits: (1) Probabilistic reasoning about ambiguous situations (home security), (2) Entailment-based aggregation vs. frequency-based methods, (3) Reliable planning capabilities, (4) Ability to estimate unstated quantities through Bayesian reasoning.

Conclusion: The authors outline four technical requirements for the community to build: (1) Belief annotation over RDF, (2) Probabilistic entailment regimes, (3) Semantic calibration layers, and (4) Protocols for exchanging and disagreeing over calibrated beliefs between agents. This represents a significant research agenda for unifying symbolic knowledge representation with probabilistic reasoning.

Abstract: Knowledge graphs describe reality in crisp assertions, while the systems now consuming them, foundation models and autonomous agents, reason natively in probabilities. We argue that this mismatch is why the integration of language models and knowledge graphs remains a data-feeding pipeline rather than a unified reasoning architecture. We envision Semantic Bayesian World Models (SBWMs): a Web that describes the world not as a database of facts but as a shared, evolving fabric of beliefs over knowledge graphs, where ontological axioms constrain priors, observations update beliefs by Bayesian conditioning, and actions intervene upon the world. We work through what an agent gains from such a model: a home-security agent deciding whether the figure at the gate is a courier or a burglar, an actuarial estimate aggregated by entailment rather than by string frequency, a planning task that language models reliably fail, and the estimation of quantities that no document has ever stated. We then set out what the community must build to make them possible: belief annotation over RDF~1.2, probabilistic entailment regimes, semantic calibration layers, and protocols by which agents that have never met can exchange, and disagree over, calibrated beliefs.

</details>


### [229] [Adapting to Evolving Requirements: Agentic AI for Retail Supply Chain Operations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03860)
*Lei Zheng,Liping Yang,Zihao Li,Guodong Lyu,Chaik Ming Koh,Chung-Piaw Teo*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes a graph-constrained agentic framework for requirement-driven adaptation in retail supply chain operations, where LLMs interact with domain agents to select intervention routes and module-level changes, validated via downstream KPIs.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Retail supply chain operations require coupled decision modules that must adapt as requirements evolve. Existing LLM methods focus on individual optimization models and struggle with heterogeneous decision pipelines where requirements may admit multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects.

Method: The authors formulate requirement-driven adaptation as joint selection of intervention routes and admissible module-level changes. They propose a graph-constrained agentic framework where: (1) domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces, and (2) a central processor searches over bounded intervention paths. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs.

Result: Evaluated on 100 warehouse requirements with GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek base LLMs, the framework improves correctness and end-to-end success across all three models, raising end-to-end success from 72-76% to 79-83%.

Conclusion: The proposed graph-constrained agentic framework successfully extends LLM-based reformulation to heterogeneous decision pipelines in retail supply chains, achieving consistent improvements over direct LLM reformulation across multiple base models.

Abstract: Retail supply chain operations rely on coupled decision modules that must adapt as requirements evolve. LLMs offer a natural-language interface for this task, but existing methods primarily focus on individual optimization models. Extending them to heterogeneous decision pipelines is challenging because a requirement may admit multiple intervention paths with different downstream effects. We formulate requirement-driven adaptation as the joint selection of an intervention route and an admissible module-level change, and propose a graph-constrained agentic framework in which domain agents expose admissible reformulation interfaces and a central processor searches over bounded intervention paths. Candidates are validated and compared using downstream KPIs. In collaboration with a large retail partner, we evaluate 100 warehouse requirements elicited from practitioner interviews, with GPT, Qwen, and DeepSeek as base LLMs. Relative to direct LLM reformulation, our framework improves correctness and end-to-end success across all three models, raising end-to-end success from 72--76% to 79--83%.

</details>
