### [230] [Bioinfoysis Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03871)
*Qingyang Shao,Xin Zhang,Zhouyang Yuan,Xianying Chen,Yujia Xiang,Zihao Yang,Tong Ye,Yangqi Zhang,Jiakang Xu,Xiaoqing Yan,Xuan Luo,Keyi Li,Enci Fan,Kai Kang,Zhuohan Liu,Xingyu Jin,Chunran Teng,Tao Li,Xinyu Lv,Minghui Wang,Wenfeng Li,Yidan Gao,Siyu Liu,Mingrui Luo,Zhu Liang,Guanren Qiao,Zhiping Xu*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Bioinfoysis is a multi-agent harness for bioinformatics that represents each request as a persistent, artifact-grounded analysis run. It combines global planning with step-wise, evidence-driven replanning, using structured handoffs to bind intermediate results to responsible agents and checklist steps, while validating generated outputs before downstream use.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM agents for bioinformatics focus primarily on producing final answers, treating planning, tool use, and code execution as transient interactions. This design is poorly suited to long-horizon bioinformatics tasks where conclusions must remain connected to the data, computations, and intermediate evidence that support them.

Method: Bioinfoysis combines global planning with step-wise, evidence-driven replanning: the planner maintains an executable checklist and revises pending steps using structured handoffs returned after each worker execution. These handoffs bind intermediate results to their responsible agent, checklist step, and plan generation. A controlled runtime validates generated scripts, tables, and figures before they are used in downstream analysis. Role-specific context, persistent memory, and governed bioinformatics skills support reliable execution.

Result: On BixBench, Bioinfoysis achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 82.4%. Across four underlying language models, Bioinfoysis increases average accuracy from 27.81% to 64.13% on SeqQA2 and from 3.13% to 31.25% on DbQA2.

Conclusion: Reliable bioinformatics automation depends not only on model capability, but also on the harness that governs planning, execution, memory, and evidence flow. The system demonstrates that architecture design is crucial for long-horizon bioinformatics tasks.

Abstract: Large language model agents have shown promise in bioinformatics, but most existing systems focus primarily on producing final answers, treating planning, tool use, and code execution as transient interactions. This design is poorly suited to long-horizon bioinformatics tasks, where conclusions must remain connected to the data, computations, and intermediate evidence that support them. We introduce \textbf{Bioinfoysis}, a multi-agent harness that represents each request as a persistent, artifact-grounded analysis run. Bioinfoysis combines global planning with step-wise, evidence-driven replanning: the planner maintains an executable checklist and revises pending steps using structured handoffs returned after each worker execution. These handoffs bind intermediate results to their responsible agent, checklist step, and plan generation, preventing stale evidence from being silently reused after replanning. A controlled runtime validates generated scripts, tables, and figures before they are used in downstream analysis or reporting, while role-specific context, persistent memory, and governed bioinformatics skills support reliable execution over long analysis trajectories. We evaluate Bioinfoysis on BixBench and two question-answering tracks of LAB-Bench 2. On BixBench, Bioinfoysis achieves state-of-the-art accuracy of 82.4\%. Across four underlying language models, Bioinfoysis increases average accuracy from 27.81\% to 64.13\% on SeqQA2 and from 3.13\% to 31.25\% on DbQA2. These results demonstrate that reliable bioinformatics automation depends not only on model capability, but also on the harness that governs planning, execution, memory, and evidence flow. We hope that the emergence of Bioinfoysis will play a driving and leading role in the development of the bioinformatics community. Our demo website can be seen in https://report.bioinfoysis.com/.

</details>


### [231] [STAIR (STructure Aware Information Retriever): A novel dataset and LLM based retriever for document structure augmentation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03874)
*Vineet Kumar,Meghanadh Pulivarthi,vishwajeet kumar,Jaydeep Sen,Riyaz Ahmad Bhat,Sachindra Joshi*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: STAIR is a novel retrieval system that leverages Table of Contents (ToC) global structure to improve retrieval augmented generation in LLMs, addressing the "lost in the middle" problem and reducing hallucinations through a fine-tuned Differentiable Search Index (DSI) approach.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current RAG systems chunk long context into length-based pieces, losing semantic global structure. LLMs also suffer from "lost in the middle" problem even with long context support. This paper aims to exploit global structure (like ToC) to enable more accurate and hallucination-free retrieval.

Method: Fine-tuned Differentiable Search Index (DSI) system enhanced with Table of Contents (ToC) information. The ToC helps the LLM efficiently store and retrieve information from its model parameters. Benchmark created: SearchTome - 18 books across 6 diverse domains.

Result: STAIR achieves Recall@1 of 82.6% vs DSI 76.9% (statistically significant), BM25 59.5%, DPR 68.7%, and Mistral 13.8%. Hallucination rate less than 0.05%. Can generalize with very few training samples.

Conclusion: ToC-based retrieval is a promising novel direction that builds low-hallucination generative IR systems. STAIR significantly outperforms baselines, and the released SearchTome benchmark enables further research in this direction.

Abstract: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a key component for generating accurate and hallucination free answers using Large Language Models (LLMs). LLMs are improving at handling long context, but still suffer from "lost in the middle" problem. Thus, precise and accurate retrieval is important. Current retrievers chunk long context into length-based manageable chunks - in the process throwing away rich and informative semantic global structure in the corpus. We introduce a novel retrieval system STAIR that empowers an LLM to exploit global structure in a corpus such as a Table of Contents (ToC) to efficiently store and retrieve information from its model parameters. Our thorough and careful ablation studies with a finetuned Differentiable Search Index (DSI) system show that ToC helps build a low hallucination (less than 0.05%) generative Information Retrieval (IR) system and can generalize to examples where very few training samples are available. To further research in this novel direction of ToC based retrieval we release SearchTome - a diverse benchmark created from 18 books across 6 diverse domains to further research in this novel direction. STAIR achieves a high Recall@1 score of 82.6% on SearchTome as compared to DSI (76.9%), where the difference is found to be statistically significant. STAIR easily beats other strong baselines such as BM25 (59.5%), DPR (68.7%) and out-of-the-box Mistral (13.8%).

</details>


### [232] [Xiaomi-TabLDM: A Tabular Foundation Model Technical Report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03880)
*Xiaomi-TabLDM Team,:,Penghui Wang,Wei Liu,Hong Wang,Chengyue Huang,Yuxi Sun,Zirui Wang,Hongming Huang,Quan Wang,Chunxiao Liu,Erli Meng,Bin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Xiaomi-TabLDM is a tabular large data foundation model for classification and regression that uses in-context learning, achieving superior prediction accuracy without task-specific fine-tuning. It is pretrained on synthetic data generated from structural causal models (SCMs).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to create a flexible tabular foundation model that can handle classification and regression tasks through in-context learning, without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. The key insight is that pretraining on synthetic data from structural causal models (SCMs) can enable more flexible context utilization and more efficient capacity scaling.

Method: The paper proposes: 1) A three-stage training strategy with dual-stream feature grouping, lightweight Attention Residual, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) to learn richer feature interactions and expert specialization; 2) Large-scale synthetic pretraining using SCMs to expand coverage and diversity of tabular data; 3) Test-time compute scaling to improve predictive performance at inference time.

Result: 1) Strong regression performance: ranks 1st on OpenML-CTR23 and 2nd on regression across TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO; 2) Favorable performance-efficiency trade-off: on TabArena regression, achieves second-highest Elo while using 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than top-ranked TabFM; 3) Test-time scaling consistently improves predictive performance over the base model.

Conclusion: Xiaomi-TabLDM demonstrates that synthetic data pretraining from SCMs can be an effective approach for building tabular foundation models. The model achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple benchmarks with significantly lower computational costs, and test-time scaling provides additional performance gains. The approach enables more flexible context utilization and efficient capacity scaling for diverse tabular tasks.

Abstract: We introduce Xiaomi-TabLDM, a tabular large data foundation model for classification and regression via in-context learning, which delivers superior prediction accuracy without requiring task-specific fine-tuning. Pretrained exclusively on synthetic data generated from structural causal models (SCMs), our model enables more flexible context utilization and more efficient capacity scaling.
  i) A new performance standard. Strong regression performance across benchmarks: Xiaomi-TabLDM ranks 1st on OpenML-CTR23 and 2nd on regression across TALENT, TabArena, and BCCO, demonstrating consistently strong regression performance across four complementary benchmark suites. Favorable performance--efficiency trade-off: Xiaomi-TabLDM combines strong predictive performance with substantially lower computational cost. For example, on TabArena regression, it achieves the second-highest Elo while using 82% less training time and 68% less prediction time than the top-ranked TabFM.
  ii) Large-scale synthetic pretraining. Xiaomi-TabLDM expands the coverage and diversity of synthetic tabular data used for pretraining. We also adopt a three-stage training strategy together with dual-stream feature grouping, lightweight Attention Residual, and sparse Mixture-of-Experts, enabling Xiaomi-TabLDM to learn richer feature interactions and expert specialization across diverse tabular tasks.
  iii) Test-time scaling. Xiaomi-TabLDM further extends tabular prediction through test-time compute scaling, where allocating additional computation at inference time consistently improves predictive performance over the base model.

</details>


### [233] [Inferring Affective Consciousness in an Artificial Agent: A Case Study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03883)
*Mark Solms,St John Grimbly,Bruce Bassett,Evert Boonstra,Rowan Hodson,Nicolas Kuske,Kival Mahadew,Benjamin Rosman,Charel van Hoof,Jonathan Shock*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper argues that hedonic place preference behavior (attraction to pleasure-producing substances lacking nutritional value) may not necessarily indicate subjective feelings. The authors demonstrate that a simple artificial agent with an affective system can exhibit such behavior while being entirely deterministic, challenging assumptions about the physical basis of consciousness and free will.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To challenge the assumption that hedonic place preference behavior in creatures indicates genuine subjective experience or feelings, by showing that similar behavior can emerge from a deterministic artificial system.

Method: The authors engineer a simple artificial agent that instantiates an affective system with felt uncertainty about intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources, and observe whether it displays hedonic place preference behavior.

Result: The artificial agent displays hedonic place preference behavior through an apparently subjective form of information processing while remaining entirely deterministic.

Conclusion: The findings suggest that hedonic place preference behavior may not be a reliable indicator of subjective experience or consciousness, with implications for our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will.

Abstract: Creatures that display 'hedonic place preference behaviour' are thought by many scientists to experience feelings, on the assumption that their attraction to pleasure-producing substances which lack nutritional value (e.g. cocaine, morphine) cannot easily be attributed to unconscious instinctual behaviour. In this paper, we discuss how a simple artificial agent that instantiates attributes of an affective system engaging in felt uncertainty about its intrinsic needs in relation to environmental resources can similarly display hedonic place preference behaviour -- through an apparently subjective form of information processing -- while simultaneously being entirely deter-ministic. We outline some implications of this artificially engineered behaviour for our understanding of the physical basis of consciousness and the experience of free will.

</details>


### [234] [Lose the Order, Keep the Hierarchy: Deordering HTN Plans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03912)
*Takudzwa Togarepi,Gaspard Quenard,Damien Pellier,Humbert Fiorino*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper adapts two classical planning plan deordering techniques to the Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning domain, enabling the removal of unnecessary ordering constraints while respecting hierarchical decomposition constraints. The approaches were evaluated on IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks and showed substantial reduction in ordering constraints compared to Optiplan.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While HTN planning has been extensively studied for plan generation, post-plan optimization—particularly plan deordering—has received comparatively less attention. Plan deordering is well-established in classical planning but remains under-researched in the HTN setting, despite its potential to improve plan efficiency by removing unnecessary ordering constraints.

Method: The authors adapt two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning by extending them to account for hierarchical decomposition constraints inherent to HTN planning. The proposed approaches are evaluated on the IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks.

Result: Both implementations achieved a substantial reduction in the number of ordering constraints. A reduction in critical path length was also observed, though the improvements were less pronounced than the constraint reductions.

Conclusion: The adapted deordering techniques successfully extend classical planning methods to the HTN domain, providing significant reduction in ordering constraints while maintaining plan validity. This demonstrates the feasibility and value of post-plan optimization in HTN planning.

Abstract: Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning is a powerful planning formalism based on task decomposition. Although most of the literature studied plan generation, comparatively less attention has been paid to post-plan optimization. In particular, plan deordering has been extensively studied in classical planning but remains under-researched in the HTN setting. Plan deordering removes unnecessary ordering constraints between actions in a plan whilst keeping the plan valid. In this paper, we adapt two established plan deordering techniques from classical planning by extending the techniques to account for hierarchical decomposition constraints. We evaluate our proposed approaches on the IPC 2023 Partial-Order HTN benchmarks and we compare them against Optiplan, an HTN planner that generates partially ordered plans directly. Our results show a substantial reduction in number of ordering constraints in both our implementations. Although we also observe a reduction in critical path length, the improvements are less pronounced.

</details>


### [235] [Value-Preserving Architectures for Agentic AI Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03920)
*Alessandro Pesare,Tommaso Dolci,Katja Hose,Emanuel Sallinger*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper investigates how architectural design decisions in LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) can preserve human-centered values like privacy, fairness, and safety. It proposes three value-preserving architectural patterns: federated topology for privacy, distributed architecture for pluralism/diversity, and guard-agent architecture for fairness. The work aims to establish guidelines for designing trustworthy MAS.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The emergence of agentic AI and LLM-based multi-agent systems creates opportunities for automating complex tasks but raises critical concerns about preserving human-centered values (privacy, fairness, safety). While software engineering traditionally focuses on functional correctness, the integration of LLMs and AI agents into socio-technical systems necessitates responsible software engineering and value alignment. The authors argue that architectural design decisions (coordination mechanisms, communication protocols, system topologies) significantly influence system behavior and outcomes.

Method: The paper analyzes how different architectural designs support different human-centered values. It proposes three value-preserving architectural patterns: (i) a privacy-aware architecture with federated topology, (ii) a distributed architecture to promote pluralism and diversity, and (iii) a guard-agent architecture to detect and mitigate unfairness. Representative use cases are introduced to illustrate these architectures in real-world scenarios.

Result: The paper establishes a framework linking architectural design with human-centered values, laying the foundation for a unified set of architectural patterns and guidelines towards designing trustworthy MAS that preserve privacy, fairness, and safety.

Conclusion: Architectural choices in MAS influence not only functionality and performance but also promote value-oriented system behavior. By linking architectural design with human-centered values, this work provides foundational patterns and guidelines for developing trustworthy multi-agent systems that systematically preserve fundamental human values.

Abstract: The emergence of agentic AI and LLM-based multi-agent systems (MAS) presents unprecedented opportunities for automating complex tasks, while simultaneously raising critical concerns about the preservation of fundamental human-centered values, such as privacy, fairness, and safety. Although software engineering has traditionally focused on functional correctness, the adoption of LLMs and AI agents into complex socio-technical systems has intensified the need for responsible software engineering and robust value alignment. In MAS, architectural design decisions, such as coordination mechanisms, communication protocols, and system topologies, play a central role in shaping system behavior and the outcomes they produce. This paper argues that architectural choices influence not only the functionality and performance of MAS but can also promote value-oriented system behavior. Therefore, we investigate how different architectural designs support different human-centered values, discussing the following value-preserving architectural patterns: (i) a privacy-aware architecture with a federated topology, (ii) a distributed architecture to promote pluralism and diversity, and (iii) a guard-agent architecture to detect and mitigate unfairness. Finally, we introduce representative use cases to illustrate the proposed architectures in real-world scenarios. By linking architectural design with human-centered values, this work lays the foundation for a unified set of architectural patterns and guidelines towards the design of trustworthy MAS.

</details>


### [236] [Speak for Me: Giving LLMs the Situational Awareness to Participate in a Meeting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03923)
*Muneeb Khan,Frederic Kirstein,Terry Ruas,Bela Gipp*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: CAPA (Collaborative Agent Predictive Architecture) is a novel system for LLM agents to participate in online meetings on behalf of absent participants. It addresses the critical problem of agents failing to recognize when to speak, reducing silence rate from 51.4% to 2.5% while maintaining low hallucination (0.6%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current LLM agents fail to recognize when to contribute in online meeting delegation scenarios. Without structured tracking of stances, coverage, and floor, they miss speaking opportunities. Baseline prompt-only delegates stay silent on 51.4% of the absent participant's talking opportunities on the AMI corpus.

Method: CAPA uses a modular architecture with four main components: (1) Perceiver - updates meeting state from each observed turn; (2) Predictor - forecasts how the conversation will continue; (3) Controller - decides whether to speak and which proposition to surface; (4) Generator - phrases contributions in the participant's style. Additionally, two judges score forecast and action against observed turns, and a Recalibrator updates meeting state from verdicts. Evaluation uses an episode-level protocol scoring whether, when, and what a delegate contributes around the participant's idea units.

Result: On 137 AMI meetings, CAPA reduces silence rate from 51.4% to 2.5%, doubles credited recovery (26.1 → 52.2), and keeps hallucination at 0.6%. The failure mode shifts from omission to selection. Protocol's schema-constrained LLM judges align with human annotations at Cohen's kappa = 0.71. Mechanism ablations identify meeting state as the key lever closing the recognition gap, where raw-context scaling alone does not.

Conclusion: CAPA demonstrates that structured meeting state tracking through predictive architecture significantly improves LLM agents' ability to recognize and act on speaking opportunities in online meeting delegation. The architecture shifts failure modes from omission (missing contributions) to selection (choosing wrong content), making errors attributable to specific modules for targeted improvement.

Abstract: In online meeting delegation, LLM agents fail to recognize when to speak. With no structured way to track stances, coverage, and floor, they miss the moments where they should contribute. Prompt-only delegates stay silent on 51.4% of the absent participant's talking opportunities on the AMI corpus. We present CAPA (Collaborative Agent Predictive Architecture), an architecture for online meeting delegation. A Perceiver updates the meeting state from each observed turn. A Predictor forecasts how the conversation will continue. A Controller decides whether to speak and which proposition to surface. A Generator phrases the chosen contribution in the participant's style. Two judges score the forecast and the action against the next observed turn. A Recalibrator updates the meeting state from those verdicts for future decisions. To evaluate online delegation, we introduce an episode-level protocol that scores whether, when, and what a delegate contributes around the participant's actual idea units. The protocol's schema-constrained LLM judges align with human annotations at Cohen's kappa = 0.71. On 137 AMI meetings, CAPA reduces the silence rate from 51.4% to 2.5%, doubles credited recovery (26.1 --> 52.2), and keeps hallucination at 0.6%. The failure mode shifts from omission to selection, with each residual near-miss attributable to a specific module of the architecture. Mechanism ablations identify the meeting state as the lever that closes the recognition gap, where raw-context scaling alone does not.

</details>


### [237] [Towards Numerical TOHTN Planning with SMT-based HTN-SAT Encoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03938)
*Gaspard Quenard,Takudzwa Togarepi,Damien Pellier,Humbert Fiorino*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses the limitation of numerical reasoning in Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning by extending SAT-based encodings with Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) to handle numeric fluents in Totally-Ordered HTN (TOHTN) planning. A benchmark suite is also introduced for evaluation purposes.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: While HTN planning has received significant attention in recent years, existing approaches have very limited support for numerical reasoning, which is essential for many real-world planning problems that require handling quantitative constraints and fluents.

Method: The authors extend standard SAT-based encodings for HTN planning with SMT solvers to handle numeric fluents. They also create a benchmark suite for numerical TOHTN planning to provide a common evaluation basis.

Result: The experimental results demonstrate that this straightforward encoding approach serves as a competitive baseline for numerical TOHTN planning.

Conclusion: This work establishes a foundation for more expressive approaches to HTN planning with numerical reasoning capabilities, opening the way for future research in this direction.

Abstract: While HTN planning has received significant attention in recent years, support for numerical reasoning remains very limited. In this paper, we investigate numerical Totally-Ordered HTN (TOHTN) planning and show how standard SAT-based encodings can be naturally extended with SMT to handle numeric fluents. In addition, we introduce a benchmark suite for numerical TOHTN planning, providing a first common basis for evaluation in this setting. Experimental results show that this simple encoding already constitutes a competitive baseline. This work opens the way to more expressive approaches to HTN planning.

</details>


### [238] [More Criticism Does Not Make a Better Review: EquiReview-R](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03943)
*Zexing Zhang,Jichao Li,Tianyang Lei,Yude Fu,Yang Kewei*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a critical flaw in AI peer review systems: they generate many criticisms but fail to distinguish between missing important issues (omission) and making unsupported allegations (overcritique). The authors propose EquiReview-R, which treats these as separate risks and uses evidence-guided refinement rather than generation-oriented approaches. The system resolves existing concerns against evidence, searches for missing issues, and returns stop/continue/defer decisions. On a test set, it reduces major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1% while meeting non-inferiority criteria for omission detection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current AI review systems suffer from a fundamental limitation: they focus on generating more criticisms without distinguishing between two critical failure modes - (1) missing consequential weaknesses (omission) and (2) retaining allegations unsupported by evidence (overcritique). These opposite failures require different corrections, but generation-oriented systems and aggregate measures obscure this distinction. The authors identify that revision must precede further search, as most concerns in high-recall reviews lack definitive evidential disposition.

Method: The authors recast AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of a structured concern set. They introduce EquiReview-R which: (1) resolves existing concerns against localized evidence, (2) searches for missing issues from independent and review-conditioned perspectives, and (3) returns stop, continue, or defer decisions. They construct an evidence-linked trajectory corpus (ReviewTrace) to study review revision, and use computation-matched controls, controlled pairs, and ablations to isolate the effect of revision versus extra inference or shorter output.

Result: EquiReview-R achieves: non-inferiority for major omission detection; reduction of major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%; a one-sided omission upper bound of 9.9%; and stops on 52.4% of papers. Ablations confirm the gains come from revision rather than extra inference or shorter output.

Conclusion: The key insight is that revision must precede search in AI peer review. By treating omission and overcritique as separate risks and using evidence-guided refinement, EquiReview-R produces more accurate reviews. The released ReviewTrace corpus enables further research on review revision, disagreement, and provenance. This work represents a paradigm shift from generation-oriented to evidence-guided refinement approaches in AI-assisted peer review.

Abstract: AI reviewers can now produce many specific criticisms, but more criticism is not necessarily a better review. A review may miss a consequential weakness or retain an allegation that available evidence does not support. These failures require opposite corrections, yet generation-oriented systems and aggregate measures obscure the distinction. We therefore recast AI-assisted review as evidence-guided refinement of a structured concern set, with omission and overcritique treated as separate risks. Building on this formulation, we introduce EquiReview-R, which resolves existing concerns against localized evidence, searches for missing issues from independent and review-conditioned perspectives, and returns stop, continue, or defer. To expose the failure mode that motivates this design, we construct an evidence-linked trajectory corpus. Its retrospective analysis shows why revision must precede further search: nearly all concerns in a high-recall review lack a definitive evidential disposition, while an earlier refinement mechanism cannot revise them. On a frozen cohort of previously unseen papers, EquiReview-R satisfies the prespecified non-inferiority criterion for major omission, reduces major overcritique from 15.5% to 8.1%, and attains a one-sided omission upper bound of 9.9% while stopping on 52.4% of papers. Computation-matched controls, controlled pairs, and ablations show that the gain comes from revision rather than extra inference or shorter output. We release the corpus as ReviewTrace, an evidence-linked resource for studying review revision, disagreement, and provenance.

</details>


### [239] [FiMI Banking: A Sovereign Model for Indian Retail Banking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03960)
*NPCI AI Research Team,Aman Kumar,Asit Desai,Chandra Bhushan,Harsh Sharma,Harshit Bhushan,Hrithik Kadam,Keyur Doshi,Kolisetty Sai Kapardheeswar,Krishanu Adhikary,Nadeem Shaik,Navya Prakash,Nitin Kukreja,Prashant Devadiga,Shamanth MH,Shantanu Pandey,Suvradip Paul,Yatharth Dedhia*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FiMI Banking is a controlled Indian retail-banking setting developed to address the limitations of general-purpose language models in banking applications. The study evaluates two post-training approaches: preference optimization for improving safe behavior (refusing out-of-scope queries) and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-turn tool-use tasks. Results show preference optimization increases out-of-scope refusal from 52% to 80%, while reinforcement learning improves edge-case performance (0.509→0.718), order-sensitive task performance (0.590→0.679), and reduces token usage by 29%.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: General-purpose language models fail to meet banking requirements when tasks demand grounded information, correct tool use, or cautious handling of sensitive situations. Banks need conversational systems that can answer product questions, assist with account requests, and operate safely within strict operational and regulatory constraints.

Method: Built FiMI Banking dataset from vetted banking documents, structured ground truth, synthetic customer backgrounds, and banking tools. Evaluated two post-training approaches: (1) preference optimization for response-level behavior, and (2) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-turn tool-use tasks.

Result: Preference optimization substantially improved safe behavior: out-of-scope refusal rate increased from 52% to 80%. Reinforcement learning improved edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718, order-sensitive task performance from 0.590 to 0.679, while using 29% fewer generated tokens.

Conclusion: Preference optimization and verifiable-reward reinforcement learning address complementary requirements for reliable banking agents. The two approaches work synergistically—preference optimization handles safety and refusal behavior while reinforcement learning optimizes tool-use efficiency and task completion.

Abstract: Banks need conversational systems that can answer product questions, assist customers with account-related requests, and operate safely within strict operational and regulatory constraints. General-purpose language models do not reliably meet these requirements. They fall short when a task requires grounded information, correct tool use, or cautious handling of bank-specific sensitive situations. We introduce FiMI Banking, a controlled Indian retail-banking setting. We build it from vetted banking documents, structured ground truth, synthetic customer backgrounds, and banking tools. We evaluate two post-training approaches: preference optimization for response-level behavior, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for multi-turn tool-use tasks. Preference optimization improves safe behavior substantially: out-of-scope refusal rises from 52% to 80%. Reinforcement learning improves edge-case performance from 0.509 to 0.718 and order-sensitive task performance from 0.590 to 0.679, while using 29% fewer generated tokens. These results show that preference optimization and verifiable-reward reinforcement learning address complementary requirements for reliable banking agents.

</details>


### [240] [Interface-Induced Trajectory Censoring](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03966)
*Wenbo Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper reveals a critical evaluation artifact: AI agent tool-call rates are not intrinsic model properties but depend heavily on the model-interface stack. The same model can score 0% or 96% tool-call rates depending on the serving adapter used, due to silent failures where well-formed calls get censored before reaching downstream components. The effect is scale-dependent and resides in the interaction between chat templates and parsers, not in individual components.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors observed that agent evaluations report tool-call rates that can be zero even when models emit well-formed calls, due to interface censorship. This motivated investigation into whether tool-call rates are truly model properties or artifacts of the evaluation infrastructure.

Method: Controlled experiments on BFCL v4 and tau-bench benchmarks, varying only the serving adapter while holding weights, cases, decoding, and seeds fixed. A 2x2 factorial design tested chat template and parser combinations. Scale dependence was probed across Qwen2.5-Coder (21x range) and Llama-3.1-8B with strict:true flag modifications. A 98-line preflight check was developed to detect silent failures.

Result: The same model scores 0.00 or 0.96/0.19 depending on the adapter. The effect is entirely in the interaction (no main effects). On tau-bench retail tasks, server-parsed calls went from 0 to 636. Qwen2.5-Coder shows server parsing 0/100 at all sizes while well-formed calls rise to 80/100 at 32B. In verl's AgentLoop at 7B, 45/115 generations have complete calls but 0 are accepted/executed. Adapter repair increases parsing 0→84 and rescues 0→9, but pass rate only improves 53→62 (not significant).

Conclusion: The observed tool-call rate is not a property of the model alone but a property of the model-interface stack. This finding has major implications for benchmark evaluation, as silent failures can mask true model capabilities. The authors provide a diagnostic tool to catch these failures and call for more rigorous evaluation protocols.

Abstract: Agent evaluations report a tool-call rate read off the serving stack. That number can be zero while the model is emitting well-formed calls: the interface censors the trajectory before anything downstream sees it.
  On BFCL v4's own data, executor and scorer, holding weights, cases, decoding and seeds fixed and changing only the serving adapter, the same model scores 0.00 or 0.96 / 0.19. A 2x2 over chat template and parser locates the effect exactly: both main effects are exactly zero and all of it sits in the interaction -- no component is defective, and repairing one side of the contract buys precisely nothing. On tau-bench's 115 interactive retail tasks the same swap moves server-parsed calls from 0 to 636 and tasks reaching any tool execution from 0 to 103. Our probe reproduces the funnel across a 21x scale range of Qwen2.5-Coder: the server parses 0/100 at every size while well-formed emitted calls rise to 80/100 at 32B (~72 after calibration against an adjudicated gold standard). Under a matched envelope, across a comparable scale span, the silent fraction stays at 0-2, a prediction committed to the repository before the run. Llama-3.1-8B's 23% rate of calling the task function itself as a tool falls to 0 under one strict:true flag.
  The mismatch reaches inside the training loop, and its consequence is scale-dependent: in verl's AgentLoop at 7B, 45 of 115 generations carry a complete call; 0 are accepted, 0 execute, 0 return an observation. At 1.5B the same zero is over-determined, so we report the two scales separately. At evaluation time, repairing the adapter restores the mechanism but not a significant outcome gain: parsing 0->84, rescues 0->9, pass rate 53->62 (n.s.). We release a 98-line preflight check that catches every silent failure here. The observed tool-call rate is not a property of the model alone; it is a property of the model-interface stack that measures it.

</details>


### [241] [Common-Witness Certificates and Sharp Feature Bounds for Counterfactual Image Auditing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03973)
*Usef Faghihi,Amir Saki*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper addresses a fundamental problem in image editing: regional constraints can be satisfied individually but fail globally when no single latent explanation exists for the complete output. The authors develop a formal framework using witness grades and witness nerves to detect and quantify this local-to-global failure, providing tools for auditing causal claims in image analysis without requiring full causal identification.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Image editors may satisfy every regional plausibility constraint separately even when no single latent explanation fits the complete output. This local-to-global inconsistency represents a critical auditing challenge - existing methods cannot detect when regional edits are mutually incompatible. The motivation is to develop a framework that can audit declared feature relations and detect inconsistencies without requiring unrestricted pixel-level counterfactual identification.

Method: The framework uses several mathematical tools: (1) witness grade and witness nerve for formalizing local-to-global failure; (2) Helly-type arguments for generating incompatibility certificates for quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases; (3) blocker-hypergraph formula for exact repair counts; (4) simultaneous confidence regions for regime marginals providing finite-sample outer coverage. The method separates auditing from causal identification - shared exogeneity allows coupling of regime marginals, while externally justified witness relations yield sharp partial-identification bounds.

Result: The method demonstrates: (1) predicted local-global separation in controlled experiments on MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB datasets; (2) sharp bounds are testable; (3) certificate recovery works in synthetic experiments; (4) structured computation enables practical implementation. The approach provides exact repair counts and incompatibility certificates rather than approximate solutions.

Conclusion: The framework successfully audits declared feature relations in image editing without identifying unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals. It provides sharp partial-identification bounds, incompatibility certificates, and exact repair counts through mathematical tools from topological (nerve theorems) and combinatorial (hypergraph) domains. The method is practical for real-world image analysis while maintaining theoretical rigor through finite-sample confidence regions.

Abstract: An image editor may satisfy every regional plausibility constraint separately even when no single latent explanation fits the complete output. We formalize this local-to-global failure using a common witness grade and witness nerve. The framework separates auditing from causal identification: shared exogeneity alone allows every coupling of the regime marginals, whereas an externally justified witness relation yields sharp partial-identification bounds for prespecified image features. Helly-type arguments provide short incompatibility certificates for quasiconvex losses, heterogeneous action strata, and finite witness atlases; a blocker-hypergraph formula gives exact repair counts. Simultaneous confidence regions for the regime marginals give finite-sample outer coverage of the complete identified interval. Controlled MNIST, Morpho-MNIST, and smallNORB studies demonstrate the predicted local-global separation, while synthetic experiments test sharp bounds, certificate recovery, and structured computation. The method audits a declared feature relation and does not identify unrestricted pixel-level counterfactuals.

</details>


### [242] [The Dually Flat Geometry of Planning as Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04005)
*Nikola Milosevic,Asaki Kataoka,Nicolas Hinrichs,Kenji Doya,Nico Scherf*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper presents an information-geometric framework for reinforcement learning by embedding the planning criterion into the dynamics through a resetting planning process. The resulting visitation measure forms a dually flat statistical manifold, enabling planning-as-inference to generalize to nonlinear functionals with natural-gradient updates.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors seek to provide an alternative characterization of the occupancy measure in reinforcement learning and to connect planning with inference using information geometry. They aim to identify the natural object on which information geometry of decision making can be expressed.

Method: The method involves embedding the planning criterion into the dynamics through a "resetting planning process" and analyzing the resulting stationary measure (visitation measure). The framework uses concepts from information geometry, including dually flat statistical manifolds, affine charts, and natural gradient methods.

Result: The achievable visitation measures form a dually flat statistical manifold with two affine charts: visitation probabilities and log-policies, dual under conditional entropy. This structure allows planning-as-inference to generalize from linear rewards to nonlinear functionals of the visitation measure, with each iteration solved by one natural-gradient step. The temporal-difference error is given the interpretation of a marginal-utility estimate.

Conclusion: This geometric framework provides a unified structure for reinforcement learning and theoretical neuroscience, connecting planning and inference through information geometry and enabling generalization to nonlinear planning objectives.

Abstract: We present an alternative characterization of the occupancy measure of reinforcement learning, obtained by embedding the planning criterion into the dynamics through a resetting planning process. Its stationary measure, which we term visitation measure, is the object on which the information geometry of decision making is most naturally expressed. The achievable visitation measures form a dually flat statistical manifold whose two affine charts are the visitation probabilities and the log-policies, dual under the conditional entropy. This structure makes planning-as-inference generalize from linear rewards to nonlinear functionals of the visitation, each iterate solved by one natural-gradient step, and gives the temporal-difference error the interpretation of a marginal-utility estimate. We develop the geometry and its consequences for reinforcement learning and theoretical neuroscience.

</details>


### [243] [LLM4CKD: Large Language Models for Early Stage Chronic Kidney Disease Screening](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04013)
*Muhammad Ashad Kabir,Sirajam Munira*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This study evaluates large language models (LLMs) for chronic kidney disease (CKD) screening using zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning, comparing them with traditional ML, DL, and tabular foundation models. LLMs can achieve competitive performance with minimal examples but show instability with increased input complexity, while traditional methods improve more consistently with larger datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Early CKD screening is critical for timely intervention, but traditional ML/DL approaches require labeled data and model training, limiting real-world applicability. This study explores whether LLMs can serve as a more flexible, training-free alternative for CKD screening.

Method: The researchers developed a framework using clinically selected tabular features combined with structured prompt templates to enable LLM-based inference without task-specific training. They evaluated LLM performance across multiple prompt styles, feature configurations, and data settings (zero-shot and few-shot), comparing results against ML, DL, tabular foundation model (TFM) baselines, and existing CKD screening tools.

Result: LLMs achieved competitive performance using only a small number of examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings. However, LLM performance remains model-dependent and less stable as input complexity increases. In contrast, ML, DL, and TFM models showed more consistent improvement with larger training data.

Conclusion: There is a trade-off between data efficiency and stability. LLMs may serve as a flexible complementary approach for CKD screening when labeled data are limited, but traditional ML/DL/TFM methods remain more stable for larger-scale deployment.

Abstract: Early screening of chronic kidney disease (CKD) is critical for timely intervention, yet most machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) approaches require labeled data and model training, limiting their use in real-world screening settings. This study evaluates the effectiveness of large language models (LLMs) for CKD screening under zero-shot and few-shot in-context learning settings and compares them with traditional ML and DL methods. We propose a framework that uses clinically selected tabular features and structured prompt templates to enable LLM-based inference without task-specific training. LLM performance is evaluated across multiple prompt styles, feature configurations, and data settings, and compared with standard ML, DL, and tabular foundation model (TFM) baselines, and existing CKD screening tools. The results show that LLMs can achieve competitive performance using only a small number of examples, often matching or outperforming traditional approaches in low-data settings. However, their performance remains model-dependent and less stable as input complexity increases. In contrast, ML, DL, and TFM models show more consistent improvement with larger training data. Overall, the findings highlight a trade-off between data efficiency and stability, suggesting that LLMs may serve as a flexible complementary approach for CKD screening when labeled data are limited.

</details>


### [244] [InSituMeasure: Probing Situated Measurement Grounding in Industrial Scenes with Multimodal Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04014)
*Chao Shen,Xinyuan Li,Yunfan Zhou,Jianguo Yao,Haibing Guan,Zhihai Wang,Xijun Li*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: InSituMeasure is a benchmark evaluating Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) on continuous-valued gauge measurement in realistic industrial settings. The study reveals a significant gap between general multimodal capabilities and reliable measurement, with the best model achieving only 25.7% joint value-unit accuracy.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing benchmarks fail to capture realistic measurement scenarios: they isolate measurement from knowledge-grounded settings, lack specialized instruments, real-world noise, and diagnostic annotations. This reduces realism and constrains root-cause analysis of MLLM failures in continuous-valued measurement tasks.

Method: The authors introduce InSituMeasure with 2,922 real industrial monitoring scenes across eight functional categories of professional engineering instruments. They define metrics for: (1) numerical accuracy under predefined tolerances, (2) unit consistency, (3) rejection of fake/unanswerable tasks, and (4) alignment between model failures and annotated error factors. They evaluate 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs.

Result: The best model achieves only 25.7% joint value-unit accuracy and 51.8% confidence-diagnosis F1, revealing a substantial gap between general multimodal competence and reliable situated measurement. Key failure sources include text-induced shortcuts, overconfident responses, and authentic industrial noise (mixed disturbances, viewpoint deviation, occlusion, environmental interference).

Conclusion: MLLMs remain unreliable for continuous-valued measurement in real-world industrial settings. The benchmark reveals specific failure modes and provides dense gauge-attribute annotations with noise tags for failure diagnosis, enabling targeted improvements in situated measurement grounding.

Abstract: For trained operators, gauge reading requires little specialized knowledge, low cognitive effort, and high repeatability. Yet Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) remain unreliable in continuous-valued measurement despite strong results on general multimodal benchmarks. Existing benchmarks expose this weakness but isolate measurement from realistic, knowledge-grounded settings, with limited situated context, specialized instruments, real-world noise, and matched diagnostic annotations, reducing realism and constraining root-cause analysis. We introduce InSituMeasure to evaluate situated measurement grounding. It contains 2,922 real industrial monitoring scenes across eight functional categories of professional engineering instruments, with dense gauge-attribute annotations and noise tags for failure diagnosis. We define metrics for numerical accuracy under predefined tolerances and unit consistency, rejection of fake or unanswerable tasks, and alignment between model failures and annotated error factors. Across 24 state-of-the-art MLLMs, the best model reaches only 25.7\% joint value-unit accuracy and 51.8\% confidence-diagnosis F1, revealing a substantial gap between general multimodal competence and reliable situated measurement. Further analysis identifies failures from text-induced shortcuts, overconfident responses, and authentic industrial noise, including mixed disturbances, viewpoint deviation, occlusion, and environmental interference.

</details>


### [245] [FLY-EVAL++: An Evidence-Driven Evaluation Protocol for Safety-Constrained Flight Prediction with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04021)
*Yalun Wu,Junfeng Fang,Jiawei Wang,Haotian Liu,Qijun Yang,Minghan Yang,Hongcheng Guo,Zhoujun Li,Boyang Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: FLY-EVAL++ is proposed as an evidence-driven evaluation protocol for assessing LLMs in safety-critical, physics-governed environments. It combines deterministic verification of protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety constraints with fixed rubric-guided aggregation. When applied to Flight Trajectory and Attitude Prediction (FTAP) across 66 LLMs, safety compliance emerged as the most discriminative dimension, with models showing >28 point differences in safety scores despite comparable predictive performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Existing LLM evaluation protocols in safety-critical, physics-governed environments are insufficient because accuracy-based metrics fail to capture critical failure modes: predictions numerically close to ground truth can still violate operational constraints, combine fields in physically inconsistent ways, or produce unusable structured outputs. Current evaluation protocols do not reliably measure these failure modes.

Method: FLY-EVAL++ combines deterministic verification of protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety constraints with fixed rubric-guided aggregation into interpretable multi-dimensional scores. For FTAP instantiation, the approach extends PilotBench with history-conditioned and multi-step prediction tasks. Evaluation covers 66 LLMs.

Result: Safety compliance is the most discriminative dimension of model behavior. Models with comparable predictive performance differ by more than 28 points in safety score. Recurrent failures observed include: (1) safety violations under physically plausible predictions, and (2) instability in multi-step rollouts.

Conclusion: Evaluation in safety-critical domains should measure constraint satisfaction and structured validity explicitly rather than relying on accuracy-centric reporting alone. This work demonstrates the necessity of multi-dimensional evaluation frameworks that go beyond traditional accuracy metrics to ensure safety and reliability.

Abstract: Evaluating large language models (LLMs) in safety-critical, physics-governed environments requires more than accuracy-based metrics, because predictions that are numerically close to the ground truth can still violate operational constraints, combine fields in physically inconsistent ways, or fail to produce usable structured outputs. Existing evaluation protocols do not measure these failure modes reliably. We propose FLY-EVAL++, an evidence-driven evaluation protocol that combines deterministic verification of protocol compliance, physical feasibility, and safety constraints with fixed rubric-guided aggregation into interpretable multi-dimensional scores. We instantiate FLY-EVAL++ for Flight Trajectory and Attitude Prediction (FTAP) by extending the PilotBench setting with history-conditioned and multi-step prediction tasks. Across 66 LLMs, safety compliance is the most discriminative dimension of model behavior: models with comparable predictive performance differ by more than 28 points in safety score, and we observe recurrent failures including safety violations under physically plausible predictions and instability in multi-step rollouts. These results show that evaluation in safety-critical domains should measure constraint satisfaction and structured validity explicitly rather than rely on accuracy-centric reporting alone.

</details>


### [246] [Instruction Duplication as an Inference-Time Control Primitive](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04024)
*Victor Lavrenko*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces "instruction duplication," a simple inference-time technique that repeats the procedural instruction to improve language model performance without retraining. Across extensive experiments (7 models, 300 questions, 8 placement conditions), this method increases the deterministic All-8 diagnostic from 90.22% to 93.17%, with practical benefits emerging in downstream systems that consume the generated trajectory.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to improve procedural instruction following in language models, particularly when generated trajectories are inspected or repaired downstream. The authors seek a minimal, black-box inference-time control that doesn't require retraining or decoding changes.

Method: The method involves "instruction duplication" - repeating only the procedural instruction (not the full prompt) at inference time. The technique was tested across 7 instruction-tuned models, 300 medical multiple-choice questions, 8 placement conditions, totaling 16,800 scheduled generations. Multiple evaluation metrics were used: All-8 diagnostic (responses passing all 8 observable tests), TF-IDF recall, final-answer accuracy, premature commitment rate, and a blinded challenge audit.

Result: Key results: Moving from one to two copies raised All-8 diagnostic from 90.22% to 93.17% (+2.95 percentage points), eliminating 30.2% of remaining failures. TF-IDF recall improved from 73.44% to 74.81% (Holm-adjusted p < .001). Final-answer accuracy remained flat at 60.21%. Premature commitment increased from 1.52% to 2.30% (p_Holm = .00536). The blinded audit showed 10/30 directional confirmations, 20/30 ties, with no reversals; the prespecified 28/30 criterion was not met. In downstream applications (Answer Engineering), duplication improved SSNHL endpoint from 84.2% to 97.1% and conductive diagnostic branch preservation from 78.6% to 73.8% (a decrease but still 14.9 points above baseline).

Conclusion: Instruction duplication is a low-complexity, placement-sensitive control mechanism whose practical value emerges through downstream systems that consume the exposed trajectory. While the main effect is modest and the blinded audit criterion wasn't met, the technique can matter operationally when downstream systems act on generated trajectories. The effect is context-dependent - beneficial for some tasks but not all.

Abstract: Procedural instruction following is a basic requirement for controllable language-model systems, especially when generated trajectories are inspected or repaired downstream. We introduce instruction duplication, a minimal black-box inference-time control that repeats only the procedural instruction, without retraining or decoding changes. Across seven instruction-tuned models, 300 medical multiple-choice questions, eight placement conditions, and 16,800 scheduled generations, moving from one to two copies raises the deterministic All-8 diagnostic--responses passing all eight observable tests--from 90.22% to 93.17% (+2.95 percentage points), eliminating 30.2% of the failures remaining after one copy. Pre-provisional TF-IDF recall rises from 73.44% to 74.81% (+1.38 points; Holm-adjusted p < .001), while final-answer accuracy remains exactly 60.21%. Premature commitment increases from 1.52% to 2.30% (p_Holm = .00536). A blinded challenge audit yields 10/30 directional confirmations, 20/30 perceptual ties, and no reversals; its prespecified 28/30 confirmation criterion is not met. Yet this distinction can matter operationally when a downstream system acts on the generated trajectory. In Answer Engineering (AE), where explicit trajectory state determines local repair, the published reason-first no-editing SSNHL endpoint was 25.1%; system-only AE was later reproduced at 84.2%, and the same trailing duplicate raised it to 97.1%. For conductive diagnostic branch preservation, the corresponding values are 58.9% published without editing, 78.6% with reproduced AE, and 73.8% with AE plus duplication--a within-AE decrease, but still 14.9 points above the no-editing baseline. Instruction duplication is therefore a low-complexity, placement-sensitive control whose practical value can emerge through the downstream system that consumes the exposed trajectory.

</details>


### [247] [IRWOZ 2.0: A Large Language Model-driven Dialogue Dataset for Industrial Robot Conversations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04030)
*Chen Li,Dimitrios Chrysostomou*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: IRWOZ 2.0 is an improved dataset for industrial human-robot interaction dialogue systems, addressing noise issues in the original version through LLM-enhanced generation and quality refinements. The dataset expands to 390 dialogues across 4 industrial domains, achieving significant improvements in dialogue state tracking (BLEU-4 score increased from 0.1651 to 0.5604).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The original IRWOZ dataset contained substantial noise in dialogue states and utterances, which limited state-tracking accuracy in industrial human-robot interaction (HRI) dialogue systems. This limitation hindered the development of effective industrial HRI systems.

Method: The researchers addressed these limitations through: (1) LLM-enhanced generation using Mistral and Claude-3.5, (2) manual corrections, and (3) automated typo removal. The improved dataset was expanded to 390 dialogues across 4 industrial domains: Assembly, Delivery, Position, and Relocation.

Result: Benchmark experiments on dialogue state tracking demonstrated significant improvements, with GPT-2's BLEU-4 score increasing from 0.1651 to 0.5604 compared to the original IRWOZ dataset.

Conclusion: IRWOZ 2.0 provides a higher-quality dataset for industrial HRI research, with substantially improved dialogue state tracking accuracy. The dataset has been publicly released to support further industrial HRI research.

Abstract: IRWOZ has improved industrial human-robot interaction (HRI) dialogue systems through domain-specific annotations. However, its initial version contains substantial noise in dialogue states and utterances, limiting state-tracking accuracy. We introduce IRWOZ 2.0, which addresses these limitations through large language model (LLM) enhanced generation (Mistral/Claude-3.5) and quality refinements. Our improved dataset expands to 390 dialogues across 4 industrial domains (Assembly, Delivery, Position, Relocation), featuring manual corrections and automated typo removal. Benchmark experiments on dialogue state tracking demonstrate significant improvements, with GPT-2's BLEU-4 score increasing from 0.1651 to 0.5604 compared to original IRWOZ. To support industrial HRI research, we publicly released IRWOZ 2.0 dataset at https://ieee-dataport.org/documents/irwoz-20-large-language-model-driven-dialogue-dataset-industrial-robot-conversations

</details>


### [248] [Spurious Advantage Hidden in GRPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04063)
*Jiamian Wang,Samyadeep Basu,Koustava Goswami,Tong Yu,Zhiqiang Tao*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: GRPO assigns high advantage to rollouts that reach correct answers, but cannot distinguish between correct reasoning and random guessing. This "spurious advantage" problem misleads policy learning. SIGNBALANCE fixes this by using sign-based, zero-mean balanced advantage estimation.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: GRPO's advantage estimator uses within-group reward statistics to assign magnitude to rollouts. However, it cannot distinguish between rollouts that reach correct answers through proper reasoning versus those that guess correctly. This "spurious advantage" problem misleads the policy toward guess-like behaviors, particularly in three scenarios: bounded-answer tasks with small candidate sets, open-answer sets with bounded sub-cases, and search agents with budget exploring many paths.

Method: SIGNBALANCE uses three key modifications: (1) keeps the verifier sign (positive for correct, negative for incorrect), (2) uses a global scale rather than group-specific statistics, and (3) restores zero-mean balance via a stop-gradient per-class rescaling mechanism.

Result: SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math tasks while improving performance on bounded-answer math tasks and search agent benchmarks at different scales.

Conclusion: The spurious advantage problem in GRPO can be effectively addressed by composition-free magnitude estimation that preserves sign information and maintains zero-mean balance. SIGNBALANCE successfully eliminates the bias toward guess-like behaviors while maintaining performance on open-answer tasks.

Abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is widely studied for reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where its advantage estimator assigns each rollout a magnitude from within-group reward statistics. In the common case, this magnitude rewards rollouts that reach the correct answer through reasoning. Yet, an overlooked case shares the same surface: a rollout may land on it by guessing, and the formula still assigns a high magnitude, which we identify as the spurious advantage. This arises in three cases: bounded-answer tasks with a small candidate set; open-answer sets hosting bounded sub-cases; and search agents whose budget opens many paths to the same answer. In all three, this misleads the policy toward guess-like behaviors. We propose SIGNBALANCE, whose magnitude is composition-free: it keeps the verifier sign, uses a global scale, and restores zero-mean balance via a stop-gradient per-class rescaling. Across math and search agent benchmarks at different scales, SIGNBALANCE matches GRPO on open-answer math and improves on bounded-answer math and search agents. Code will be released.

</details>


### [249] [Why Gated DeltaNet Survives 4-Bit Quantization: NVFP4 W4A4 for the Recurrent Half of a Hybrid 27B LLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04098)
*Sergii Kozyrev,Davyd Maiboroda*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: Minima is a hybrid LLM (Qwen3.8-27B with Gated DeltaNet) quantized to 4-bit weight and activation (NVFP4 W4A4) across all 496 linear layers, challenging the intuition that recurrent GDN layers require higher precision. The model matches BF16 baseline across perplexity, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, AIME'25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench, and RULER benchmarks while being smallest (17.5 GiB) and fastest (+14-19% prefill).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The authors test the intuition that errors in recurrent states (like Gated DeltaNet) accumulate over long contexts, justifying keeping GDN blocks at 8- or 16-bit precision in previous quantizations. They hypothesize that the delta-rule recurrence and gate parameterizations may actually be robust to quantization.

Method: The authors built Minima using NVFP4 W4A4 quantization on all 496 linear layers including GDN blocks. They evaluated across: (i) perplexity at 4K/32K context, (ii) MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, AIME'25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench, (iii) RULER retrieval to 64K. They conducted a four-part mechanism study examining: block scaling, gate projections, delta-rule recurrence, and per-token quantization costs.

Result: Minima matches BF16 within seed noise (5-task average -0.52) while being the smallest (17.5 GiB) and fastest prefill (+14-19%) recipe. The 32K perplexity gap shrinks with position. Mechanism study reveals: (i) NVFP4's 16-element block scaling localizes outliers; (ii) gate projections are least sensitive (~11% GEMM error compresses to ~2% output error); (iii) delta-rule recurrence holds injected noise at flat plateau over 32K tokens and forgets state impulse within hundreds of steps; (iv) per-token quantization cost washes out with context. The paper also addresses global-scale mismatch in fused GEMMs and shows calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales are performance-free.

Conclusion: The recurrent half of a hybrid LLM is the easiest half to quantize. The delta-rule recurrence naturally stabilizes noise, gate parameterizations compress errors, and block scaling handles outliers. This provides both a practical recipe (quantize everything, ship KV scales) and a mechanistic explanation for why hybrid LLM recurrences are robust to quantization.

Abstract: Hybrid LLMs pair softmax attention with linear-attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), whose recurrent state summarizes the context in fixed size. Early community 4-bit quantizations of Qwen3.8-27B (48 GDN layers, 16 attention layers) left the GDN block in 8- or 16-bit precision -- especially its decay and write-strength gates -- on the intuition that errors in a recurrence accumulate over long contexts. We test that intuition by building Minima: NVFP4 W4A4 on all 496 linear layers, GDN included. Across perplexity at 4K/32K, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, AIME'25, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench, and RULER retrieval to 64K, Minima matches BF16 within seed noise (5-task average -0.52) while being the smallest (17.5 GiB) and fastest-prefill (+14-19%) recipe we compare, and its 32K perplexity gap shrinks with position. A four-part mechanism study explains why: (i) NVFP4's 16-element block scaling localizes the residual stream's extreme outliers, equalizing activation error across layer roles; (ii) the supposedly fragile gate projections are the least sensitive -- softplus/exponential and sigmoid parameterizations compress ~11% GEMM error to ~2% output error; (iii) the delta-rule recurrence holds injected noise at a flat plateau over 32K tokens and forgets a state impulse within hundreds of steps, because each write overwrites the state along the current key direction; (iv) the per-token quantization cost washes out with context instead of compounding. We also repair a global-scale mismatch that arises when per-module-calibrated NVFP4 checkpoints are served by kernels that fuse those modules into one GEMM, and show calibrated FP8 KV-cache scales are performance-free. The result: a practical recipe -- quantize everything, ship KV scales -- and a mechanistic account of why the recurrent half of a hybrid LLM is the easy half to quantize. Checkpoint: https://huggingface.co/minima-ai/mnma_qwen3.8_27b_nvfp4

</details>


### [250] [Epistemic Warrant for LLM Recommendations: Characterizing the Basis for Reliance When Ground Truth Is Unavailable](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04127)
*Shai Vardi,João Sedoc*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper introduces "epistemic warrant" as a theoretical construct to help users assess whether to rely on specific LLM recommendations, operationalized through a four-tier reliance certificate system.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Users lack a principled basis for assessing whether to trust individual LLM recommendations in organizational decisions, as existing approaches evaluate broad model properties rather than the underlying basis for specific recommendations.

Method: The authors adapt epistemological foundations to create a decision-level construct that characterizes the stability of model preference and its scope. They validate it through known-groups tests and crowd worker consensus, and compare it with verbalized confidence and decision difficulty.

Result: The four-tier reliance certificate (unstable, context-dependent, locally supported, broadly supported) successfully recovers expert-prespecified warrant orderings, aligns with crowd worker consensus, and provides information distinct from verbalized confidence.

Conclusion: Epistemic warrant offers a theoretically grounded, implementable approach for characterizing the warrant of individual LLM recommendations when objective ground truth is unavailable.

Abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to support organizational decisions, yet users often lack a principled basis for assessing whether to rely on a specific recommendation. Existing approaches typically evaluate broad model properties, such as reliability, uncertainty, or robustness, or focus on user trust, rather than the underlying basis for relying on an individual recommendation. Adapting theoretical foundations from epistemology, we introduce epistemic warrant, a decision-level construct that characterizes the stability of a model's preference and the scope over which that preference holds. We operationalize this construct through a four-tier reliance certificate for pairwise recommendations, distinguishing among unstable, context-dependent, locally supported, and broadly supported recommendations. We validate the construct using contemporary methodologies: known-groups tests successfully recover expert-prespecified warrant orderings, and stronger warrants systematically align with independent consensus from crowd workers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that epistemic warrant provides information distinct from verbalized confidence and is not readily explained by decision difficulty. Ultimately, this framework offers a theoretically grounded, implementable approach for characterizing the warrant of individual LLM recommendations when objective ground truth is unavailable.

</details>


### [251] [Environment Evolution for Terminal Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04128)
*Zhiyuan Fan,Tinghao Yu,Yuanjun Cai,Jiang Zhou,Jiangtao Guan,Jincheng Liu,Yun Yang,Dingxin Hu,Zhuo Han,Xing Wu,Feng Zhang,Lilin Wang*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: This paper proposes "environment evolution" as a method to train terminal agents by incrementally increasing environment difficulty off-policy. It derives three evolution directions from multi-turn learning objectives and implements them through a multi-agent harness. The method was validated on Qwen3.6 models, achieving 14.4-18.0 percentage point improvements on Terminal-Bench 2.1.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current frontier models make synthesized environments less challenging, limiting learning signals. Existing co-evolution methods rely on on-policy rollouts, limiting generalization and continuous learning signals as models improve. There was a need for a method that can provide continuous, progressively difficult environments off-policy.

Method: The paper derives three evolution directions from the multi-turn learning objective that influence environment difficulty. Evolution is implemented through a loop-engineered multi-agent harness. Environment difficulty is increased off-policy and scheduled generation by generation during training.

Result: Quantitative rollout experiments with Hy4 preview, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Sol show that environment evolution consistently produces more difficult environments. Training with Qwen3.6-27B improved by 14.4 percentage points and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B improved by 18.0 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Conclusion: Environment evolution is an effective approach for training terminal agents. It provides continuous learning signals by scheduling progressively difficult environments, achieving significant performance improvements on benchmark tests. The method works off-policy, addressing limitations of previous co-evolution approaches.

Abstract: Scaling interactive and verifiable environments is critical for training terminal agents. As frontier models become more capable, environments synthesized from scratch become less challenging and thus provide limited learning signals. Recent co-evolution methods iteratively synthesize environments near the model's learnable frontier based on weaknesses exposed during rollouts. However, their dependence on on-policy rollouts limits generalization and the continuous provision of learning signals as the model becomes stronger. In this paper, we propose environment evolution, which incrementally increases environment difficulty off-policy and schedules the evolved environments generation by generation during training to provide continuous learning signals. We derive three evolution directions that influence environment difficulty from the multi-turn learning objective and then implement evolution along these directions through a loop-engineered multi-agent harness. Quantitative rollout experiments with Hy4 preview, Claude Opus 5, and GPT-5.6 Sol show that environment evolution consistently produces more difficult environments. We validate its effectiveness on Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B through simple long-horizon RL training, improving their performance by 14.4 and 18.0 percentage points on Terminal-Bench 2.1, respectively.

</details>


### [252] [The Natural Language Interaction Protocol and Standard for AI Agents](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04135)
*Luyi Xing,Rasit Onur Topaloglu,Ranjan Sinha,Abhay Ratnaparkhi,Samuel Ndichu,Christopher Nguyen,Anindita Das,Tom Sheffler,Mohamed Rahouti,Zichuan Li,Xiaojing Liao,Sanjay Aiyagari*

Main category: cs.AI

TL;DR: NLIP (Natural Language Interaction Protocol) is a standardized application-layer protocol for AI agent interoperability, developed by a consortium and standardized by Ecma International. It provides a lightweight semantic message envelope that works over existing transport protocols (HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket, AMQP) and enables adaptation between heterogeneous agent frameworks, AI models, and enterprise services.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: AI agents are increasingly deployed across organizations using heterogeneous frameworks, models, tool interfaces, protocols, and execution environments. To realize their social and business impact, these agents need to interoperate through a common communication protocol. Existing protocols lack standardization for AI-agent interaction at the application layer.

Method: The paper presents the design rationale of NLIP, including its message model, transport bindings, and security-by-design considerations. It also describes a reference implementation, representative applications, adoption signals, and compares NLIP with emerging agent protocols like MCP and A2A.

Result: NLIP provides a standards-based solution that enables interoperability between heterogeneous AI agents, supporting communication over multiple transport protocols (HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket, AMQP) and allowing adaptation between clients, agents, context stores, ontologies, tools, enterprise services, and heterogeneous underlying protocols.

Conclusion: NLIP represents a mature, industry-consensus standard for AI agent communication, with adoption signals from multiple companies and universities, and is positioned alongside emerging protocols like MCP and A2A in the evolving AI agent ecosystem.

Abstract: AI agents are increasingly being developed and deployed across organizations using heterogeneous agent-development frameworks, AI models, tool interfaces, protocols, and execution environments. To realize their potential social and business impact, these agents must be able to interoperate through a common communication protocol. The Natural Language Interaction Protocol (NLIP), developed by researchers and practitioners across companies and universities and standardized by Ecma International, addresses this need by defining a standards-based application-layer protocol for AI-agent interaction. NLIP provides a lightweight semantic message envelope that can be carried over existing transports such as HTTP/HTTPS, WebSocket, and AMQP, while allowing NLIP-aware agents and gateways to adapt between clients, agents, local context stores, ontologies, tools, enterprise services, and heterogeneous underlying protocols. This paper presents the motivation and design rationale of NLIP, its message model and transport bindings, security-by-design considerations, reference implementation, representative applications, adoption signals, and relationship to emerging agent protocols such as MCP and A2A.

</details>


### [253] [Efficient Test-Time Adaptation through Human-AI Interaction](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04141)
