Result: Top hosted system achieves exec@10 = 1.00 but only exec@1 = 0.331. Rank-1 misses are paired buggy variants 91.5-99.4% of the time across four leading systems. Canonical scores below at least one distractor in 67-78% of queries on leading systems.

Conclusion: Current embedding-based code retrieval systems struggle to functionally discriminate correct code from near-clone buggy variants at rank-1, despite high recall at top-10. This reveals a critical gap in retrieval capability for coding agents and retrieval-augmented generation.

Abstract: Embedding-based code retrieval is a core component of coding agents and retrieval-augmented code generation, where retrieving correct code matters more than retrieving lexically similar code. Existing code-retrieval benchmarks do not plant controlled, execution-verified single-edit variants of each query's canonical implementation in the search pool, leaving the question of whether embeddings can functionally discriminate correct from near-clone-but-incorrect code unanswered in a retrieval setting. Resolving this requires a benchmark whose search pool itself contains the relevant counterfactuals -- execution-verified buggy variants near-identical to each canonical -- so that a retriever's rank ordering can be directly tested for functional discrimination rather than topical or identity overlap. We introduce ExecRetrieval, 939 Python tasks each paired with one execution-verified canonical implementation and up to four execution-verified buggy distractors, each generated by a mechanical mutation making a single targeted edit, and evaluate 23 dense embedding configurations plus BM25 under provider-native invocation with paired McNemar tests and query-level bootstrap intervals. With near-clone counterfactuals in the pool, the top hosted system reaches exec@10 = 1.00 but only exec@1 = 0.331; rank-1 misses are paired buggy variants 91.5-99.4% of the time across the four leading systems, and the canonical scores below at least one of its four paired distractors in 67-78% of queries on the leading systems. The full dataset, execution oracle, embedding matrices, environment snapshot, and pairwise statistical tests are released at the URL in Appendix D.

</details>

### [275] [CAPQ-FAST: Content-Adaptive Perceived Quality Assessment for Faster Audiovisual Playback](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03498)
*Jiarun Song,Yuxin Song,Fuzheng Yang,Weisi Lin*

Main category: cs.MM

TL;DR: Summary generation failed


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Motivation analysis unavailable

Method: Method extraction failed

Result: Result analysis unavailable

Conclusion: Conclusion extraction failed

Abstract: Faster playback has become a common feature in modern online audiovisual services, allowing users to consume content in less time while still maintaining a coherent viewing experience. However, different modalities of media content, such as video, audio (including speech and music), and audiovisual, exhibit varying requirements for understandability and information integrity under faster playback. These differences lead to noticeable variations in perceived quality depending on the content type. Nevertheless, users' perceived quality at different playback speeds remains insufficiently investigated. To address this gap, this paper conducts a series of subjective experiments to analyze the relationship between playback speed and perceived quality for video, audio, and audiovisual content. Content-specific intrinsic features are extracted to capture temporal dynamics, including temporal information (TI) for video, words per minute (WPM) for speech, and beats per minute (BPM) for music. Predictive models of perceived quality under faster playback are then developed separately for video, speech, and music. By integrating these models, a unified content-adaptive perceived quality assessment model (CAPQ-FAST) is proposed for faster audiovisual playback. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model effectively predicts perceived quality under different playback speeds. This model can help service providers better understand users' viewing intentions and perceptual experiences under faster playback, thereby enabling more adaptive personalized recommendations and playback control to enhance user experience adaptability.

</details>

### [276] [SISER: Speaker-Invariant Speech Emotion Recognition with Entropy-Based Adversarial Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.02941)
*Eunseo Choi,Hyunku Kang,Chanwoo Kim*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: SISER proposes a speaker-invariant speech emotion recognition system that combines wav2vec 2.0 pre-trained representations with ECAPA-TDNN-based adversarial training to address data scarcity and inter-speaker variability. The method achieves 60.63% UA on IEMOCAP, outperforming baseline (51.15%) and wav2vec 2.0 without speaker suppression (56.46%).


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Speech emotion recognition suffers from two fundamental challenges: (1) scarcity of labeled data, and (2) inter-speaker variability that hinders generalization. Existing adversarial approaches address speaker variability but fail to leverage powerful pre-trained representations.

Method: SISER integrates wav2vec 2.0 as a feature encoder with ECAPA-TDNN as a speaker discriminator within an entropy-based adversarial training scheme. The approach uses self-supervised representations from wav2vec 2.0 to reduce dependency on large labeled datasets, while ECAPA-TDNN provides stronger adversarial signal for speaker identity suppression compared to shallow classifiers.

Result: On IEMOCAP dataset, SISER achieves 60.63% UA (Unweighted Accuracy), significantly outperforming the baseline (51.15%) and wav2vec 2.0 without speaker suppression (56.46%). Ablation studies confirm that the choice of speaker classifier architecture is a key factor in performance.

Conclusion: Combining pre-trained self-supervised representations (wav2vec 2.0) with a strong speaker discriminator (ECAPA-TDNN) in an adversarial training framework effectively addresses both data scarcity and inter-speaker variability in SER. The architecture of the speaker classifier is crucial for optimal performance.

Abstract: Speech emotion recognition (SER) faces two fundamental challenges: scarcity of labeled data and inter-speaker variability, both of which hinder generalization of emotion recognition systems. While prior adversarial approaches address speaker variability, they fall short in leveraging powerful pre-trained representations. We propose SISER (Speaker-Invariant Speech Emotion Recognition), integrating wav2vec 2.0 as a feature encoder and ECAPA-TDNN as a speaker discriminator within an entropy-based adversarial training scheme. wav2vec 2.0 provides rich self-supervised representations that alleviate dependency on large labeled datasets, while ECAPA-TDNN enables suppression of speaker identity via a stronger adversarial signal than shallow classifiers. Evaluated on IEMOCAP, SISER achieves a UA of 60.63%, outperforming the baseline (51.15%) and wav2vec 2.0 without speaker suppression (56.46%), with ablation emphasizing that the choice of speaker classifier architecture is a key factor.

</details>


### [277] [CRAW: Codec Robust Audio Watermarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03107)
*David Chernin,Ethan Fetaya*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper introduces CRAW, a codec-robust audio watermarking framework that addresses the vulnerability of existing post-hoc watermarking methods to neural codecs and denoisers. The approach combines distortion-aware training, attention-based pooling, inference-time perceptual masking, and error-correcting codes to achieve robust synthetic speech detection while maintaining high perceptual quality.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Recent advances in generative speech models have made it increasingly difficult to distinguish authentic from synthetic audio, enabling new forms of fraud and misinformation. While audio watermarking offers a promising defense by embedding an imperceptible signal into generated speech, existing post-hoc watermarking methods fail under neural codecs and denoisers—transformations routinely applied during real-world storage, transmission, and processing—severely limiting their practical utility.

Method: CRAW combines four key techniques: (1) distortion-aware training to improve robustness against neural re-synthesis, (2) an attention-based pooling mechanism for effective feature aggregation, (3) inference-time perceptual masking to preserve watermark information, and (4) an error-correcting code to recover fidelity lost during robust training.

Result: Experiments demonstrate that CRAW achieves state-of-the-art robustness against neural codecs, denoisers, and vocoders while maintaining perceptual quality comparable to existing post-hoc watermarking methods.

Conclusion: CRAW successfully balances robustness against neural transformations and perceptual quality, addressing a critical gap in practical audio watermarking for synthetic speech detection. The code is publicly available.

Abstract: Recent advances in generative speech models have made it increasingly difficult to distinguish authentic from synthetic audio, enabling new forms of fraud and misinformation. Audio watermarking offers a promising defense by embedding an imperceptible signal into generated speech that can later be detected to verify its provenance. However, recent studies have shown that existing post-hoc watermarking methods fail under neural codecs and denoisers, transformations routinely applied during real-world storage, transmission, and processing, severely limiting their practical utility. Here we introduce CRAW, a codec-robust audio watermarking framework that jointly improves robustness against neural re-synthesis while maintaining high perceptual quality. CRAW combines distortion-aware training with an attention-based pooling mechanism, inference-time perceptual mask- ing, and an error-correcting code to recover the fidelity lost during robust training. Experiments demonstrate that CRAW achieves state-of-the-art robustness against neural codecs, denoisers, and vocoders while maintaining perceptual quality comparable to existing post-hoc watermarking methods. The code is available at https://github.com/DavidC1212/craw.

</details>


### [278] [Local Chord Corruption Is Not Recognizer Replay: Chord-Condition Propagation in MIDI-SAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03584)
*Weiwen Huang*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper compares two testing approaches for singing accompaniment generation (SAG) systems: synthetic chord corruption (controlled stress test) and complete automatic chord recognition (ACR) replay (real-world evaluation). Using CNN-CRF and DeepChroma+CRF predictors through a fixed MIDI-SAG generator across 30 tracks, the study finds that synthetic corruption produces larger localized effects, while complete replay provides more comprehensive evaluation of chord-condition propagation in deployed systems.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: The motivation is to understand the difference between controlled stress testing (synthetic corruption) and real-world evaluation (complete ACR replay) for singing accompaniment generation systems. The authors aim to determine which approach provides better insights into system performance and failure modes.

Method: The authors replayed predictions from two chord recognition models (CNN-CRF and DeepChroma+CRF) through one fixed MIDI-SAG generator while controlling track, seed, context, and scoring window. They tested across 30 paired tracks with three seeds each, using STFT, CQT, and CENS representations. They evaluated effects including changed-target, inside-output, and compared replay distance under different matching conditions (joint matching, relation composition).

Result: Key findings: 1) Central four-second tritone produced larger changed-target and inside-output effects than CNN-CRF replay in all representations; 2) CENS target gap was positive on 29/30 tracks (mean 0.462); 3) Matching replay support and relation composition reduced mismatch, with joint matching giving lowest replay distance; 4) Relative-root substitutions produced 2.88-fold larger CENS output change than same-root quality flips; 5) Matched surrogate was closer to replay for both recognizer paths.

Conclusion: Localized corruption tests mechanisms, whereas complete replay evaluates deployed chord-condition propagation. The two approaches serve different purposes: synthetic corruption is better for understanding specific failure mechanisms, while complete ACR replay provides more realistic evaluation of deployed system performance.

Abstract: Synthetic chord corruption provides a controlled stress test for singing accompaniment generation (SAG), whereas complete automatic chord recognition (ACR) replay measures the condition delivered to a deployed system. We compare them by replaying CNN-CRF and DeepChroma+CRF predictions through one fixed MIDI-SAG generator, holding track, seed, context, and scoring window constant. Across 30 paired tracks and three seeds, a central four-second tritone produced larger changed-target and inside-output effects than CNN-CRF replay in STFT, CQT, and CENS; the CENS target gap was positive on 29/30 tracks (mean 0.462). Matching replay support and relation composition reduced this mismatch, with joint matching giving the lowest replay distance in the full-30 analysis. Relative-root substitutions produced 2.88-fold larger CENS full-window output change than same-root quality flips at near-equal dose. The matched surrogate was closer to replay for both recognizer paths. We conclude that localized corruption tests mechanisms, whereas complete replay evaluates deployed chord-condition propagation.

</details>


### [279] [VoxReason: Listener-Free Evaluation of Source-Grounded Speech Planning Before Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03203)
*Mengzhe Geng*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: VoxReason introduces a listener-free evaluation framework to measure whether expressive speech synthesis decisions (affect, pitch, energy, rate, etc.) are grounded in source records before waveform rendering. The system outputs source-cited speaking plans with evidence citations, verified by a deterministic checker for citation legality, slot agreement, schema validity, and counterfactual locality. Experiments show slot accuracy alone is insufficient (key-lookup oracle achieves 1.000 accuracy), while a 7B model with SFT+CF repair achieves 0.919 plan-slot accuracy and 1.000 locality on source-key-disjoint cases.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current expressive speech systems make delivery decisions (affect, pitch, energy, pause, emphasis, stance) before any waveform is rendered, but downstream audio evaluation cannot determine whether these choices were licensed by the source record. This represents a source-use failure that occurs before synthesis. The authors seek to make this pre-synthesis decision measurable as a listener-free task for source-grounded speech planning.

Method: VoxReason measures source-grounded speech planning before synthesis. Systems output source-cited speaking plans with evidence citations. A deterministic verifier checks: (1) citation legality, (2) slot agreement, (3) unsupported state, (4) schema validity, and (5) one-cue counterfactual locality. Experiments include: (1) 1,440 checked source-label cases with shortcut controls (key-lookup oracle, emotion prior), (2) 100-case learned source-key-disjoint comparison using a 7B locality model with SFT+CF repair.

Result: Key findings: (1) A key-lookup oracle achieves 1.000 plan-slot accuracy on seen keys, demonstrating slot accuracy alone is unsafe; (2) An emotion prior reaches 0.958 slot accuracy on source-key-disjoint cases without citing intensity or identity; (3) 7B locality SFT+CF repair improves plan-slot accuracy/locality from 0.684/0.141 to 0.919/1.000; (4) Removing source records lowers citation-required grounded score by 0.488. Waveform quality evaluation is outside scope.

Conclusion: Slot accuracy alone is insufficient for evaluating source-grounded speech planning; locality and citation quality are critical metrics. The proposed VoxReason framework effectively measures whether delivery choices are properly licensed by source records through deterministic verification. Future work should integrate waveform quality evaluation.

Abstract: Expressive speech systems make a decision before any waveform is rendered: how an utterance is delivered. In dialogue agents, narration, and role-conditioned TTS, that hidden planning step sets affect, pitch, energy, rate, pause, emphasis, and stance, yet downstream audio scores rarely reveal whether those choices were licensed by the source record, a source-use failure that occurs before any waveform exists. VoxReason makes that pre-synthesis decision measurable as a listener-free task for source-grounded speech planning. Before synthesis, VoxReason measures whether delivery choices are grounded in cited source records. Systems output a source-cited speaking-plan with evidence citations, and a deterministic verifier checks citation legality, slot agreement, unsupported state, schema validity, and one-cue counterfactual locality. On 1,440 checked source-label cases, shortcut controls show why slot accuracy alone is unsafe: a key-lookup oracle reaches 1.000 plan-slot accuracy on seen keys, while an emotion prior still reaches 0.958 slot accuracy on source-key-disjoint cases without citing intensity or identity. In a separate 100-case learned source-key-disjoint comparison, a 7B locality SFT+CF repair improves plan-slot accuracy/locality from 0.684/0.141 to 0.919/1.000, and removing source records lowers citation-required grounded score by 0.488. Rendered waveform quality remains outside the present evaluation.

</details>


### [280] [Is Semantics Enough for Speech Mean Opinion Score Prediction?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03283)
*Tianyu Lan,Yufei Shi,Yang Ai,Honghao Sun,Huipeng Du,Zhenhua Ling*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper investigates different representation paradigms for predicting Mean Opinion Score (MOS) in synthesized speech, comparing self-supervised learning (SSL) models, acoustic-only neural audio codecs (NACs), and unified NACs that combine semantic and acoustic modeling. The key finding is that features synergizing semantic understanding with fine-grained acoustic modeling achieve the highest performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Current automatic MOS predictors rely heavily on self-supervised learning (SSL) models that prioritize high-level semantics, potentially sacrificing critical acoustic details needed for accurate speech quality assessment.

Method: The authors systematically benchmark representations from three paradigms: (1) SSL models, (2) acoustic-only neural audio codecs (NACs), and (3) unified NACs that integrate semantics into reconstruction-based architectures. Evaluation is conducted on the standard BVCC dataset and multiple out-of-domain (OOD) datasets.

Result: Features that combine semantic understanding with fine-grained acoustic modeling achieve a higher performance upper bound in speech quality assessment compared to semantics-only approaches.

Conclusion: Semantics alone are insufficient for robust MOS prediction. A dual focus on both semantic content and acoustic fidelity is essential for building effective speech quality assessment models.

Abstract: Mean Opinion Score (MOS) is the gold standard for evaluating synthesized speech naturalness. However, current automatic MOS predictors are dominated by self-supervised learning (SSL) models that prioritize high-level semantics, potentially compromising their ability to capture critical acoustic details. In this paper, we systematically investigate representations from three paradigms: SSLs, acoustic-only neural audio codecs (NACs), and unified NACs that integrate semantics into reconstruction-based architectures. Extensive benchmarking on the standard BVCC and multiple out-of-domain (OOD) datasets demonstrates that features synergizing semantic understanding with fine-grained acoustic modeling achieve a higher performance upper bound in speech quality assessment. Ultimately, our findings highlight that semantics alone are not enough; a dual focus on semantic content and acoustic fidelity is essential for robust MOS prediction.

</details>


### [281] [Beyond .WAV: Design and Software Verification of VocalCap, a Traceable Browser-Based Audio Capture System for Vocal Biomarker Research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03320)
*Augusto Camargo*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: VocalCap is an institution-controlled, browser-based system for self-guided voice capture by untrained participants. It preserves comprehensive provenance metadata including capture execution, technical quality, byte-level integrity, and transformation history. The system was tested with 39 pilot recordings, resolving channel topology issues through active-channel selection.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Remote voice studies typically retain only final audio files with limited evidence about how they were captured, transferred, processed, and accepted. There is a need for systems that preserve complete provenance and technical integrity of voice recordings.

Method: VocalCap uses a versioned protocol driving a workflow where each accepted recording retains: (1) browser-native objects, (2) client-lossless Float32 WAV, and (3) server-canonical mono PCM16 WAV. IndexedDB preserves artifacts until server confirmation. The system was tested with malformed objects, exact-zero interruptions, channel-topology variants, and interrupted operations. A post hoc technical audit of 39 pilot recordings was conducted.

Result: Among 39 pilot recordings, 25 were sample-identical stereo files and 14 had signal confined to the left channel. Topology-aware active-channel selection limited RMS level difference to less than 0.001 dB in all 14 affected files. Production verification completed two five-task profiles in Chromium and WebKit, yielding 10 accepted recordings and 30 retained artifacts that passed server-side integrity and format checks.

Conclusion: VocalCap's software behavior has been verified under tested browser-engine conditions. However, device-level acoustic agreement, target-population usability, clinical validity, and biomarker performance remain subjects for separate studies.

Abstract: Remote voice studies often retain a final audio file with limited evidence about how it was captured, transferred, processed, and accepted. This paper presents VocalCap, an institution-controlled, browser-based system for self-guided capture of voice and related acoustic signals by participants without technical training. A versioned protocol drives the workflow. Each accepted recording retains a browser-native object, a client-lossless Float32 WAV derived from the same MediaStream, and a server-canonical mono PCM16 WAV, linked to evidence of capture execution, technical quality, byte-level integrity, recovery, and transformation provenance. IndexedDB preserves accepted browser artifacts until server confirmation, while session completion requires successful verification of every task and artifact. Software tests challenged the acquisition contracts with malformed or altered objects, exact-zero interruptions, channel-topology variants, and interrupted or repeated operations. A post hoc technical audit of 39 consented pilot recordings found 25 sample-identical stereo files and 14 files with signal confined to the left channel. Topology-aware active-channel selection limited the canonical root-mean-square level difference to less than 0.001 dB in all 14 affected files; equal-weight stereo averaging would have introduced approximately 6.02 dB of attenuation. Production end-to-end verification completed two five-task profiles in Chromium and WebKit, yielding 10 accepted recordings and 30 retained artifacts that passed server-side integrity and format checks. The results verify VocalCap's software behavior under the tested browser-engine conditions. Device-level acoustic agreement, target-population usability, clinical validity, and biomarker performance remain subjects for separate studies.

</details>


### [282] [Neural Music Enhancement with Dual Time-Frequency Spectral Representations for Prediction and Discrimination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03357)
*Fei Liu,Yang Ai,Zhen-Hua Ling*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: DSME is a music enhancement model using dual time-frequency spectral representations (STFT and CQT) within a generative adversarial framework to address background noise and reverberation in non-professional music recordings.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Non-professional music recordings shared online often suffer from background noise and reverberation, which degrades perceived quality and limits reuse. There is a need for effective music enhancement methods.

Method: DSME uses a dual-spectrum approach: STFT spectra for generation (leveraging fixed window, invertibility, and predictability) and CQT spectra for discrimination (exploiting log-frequency, variable-window structure aligned with musical octaves). An octave-segmented CQT discriminator is designed, and a chroma-spectrum loss is introduced to emphasize pitch and harmonic consistency.

Result: Experiments show DSME outperforms baselines in both objective and subjective tests, validating the effectiveness of the dual-spectrum approach.

Conclusion: The dual time-frequency spectral representation approach (combining STFT and CQT) is effective for music enhancement, achieving superior performance over existing methods.

Abstract: Non-professional music recordings shared online often suffer from background noise and reverberation, degrading perceived quality and limiting reuse. This paper proposes DSME, a music enhancement model based on dual time-frequency spectral representations. Within a generative adversarial framework, DSME uses short-time Fourier transform (STFT) spectra for generation and constant-Q transform (CQT) spectra for discrimination. Leveraging STFT's fixed window, invertibility, and predictability, the generator estimates clean amplitude-phase spectra from degraded inputs and reconstructs waveforms via inverse STFT. Exploiting CQT's log-frequency, variable-window structure aligned with musical octaves, we design an octave-segmented CQT discriminator. We also introduce a chroma-spectrum loss to emphasize pitch and harmonic consistency. Experiments show DSME outperforms baselines in objective and subjective tests, validating the effectiveness of the dual-spectrum approach.

</details>


### [283] [PACodec: A Low-bitrate Neural Speech Codec with Parallel Additive Vector Quantization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03363)
*Fei Liu,Yang Ai,Xiao-Hang Jiang,Zhen-Hua Ling*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: PACodec is a novel low-bitrate neural speech codec using parallel additive vector quantization (PAVQ) with a "global-local-global" (GLG) design, where multiple independent VQs quantize global features in parallel and aggregate outputs through addition. It achieves 30% bitrate reduction compared to baselines while maintaining decoding quality, and exhibits disentanglement properties capturing speech content, timbre, and acoustic details.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Mainstream neural speech codecs use residual vector quantization (RVQ) with sequentially dependent vector quantizers, which is inefficient in bitrate usage. There is a need for a more efficient quantization approach that can reduce bitrate while maintaining quality.

Method: PACodec proposes PAVQ with a GLG design: global encoded features are quantized in parallel by multiple independent VQs, each attending to local components of the representation. Their outputs are aggregated through addition to yield the final global quantization result for decoding.

Result: PACodec achieves 30% bitrate reduction compared to baseline methods at the same decoding quality, with only minor model complexity increase. Each independent VQ captures different aspects of speech (content, timbre, acoustic details), demonstrating disentanglement-friendly properties.

Conclusion: PAVQ with GLG design enables efficient bitrate usage through parallel quantization. The proposed PACodec is suitable for low-bitrate applications and shows potential for downstream tasks like voice conversion due to its disentanglement properties.

Abstract: This paper proposes PACodec, a novel low-bitrate neural speech codec based on parallel additive vector quantization (PAVQ). Unlike the mainstream residual vector quantization (RVQ) used in most neural speech codecs, where vector quantizers (VQs) are sequentially dependent, the PAVQ strategy adopted in PACodec aggregates parallel quantization results to optimize bitrate usage. Specifically, the PAVQ adopts a "global-local-global" (GLG) design: the global encoded features are quantized in parallel by multiple independent VQs, each attending to a local component of the representation, and their outputs are aggregated through addition to yield the final global quantization result for decoding. Experimental results show that PACodec, as each VQ focuses only on local information, supports smaller codebooks and reduces bitrate by 30% compared with baselines at the same decoding quality, with only minor model complexity. Further analysis shows that, owing to the GLG framework of PAVQ, the proposed PACodec is disentanglement-friendly, and each independent VQ captures different aspects of speech, e.g., content, timbre, and acoustic details, suggesting potential for application to downstream tasks such as voice conversion.

</details>


### [284] [StrixAE: An Intelligent Agent for Audio Enhancement under Complex Distortion Coupling in Real-World Scenarios](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03414)
*Chenglin Wu,Junjie Wu,Jinhang Chen,Mingyang Chen,Zixu Lin,Jiabian Chen,Xinghao Ding,Xiaotong Tu*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: StrixAE is an MLLM-based agent that coordinates multiple audio enhancement and personalization models for real-world audio restoration. It uses a two-stage training: CoT fine-tuning on AcoustBench followed by Audio Perception Reinforcement Learning (APRL) that optimizes format validity, structural coherence, and perceptual quality. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on real-world test datasets.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Real-world audio enhancement involves complex distortion couplings and requires personalized enhancement, but existing solutions fail to address both simultaneously. There's a need for robust, autonomous systems that can handle diverse real-world scenarios without hallucinated tools or unreliable enhancement plans.

Method: StrixAE uses a multimodal LLM as a controller to coordinate multiple audio enhancement and personalization models. Training involves two stages: (1) Chain-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning on AcoustBench for basic reasoning and tool invocation; (2) Audio Perception Reinforcement Learning (APRL) with structured rewards enforcing executable pipelines, logical section ordering, format validity, structural coherence, and perceptual quality.

Result: Outperforms most existing open-source and proprietary solutions on real-world test datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple perceptual metrics with strong generalization robustness.

Conclusion: The MLLM-based agent approach with APRL training enables reliable, interpretable enhancement plans without hallucinated tools, successfully addressing complex distortion coupling and personalized enhancement simultaneously in real-world scenarios.

Abstract: Audio enhancement in real-world scenarios involves complex distortion couplings and requires personalized enhancement. Existing solutions struggle to address both simultaneously. To improve robustness and enable autonomous operation in such scenarios, we propose StrixAE, an agent based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). StrixAE leverages the MLLM as a controller to coordinate multiple audio enhancement and personalization models. To further enhance system robustness, reduce artifacts, and improve generalization across diverse real-world scenarios, StrixAE is trained through a two-stage process: first, CoT supervised fine-tuning on AcoustBench to ground basic reasoning and tool invocation; second, Audio Perception Reinforcement Learning (APRL), a reward design specifically tailored for audio restoration pipelines that jointly optimizes format validity, structural coherence, and perceptual quality. Unlike generic RL fine-tuning, APRL introduces structured rewards that enforce executable pipelines and logical section ordering, enabling the agent to produce reliable, interpretable enhancement plans without hallucinated tools. Based on real-world test datasets, our proposed method outperforms most existing open-source and proprietary solutions, achieving state-of-the-art performance across multiple perceptual metrics and demonstrating strong generalization robustness.

</details>


### [285] [Test-time adaptation for speech enhancement with an autoregressive speech prior](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03622)
*Sofiene Kammoun,Simon Leglaive,Xavier Alameda-Pineda,Timo Gerkmann*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: A test-time adaptation (TTA) method for speech enhancement that uses an autoregressive prior trained on clean speech latent representations from a neural audio codec. Adaptation is performed via KL divergence minimization between enhanced and clean speech distributions, requiring no labeled target data.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: To improve speech enhancement models under mismatched acoustic conditions (training-testing noise mismatch) without requiring access to labeled target data, which is a common practical challenge in real-world deployment.

Method: Single-utterance TTA approach using: (1) a neural audio codec to extract clean speech latent representations, (2) an autoregressive prior trained on these clean speech latents, (3) KL divergence minimization between the enhanced speech distribution and the clean speech prior for adaptation.

Result: Consistent improvements in speech quality across multiple noisy speech datasets, with particularly notable gains under training-testing noise mismatch conditions.

Conclusion: The proposed TTA method effectively adapts pretrained speech enhancement models to unseen acoustic conditions using only unlabeled test data, demonstrating practical potential for deployment in real-world mismatched acoustic environments.

Abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) offers a promising direction for improving speech enhancement models under mismatched acoustic conditions, without requiring access to labeled target data. In this work, we propose a single-utterance TTA method that regularizes a pretrained speech enhancement model using an autoregressive prior trained on clean speech latent representations extracted from a neural audio codec. Adaptation is performed by minimizing the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the enhanced speech distribution and the clean speech prior. Experiments across multiple noisy speech datasets show consistent improvements in speech quality, particularly under training-testing noise mismatch conditions. Code and audio examples are available online.

</details>


### [286] [Masked Autoregressive Speech Enhancement with Continuous Neural Audio Codec Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03940)
*Yoto Fujita,Simon Leglaive,Laurent Girin*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper proposes MARSE (masked autoregressive speech enhancement), a method for speech enhancement using continuous latent representations from neural audio codecs (NACs) with iterative decoding of masked clean speech frames. The method offers a flexible trade-off between SE performance and computational cost.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: Previous work on speech enhancement based on masked generative modeling relied on discrete token representations from neural audio codecs. This study is motivated by the finding that continuous latent representations of NACs can be advantageous for SE in terms of speech quality and intelligibility.

Method: The proposed MARSE method uses iterative decoding of masked clean speech frames with continuous NAC representations. The study investigates different decoding policies while keeping constant: a Conformer model as the DNN, the DAC codec as the NAC, and the same training setup.

Result: The results demonstrate that MARSE enables a flexible trade-off between speech enhancement performance and computational cost, depending on the decoding policy chosen.

Conclusion: MARSE provides a practical approach for speech enhancement that balances performance and computational efficiency, with audio examples and code made available online.

Abstract: Most previous work on speech enhancement (SE) based on masked generative modeling relied on discrete token representations of audio signals, obtained using neural audio codecs (NACs). However, a recent study has shown that continuous latent representations of NACs can be advantageous for SE in terms of speech quality and intelligibility. In this work, we propose masked autoregressive SE (MARSE), a method for SE based on iterative decoding of masked clean speech frames using continuous NAC representations of speech. In particular, we investigate a set of different decoding policies, ceteris paribus, that is, using the same DNN (a Conformer model), the same NAC (the DAC codec) and the same training setup. The results show that MARSE enables a flexible trade-off between SE performance and computational cost. Audio examples and code are available online.

</details>


### [287] [Compressing Streaming Neural Audio Encoders via Latent-Space Distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.04102)
*Prasanth Yadla,Mohammad Samragh,Dongseong Hwang,Mingbin Xu,Yuanyuan Zhang,Chung-Cheng Chiu,Yongqiang Wang,Yuan Liu,Zhen Huang,Xiaodan Zhuang*

Main category: cs.SD

TL;DR: This paper presents a method to compress tokenizers for on-device speech recognition on Apple devices using knowledge distillation. Rather than distilling discrete tokens or output distributions, the method trains a student encoder to regress the teacher's pre-quantizer latent representations - the actual input the language model consumes. This approach achieves 2.8x compression while maintaining 98.1% of the teacher's word error rate (WER) performance.


<details>
  <summary>Details</summary>
Motivation: On Apple devices, System-wide Dictation runs entirely on-device with a sparsely activated language model (under Instruction-Following Pruning). The always-on tokenizer competes for the same DRAM memory as the language model's active experts. Since the tokenizer's parameter count directly impacts power and latency, compressing it becomes critical for efficient on-device speech recognition.

Method: The method uses knowledge distillation with a novel supervision target: the pre-quantizer latent (the last representation shared by the two token interfaces). The student encoder is trained to regress the teacher's per-frame latent under a squared-error objective, with a single affine layer to handle teacher-student width mismatch. This approach works for both token interfaces and applies to tokenizers pretrained alone or jointly trained with a language model.

Result: At 2.8x compression, the distilled student stays within 1.9% relative WER of its teacher on five of six teacher-student pairs without any fine-tuning. It also improves on an independently trained tokenizer of identical capacity by 3.9% relative WER.

Conclusion: Distilling to pre-quantizer latents is an effective approach for tokenizer compression, achieving significant model reduction (2.8x) with minimal performance degradation (1.9% relative WER increase). This single recipe works across different training setups and token interfaces, making it a practical solution for on-device speech recognition systems.

Abstract: System-wide Dictation on Apple devices runs entirely on-device, and the speech it transcribes reaches the foundation model through a tokenizer: an encoder that maps short windows of waveform onto the representation the language model reads. Because that model is sparsely activated under Instruction-Following Pruning, only a small subset of its experts occupies DRAM at any time, so the always-on tokenizer competes for the same memory, and its parameter count bears directly on power and latency. In this work we study how to compress such a tokenizer by distillation, taking as the supervision target neither the discrete token nor the output distribution but the pre-quantizer latent the model actually consumes - the last representation the two token interfaces share. We train only the student encoder to regress the teacher's per-frame latent under a squared-error objective, with a single affine layer absorbing the teacher-student width mismatch. Because the target precedes both the quantizer and the language-model bridge, one recipe covers both token interfaces we support, and applies both to a tokenizer pretrained alone and to one jointly trained with a language model. At 2.8x compression the distilled student stays within 1.9% relative WER of its teacher on five of six teacher-student pairs without any fine-tuning, and improves on an independently trained tokenizer of identical capacity by 3.9% relative.

</details>
